Part I. Problems and Methods

Methodological Commitments and Boundary DeclarationsChapter 0

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Place of This Chapter in the Work Chapter 0 is the "meta-level" chapter of the whole work. It precedes the Introduction and is tasked with laying the methodological foundation for the entire theoretical edifice. It does not belong to any particular layer of the protocol stack; rather, it is the "meta-protocol" of the protocol stack itself — it specifies how this work is to be read, how it is to be used, and how it is to be revised. III. The Core Tasks of This Chapter This chapter undertakes four core tasks: Task 1: Characterization. To specify clearly the threefold character of this work as a "provisional convention," a "concept prototype," and an "open system." Task 2: Methodological commitments. To articulate the methodological positions of interdisciplinary integration, the balance between formalization and intuition, the tension between speculation and prudence, and the relation between the normative and the descriptive. Task 3: Boundary declarations. To state systematically the boundary conditions of use restrictions, maturity, ethical constraints, and revisability. Task 4: The reader's contract. To establish an explicit contract between author and reader, stating what this work does and does not promise, and what it expects of the reader. IV. The Deliverables of This Chapter After completing this chapter, the reader will have:

  • An accurate understanding of the character of this work
  • A clear grasp of its methodological commitments
  • A definite awareness of the boundaries of its use
  • A "reading contract" with the author
  • A basis for judging whether this work suits the reader's own needs

V. Reading Advice This chapter is the "user manual" of the whole work; all readers are advised to read it in full. Readers with limited time may prioritize: §0.1.1 (Provisional Convention) → §0.3.1 (Restrictions on Use) → §0.4 (The Reader's Contract) Academic researchers should focus on: §0.2 (Methodological Commitments) → §0.3.2 (Maturity Declaration) Estimated reading time: about 1.5-2 hours for a complete reading. ⚠ Important notice: the boundary declarations in this chapter serve a "disclaimer" function in the sense of legal effect; please read §0.3.1 (Restrictions on Use) carefully.

§0.1 The Characterization of This Work

§0.1.1 A Theory as a "Provisional Convention" I. Introducing the Concept of a "Provisional Convention" Definition 0.1 (Provisional Convention) A provisional convention is a theoretical framework that: (1) is regarded, under current epistemic conditions, as the best available option; (2) explicitly acknowledges its own fallibility and revisability; (3) sets out definite revision-triggering conditions and revision procedures; (4) does not claim eternal validity or the status of absolute truth. Formal statement: $$\text{ProvisionalConvention}(T) \leftrightarrow \text{BestAvailable}(T, t) \wedge \text{Fallible}(T) \wedge \text{RevisionConditions}(T) \wedge \neg\text{AbsoluteTruth}(T)$$ where:

  • $T$ = the theoretical framework
  • $t$ = the current point in time
  • $\text{BestAvailable}(T, t)$ = at time $t$, $T$ is the best available option
  • $\text{Fallible}(T)$ = $T$ is fallible
  • $\text{RevisionConditions}(T)$ = $T$ has definite revision conditions
  • $\text{AbsoluteTruth}(T)$ = $T$ claims the status of absolute truth

II. Why This Work Is a "Provisional Convention" This work positions itself as a "provisional convention" on three grounds: Reason One: An epistemic reason — grounded in the New View of Cognition (NK) According to the New View of Cognition (NK), to be argued in detail in Chapter 3, knowledge has the following features:

  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): The knower is not a spectator of the world but a participant. The act of cognition itself alters the object of cognition.
  • NK-2 (social knowledge): Knowledge is a social achievement, depending on the collaboration and verification of an epistemic community.
  • NK-4 (epistemic humility): Given the participatory and social character of cognition, the knower should remain humble about his or her cognitive claims.

Applying these principles to this work itself, we obtain: $$\text{NK-4} \rightarrow \text{Humility}(\text{ThisWork}) \rightarrow \text{ProvisionalConvention}(\text{ThisWork})$$ Proposition 0.1 (The Self-Application Principle) The epistemic stance of this work (the New View of Cognition) requires this work to treat itself as a provisional convention. Any theory that claims the status of absolute truth contradicts the core propositions of the New View of Cognition. Reason Two: A historical reason — lessons from the history of science The history of science shows that even the most successful theories may be revised or superseded: | Theory | Status | Subsequent development | |------|------|----------| | Newtonian mechanics | 200 years of "absolute truth" | Revised by relativity and quantum mechanics | | Classical thermodynamics | Foundation of engineering | Deepened by statistical mechanics | | Darwinian evolution | Foundation of biology | Extended by the modern evolutionary synthesis | The problem this work addresses — the normative foundations of interstellar civilization — is far more speculative than any of the theories above. If physical theories require revision, this work should expect revision all the more. Reason Three: A practical reason — openness toward the future The core concern of this work is the governance of interstellar civilization. This concern points to future scenarios that have not yet arrived:

  • the emergence of AGI (artificial general intelligence)
  • possible contact with extraterrestrial intelligence
  • the interstellar expansion of human civilization
  • the emergence of new kinds of intelligent agents

The specific features of these scenarios cannot be fully foreseen at present. This work must therefore remain open, so that it can be adaptively revised as new scenarios arise. III. The Operational Meaning of a "Provisional Convention" Positioning this work as a "provisional convention" has the following operational implications: Implication One: Revision-triggering conditions This work sets out the following revision-triggering conditions: | Trigger type | Trigger condition | Scope of revision | |----------|----------|----------| | Empirical | A new scientific finding conflicts with a core proposition | The proposition concerned and its corollaries | | Logical | An internal logical contradiction is discovered | The propositions involved in the contradiction | | Contextual | A new scenario falls outside the framework's scope | Extension or restriction of the framework | | Consensus | The scholarly community reaches a consensus to revise | The content covered by the consensus | Formal statement: $$\text{RevisionTrigger} = \text{Empirical} \vee \text{Logical} \vee \text{Contextual} \vee \text{Consensus}$$ Implication Two: Revision procedure This work adopts a versioned revision procedure (see §0.3.4 for details): Revision procedure: (1) Trigger identification: determine whether a revision-triggering condition is satisfied (2) Impact assessment: assess the impact of the revision on other parts (3) Proposal: put forward a revision proposal (4) Community deliberation: submit it for deliberation by the scholarly community (5) Version update: update the version number and record the changes Implication Three: Version-numbering rules This work adopts Semantic Versioning: $$\text{Version} = \text{MAJOR}.\text{MINOR}.\text{PATCH}$$ | Version type | Type of change | Example | |----------|----------|------| | MAJOR | Incompatible major change (core propositions altered) | v1.0.0 → v2.0.0 | | MINOR | Backward-compatible feature addition (new indicators, adjusted weights) | v1.0.0 → v1.1.0 | | PATCH | Backward-compatible problem fix (error correction, clarification of wording) | v1.0.0 → v1.0.1 | Current version: v0.9.0 The version number v0.9.0 means:

  • MAJOR = 0: has not yet reached the stability of an official release
  • MINOR = 9: the ninth iteration of the main content
  • PATCH = 0: no patch fixes in the current iteration

IV. Distinguishing a "Provisional Convention" from "Relativism" An important clarification: positioning this work as a "provisional convention" is not equivalent to adopting a relativist stance. Definition 0.2 (Relativism) Relativism holds that there is no objective truth or normative standard that is cross-cultural, cross-era and cross-agent. All truths and norms are relative to a particular culture, era or agent. Definition 0.3 (Fallibilism) Fallibilism holds that our knowledge claims may be mistaken, but this does not mean that there is no objective truth. We should pursue truth while acknowledging that we may not yet have attained it. This work adopts a fallibilist stance, not a relativist one: | Dimension | Relativism | Fallibilism (the stance of this work) | |------|----------|----------------------| | Objective truth | Does not exist | Exists, but we may not yet have attained it | | Progress of knowledge | Impossible (only change) | Possible (approximating truth through revision) | | Standard of criticism | No cross-cultural standard | Exists, but requires continual revision | | Practical attitude | Any view is equally valid | Some views are better than others | Formal statement: $$\text{Fallibilism} \leftrightarrow \text{ObjectiveTruth} \wedge \text{PossibleError} \wedge \text{ProgressPossible}$$ $$\text{Relativism} \leftrightarrow \neg\text{ObjectiveTruth} \wedge \neg\text{ProgressPossible}$$ Proposition 0.2 (Compatibility of Fallibilism and the Provisional Convention) The status of provisional convention is compatible with fallibilism and incompatible with relativism. This work acknowledges that it may be mistaken, but it does not acknowledge that all views are equally valid. Revision of this work aims at a better approximation of truth, not mere change.

§0.1.2 The Framework as a "Concept Prototype" I. Introducing the Concept of a "Concept Prototype" Definition 0.4 (Concept Prototype) A concept prototype is a theoretical framework that: (1) provides preliminary definitions of core concepts and their interrelations; (2) exhibits the basic structure and operating logic of the framework; (3) has not yet undergone sufficient empirical and practical validation; (4) is intended to provide a starting point for subsequent refinement. Formal statement: $$\text{ConceptualPrototype}(F) \leftrightarrow \text{CoreConcepts}(F) \wedge \text{BasicStructure}(F) \wedge \neg\text{FullyValidated}(F) \wedge \text{StartingPoint}(F)$$ II. The Technology Readiness Level (TRL) Framework To describe precisely the maturity of the components of this work, we draw on NASA's Technology Readiness Level (TRL) framework and develop a "Conceptual Readiness Level" (CRL) suitable for theoretical frameworks: Table 0.1 Definitions of the Conceptual Readiness Level (CRL) | CRL | Name | Definition | Validation status | |---------|------|------|----------| | CRL 1 | Observation of basic principles | Basic principles identified but not yet formalized | No validation | | CRL 2 | Concept formation | Preliminary concept definitions formed but not systematized | Conceptual level | | CRL 3 | Concept validation | Concepts have passed a preliminary test of logical consistency | Logical level | | CRL 4 | Framework integration | Concepts integrated into a coherent theoretical framework | Framework level | | CRL 5 | Simulation validation | The framework is validated in a simulation environment | Simulation level | | CRL 6 | Case application | The framework is applied to historical or contemporary cases | Case level | | CRL 7 | Pilot experiment | The framework is piloted in a controlled environment | Pilot level | | CRL 8 | Practical validation | The framework is tested in real-world settings | Practical level | | CRL 9 | Mature application | The framework is fully validated and can be widely applied | Mature level | III. Maturity Assessment of the Components of This Work Table 0.2 CRL assessment of the components of this work | Component | Name | CRL | Note | |------|------|---------|------| | The Three New Views | NC, NL, NK | CRL 4 | Concept integration complete; logical consistency checked | | Bridge principles | BP-1, BP-2, BP-3 | CRL 3-4 | Concept validation complete; integration under way | | Normative principles | PRF, PNR, PR | CRL 4 | Framework integration complete | | Indicator system | UCS, RFD, CRV, etc. | CRL 2-3 | Concept formed; partly logically validated | | Institutional design | Multi-agent adjudication chamber, etc. | CRL 2 | Concept-formation stage | | Protocol stack | L₀-L₄ architecture | CRL 4 | Framework integration complete | Important declaration: all components of this work are at the CRL 2-4 stage, i.e. the "concept prototype" stage. This means:

  1. They may be used for: academic research, thought experiments, simulation modelling, policy discussion
  2. They must not be used for: mandatory assessment, legal adjudication, resource-allocation decisions

IV. The Value and Limits of a "Concept Prototype" The value of a concept prototype: | Dimension of value | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Exploratory value | Opens new research directions and poses new questions | | Integrative value | Integrates cross-disciplinary insights and builds conceptual bridges | | Heuristic value | Stimulates further research and provides a framework for thought | | Dialogical value | Provides a common point of reference for scholarly dialogue | The limits of a concept prototype: | Dimension of limitation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Insufficient validation | Not yet sufficiently empirically validated | | Difficulty of operationalization | Challenges in moving from concept to operation | | Blurred boundaries | The boundaries of applicability are not yet clear | | Unknown stability | Stability under new scenarios is untested | Proposition 0.3 (Appropriate Use of a Concept Prototype) A concept prototype should be used for exploration, integration, inspiration and dialogue, not for mandatory decision-making. Using a concept prototype for mandatory decision-making misuses its character and may lead to improper consequences. Formal statement: $$\text{AppropriateUse}(\text{Prototype}) = \{\text{Exploration}, \text{Integration}, \text{Inspiration}, \text{Dialogue}\}$$ $$\text{InappropriateUse}(\text{Prototype}) = \{\text{MandatoryDecision}, \text{LegalJudgment}, \text{ResourceAllocation}\}$$ V. §0.1.3 This Work as an "Open System" I. Introducing the Concept of an "Open System" Definition 0.5 (Open System) An open system is a theoretical framework that: (1) maintains continuous interaction with its external environment (the scholarly community, fields of practice, new scenarios); (2) can absorb external inputs (criticism, new evidence, new insights) and make internal adjustments; (3) produces external outputs (research agendas, policy recommendations, conceptual tools); (4) evolves and develops through this interaction. This concept borrows from the notion of an open system in thermodynamics, but applies it in the context of a theoretical framework. Formal statement: $$\text{OpenSystem}(T) \leftrightarrow \text{ExternalInteraction}(T) \wedge \text{InputAbsorption}(T) \wedge \text{OutputGeneration}(T) \wedge \text{Evolution}(T)$$ II. The Link between the Open System and the Three New Views Positioning this work as an "open system" is highly consistent with the core propositions of the Three New Views: Link with the New Cosmology (NC): The New Cosmology emphasizes relationality (NC-1) and processuality (NC-2). Treating this work as an open system means acknowledging the relationality between this work and its environment (the scholarly community, fields of practice), and the processuality of this work as a continuous process of evolution. $$\text{NC-1}(\text{relationality}) \rightarrow \text{the relationality of ThisWork and its environment}$$ $$\text{NC-2}(\text{processuality}) \rightarrow \text{ThisWork as an evolutionary process}$$ Link with the New View of Life (NL): The New View of Life emphasizes negentropic persistence (NL-2). As a "conceptual living entity," a theoretical framework likewise depends for its persistence on drawing "conceptual negentropy" from its environment — new insights, criticism, evidence — in order to maintain and increase its organizational complexity. $$\text{NL-2}(\text{negentropic persistence}) \rightarrow \text{ThisWork needs conceptual negentropy to persist}$$ Link with the New View of Cognition (NK): The New View of Cognition emphasizes the social character of knowledge (NK-2) and its negotiability (NK-4). Treating this work as an open system means acknowledging that its development depends on the collaboration of the scholarly community, and that its content is negotiable and revisable. $$\text{NK-2}(\text{social knowledge}) \rightarrow \text{ThisWork depends on the scholarly community}$$ $$\text{NK-4}(\text{negotiability}) \rightarrow \text{the content of ThisWork is negotiable}$$ Proposition 0.4 (Self-Application of the Three New Views) The framework of the Three New Views in this work requires this work to treat itself as an open system. A theoretical framework that asserts relationality, processuality and sociality would fall into self-contradiction if it treated itself as closed, static and independent. III. The Input-Output Structure of an Open System Table 0.3 The input-output structure of this work as an open system | Dimension | Input | Internal processing | Output | |------|------|----------|------| | Academic | Criticism, rebuttals, alternatives | Evaluation, integration, revision | Revised versions, response papers | | Empirical | New scientific findings, new data | Consistency checks, framework adjustment | Updated propositions, new predictions | | Practical | Policy feedback, implementation experience | Feasibility assessment, institutional adjustment | Policy recommendations, implementation guides | | Contextual | New scenarios, new challenges | Applicability assessment, framework extension | Extended framework, new applications | Formal statement: $$\text{OpenSystem}_{\text{ThisWork}} = \langle I, P, O, E \rangle$$ where:

  • $I$ = the set of inputs (criticism, evidence, feedback, new scenarios)
  • $P$ = the processing function (evaluation, integration, revision, extension)
  • $O$ = the set of outputs (revised versions, policy recommendations, research agendas)
  • $E$ = the evolutionary trajectory (version history, conceptual development)

The boundary can be neither entirely closed (which would lead to rigidity) nor entirely open (which would lead to dissolution). V. The Open System and the Founding of "Interstellar Civilization Studies" The positioning of this work as an open system is highly consistent with its goal of founding "Interstellar Civilization Studies." Definition 0.6 (Interstellar Civilization Studies) Interstellar Civilization Studies is an interdisciplinary field that studies the existence, development, interaction and governance of intelligent civilizations on a cosmic scale. It integrates perspectives from physics, biology, cognitive science, ethics, political science, law and other disciplines to provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for the normative problems of the interstellar-civilization era. As the founding work of an emerging discipline, this work must be an open system, for the following reasons: | Reason | Explanation | |------|------| | The discipline is newly founded | A new discipline needs to keep absorbing contributions from many fields | | The object evolves | The object of study (interstellar civilization) is itself evolving | | Methods develop | Research methods need continual development and refinement | | Community building | The scholarly community must be built through open participation | Proposition 0.5 (Open Systems and the Founding of a Discipline) The founding work of a new discipline should be an open system. A closed founding work would hinder the healthy development of the discipline, whereas an open one provides space for its continuous evolution.

§0.2 Methodological Commitments

§0.2.1 The Method of Interdisciplinary Integration I. The Necessity of Interdisciplinary Integration The problem this work addresses — the normative foundations of interstellar civilization — is essentially interdisciplinary. It involves: | Discipline | Related problems | |----------|----------| | Physics | The basic structure of the cosmos, thermodynamic constraints, the boundaries of information theory | | Biology | The nature of life, the origin of consciousness, the direction of evolution | | Cognitive science | The nature of cognition, the diversity of intelligence, the conditions of agency | | Ethics | The source of normativity, the criteria of moral status, the attribution of responsibility | | Political science | Principles of governance, institutional design, the distribution of power | | Law | The definition of legal persons, the basis of rights, the resolution of disputes | No single discipline can answer the normative problems of interstellar civilization on its own. Interdisciplinary integration is therefore not an optional methodological preference but an intrinsic requirement of the problem itself. Proposition 0.6 (The Necessity of Interdisciplinary Integration) The normative problems of interstellar civilization are essentially interdisciplinary. Any attempt to answer them from a single disciplinary perspective will be incomplete. Formal statement: $$\text{NormativeFoundation}_{\text{InterstellarCiv}} \not\subseteq \text{Domain}(D_i) \quad \forall D_i \in \{\text{Physics}, \text{Biology}, \text{CogSci}, \text{Ethics}, ...\}$$ $$\text{NormativeFoundation}_{\text{InterstellarCiv}} \subseteq \bigcup_{i} \text{Domain}(D_i) \cap \text{Integration}$$ II. Three Operating Principles of Interdisciplinary Integration To prevent interdisciplinary integration from degenerating into "shallow collage" or "pseudo-scientific analogy-hunting," this work lays down three strict operating principles: Principle A: The empirical core is not to be disturbed Definition 0.7 (Empirical Core) The empirical core is the body of well-validated empirical propositions and theoretical structures within a discipline that are widely accepted by its scholarly community. Content of the principle: This work does not propose competing revisions to the empirical core of mature scientific theories. Specific constraints: | Type of constraint | Specific content | Example | |----------|----------|------| | Physical | Does not challenge the empirical predictions of thermodynamics, relativity or quantum mechanics | Does not claim that "negentropy can increase without limit" | | Biological | Does not challenge evolution or the core findings of molecular biology | Does not claim that "life can violate thermodynamics" | | Cognitive-scientific | Does not challenge the core empirical findings of cognitive science | Does not claim that "consciousness is independent of physical processes" | Formal statement: $$\forall D_i, \forall p \in \text{EmpiricalCore}(D_i): \neg\text{Challenge}(\text{ThisWork}, p)$$ Principle B: Structural use, not concept hijacking Definition 0.8 (Structural Use) Structural use is the borrowing of the formal structure of one discipline (e.g. a mathematical model or logical framework) for analysis in another domain, while making explicit the analogical character and the boundaries of such borrowing. Definition 0.9 (Concept Hijacking) Concept hijacking is the transplanting of a technical term from one discipline into another domain while stripping it of its original precise meaning, in order to manufacture a false sense of scientific authority. Content of the principle: This work engages only in structural use; concept hijacking is strictly forbidden. Specific constraints: | Source | Structural use (permitted) | Concept hijacking (forbidden) | |----------|------------------|------------------| | Thermodynamics | Borrowing the formal structure of "entropy increase" to analyse system evolution | Claiming that "social entropy" can be computed exactly with thermodynamic formulas | | Quantum mechanics | Borrowing the conceptual framework of "superposition" to discuss uncertainty | Claiming that "consciousness is a quantum effect" without empirical evidence | | Information theory | Borrowing "information entropy" to analyse cognitive systems | Claiming that "consciousness just is information" while ignoring the hard problem | Formal statement: $$\text{StructuralUse}(S, D_1, D_2) \leftrightarrow \text{FormalAnalogy}(S) \wedge \text{BoundaryDeclared}(S) \wedge \neg\text{OntologicalClaim}(S)$$ $$\text{ConceptHijacking}(C, D_1, D_2) \leftrightarrow \text{TermTransfer}(C) \wedge \neg\text{MeaningPreserved}(C) \wedge \text{FalseAuthority}(C)$$ Principle C: Interdisciplinary bridges are truncatable Content of the principle: The interdisciplinary analogies and structural mappings in this work can be partly or entirely removed while preserving the normative and institutional backbone. Specific meaning: | Level | Content | Truncatability | |------|------|----------| | Core argument | The derivation from the Three New Views to the normative principles | Not truncatable | | Scientific analogy | Using physical concepts to elucidate the Three New Views | Truncatable | | Structural mapping | Using mathematical models to formalize indicators | Partly truncatable | This principle ensures that even if some interdisciplinary analogies prove inappropriate, the core argument of this work can still stand independently. Formal statement: $$\text{CoreArgument}(\text{ThisWork}) \not\rightarrow \text{InterdisciplinaryAnalogy}(\text{ThisWork})$$ $$\text{Valid}(\text{CoreArgument}) \not\leftarrow \text{Valid}(\text{InterdisciplinaryAnalogy})$$ III. Specific Methods of Interdisciplinary Integration Method One: Conceptual bridging Building conceptual bridges between disciplines and identifying structural similarities. Examples of conceptual bridging: Physical concept Bridging relation Concept in this work

──────────────────────────

Negentropy ←─structural analogy─→ condition for the maintenance of life Phase space ←─structural analogy─→ space of possibilities Dissipative structure ←─structural analogy─→ self-organization of civilization Method Two: Layered integration Integrating the contributions of different disciplines into different layers of the protocol stack. | Protocol-stack layer | Main disciplinary contributions | |------------|--------------| | L₀ (physical-constraint layer) | Physics, thermodynamics, information theory | | L₁ (onto-epistemic layer) | Philosophy, cognitive science, complexity science | | L₂ (normative-principle layer) | Ethics, political philosophy | | L₃ (institutional-design layer) | Political science, law, institutional economics | | L₄ (operating-procedure layer) | Engineering, management, policy science | Method Three: Multiple validation Validating the same proposition from several disciplinary perspectives in order to increase its credibility. $$\text{Credibility}(p) = f\left(\sum_{i} w_i \cdot \text{Support}(p, D_i)\right)$$ where:

  • $p$ = the proposition
  • $D_i$ = discipline $i$
  • $\text{Support}(p, D_i)$ = the degree to which discipline $i$ supports proposition $p$
  • $w_i$ = the weight of discipline $i$

§0.2.2 The Balance between Formalization and Intuition I. The Value and Limits of Formalization The value of formalization: | Dimension of value | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Precision | Eliminates the ambiguity of natural language | | Testability | Allows arguments to be tested rigorously | | Transmissibility | Facilitates cross-cultural and cross-linguistic communication | | Computability | Provides a basis for computer-assisted analysis | The limits of formalization: | Dimension of limitation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Limits of expressiveness | Some concepts are hard to formalize fully | | Reduced readability | Excessive formalization reduces readability | | False precision | Formalization may conceal conceptual vagueness | | Constraint on creativity | Premature formalization may constrain conceptual exploration | II. The Value and Limits of Intuition The value of intuition: | Dimension of value | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Discovery | Intuition is an important source of conceptual discovery | | Integration | Intuition can integrate complex information | | Communication | Intuitive formulations are easier to understand | | Checking | Intuition can check the reasonableness of formalized results | The limits of intuition: | Dimension of limitation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Subjectivity | Intuition varies from person to person | | Risk of bias | Intuition may reflect cognitive bias | | Non-transmissibility | Intuition is hard to convey precisely | | Non-testability | Purely intuitive claims are hard to test | III. The Balancing Strategy of This Work Strategy One: Layered presentation This work uses a layered strategy, employing different degrees of formalization at different levels: | Level of presentation | Degree of formalization | Intended reader | |----------|------------|----------| | Core text | Medium | General academic readers | | Technical appendices | High | Specialist researchers | | Abstracts / guides | Low | Skimmers | Strategy Two: Dual formulation For core propositions, this work provides both a natural-language and a formal formulation: Example of dual formulation: Natural-language formulation: "The action of any agent should protect (rather than compress) the space of possibilities for meaningful choice of all affected subjects (including possible future subjects)." Formal formulation: ∀A∀a: Permissible(a) → ¬Compress(a, PS_affected) Strategy Three: Intuition checking Formalized results should be subject to intuition checking. If a formalized result conflicts with a strong intuition, either the formalization process or the intuition itself needs to be re-examined. $$\text{FormalizationValid}(F) \leftarrow \text{LogicallySound}(F) \wedge \text{IntuitionConsistent}(F)$$ Strategy Four: Declaring the boundaries of formalization For each formal formulation, its boundaries of applicability and simplifying assumptions are made explicit. Proposition 0.7 (The Complementarity of Formalization and Intuition) Formalization and intuition are not opposed but complementary. Formalization provides precision and testability; intuition provides discovery and integration. The best theoretical construction requires the collaboration of both.

§0.2.3 The Tension between Speculation and Prudence I. The Necessity of Speculation The problem this work addresses — the normative foundations of interstellar civilization — essentially concerns scenarios that have not yet occurred: | Speculative scenario | Current state | Necessity of speculation | |------------|----------|------------| | Emergence of AGI | Not yet realized | A normative framework needs to be established in advance | | Extraterrestrial contact | Has not occurred | Principles of response need to be established in advance | | Interstellar colonization | Has not begun | A governance framework needs to be established in advance | | Posthuman transformation | Not yet complete | Ethical guidance needs to be established in advance | Proposition 0.8 (The Necessity of Speculation) For decisions with long-term irreversible consequences, prior speculative thinking is necessary. Waiting until the scenario is fully clear before undertaking normative reflection may be too late. Formal statement: $$\text{LongTermIrreversible}(D) \rightarrow \text{Necessary}(\text{SpeculativeThinking}(D))$$ II. The Necessity of Prudence Speculative thinking must be constrained by prudence, for the following reasons: | Reason for prudence | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Epistemic limitation | Our knowledge of future scenarios is limited | | Risk of bias | Speculation may reflect present-day biases | | Risk of misleading | Mistaken speculation may mislead decision-making | | Waste of resources | Excessive speculation may waste cognitive resources | Proposition 0.9 (The Necessity of Prudence) Speculative thinking must be constrained by prudence. Unconstrained speculation may lead to mistaken conclusions and improper action. III. Strategies for Managing the Tension Strategy One: Labelling the level of speculation This work labels propositions with their level of speculation: | Level of speculation | Definition | Example | |----------|------|------| | S1 (low) | Inference based on sufficient evidence | Thermodynamic constraints will continue to hold | | S2 (moderate) | Inference based on reasonable extrapolation | AI capabilities will continue to grow | | S3 (high) | Inference based on limited evidence | AGI may emerge in this century | | S4 (very high) | Inference based on pure theory | Extraterrestrial civilizations may exist | Strategy Two: Contextual conditioning Speculative propositions are stated in conditional form, making their underlying assumptions explicit: $$\text{If } \text{Condition}(C) \text{ then } \text{Conclusion}(P)$$ Example: "If AGI emerges in this century (condition), then a framework for assessing agent status needs to be established in advance (conclusion)." Strategy Three: Robustness first Under speculative scenarios, prefer strategies that are effective across many possible scenarios (robust strategies) over strategies that are optimal only in a specific scenario. $$\text{Prefer}(\text{RobustStrategy}) \text{ over } \text{Prefer}(\text{OptimalStrategy}_{\text{specific}})$$ Strategy Four: Preference for reversibility Under speculative scenarios, prefer reversible decisions, so that they can be corrected if the speculation proves mistaken. $$\text{Speculation}(S) \rightarrow \text{Prefer}(\text{ReversibleDecision})$$ This strategy is highly consistent with the "Reversibility Principle" to be argued in Chapter 13 of this work.

§0.2.4 The Relation between the Normative and the Descriptive I. The Classic Formulation of the "Is-Ought" Problem Hume's Law states that one cannot derive an "ought" (a normative proposition) from a pure "is" (a descriptive proposition). Formal statement: $$\{p_1, p_2, ..., p_n\} \vdash q \text{ and } \forall p_i: \text{Descriptive}(p_i) \rightarrow \neg\text{Normative}(q)$$ This law poses a challenge for this work: if the Three New Views are descriptive (descriptions of the cosmos, life and cognition), how can normative principles be derived from them? II. The Response Strategy of This Work This work does not seek to violate Hume's Law, but adopts the following strategies: Strategy One: Introducing bridge principles This work introduces "bridge principles." They are not purely descriptive propositions but mixed propositions containing a normative component. Definition 0.10 (Bridge Principle) A bridge principle is an intermediary principle connecting descriptive and normative propositions. It contains a minimal normative assumption about "rational agents," which makes the transition from description to norm possible. Formal statement: $$\text{Descriptive}(D) + \text{BridgePrinciple}(B) \vdash \text{Normative}(N)$$ where $B$ contains a normative component, so the derivation does not violate Hume's Law. Strategy Two: The constitutive argument This work adopts a "constitutive argument" strategy: certain normative requirements are constitutive conditions of rational agency. Structure of the argument:

  1. Premise One (descriptive): X is a rational agent
  2. Premise Two (constitutive): The constitutive conditions of rational agency include C
  3. Conclusion (normative): X ought to satisfy C

This argument does not violate Hume's Law, because Premise Two is not purely descriptive but is a constitutive claim about rational agency. Strategy Three: Reflective equilibrium This work adopts a Rawlsian method of "reflective equilibrium": seeking a mutually supportive equilibrium among concrete intuitions, mid-level principles and abstract theory. The structure of reflective equilibrium:

┌─────────────────────┐
│    Abstract theory   │
│   (the Three New Views)  │
└──────────┬──────────┘
│

▼

┌─────────────────────┐
│   Mid-level principles  │
│ (normative principles, bridge principles) │
└──────────┬──────────┘
│

▼

┌─────────────────────┐
│   Concrete intuitions  │
│ (moral intuitions, case judgments) │
└─────────────────────┘

The three levels adjust to one another in the search for equilibrium. III. The Metaethical Stance of This Work Statement of stance: In metaethics this work adopts an "open stance" and does not presuppose any particular metaethical theory (such as moral realism, constructivism or expressivism). Reasons: | Reason | Explanation | |------|------| | Metaethical disputes are unresolved | The core disputes of metaethics remain unsettled | | Practical priority | The aim of this work is practical guidance, not metaethical argument | | Consideration of compatibility | An open stance allows compatibility with many metaethical theories | Proposition 0.10 (Metaethical Openness) The normative framework of this work is compatible with many metaethical positions. Readers may interpret the normative claims of this work according to their own metaethical preferences. Formal statement: $$\text{Compatible}(\text{ThisWork}, \text{MoralRealism}) \wedge \text{Compatible}(\text{ThisWork}, \text{Constructivism}) \wedge ...$$

§0.3 The System of Boundary Declarations

§0.3.1 Restrictions on Use I. The Necessity of Restrictions on Use As a "concept prototype" (CRL 2-4), this work must be subject to strict restrictions on use. Improper use may lead to: | Type of improper use | Potential consequence | |--------------|----------| | Use for mandatory assessment | Injustice to individuals or organizations | | Use for legal adjudication | Improper legal consequences | | Use for resource allocation | Unfair distribution of resources | | Use for political manipulation | Use to justify improper policies | II. The Specific Content of the Restrictions on Use Declaration 0.1 (Restrictions on Use) This work expressly declares the following restrictions on use: Restriction One: Use for mandatory assessment is forbidden The indicator systems of this work (UCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIA) must not be used for mandatory assessment or ranking of any individual, organization, state or civilization. Formal statement: $$\neg\text{Permitted}(\text{MandatoryAssessment}(\text{Indicators}_{\text{ThisWork}}, \text{Entity}))$$ Restriction Two: Use for legal adjudication is forbidden The normative principles and institutional designs of this work must not serve as the direct basis of legal adjudication. This work has no legal force. Formal statement: $$\neg\text{LegalAuthority}(\text{ThisWork})$$ Restriction Three: Use for resource-allocation decisions is forbidden The framework of this work must not serve as the sole or primary basis for resource-allocation decisions. Restriction Four: Use for political manipulation is forbidden This work must not be selectively cited to justify improper policies or political manipulation. III. Permitted Scope of Use Declaration 0.2 (Permitted Scope of Use) The following uses of this work are permitted: | Permitted type of use | Specific content | |--------------|----------| | Academic research | As a reference framework for academic research | | Thought experiments | As a conceptual tool for thought experiments | | Policy discussion | As a reference view in policy discussion | | Education and training | As teaching material for education and training | | Simulation modelling | As a conceptual basis for simulation modelling | | Public dialogue | As a discussion framework for public dialogue | Formal statement: $$\text{PermittedUse}(\text{ThisWork}) = \{\text{Research}, \text{ThoughtExperiment}, \text{PolicyDiscussion}, \text{Education}, \text{Simulation}, \text{PublicDialogue}\}$$ IV. Responsibilities of Users Declaration 0.3 (Statement of User Responsibility) Any individual or organization using this work should bear the following responsibilities: | Type of responsibility | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Respect for boundaries | Respect the boundaries of use declared by this work | | Complete citation | Maintain the integrity of context when citing | | Acknowledgment of limitations | Acknowledge the limitations of this work | | Acceptance of consequences | Bear responsibility for the consequences of use |

§0.3.2 Maturity Declaration I. The Purpose of the Maturity Declaration The purpose of the maturity declaration is to give readers an accurate understanding of the stage of development of each component of this work, so that they can make appropriate decisions about its use. II. §0.3.3 Ethical Declaration I. The Necessity of an Ethical Declaration This work touches on sensitive ethical questions, including: | Sensitive area | Specific question | |----------|----------| | Status of agents | Who qualifies to be regarded as a moral agent? | | Moral status | How are the moral statuses of different agents compared? | | Intergenerational justice | What responsibilities do present generations owe to future generations? | | Cross-species ethics | What responsibilities do humans owe to other species? | | AI ethics | Can AI systems have moral status? | Discussion of these questions may be misunderstood or misused, and therefore requires an explicit ethical declaration. II. The Specific Content of the Ethical Declaration Declaration 0.6 (Ethical Declaration) This work makes the following ethical commitments: Commitment One: The principle of non-discrimination The framework of this work must not be used to discriminate against any individual or group. Indicators such as UCS are intended to provide analytical tools, not to establish discriminatory hierarchies. Formal statement: $$\neg\text{Permitted}(\text{Discrimination}(\text{Entity}, \text{Framework}_{\text{ThisWork}}))$$ Commitment Two: The principle of human dignity This work recognizes and respects the inviolability of human dignity. Its discussion of the moral status of non-human agents does not imply any lowering of the moral status of human beings. Commitment Three: The principle of prudence This work adopts a prudent attitude in matters of sensitive ethical controversy. On questions where no consensus exists, it presents multiple views rather than imposing a particular position. Commitment Four: The principle of transparency This work is transparent about its ethical stance. Readers have the right to know the ethical assumptions and value orientations of this work. Commitment Five: The principle of contestability The ethical claims of this work are contestable. Criticism of and challenges to its ethical stance are welcome. III. Principles for Handling Sensitive Topics Table 0.5 Principles for handling sensitive topics | Sensitive topic | Principle of handling | Specific measure | |----------|----------|----------| | Moral status of AI | Open exploration | Present multiple views without prejudging the conclusion | | Animal rights | Respect for pluralism | Acknowledge the reasonableness of different ethical traditions | | Intergenerational trade-offs | Prudent balance | Avoid extreme claims of intergenerational sacrifice | | Comparison of civilizations | Avoid hierarchies | Do not establish a hierarchy of superiority among civilizations | | Authority to intervene | Restrict claims | Do not claim the legitimacy of unilateral intervention | IV. Ethical Review Mechanisms Declaration 0.7 (Commitment to Ethical Review) This work undertakes to establish the following ethical review mechanisms: | Type of review | Subject of review | Reviewer | |----------|----------|----------| | Internal review | Checking ethical consistency | The author team | | Peer review | Checking ethical reasonableness | Academic peers | | Public review | Checking social acceptability | Public feedback | | Continuous review | Checking long-term impact | Continuous monitoring |

§0.3.4 Revisability Declaration I. The Theoretical Basis of Revisability The theoretical basis of the revisability declaration comes from three core positions of this work: | Position | Relation to revisability | |------|------------------| | The provisional-convention stance | A provisional convention is by nature revisable | | The New View of Cognition (NK-4) | Epistemic humility requires acknowledging fallibility | | The open-system stance | An open system evolves through revision | Proposition 0.11 (The Inevitability of Revisability) The core positions of this work (provisional convention, the New View of Cognition, open system) logically entail its revisability. A work that claimed to be non-revisable would contradict these core positions. Formal statement: $$(\text{ProvisionalConvention} \wedge \text{NK-4} \wedge \text{OpenSystem}) \rightarrow \text{Revisable}(\text{ThisWork})$$ II. The Layered Structure of Revisability The revisability of this work has a layered structure, with different degrees of difficulty of revision at each layer: Table 0.6 The layered structure of revisability | Layer | Content | Difficulty of revision | Revision condition | |------|------|----------|----------| | Meta-level | The principle of revisability itself | Extremely high | Only if a self-contradiction is found | | Core level | The core propositions of the Three New Views | High | A major scientific breakthrough or logical defect | | Principle level | Normative principles, bridge principles | Moderately high | Argumentative defect or new-scenario challenge | | Framework level | The protocol-stack architecture, the indicator framework | Medium | Difficulty of operationalization or poor effect | | Detail level | Specific parameters, procedural details | Low | Continuous optimization | Formal statement: $$\text{RevisionDifficulty}(\text{Meta}) > \text{RevisionDifficulty}(\text{Core}) > \text{RevisionDifficulty}(\text{Principle}) > \text{RevisionDifficulty}(\text{Framework}) > \text{RevisionDifficulty}(\text{Detail})$$ III. Revision-Triggering Conditions Declaration 0.8 (Revision-Triggering Conditions) This work lays down the following revision-triggering conditions: Trigger One: Empirical trigger When a new scientific finding comes into irreconcilable conflict with a core proposition of this work, the revision procedure is triggered. Formal statement: $$\text{NewEvidence}(E) \wedge \text{Conflict}(E, \text{CoreProposition}(P)) \wedge \neg\text{Reconcilable}(E, P) \rightarrow \text{TriggerRevision}(P)$$ Trigger Two: Logical trigger When a logical contradiction is found within this work, the revision procedure is triggered. Formal statement: $$\text{LogicalContradiction}(P_1, P_2) \rightarrow \text{TriggerRevision}(P_1 \vee P_2)$$ Trigger Three: Contextual trigger When a new scenario falls outside the scope of the framework of this work, and that scenario is important, the revision procedure is triggered. Formal statement: $$\text{NewContext}(C) \wedge \neg\text{Applicable}(\text{Framework}, C) \wedge \text{Important}(C) \rightarrow \text{TriggerRevision}(\text{Framework})$$ Trigger Four: Consensus trigger When the scholarly community reaches a consensus to revise, the revision procedure is triggered. Formal statement: $$\text{AcademicConsensus}(\text{Revision}(P)) \rightarrow \text{TriggerRevision}(P)$$ IV. Revision Procedure Declaration 0.9 (Revision Procedure) This work adopts the following revision procedure:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Flow of the revision procedure                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Step 1: Trigger identification                                 │
│  ├─ Determine whether a revision-triggering condition is met    │
│  ├─ Record the source and evidence of the trigger               │
│  └─ Preliminarily assess the scope of revision                  │
│           │                                                     │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  Step 2: Impact assessment                                      │
│  ├─ Assess the impact of the revision on other parts            │
│  ├─ Identify dependencies                                       │
│  └─ Assess the costs and benefits of revision                   │
│           │                                                     │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  Step 3: Proposal                                               │
│  ├─ Put forward a revision proposal                             │
│  ├─ Provide reasons for the revision                            │
│  └─ Explain the differences from the previous version           │
│           │                                                     │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  Step 4: Community deliberation                                 │
│  ├─ Submit for deliberation by the scholarly community          │
│  ├─ Collect feedback                                            │
│  └─ Adjust the proposal in light of feedback                    │
│           │                                                     │
│           ▼                                                     │
│  Step 5: Version update                                         │
│  ├─ Update the version number                                   │
│  ├─ Record the change log                                       │
│  └─ Release the new version                                     │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

V. Version-Control Conventions Declaration 0.10 (Version-Control Conventions) This work adopts Semantic Versioning: Version-number format: $$\text{Version} = \text{MAJOR}.\text{MINOR}.\text{PATCH}$$ Version-number rules: | Version type | Type of change | Trigger condition | Example | |----------|----------|----------|------| | MAJOR | Incompatible major change | Core propositions altered, framework restructured | v1.0.0 → v2.0.0 | | MINOR | Backward-compatible feature addition | New indicators, adjusted weights, extended application | v1.0.0 → v1.1.0 | | PATCH | Backward-compatible problem fix | Error correction, clarification of wording, formatting | v1.0.0 → v1.0.1 | Change-log format: Change-log template: [version number] - date Added

  • description of additions

Changed

  • description of changes

Fixed

  • description of fixes

Removed

  • description of removals

Rationale

  • explanation of the reasons for the change

VI. Rollback Mechanism Declaration 0.11 (Rollback Mechanism) This work establishes a rollback mechanism, allowing a return to a previous version when necessary: Rollback-triggering conditions: | Trigger condition | Explanation | |----------|------| | The revision causes serious problems | The new version introduces more serious problems than the previous one | | The revision lacks consensus | The scholarly community is deeply divided over the revision | | The evidence for the revision is insufficient | The evidence supporting the revision proves inadequate | Rollback procedure:

  1. Identify the need for rollback
  2. Assess the impact of rollback
  3. Community deliberation
  4. Execute the rollback
  5. Record the reasons for the rollback

Formal statement: $$\text{RollbackCondition}(V_{\text{new}}) \rightarrow \text{Rollback}(V_{\text{new}}, V_{\text{old}})$$

§0.4 The Contract with the Reader §0.4.1 What This Work Promises I. Content Promises Commitment 0.1 (Content Promises) This work promises readers the following content: | Type of commitment | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Clarification of the problem | A clear articulation of the core challenges of the normative problems of interstellar civilization | | Provision of a framework | A conceptual framework for addressing these challenges | | Presentation of arguments | The complete chain of argument from premises to conclusions | | Development of tools | Operational indicators and institutional prototypes | | Boundary declarations | A clear statement of the scope and limits of the framework | II. Quality Promises Commitment 0.2 (Quality Promises) This work promises readers the following quality standards: | Dimension of quality | Content of the commitment | |----------|----------| | Logical consistency | No logical contradiction among core propositions | | Transparency of argument | The premises and inferential steps of arguments are clearly visible | | Accuracy of citation | Accurate and fair citation of other scholars' views | | Honesty about boundaries | Honest acknowledgment of the limits and uncertainties of the framework | | Criticizability | The framework is designed to be criticizable | III. Attitudinal Promises Commitment 0.3 (Attitudinal Promises) This work promises readers the following attitudes: | Dimension of attitude | Content of the commitment | |----------|----------| | Epistemic humility | Acknowledging that it may be mistaken | | Open dialogue | Welcoming criticism and alternative views | | Continuous improvement | A commitment to continuous improvement in light of feedback | | Academic integrity | Observing the norms of academic integrity |

§0.4.2 What This Work Does Not Promise I. What Is Not Promised Declaration 0.12 (Declaration of Non-Promise) This work expressly declares that it does not promise the following: Non-promise One: Absolute truth This work does not promise that its content is absolute truth. It is a provisional convention and may require revision. Non-promise Two: A complete answer This work does not promise to provide a complete answer to the normative problems of interstellar civilization. It is an open research programme, not a closed theoretical system. Non-promise Three: Immediate usability This work does not promise that its framework can be used immediately for actual decision-making. It is a concept prototype that requires further development and validation. Non-promise Four: Value neutrality This work does not promise value neutrality. It contains normative claims, and these claims reflect particular value orientations. Non-promise Five: Universal acceptance This work does not promise that its views will be universally accepted. Many of its claims are controversial. II. Reasons for the Non-Promises Table 0.7 Explanation of the reasons for the non-promises | Content not promised | Explanation of the reason | |------------|----------| | Absolute truth | Consistent with the requirement of epistemic humility in the New View of Cognition (NK-4) | | A complete answer | The complexity of the problem exceeds the capacity of any single work | | Immediate usability | A concept prototype requires further development before practical application | | Value neutrality | Normative problems essentially involve value judgments | | Universal acceptance | Academic progress depends on criticism and debate |

§0.4.3 Expectations of the Reader I. Expectations about the Attitude of Reading Expectation 0.1 (Expectation about the Attitude of Reading) This work expects readers to adopt the following attitudes in reading: | Dimension of expectation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Critical reading | Do not accept blindly; maintain critical thinking | | Principle of charity | Try to understand the author's intent before criticizing | | Grasp of the whole | Grasp the overall framework before judging the parts | | Respect for boundaries | Respect the boundaries of use declared by this work | II. Expectations about the Manner of Use Expectation 0.2 (Expectation about the Manner of Use) This work expects readers to use it in the following ways: | Dimension of expectation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Academic use | As a reference for academic research and discussion | | Critical use | As an object of critical analysis | | Developmental use | As a starting point for further development | | Responsible use | Bearing responsibility for the consequences of use | III. Expectations about Feedback Expectation 0.3 (Expectation about Feedback) This work expects readers to provide the following types of feedback: | Type of feedback | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Correction of errors | Pointing out logical, factual or citation errors | | Challenge to arguments | Questioning the validity of an argument or the reasonableness of a premise | | Alternatives | Proposing alternative concepts, arguments or frameworks | | Application feedback | Reporting experience of and problems with applying the framework | | Suggestions for extension | Suggesting directions for extending the framework | Channels for feedback: This work welcomes feedback through the following channels:

  • Criticism and responses in the form of academic papers
  • Discussion at academic conferences
  • Formal book reviews
  • Academic correspondence

IV. Formal Statement of the Reader's Contract Contract 0.1 (The Reader's Contract) The contract between this work and the reader can be stated formally as follows: $$\text{Contract}(\text{Author}, \text{Reader}) = \langle \text{Commitments}_A, \text{NonCommitments}_A, \text{Expectations}_R \rangle$$ where:

  • $\text{Commitments}_A$ = the set of the author's commitments (§0.4.1)
  • $\text{NonCommitments}_A$ = the set of the author's non-commitments (§0.4.2)
  • $\text{Expectations}_R$ = the set of expectations of the reader (§0.4.3)

The binding force of the contract: This contract has no legal binding force but does have binding force in academic ethics. Conduct that violates the contract (for example, the author breaching commitments, or the reader violating the boundaries of use) will invite criticism from the scholarly community.

│  │  3. Ethical declaration: non-discrimination, human dignity, prudence, transparency, contestability │   │
│  │  4. Revisability declaration: revision-triggering conditions, revision procedure, version control │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The system of boundary declarations ensures that this work is used appropriately, preventing misuse and abuse. │   │

│  │                                                           │   │

│  │  - Author's commitments: clarification of the problem, provision of a framework, transparent argument, honest boundaries │   │
│  │  - Author's non-commitments: absolute truth, a complete answer, immediate usability │   │
│  │  - Expectations of the reader: critical reading, respect for boundaries, constructive feedback │   │

Footnotes

Chapter 0 Footnotes

[1] Semantic Versioning: Semantic versioning is the standard method of software version management, proposed by Tom Preston-Werner. See: Preston-Werner, T. (2013). Semantic Versioning 2.0.0. https://semver.org/ [2] Technology Readiness Level (TRL): TRL is the standard framework developed by NASA for assessing technological maturity. See: Mankins, J. C. (1995). "Technology Readiness Levels." NASA White Paper. The "Conceptual Readiness Level" (CRL) developed in this work is an analogical application of TRL to the domain of theoretical frameworks. [3] Hume's Law: In A Treatise of Human Nature, Hume pointed out that one cannot derive "ought" from "is". See: Hume, D. (1739). A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Part I, Section I. For contemporary discussion of Hume's Law, see: Pigden, C. R. (Ed.). (2010). Hume on Is and Ought. Palgrave Macmillan. [4] Naturalistic Fallacy: Moore introduced this concept in Principia Ethica. See: Moore, G. E. (1903). Principia Ethica. Cambridge University Press. On the relationship between the naturalistic fallacy and Hume's Law, see: Frankena, W. K. (1939). "The Naturalistic Fallacy." Mind, 48(192), 464-477. [5] Reflective Equilibrium: Rawls developed this methodological concept in A Theory of Justice. See: Rawls, J. (1971). A Theory of Justice. Harvard University Press, pp. 48-51. For a detailed discussion of reflective equilibrium, see: Daniels, N. (1979). "Wide Reflective Equilibrium and Theory Acceptance in Ethics." Journal of Philosophy, 76(5), 256-282. [6] Fallibilism: The classic formulation of fallibilism comes from Peirce. See: Peirce, C. S. (1897). "Fallibilism, Continuity, and Evolution." In Collected Papers of Charles Sanders Peirce. [7] Open System: The concept of the open system originates from von Bertalanffy's general system theory. See: von Bertalanffy, L. (1968). General System Theory: Foundations, Development, Applications. George Braziller. [8] Constitutive Argument: The constitutive argument is a form of Kantian transcendental argument. On the application of constitutive argument in ethics, see: Korsgaard, C. M. (1996). The Sources of Normativity. Cambridge University Press. [9] Interdisciplinary Research Methodology: on methodological discussion of interdisciplinary research, see: Repko, A. F., & Szostak, R. (2020). Interdisciplinary Research: Process and Theory (3rd ed.). SAGE. [10] Conceptual Prototype and Design Thinking: The methodology of the conceptual prototype comes from the design-thinking tradition. See: Brown, T. (2009). Change by Design: How Design Thinking Transforms Organizations and Inspires Innovation. HarperBusiness.

Three Puzzles and a Theoretical PreviewIntroduction

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Place of This Chapter in the Work The Introduction is the "unfolding of the problem" and the "theoretical preview" chapter of the whole work. It follows Chapter 0 (methodological commitments) and precedes Part One (the Three New Views). It serves as the bridge from the "meta-level" to the "substantive level": Chapter 0 establishes how this work is to be read, while the Introduction unfolds what problems this work is to solve and the basic outline of the answers. III. The Core Tasks of This Chapter This chapter undertakes four core tasks: Task 1: Diagnosis of the challenge. To articulate the distinctive challenges facing the governance of interstellar civilization and to argue why existing frameworks are inadequate to meet them. Task 2: Unfolding the puzzles. To unfold systematically the three core puzzles (the cosmic grounding of normativity, rationality under deep uncertainty, and the attribution of long-range responsibility) and to reveal their internal connections. Task 3: Theoretical preview. To preview the outline of this work's answers (the Three New Views, the normative principles, the operational framework), so that readers grasp the overall picture before entering the main text. Task 4: Structural navigation. To provide a structural map of the work and suggested reading paths, helping readers of different backgrounds find a route suited to them. IV. The Deliverables of This Chapter After completing this chapter, the reader will have:

  • A clear understanding of the governance challenges of interstellar civilization
  • An in-depth grasp of the three core puzzles
  • An overall grasp of the outline of this work's answers
  • A navigation map of the structure of the work
  • A reading path suited to the reader's own needs

V. Reading Advice This chapter is the necessary preparation for entering the main text; all readers are advised to read it in full. Readers with limited time may prioritize: §D.2 (The Three Core Puzzles) → §D.3.4 (Preview of the Overall Architecture) → §D.4.3 (Suggested Reading Paths) Readers with a philosophical background should focus on: §D.2.1 (The Cosmic Grounding of Normativity) → §D.3.1 (Preview of the Three New Views) Readers with a policy background should focus on: §D.1 (The Governance Challenge) → §D.3.3 (Preview of the Operational Framework) Estimated reading time: about 2-2.5 hours for a complete reading. VI. Continuity with Chapter 0 The methodological commitments established in Chapter 0 are concretely applied in this chapter:

  • The "provisional convention" stance → the theoretical preview of this chapter is a revisable preliminary outline
  • The "concept prototype" stance → the framework previewed in this chapter is at the CRL 3-4 stage
  • The "open system" stance → the problem diagnosis of this chapter welcomes additions and corrections
