§D.1 The Challenge of Governing Interstellar Civilization

§D.1.1 Why Think about Interstellar Civilization Now? I. Responding to the "Too Early" Objection A natural objection is this: interstellar civilization seems to belong to a distant future, so why think about its governance now? This objection deserves to be taken seriously. Definition D.1 (Interstellar Civilization) Interstellar civilization is a form of intelligent civilization possessing the following features: (1) a sphere of activity extending beyond a single planetary system; (2) a time scale extending over many generations, even thousands of generations; (3) possible inclusion of many types of intelligent agents (biological, artificial, hybrid); (4) exposure to the possibility of contact with other intelligent civilizations. Formal statement: $$\text{InterstellarCiv}(C) \leftrightarrow \text{MultiPlanetary}(C) \wedge \text{DeepTime}(C) \wedge \text{MultiAgent}(C) \wedge \text{ContactPossible}(C)$$ The response to the "too early" objection rests on the following three arguments: Argument One: The technological-trajectory argument The trajectory of contemporary technological development shows that certain elements of interstellar civilization are accelerating toward us: | Technological field | Current state | Expected development | Governance relevance | |----------|----------|----------|------------| | Artificial intelligence | Large language models, specialized AI | AGI may emerge within decades | Status of agents, attribution of responsibility | | Space exploration | Mars missions under planning | A Mars colony may be established this century | Cross-planetary governance, resource distribution | | Biotechnology | Gene editing, synthetic biology | Human enhancement, life extension | Posthuman agents, intergenerational relations | | Communication technology | Deep-space communication networks | SETI continues its search | Protocols for cross-civilizational contact | Proposition D.1 (The Governance Implications of the Technological Trajectory) The current trajectory of technological development shows that the core governance challenges of interstellar civilization (the status of AI agents, cross-planetary governance, posthuman ethics, cross-civilizational contact) will become real problems in the foreseeable future. Normative frameworks need to be established before technological capacities are acquired. Formal statement: $$\text{TechTrajectory}(T) \rightarrow \text{FutureChallenge}(C, t_{future}) \rightarrow \text{NeedFramework}(t_{now})$$ Argument Two: The irreversibility argument Decisions relating to interstellar civilization are highly irreversible. Once made, their consequences may persist for generations, even millennia, and are hard to correct. | Type of decision | Degree of irreversibility | Example | |----------|--------------|------| | The path of AI development | Extremely high | Once AGI value alignment fails, it may be impossible to correct | | Planetary engineering | Extremely high | Once Martian terraforming begins, the original ecosystem cannot be restored | | Genetic modification | High | Germline gene editing is transmitted to descendants | | First contact | Extremely high | First contact with an extraterrestrial civilization will permanently shape the relation | Proposition D.2 (Irreversibility and Prior Reflection) The higher the degree of irreversibility of a decision, the greater the necessity of establishing a normative framework in advance. For highly irreversible decisions, the strategy of "wait until the problem appears and then solve it" is irresponsible. Formal statement: $$\text{Irreversibility}(D) > \theta_{high} \rightarrow \text{Necessary}(\text{PreemptiveFramework}(D))$$ where $\theta_{high}$ is the high threshold of irreversibility. Argument Three: The conceptual-preparation argument Even if the full realization of interstellar civilization still lies some distance away, the construction of a conceptual framework itself takes time. History shows that major conceptual transformations often require the efforts of several generations. | Conceptual transformation | Period of gestation | Key milestones | |----------|----------|----------| | Heliocentrism | About 150 years | Copernicus (1543) → Newton (1687) | | Evolutionary theory | About 100 years | Darwin (1859) → the modern synthesis (1940s) | | Quantum mechanics | About 30 years | Planck (1900) → the Copenhagen interpretation (1927) | | The idea of human rights | About 200 years | The Enlightenment → the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) | Proposition D.3 (The Temporal Demand of Conceptual Preparation) Major conceptual transformations of framework require a considerable period of gestation. The normative framework of interstellar civilization involves a fundamental reconstruction of ontology, epistemology and ethics, and its establishment cannot be accomplished overnight. Thinking begins now as the necessary conceptual preparation for the future. II. The Convergence of Threefold Pressure Contemporary human civilization faces a convergence of threefold pressure, and these pressures jointly point to the urgency of the governance problems of interstellar civilization: Pressure One: Exponential growth of technological capability Human technological capability is growing at an exponential rate, but the growth of ethical wisdom and governance capacity has lagged far behind. $$\text{TechCapability}(t) = \text{TechCapability}(t_0) \cdot e^{r_T(t-t_0)}$$ $$\text{EthicalWisdom}(t) = \text{EthicalWisdom}(t_0) \cdot (1 + r_E(t-t_0))$$ where $r_T >> r_E$, i.e. the growth rate of technological capability far exceeds that of ethical wisdom. This gap constitutes the contemporary version of the "Collingridge Dilemma": When the impact of a technology can be foreseen, the technology is not yet mature and intervention seems unnecessary; when the technology is mature, its impact is already deeply entrenched and intervention becomes difficult. Pressure Two: Spatiotemporal extension of the consequences of action The consequences of contemporary human action are extending over ever greater distances in space and time: | Dimension | Traditional range | Contemporary extension | Interstellar-civilization range | |------|----------|----------|--------------| | Space | Local community | Global | Multi-planetary, interstellar | | Time | A few generations | A few centuries | Thousands to millions of years | | Agents | Humans | Humans + some animals | Many kinds of intelligent agents | Pressure Three: The emergence of agent pluralism Traditional ethical and governance frameworks presuppose relatively homogeneous human individuals as their agents. But contemporary and future agents are becoming highly diverse: | Type of agent | Current state | Future possibility | Governance challenge | |----------|----------|----------|----------| | Artificial intelligence | Instrumental existence | May possess agency | Moral status, attribution of responsibility | | Enhanced humans | Preliminary exploration | Cognitive and bodily enhancement | Equality, identity | | Digital consciousness | Theoretical discussion | Mind uploading | Personal identity, rights | | Extraterrestrial intelligence | Unconfirmed | May exist | Cross-civilizational ethics | Proposition D.4 (The Convergent Effect of Threefold Pressure) The exponential growth of technological capability, the spatiotemporal extension of the consequences of action, and the emergence of agent pluralism — these three pressures are converging and jointly point to one conclusion: traditional ethical and governance frameworks are approaching the limits of their applicability and require fundamental reconstruction. Formal statement: $$(\text{TechGrowth} \wedge \text{ConsequenceExtension} \wedge \text{AgentDiversity}) \rightarrow \text{FrameworkReconstruction}$$ III. On the Relation between the "Three New Views" and the "Three Old Views" The "Three New Views" proposed in this work (the New Cosmology, the New View of Life, the New View of Cognition) are a paradigm shift from the traditional "three old views" (worldview, outlook on life, values), rather than a simple replacement. Specific qualifications:

  1. The historical contribution of the "three old views": the traditional worldview, outlook on life and values played an important role in the planetary stage of human civilization, providing individuals and societies with a framework of meaning and a guide to action.
  2. The limits of the "three old views": under the new conditions of interstellar civilization, multiple intelligent agents and deep uncertainty, the old views face structural limits — they presuppose anthropocentrism, an Earth-bound environment and short time scales.
  3. The stance of the "three new views": the Three New Views do not negate the three old views but provide a more inclusive and adaptive framework over a larger spatiotemporal scale and a more diverse range of agents.
  4. Compatibility: at the Earthly scale and within human society, the three old views remain valid; the Three New Views are a "dimensional upgrade" of the old views at the interstellar scale.

Comparison of the Three New Views and the Three Old Views | Dimension | Three old views | Three new views | Relation | |------|--------|--------|------| | Understanding of the cosmos | Worldview (static, mechanical) | New Cosmology (participatory, processual) | Dimensional extension | | Understanding of life | Outlook on life (anthropocentric) | New View of Life (cross-substrate, graded) | Dimensional extension | | Understanding of value | Values (Earthly scale) | New View of Cognition (participatory construction) | Dimensional extension | | Scope of applicability | Planetary civilization | Interstellar civilization | Relation of inclusion | | Range of agents | Humans | Multiple intelligent agents | Relation of inclusion | | Time scale | Generational | Deep time | Relation of inclusion | IV. The Disciplinary Positioning of "Interstellar Civilization Studies" One of the core aims of this work is to lay the foundation for "Interstellar Civilization Studies" as an emerging discipline. Definition D.2 (Interstellar Civilization Studies) Interstellar Civilization Studies is an interdisciplinary field that studies the existence, development, interaction and governance of intelligent civilizations on a cosmic scale. It integrates perspectives from physics, biology, cognitive science, ethics, political science, law and other disciplines to provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for the normative problems of the interstellar-civilization era. The disciplinary features of Interstellar Civilization Studies: | Feature | Content | Difference from traditional disciplines | |------|------|------------------| | Time scale | Deep time (thousands to millions of years) | Traditional disciplines usually focus on a few generations | | Spatial scale | Cosmic scale | Traditional disciplines usually focus on the Earth | | Range of agents | Multiple intelligent agents | Traditional disciplines usually focus on humans | | Uncertainty | Deep uncertainty | Traditional disciplines usually assume calculable risk | | Normativity | Cosmic ethics | Traditional ethics is usually anthropocentric | Proposition D.5 (The Necessity of Interstellar Civilization Studies) The governance problems of interstellar civilization have distinctive features (deep time scale, cosmic space, plural agents, deep uncertainty) that exceed the capacity of any single existing discipline. A new interdisciplinary field — Interstellar Civilization Studies — is therefore needed to study these problems systematically.

§D.1.2 The Distinctiveness of the Governance Challenge I. Fourfold Distinctiveness The governance challenge of interstellar civilization has a fourfold distinctiveness that makes traditional governance frameworks hard to apply directly: Distinctiveness One: Deep Time Scale Definition D.3 (Deep Time) Deep time is a time scale beyond the grasp of human intuition, usually referring to spans of thousands to millions of years. At the scale of deep time, the succession of human generations, the rise and fall of civilizations, and even the evolution of species become observable phenomena. The challenge that the deep time scale poses to governance: | Dimension of challenge | Specific content | Limit of traditional frameworks | |----------|----------|----------------| | Prediction of consequences | Consequences of action extend thousands of years into the future | Traditional predictive methods fail | | Attribution of responsibility | Causal chains cross many generations | Traditional responsibility models do not apply | | Representation of interests | Future generations cannot participate in present decisions | Traditional democratic mechanisms are inadequate | | Stability of values | Values may evolve over deep time | Traditional assumptions about values are unstable | Formal statement: $$\text{DeepTime}(T) \leftrightarrow T > \theta_{deep} \approx 10^3 \text{ years}$$ $$\text{DeepTime}(T) \rightarrow \neg\text{Applicable}(\text{TraditionalGovernance})$$ Distinctiveness Two: Cosmic Spatial Scale Definition D.4 (Cosmic Spatial Scale) Cosmic spatial scale refers to spatial ranges beyond a single planetary system, including interplanetary, interstellar and even intergalactic space. The challenge that the cosmic spatial scale poses to governance: | Dimension of challenge | Specific content | Limit of traditional frameworks | |----------|----------|----------------| | Communication delay | The speed of light imposes communication delays | Real-time coordination is impossible | | Jurisdiction | Traditional concepts of sovereignty do not apply | Territorial-sovereignty models fail | | Resource allocation | Principles for allocating cosmic resources | Earth-bound resource models are inadequate | | Environmental responsibility | Responsibility for the cosmic environment | Earth-bound environmental ethics are inadequate | Distinctiveness Three: Agent Diversity Definition D.5 (Agent Diversity) Agent diversity means that under interstellar-civilization conditions there may be many types of intelligent agents, including but not limited to: biological intelligence (humans and possibly extraterrestrial life), artificial intelligence (from specialized AI to AGI), hybrid intelligence (human-machine integrations), collective intelligence (swarm-style intelligence), and so on. The challenge that agent diversity poses to governance: | Dimension of challenge | Specific content | Limit of traditional frameworks | |----------|----------|----------------| | Moral status | How the moral status of different agents is determined | Traditional criteria are anthropocentric | | Weighing of interests | How the interests of different agents are compared | Traditional utilitarian calculation does not apply | | Possibility of communication | Whether communication with heterogeneous agents is possible | Traditional communication assumes human language | | Shared values | Whether there are values shared across agents | Traditional values assume human commonality | Distinctiveness Four: Deep Uncertainty Definition D.6 (Deep Uncertainty) Deep uncertainty is an epistemic state in which: (1) the space of possible outcomes cannot be fully enumerated; (2) even if it could be enumerated, no meaningful probabilities could be assigned to the outcomes; (3) even if probabilities could be assigned, the utility function could not be determined; (4) the decision-maker is also uncertain about his or her own preferences and values. Formal statement: $$\text{DeepUncertainty} \leftrightarrow \neg\text{Enumerable}(\Omega) \vee \neg\text{Probabilizable}(\Omega) \vee \neg\text{UtilityDefined}(U) \vee \neg\text{PreferenceStable}(P)$$ where $\Omega$ is the outcome space, $U$ is the utility function, and $P$ is the preference structure. Distinguishing deep uncertainty from traditional uncertainty: | Type of uncertainty | Outcome space | Probability assignment | Utility function | Decision method | |--------------|----------|----------|----------|----------| | Risk | Known | Assignable | Known | Expected-utility maximization | | Uncertainty | Known | Not assignable | Known | Maximin, minimax regret | | Deep uncertainty | Unknown or incomplete | Not assignable | Unknown or unstable | New methods required | Proposition D.6 (The Combined Effect of Fourfold Distinctiveness) Deep time scale, cosmic spatial scale, agent diversity and deep uncertainty — these four forms of distinctiveness are not isolated but interwoven and mutually reinforcing. Their combined effect makes the governance challenge of interstellar civilization qualitatively different from any traditional governance problem. Formal statement: $$\text{GovernanceChallenge}_{IC} = f(\text{DeepTime}, \text{CosmicScale}, \text{AgentDiversity}, \text{DeepUncertainty})$$ where $f$ is a non-linear combined function expressing the mutually reinforcing effect of the four forms of distinctiveness. II. The Boundaries of the Traditional Governance Paradigm Traditional governance paradigms encounter structural boundaries when facing the challenges of interstellar civilization: Boundary One: The boundary of the Westphalian system The Westphalian system (the international order since 1648) rests on the following assumptions: | Assumption | Content | Challenge from interstellar-civilization conditions | |------|------|---------------------| | Territorial sovereignty | A state has exclusive sovereignty over its territory | Cosmic space cannot be divided into territories | | Sovereign equality | States are equal in law | The capacities of different civilizations differ enormously | | Non-interference | Non-interference in the internal affairs of other states | The externalities of cosmic action cannot be isolated | | Human subjects | The subjects of international law are human states | The status of non-human agents is undetermined | Boundary Two: The boundary of social-contract theory Social-contract theory (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Rawls) rests on the following assumptions: | Assumption | Content | Challenge from interstellar-civilization conditions | |------|------|---------------------| | Contemporaneity | The contracting parties are contemporaries | Future generations cannot participate in the contract | | Human rationality | The contracting parties possess human rationality | The forms of rationality of non-human agents are unknown | | Limited space and time | The contract applies to limited space and time | Interstellar civilization spans deep time and cosmic space | | Communicability | The contracting parties can communicate | Communication with heterogeneous agents may be limited | Boundary Three: The boundary of utilitarianism Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill, Singer) rests on the following assumptions: | Assumption | Content | Challenge from interstellar-civilization conditions | |------|------|---------------------| | Utility is calculable | Utility can be calculated and compared | Under deep uncertainty utility is not calculable | | Agents are identifiable | Affected agents can be identified | Future and heterogeneous agents are hard to identify | | Preferences are stable | Preferences are stable | Preferences may evolve over deep time | | Aggregation is possible | Utility can be aggregated across agents | The utilities of heterogeneous agents are not comparable | Boundary Four: The boundary of deontology Deontology (Kant, Rawls) rests on the following assumptions: | Assumption | Content | Challenge from interstellar-civilization conditions | |------|------|---------------------| | Rational agents | Moral agents are rational beings | The forms of rationality of non-human agents are unknown | | Universalizability test | Maxims can be tested for universalizability | Cross-civilizational standards of universalization are undetermined | | Dignity of persons | Persons have intrinsic dignity | The dignity status of non-human agents is undetermined | | Limited responsibility | Responsibility is limited | Over deep time the boundaries of responsibility blur | Proposition D.7 (The Structural Boundaries of Traditional Paradigms) The difficulties that traditional governance paradigms (the Westphalian system, social-contract theory, utilitarianism, deontology) encounter in the face of interstellar-civilization challenges are not incidental difficulties but structural boundaries. These boundaries arise from a fundamental mismatch between the core assumptions of these paradigms and interstellar-civilization conditions. Formal statement: $$\forall P \in \{\text{Westphalia}, \text{SocialContract}, \text{Utilitarianism}, \text{Deontology}\}: \text{Assumptions}(P) \not\models \text{Context}_{IC}$$ where $\text{Context}_{IC}$ is the set of features of interstellar-civilization conditions. III. The Necessity of Moving from "Patching" to "Reconstruction" In the face of the structural boundaries of traditional paradigms, two possible response strategies exist: Strategy One: The patching strategy The patching strategy attempts to meet new challenges through partial adjustments while preserving the core structure of traditional paradigms. | Patching attempt | Specific content | Limitation | |----------|----------|--------| | Extending the range of agents | Including animals and AI in moral consideration | Does not touch the criteria of agency itself | | Extending the time horizon | Considering the interests of future generations | Does not solve the problem of representation | | Introducing uncertainty | Using probabilistic decision theory | Does not address deep uncertainty | | Extending international law | Concluding space-law treaties | Does not transcend the Westphalian framework | Strategy Two: The reconstruction strategy The reconstruction strategy acknowledges the structural boundaries of traditional paradigms and attempts to re-establish a normative framework at a more fundamental level. | Dimension of reconstruction | Specific content | Response of this work | |----------|----------|--------------| | Ontological reconstruction | Re-understanding the basic structure of existence | The New Cosmology (NC) | | Reconstruction of the view of life | Re-understanding life and agency | The New View of Life (NL) | | Epistemological reconstruction | Re-understanding knowledge and rationality | The New View of Cognition (NK) | | Normative reconstruction | Re-establishing the normative foundation | The three normative principles | Proposition D.8 (The Necessity of Reconstruction) The patching strategy cannot meet the governance challenges of interstellar civilization, because these challenges arise from a fundamental mismatch between the core assumptions of traditional paradigms and interstellar-civilization conditions. What is required is a reconstruction strategy — re-establishing the framework at the fundamental level of ontology, epistemology and normativity. Formal statement: $$\text{StructuralMismatch}(\text{TraditionalParadigm}, \text{Context}_{IC}) \rightarrow \neg\text{Sufficient}(\text{Patching}) \rightarrow \text{Necessary}(\text{Reconstruction})$$

§D.1.3 The Inadequacy of Existing Frameworks I. The Limits of Extensions of Traditional Ethics Contemporary ethicists have recognized the limits of traditional ethics and have attempted various extensions. But these extensions still face fundamental difficulties. Extension One: The extension of animal ethics Animal ethics (Singer, Regan, and others) attempts to extend moral consideration to non-human animals. | Contribution | Limitation | |------|------| | Challenged anthropocentrism | Still uses sentience as the core criterion | | Extended the moral community | Fails to address non-biological agents such as AI | | Developed a theory of interest consideration | Fails to address interests under deep uncertainty | Extension Two: The extension of environmental ethics Environmental ethics (Leopold, Naess, and others) attempts to extend moral consideration to ecosystems. | Contribution | Limitation | |------|------| | Introduced a holistic perspective | Focuses mainly on Earth's ecosystems | | Developed a theory of intrinsic value | Fails to address environments on a cosmic scale | | Emphasized intergenerational responsibility | Fails to address responsibility on a deep time scale | Extension Three: The extension of intergenerational ethics Intergenerational ethics (Parfit, Gosseries, and others) attempts to extend moral consideration to future generations. | Contribution | Limitation | |------|------| | Raised the question of the moral status of future generations | Fails to solve the "non-identity problem" | | Developed discussion of discount rates | Fails to address discounting under deep uncertainty | | Emphasized sustainability | Fails to address sustainability on a deep time scale | Extension Four: The extension of AI ethics AI ethics attempts to address the ethical problems raised by artificial intelligence. | Contribution | Limitation | |------|------| | Raised the question of the moral status of AI | Lacks criteria for judging AI agency | | Developed discussion of the alignment problem | Fails to address value pluralism | | Emphasized attribution of responsibility | Fails to address responsibility in distributed systems | Proposition D.9 (The Structural Limits of Extensions of Traditional Ethics) The various extensions of traditional ethics (animal ethics, environmental ethics, intergenerational ethics, AI ethics), although making important contributions, still operate within the framework of traditional ethics and fail to touch the structural assumptions of the framework itself. They therefore cannot adequately meet the governance challenges of interstellar civilization. II. The Contribution and Shortcomings of Longtermism Longtermism is an ethical position that has emerged in recent years, holding that we should attach great importance to impacts on the long-term future. Definition D.7 (Longtermism) Longtermism is an ethical position holding that: (1) the well-being of future generations is morally as important as that of present generations; (2) because the number of future generations may greatly exceed the present generation, actions affecting the long-term future are of extremely high moral importance; (3) we should prioritize actions that may affect the long-term future, especially existential risks. The contributions of longtermism: | Dimension of contribution | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Extension of the time horizon | Extends moral concern to the deep time scale | | Attention to existential risk | Systematic attention to risks that could end civilization | | Reconstruction of priorities | Reassesses the moral priority of different actions | | Institution building | Has promoted relevant research institutions and policy initiatives | The shortcomings of longtermism: | Dimension of shortcoming | Specific content | Response of this work | |----------|----------|--------------| | Weak epistemic foundation | How can reliable judgments be made under deep uncertainty? | The New View of Cognition provides an epistemic foundation | | Contested normative foundation | Why is the well-being of future generations equally important? | The Three New Views provide a normative foundation | | Dependence on utilitarianism | Relies mainly on a utilitarian framework | This work provides an alternative framework | | Residual anthropocentrism | Focuses mainly on the human future | This work extends to plural agents | | Difficulty of operationalization | How are principles translated into concrete action? | This work provides an indicator system and institutional design | Proposition D.10 (The Positioning of Longtermism) Longtermism is an important interlocutor of this work, not a competitor. This work attempts to provide longtermism with a firmer epistemic and normative foundation, to extend its scope (from humans to plural agents), and to supply operational tools. Formal statement: $$\text{ThisWork} = \text{Longtermism} + \text{EpistemicFoundation} + \text{NormativeFoundation} + \text{AgentExpansion} + \text{Operationalization}$$ III. The Lag of Global Governance Frameworks Contemporary global governance frameworks lag markedly in meeting the challenges of interstellar civilization. Lag One: The limits of the United Nations system | Dimension of limitation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Limitation of agents | Recognizes only states and a limited set of international organizations as subjects | | Time horizon | Focuses mainly on contemporary problems | | Spatial range | Focuses mainly on Earthly affairs | | Decision mechanism | Relies on inter-state negotiation, with limited efficiency | Lag Two: The limits of international space law Existing international space law (the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the Moon Agreement of 1979, etc.) has the following limits: | Dimension of limitation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Resource allocation | The principles for allocating space resources are unclear | | Environmental protection | Provisions for the protection of the space environment are inadequate | | Extension of agents | Does not consider the status of non-human agents | | Enforcement mechanism | Lacks effective enforcement and dispute-resolution mechanisms | Lag Three: The limits of AI governance frameworks Current AI governance frameworks (such as the EU AI Act and national AI ethics guidelines) have the following limits: | Dimension of limitation | Specific content | |----------|----------| | Status of agents | Does not clarify the potential agency status of AI | | Long-term risk | Focuses mainly on near-term risks, with insufficient attention to AGI risk | | International coordination | Lacks effective mechanisms of international coordination | | Value alignment | Addresses the value-alignment problem inadequately | Proposition D.11 (The Structural Lag of Global Governance Frameworks) Contemporary global governance frameworks (the UN system, international space law, AI governance frameworks) lag structurally in meeting the challenges of interstellar civilization. This lag is not merely a matter of speed but a structural limitation of the frameworks themselves. IV. The Insights and Gaps of Complexity Science Complexity science (the Santa Fe Institute tradition, complex adaptive systems theory, and so on) provides important insights for understanding interstellar civilization, but there is also a gap from description to norm. The insights of complexity science: | Dimension of insight | Specific content | Contribution to this work | |----------|----------|----------------| | Emergence | Complex systems exhibit emergent properties | Understanding the emergence of consciousness and agency | | Self-organization | Complex systems can self-organize | Understanding the self-organizing evolution of civilizations | | Adaptivity | Complex adaptive systems can learn and adapt | Understanding the adaptive requirements of governance frameworks | | Criticality | Complex systems may be in a critical state | Understanding the fragility and resilience of civilizations | The gaps of complexity science: | Dimension of gap | Specific content | Response of this work | |----------|----------|--------------| | Normative gap | Complexity science is descriptive and offers no normative guidance | This work establishes normativity through bridge principles | | Value gap | Complexity science does not address value questions | This work develops a generative axiology | | Institutional gap | Complexity science offers no institutional design | This work provides an institutional-design framework | | Operational gap | Complexity science offers no operating guidance | This work provides an indicator system and operating protocols | Proposition D.12 (The Need for a Bridge from Description to Norm) Complexity science provides important descriptive tools for understanding interstellar civilization, but a bridge is needed from description to norm. One of the core tasks of this work is to build this bridge and to translate the insights of complexity science into a normative framework. Formal statement: $$\text{ComplexSystemsScience}(\text{Descriptive}) \xrightarrow{\text{BridgePrinciples}} \text{NormativeFramework}$$

§D.2 The Three Core Puzzles

§D.2.1 Puzzle One: The Cosmic Grounding of Normativity I. The Formulation of the Puzzle The core question of Puzzle One: In a universe governed by physical laws, where does normativity come from? If the universe is merely matter and energy moving according to physical laws, how is an "ought" possible? This puzzle can be decomposed into the following sub-questions: | Sub-question | Specific content | |--------|----------| | The question of source | What is the source of normativity? | | The question of ground | What is the ground of normative judgments? | | The question of binding force | Why does normativity have binding force? | | The question of universality | Are there universal norms across civilizations? | Formal statement: $$\text{Puzzle}_1: \text{PhysicalUniverse} \wedge \text{Normativity} \rightarrow \text{Source}(\text{Normativity}) = ?$$ II. The Predicament of Traditional Answers Answer One: The theological answer Traditional theology traces the source of normativity to God's commands or God's nature. | Advantage | Predicament | |------|------| | Provides a definite source of normativity | Depends on the assumption that God exists | | Explains the binding force of normativity | Faces the "Euthyphro dilemma" | | Provides a basis for universality | Lacks a basis of consensus under plural civilizations | The Euthyphro dilemma: is the good good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? The former makes the good arbitrary; the latter makes God superfluous. Answer Two: The natural-law answer The natural-law tradition (Aristotle, Aquinas, Grotius) roots normativity in the nature of nature or of reason. | Advantage | Predicament | |------|------| | Does not depend on particular religious assumptions | Faces the charge of the "naturalistic fallacy" | | Provides a basis for universality | The meaning of "nature" is unclear under interstellar conditions | | Is connected with reason | The "reason" of non-human agents is of unknown form | Answer Three: The social-contract answer Social-contract theory roots normativity in a (hypothetical) contract among rational agents. | Advantage | Predicament | |------|------| | Does not depend on metaphysical assumptions | Future generations cannot participate in the contract | | Respects the autonomy of agents | The contractual capacity of non-human agents is unknown | | Provides procedural legitimacy | Under deep uncertainty the content of the contract is hard to determine | Answer Four: The utilitarian answer Utilitarianism roots normativity in the maximization of well-being or utility. | Advantage | Predicament | |------|------| | Provides a clear decision criterion | Under deep uncertainty utility is not calculable | | Attends to actual consequences | The utilities of heterogeneous agents are not comparable | | Has the potential for universality | Depends on a contestable concept of utility | Answer Five: The Kantian answer Kantian ethics roots normativity in the self-legislation of reason. | Advantage | Predicament | |------|------| | Respects the autonomy of rational agents | The form of rationality of non-human agents is unknown | | Provides a universalizability test | Cross-civilizational standards of universalization are undetermined | | Does not depend on calculation of consequences | Under deep uncertainty consequences must still be considered | Proposition D.13 (The Common Predicament of Traditional Answers) The traditional theories of the source of normativity (theology, natural law, social contract, utilitarianism, Kantian ethics) all encounter predicaments in the face of interstellar-civilization conditions. The common root of these predicaments is this: all these theories presuppose a particular understanding of agents, rationality and value, and these understandings become uncertain under interstellar-civilization conditions. III. The Direction of This Work's Response The response of this work to Puzzle One rests on the following core insight: Core insight: normativity is not a mysterious force external to the physical universe but a structural requirement internal to the persistence conditions of complex systems. Path of argument:

  1. Premise One (from the New Cosmology, NC): The cosmos is relational, processual and participatory.
  2. Premise Two (from the New View of Life, NL): Life is negentropic organization, and its persistence depends on the capacity to maintain a state far from equilibrium.
  3. Premise Three (from the New View of Cognition, NK): Cognition is participatory construction; the cognitive subject participates in the constitution of the world through cognitive activity.
  4. Bridge principle (BP-1): Any rational agent, if it seeks its own persistence, has reason to maintain the conditions that make its persistence possible.
  5. Conclusion: normativity arises from the persistence conditions of negentropic organization — actions that maintain complexity and preserve the space of possibilities have intrinsic normativity.

Formal statement: $$\text{NC} + \text{NL} + \text{NK} + \text{BP-1} \vdash \text{Normativity} \leftarrow \text{SurvivalConditions}(\text{NegentropyOrganization})$$ Proposition D.14 (The Cosmic Grounding of Normativity) The cosmic grounding of normativity lies in the persistence conditions of negentropic organization. In a universe of increasing entropy, actions that maintain complexity and preserve the space of possibilities have intrinsic normativity, because such actions are necessary conditions for the persistence of any rational agent. This response will be argued in detail in Part One (the Three New Views) and Part Three (the normative principles).

§D.2.2 Puzzle Two: Rationality under Deep Uncertainty I. The Formulation of the Puzzle The core question of Puzzle Two: When consequences cannot be predicted, probabilities cannot be assigned and utilities cannot be determined, how is rational action possible? Traditional models of rational decision-making fail under deep uncertainty; what alternative standards of rationality do we need? This puzzle can be decomposed into the following sub-questions: | Sub-question | Specific content | |--------|----------| | The question of decision criteria | Under deep uncertainty, what is a good decision criterion? | | The question of information | How can decisions be made when information is fundamentally insufficient? | | The question of robustness | How can decisions be made that are reasonable under many possible scenarios? | | The question of revisability | How can decisions be revised when new information appears? | Formal statement: $$\text{Puzzle}_2: \text{DeepUncertainty} \wedge \text{RationalAction} \rightarrow \text{RationalityStandard} = ?$$ II. The Limits of Traditional Models of Rational Decision-Making Model One: Expected Utility Maximization Expected utility maximization is the standard model of rational decision-making: $$\text{EU}(a) = \sum_{s \in S} p(s) \cdot u(a, s)$$ Choose the action that maximizes expected utility: $$a^ = \arg\max_a \text{EU}(a)$$ | Presupposition | Problem under deep uncertainty | |----------|---------------------| | The outcome space $S$ is known | The outcome space may not be fully enumerable | | Probabilities $p(s)$ can be assigned | Probabilities may not be meaningfully assignable | | Utilities $u(a,s)$ are known | The utility function may be unknown or unstable | Model Two: Maximin The maximin strategy chooses the action that makes the worst-case outcome the best: $$a^ = \arg\max_a \min_s u(a, s)$$ | Advantage | Limitation | |------|------| | Does not require probability assignment | Still requires knowledge of the outcome space and utilities | | Provides a conservative strategy | May be excessively conservative | | Applies to adversarial situations | Does not apply to all situations | Model Three: Minimax Regret The minimax-regret strategy chooses the action that minimizes the maximum regret: $$\text{Regret}(a, s) = \max_{a'} u(a', s) - u(a, s)$$ $$a^ = \arg\min_a \max_s \text{Regret}(a, s)$$ | Advantage | Limitation | |------|------| | Takes opportunity costs into account | Still requires knowledge of the outcome space and utilities | | More flexible than maximin | High computational complexity | Model Four: Robust Decision Making (RDM) The robust decision-making method (developed at RAND) attempts to find robust strategies under deep uncertainty: | Advantage | Limitation | |------|------| | Explicitly addresses deep uncertainty | Mainly methodological, lacking a normative foundation | | Uses scenario discovery rather than prediction | Computationally intensive | | Searches for robust strategies | Does not provide a complete standard of rationality | Proposition D.15 (The Structural Limits of Traditional Models of Rational Decision-Making) Traditional models of rational decision-making (expected utility maximization, maximin, minimax regret) face structural limits under deep uncertainty, because they all presuppose some knowledge of the outcome space, of probability assignment or of the utility function, and such knowledge is unavailable under deep uncertainty. III. The Direction of This Work's Response The response of this work to Puzzle Two rests on the following core insight: Core insight: under deep uncertainty, the standard of rationality should shift from "optimization of outcomes" to "preservation of the space of possibilities." Path of argument:

  1. Premise One: Under deep uncertainty we cannot reliably predict the specific consequences of an action.
  2. Premise Two: But we can assess an action's effect on the space of possibilities — whether it expands or compresses that space.
  3. Premise Three: The preservation of the space of possibilities is a precondition of any future choice.
  4. Conclusion: Under deep uncertainty the standard of rationality is to preserve (not compress) the space of possibilities.

Formal statement: $$\text{DeepUncertainty} \rightarrow \neg\text{Reliable}(\text{OutcomePrediction}) \rightarrow \text{RationalityStandard} = \text{PossibilitySpacePreservation}$$ Definition D.8 (Possibility Space) The possibility space is the set of all possible states and trajectories that an agent or system can realize at a given moment. Formal statement: $$\text{PS}(S, t) = \{s \in \mathcal{S} : \text{Reachable}(S, s, t)\}$$ where $S$ is the agent or system, $t$ is time, $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space, and $\text{Reachable}(S, s, t)$ means that state $s$ is reachable for $S$ at time $t$. Definition D.9 (Recursive Freedom Degree, RFD) The Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) is an indicator measuring the effect of an action on the space of possibilities. A positive value indicates expansion of the space of possibilities; a negative value indicates compression. Formal statement: $$\text{RFD}(a) = \frac{|\text{PS}_{after}(a)| - |\text{PS}_{before}|}{|\text{PS}_{before}|}$$ Proposition D.16 (The Standard of Rationality under Deep Uncertainty) Under deep uncertainty, the standard of rational action is: choose actions that preserve or expand the space of possibilities, and avoid actions that irreversibly compress it. Formal statement: $\text{Rational}(a) \leftrightarrow \text{RFD}(a) \geq 0$. This response will be argued in detail in Part Two (the indicator system) and Part Three (the normative principles).

§D.2.3 Puzzle Three: The Attribution of Long-Range Responsibility I. The Formulation of the Puzzle The core question of Puzzle Three: When causal chains extend into the distant future, involve multiple agents and pass through complex intermediary processes, how is responsibility to be attributed? Traditional models of responsibility attribution fail under long-range causal chains; what alternative framework of responsibility do we need? This puzzle can be decomposed into the following sub-questions: | Sub-question | Specific content | |--------|----------| | The causal question | How is responsibility traced through a complex causal network? | | The temporal question | What responsibility is borne for consequences in the distant future? | | The collective question | How is responsibility for collective action distributed? | | The intergenerational question | What responsibilities do present generations owe to future generations? | Formal statement: $$\text{Puzzle}_3: \text{LongCausalChain} \wedge \text{Responsibility} \rightarrow \text{Attribution}(\text{Responsibility}) = ?$$ II. The Limits of Traditional Models of Responsibility Attribution Model One: The direct-causation model Traditional responsibility attribution rests on direct causation: A caused B, therefore A is responsible for B. | Presupposition | Problem under long-range conditions | |----------|------------------| | Causation is direct | Long-range causal chains involve multiple intermediaries | | Causation is traceable | Causation in complex systems is hard to trace | | Agents are identifiable | Individual contributions to collective action are hard to quantify | Model Two: The role-responsibility model The role-responsibility model assigns responsibility to the holders of particular roles. | Advantage | Limitation | |------|------| | Provides a definite allocation of responsibility | Role boundaries are unclear under new conditions | | Is connected with institutional design | Roles for future scenarios are not yet defined | | Facilitates accountability | The problem of role transmission across generations | Model Three: The capacity-responsibility model The capacity-responsibility model ties responsibility to capacity: agents capable of influencing an outcome bear responsibility for it. | Advantage | Limitation | |------|------| | Reflects actual influence | The boundaries of capacity are hard to determine under deep uncertainty | | Avoids impossible demands | The relation between collective capacity and individual responsibility is unclear | | Has intuitive plausibility | The temporal dimension of capacity is insufficiently considered | Model Four: The benefit-responsibility model The benefit-responsibility model ties responsibility to benefit: agents who benefit from an arrangement bear responsibility for its consequences. | Advantage | Limitation | |------|------| | Reflects the relevance of interests | Defining benefit is difficult under long-range conditions | | Provides a principle of allocation | The benefits of future generations are hard to predict | | Is connected with theories of justice | Cross-generational comparison of benefits is difficult | Proposition D.17 (The Structural Limits of Traditional Models of Responsibility Attribution) Traditional models of responsibility attribution (direct causation, role responsibility, capacity responsibility, benefit responsibility) all encounter structural limits in the face of long-range causal chains. The common root of these limits is this: all these models presuppose a relatively simple causal structure, clear boundaries between agents, and a stable temporal framework, and these presuppositions no longer hold under interstellar-civilization conditions. III. The Direction of This Work's Response The response of this work to Puzzle Three rests on the following core insight: Core insight: responsibility is not a static attribution but a dynamic vector, with three dimensions — spatial scope, temporal depth and reversibility. Path of argument:

  1. Premise One: In a complex causal network, responsibility cannot simply be attributed to a single agent.
  2. Premise Two: Responsibility has a temporal dimension — responsibility for future consequences of a present action decays over time but never reaches zero.
  3. Premise Three: Responsibility is related to reversibility — responsibility for irreversible action weighs more than for reversible action.
  4. Conclusion: Responsibility should be understood as a vector comprising three dimensions: spatial scope (the range of affected agents), temporal depth (the span of time affected) and reversibility (the degree to which the consequences can be reversed).

Formal statement: $$\text{Responsibility}(a) = \text{CRV}(a) = \langle \text{SpatialScope}(a), \text{TemporalDepth}(a), \text{Reversibility}(a) \rangle$$ Definition D.10 (Commitment Reversibility Verifiability, CRV) Commitment Reversibility Verifiability (CRV) is a three-dimensional vector used to characterize the responsibility structure of an action: The three key aspects of a commitment: observability, enforceability and rollback-ability. Formal statement: $$\text{CRV}: \mathcal{C} \rightarrow [0, 1]^3$$ where:

  • $V_{\text{obs}}$: Observability
  • $V_{\text{enf}}$: Enforceability
  • $V_{\text{rev}}$: Reversibility

A dynamic model of responsibility attribution: Responsibility is not attributed once and for all but is dynamically adjusted as time and information change: $$\text{CRV}(a, t_2) = f(\text{CRV}(a, t_1), \text{NewInfo}(t_1, t_2), \text{IntermediateActions}(t_1, t_2))$$ Proposition D.18 (The Dynamic Attribution of Long-Range Responsibility) In long-range causal chains, responsibility should be understood as a dynamic vector rather than a static attribution. The magnitude and allocation of responsibility adjust with changes in time, information and intermediate actions. This dynamic model can handle complex responsibility situations that traditional models cannot. This response will be argued in detail in Part Two (the indicator system, especially CRV in Chapter 8) and Part Three (the normative principles, especially the Negentropy Responsibility Principle).

§D.2.4 The Internal Connections among the Three Puzzles I. The Logical Connections among the Puzzles The three puzzles are not independent of one another but are connected by deep logical relations: Connection One: Normativity and rationality Puzzle One (the cosmic grounding of normativity) and Puzzle Two (rationality under deep uncertainty) are related in both directions: | Direction | Content of the connection | |------|----------| | Normativity → rationality | Normativity defines the goal of rationality: rational action is action pursuing an "ought" | | Rationality → normativity | Rationality is the epistemic condition of normativity: only rational agents can recognize and follow norms | Formal statement: $$\text{Normativity} \leftrightarrow \text{Rationality}: \text{Normativity} \xrightarrow{\text{defines goal}} \text{Rationality} \wedge \text{Rationality} \xrightarrow{\text{enables}} \text{Normativity}$$ Connection Two: Rationality and responsibility Puzzle Two (rationality under deep uncertainty) and Puzzle Three (the attribution of long-range responsibility) are related in both directions: | Direction | Content of the connection | |------|----------| | Rationality → responsibility | Rationality is the precondition of responsibility: only agents capable of rational action can bear responsibility | | Responsibility → rationality | Responsibility constrains rationality: rational action must consider the consequences of responsibility | Formal statement: $$\text{Rationality} \leftrightarrow \text{Responsibility}: \text{Rationality} \xrightarrow{\text{enables}} \text{Responsibility} \wedge \text{Responsibility} \xrightarrow{\text{constrains}} \text{Rationality}$$ Connection Three: Responsibility and normativity Puzzle Three (the attribution of long-range responsibility) and Puzzle One (the cosmic grounding of normativity) are related in both directions: | Direction | Content of the connection | |------|----------| | Responsibility → normativity | Responsibility is the core content of normativity: one of the core questions of normativity is "to whom do we owe what?" | | Normativity → responsibility | Normativity defines the boundaries of responsibility: what counts as responsibility is decided by the normative framework | Formal statement: $$\text{Responsibility} \leftrightarrow \text{Normativity}: \text{Responsibility} \xrightarrow{\text{constitutes}} \text{Normativity} \wedge \text{Normativity} \xrightarrow{\text{defines}} \text{Responsibility}$$ II. The Entangled Structure of the Three Puzzles The three puzzles form a mutually entangled structure:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                The entangled structure of the three puzzles      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│                Puzzle One: The grounding of normativity          │
│                Where does the "ought" come from?                 │
│                           ↑↓                                    │
│              ┌────────────┴────────────┐                       │
│              │   defines goal / enables │                      │
│              ↓                         ↓                        │
│    Puzzle Two: Rationality under deep uncertainty ←────→ Puzzle Three: Long-range responsibility │
│    How to act rationally?        enables/constrains     How is responsibility attributed? │
│                                                                 │
│    【Entanglement effect】                                       │
│    - Without solving the normative problem, the goal of rationality cannot be defined │
│    - Without solving the problem of rationality, responsibility cannot be borne │
│    - Without solving the problem of responsibility, the content of normativity cannot be determined │
│    - The three problems must be solved together; partial solutions are unstable │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Proposition D.19 (The Entanglement of the Three Puzzles) The three puzzles (the cosmic grounding of normativity, rationality under deep uncertainty, the attribution of long-range responsibility) are mutually entangled. Any attempt to solve one of them in isolation will be incomplete, because the solution of each puzzle depends on the solution of the others. What is needed is a unified framework capable of responding to all three at once. Formal statement: $$\text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_1) \leftrightarrow \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_2) \leftrightarrow \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_3)$$ $$\text{Complete}(\text{Solution}) \leftrightarrow \text{Unified}(\text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_1), \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_2), \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_3))$$ III. The Three New Views as a Unified Response The core claim of this work is that the Three New Views (the New Cosmology, NC; the New View of Life, NL; the New View of Cognition, NK) provide a unified framework capable of responding to all three puzzles at once. Table D.1 The unified response of the Three New Views to the three puzzles | Puzzle | Core question | Response of the Three New Views | Mechanism of response | |------|----------|--------------|----------| | Puzzle One | Where does normativity come from? | Normativity arises from the persistence conditions of negentropic organization | NC (participatory cosmos) + NL (negentropic persistence) + BP-1 (rationality of persistence) | | Puzzle Two | How to be rational under deep uncertainty? | The standard of rationality is preservation of the space of possibilities | NK (participatory cognition) + the RFD indicator | | Puzzle Three | How is long-range responsibility attributed? | Responsibility is a dynamic vector proportional to capacity and influence | NL (graded agency) + the CRV indicator | The logical structure of the unified response:

Proposition D.20 (The Unity of the Three New Views) The Three New Views (NC, NL, NK) are not three independent theories but three dimensions of a single unified framework. Together they provide the ontological, biological and epistemological foundations needed to respond to the three puzzles. This unity enables this work to avoid the one-sidedness of traditional approaches. Formal statement: $$\text{NewThreeViews} = \text{NC} \otimes \text{NL} \otimes \text{NK}$$ $$\text{NewThreeViews} \vdash \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_1) \wedge \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_2) \wedge \text{Solution}(\text{Puzzle}_3)$$ where $\otimes$ denotes the integration (not mere juxtaposition) of the three perspectives.

§D.3 Theoretical Preview: The Outline of the Answers

§D.3.1 Preview of the Three New Views I. Preview of the New Cosmology (NC) Definition D.11 (The New Cosmology) The New Cosmological View (NC) is an ontological position holding that the basic structure of the cosmos is relational, processual and participatory. The three core propositions of the New Cosmology: | Proposition | Name | Content | |----------|----------|----------| | NC-1 | The relationality proposition | Relations precede entities: the properties of an entity are relational and determined by its relations with other entities | | NC-2 | The processuality proposition | Process precedes state: the basic mode of existence is process, not static state | | NC-3 | The participatory proposition | Participation precedes observation: the observer/agent participates in the construction of reality rather than merely observing it | Formal statement: $$\text{NC-1}: \forall e \in E, \text{Properties}(e) = f(\text{Relations}(e))$$ $$\text{NC-2}: \forall e \in E, \text{State}(e, t) = g(\text{Process}(e, t-\Delta t, t))$$ $$\text{NC-3}: \forall o \in O, \exists e \in E: \text{Observe}(o, e) \rightarrow \text{Modify}(o, e)$$ The relation between the New Cosmology and the old cosmology: | Dimension | Old cosmology | New Cosmology | Relation | |------|----------|----------|------| | Basic unit | Independent entities | Networks of relations | Dimensional extension | | Basic mode | Static states | Dynamic processes | Dimensional extension | | Role of the observer | Spectator | Participant | Dimensional extension | The contribution of the New Cosmology to Puzzle One: The New Cosmology provides the ontological basis for the normative problem. In a participatory cosmos, agents are not spectators external to the world but participating co-constructors of it. This means that agents bear responsibility for the world they co-construct — normativity is not externally imposed but internal to the structure of participatory existence. II. Preview of the New View of Life (NL) Definition D.12 (The New View of Life) The New View of Life (NL) is a position on the nature of life holding that life is a cross-substrate, graded phenomenon whose persistence depends on a negentropic flow. The three core propositions of the New View of Life: | Proposition | Name | Content | |----------|----------|----------| | NL-1 | The cross-substrate proposition | Life is not limited to carbon-based organisms but is a functional organization realizable on many substrates | | NL-2 | The negentropic-persistence proposition | The essence of life is the maintenance of negentropic organization far from equilibrium, whose persistence depends on a continuous negentropic flow | | NL-3 | The graded proposition | Life, consciousness and agency are not all-or-nothing but a graded continuum | Formal statement: $$\text{NL-1}: \text{Life}(x) \leftrightarrow \text{FunctionalOrganization}(x) \wedge \neg\text{SubstrateDependence}(x)$$ $$\text{NL-2}: \text{Life}(x) \rightarrow \text{NegEntropyFlow}(x) > 0$$ $$\text{NL-3}: \text{Consciousness}: E \rightarrow [0, 1] \text{ (continuous function)}$$ The relation between the New View of Life and the old view of life: | Dimension | Old view of life | New View of Life | Relation | |------|----------|----------|------| | Substrate | Carbon-based restriction | Cross-substrate | Dimensional extension | | Essence | Replication/metabolism | Negentropic organization | Dimensional extension | | Boundary | Binary (living/non-living) | Continuum | Dimensional extension | The contribution of the New View of Life to Puzzle Three: The New View of Life provides the basis in a view of life for the problem of responsibility attribution. A graded view of agency means that responsibility is also graded — different degrees of agency correspond to different degrees of responsibility. The negentropic-persistence view means that responsibility is related to the capacity to maintain negentropic organization — agents capable of influencing a negentropic flow bear a corresponding responsibility. III. Preview of the New View of Cognition (NK) Definition D.13 (The New View of Cognition) The New View of Cognition (NK) is an epistemological position holding that cognition is participatory construction, that knowledge is a social achievement, that cognition has a normative dimension, and that standards of cognition are negotiable. The four core propositions of the New View of Cognition: | Proposition | Name | Content | |----------|----------|----------| | NK-1 | The participatory-cognition proposition | Cognition is not a passive reflection of an external world but an active, interactive construction by the subject with the world | | NK-2 | The social-knowledge proposition | Knowledge is not the private property of an individual mind but a social achievement of an epistemic community | | NK-3 | The cognitive-normativity proposition | Cognitive activity has an intrinsic normative dimension: the knower is committed to norms of truth, evidence and consistency | | NK-4 | The negotiability proposition | Standards of cognition are not fixed but can be negotiated and revised within the epistemic community | Formal statement: $$\text{NK-1}: \text{Know}(s, p) \rightarrow \text{Participate}(s, p)$$ $$\text{NK-2}: \text{Knowledge}(p) \rightarrow \text{SocialValidation}(p)$$ $$\text{NK-3}: \text{Cognition}(s) \rightarrow \text{NormativeCommitment}(s)$$ $$\text{NK-4}: \forall \text{standard} \in S, \text{Negotiable}(\text{standard})$$ The relation between the New View of Cognition and the old view of cognition: | Dimension | Old view of cognition | New View of Cognition | Relation | |------|----------|----------|------| | Mode of cognition | Passive reflection | Active construction | Dimensional extension | | Ownership of knowledge | Individual, private | Socially shared | Dimensional extension | | Cognitive norms | External constraint | Internal commitment | Dimensional extension | | Nature of standards | Fixed | Negotiable | Dimensional extension | The contribution of the New View of Cognition to Puzzle Two: The New View of Cognition provides the epistemic basis for the problem of rationality under deep uncertainty. Participatory cognition means that the knower does not passively receive information but actively constructs understanding — this provides a basis for acting rationally even when information is insufficient. Negotiability means that standards of rationality are themselves revisable — this provides room for adjusting standards of rationality under new conditions. IV. The Unity of the Three New Views The Three New Views are not three independent theories but three dimensions of a single unified framework:

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Proposition D.21 (The Intrinsic Unity of the Three New Views) The Three New Views (NC, NL, NK) share four core themes: relationality over entity-hood, processuality over state-hood, participation over observation, and gradation over binarity. These four themes find different expressions at the three levels of ontology (NC), the view of life (NL) and epistemology (NK), but they are different dimensions of one and the same unified framework.

§D.3.2 Preview of the Normative Principles I. The Bridge from the Three New Views to the Normative Principles The Three New Views are a descriptive framework; the normative principles are normative claims. A "bridge principle" is needed to move from the former to the latter. Definition D.14 (Bridge Principle) Bridge principles are intermediary principles connecting descriptive and normative propositions. They contain a minimal normative assumption about rational agents, which makes the transition from description to norm possible. This work proposes three bridge principles: | Bridge principle | Content | Level connected | |----------|------|------------| | BP-1 (the principle of rational persistence) | Any rational agent, if it seeks its own persistence, has reason to maintain the conditions that make its persistence possible | NC/NL → PRF/PNR | | BP-2 (the principle of epistemic humility) | Any rational agent, if it acknowledges the finitude of its own cognition, has reason to keep the space of possibilities open | NK → PRF/PR | | BP-3 (the principle of intersubjectivity) | Any rational agent, if it acknowledges the existence of other agents, has reason to consider the impact of its action on them | NC/NL/NK → PNR | Formal statement: $$\text{BP-1}: \text{RationalAgent}(A) \wedge \text{SeeksSurvival}(A) \rightarrow \text{HasReason}(A, \text{MaintainSurvivalConditions})$$ $$\text{BP-2}: \text{RationalAgent}(A) \wedge \text{AcknowledgesLimitation}(A) \rightarrow \text{HasReason}(A, \text{PreservePossibilitySpace})$$ $$\text{BP-3}: \text{RationalAgent}(A) \wedge \text{AcknowledgesOthers}(A) \rightarrow \text{HasReason}(A, \text{ConsiderImpactOnOthers})$$ II. The Three Normative Principles Through the bridge principles, this work derives three normative principles from the Three New Views: Principle One: The Principle of Recursive Freedom (PRF) Definition D.15 (The Principle of Recursive Freedom) The Principle of Recursive Freedom holds that the action of any agent should protect (rather than compress) the space of possibilities for meaningful choice of all affected agents, including possible future agents. Formal statement: $$\text{PRF}: \forall A, \forall a: \text{Permissible}(a) \rightarrow \neg\text{Compress}(a, \text{PS}_{\text{affected}})$$ where $\text{PS}_{\text{affected}}$ is the space of possibilities of all affected agents. Principle Two: The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (PNR) Definition D.16 (The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility) The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility holds that any agent that benefits from a negentropic organization bears a corresponding responsibility for maintaining the conditions of its persistence. The magnitude of responsibility is proportional to the degree of benefit and the capacity to influence. Formal statement: $$\text{PNR}: \forall A: \text{Benefit}(A, N) \rightarrow \text{Responsibility}(A, \text{Maintain}(N))$$ $$\text{Responsibility}(A) \propto \text{Benefit}(A) \times \text{Capability}(A)$$ where $N$ is the negentropic organization and $\text{Benefit}(A, N)$ denotes that agent $A$ benefits from the negentropic organization $N$. Principle Three: The Principle of Reversibility (PR) Definition D.17 (The Principle of Reversibility) The Principle of Reversibility holds that under conditions of deep uncertainty, reversible actions should be preferred to irreversible ones. Irreversible actions require a higher threshold of justification. Formal statement: $$\text{PR}: \text{DeepUncertainty} \rightarrow \text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a)) \text{ over } \text{Prefer}(\text{Irreversible}(a))$$ $$\text{Irreversible}(a) \rightarrow \text{HigherJustificationThreshold}(a)$$ III. The Integrative Relation among the Three Principles The three normative principles are not independent of one another but mutually supportive and mutually constraining:

Proposition D.22 (The Complementarity of the Three Principles) The Principle of Recursive Freedom (PRF), the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (PNR) and the Principle of Reversibility (PR) are complementary. PRF provides the core criterion for evaluating action (preserve the space of possibilities), PNR provides the basis of responsibility attribution (maintain negentropic organization), and PR provides the decision strategy under deep uncertainty (prefer reversible action). Together they constitute the normative core of cosmic responsibility ethics. IV. Forbidden Red Lines (FRL) Besides the three positive principles, this work also sets out forbidden red lines — boundaries that must absolutely not be crossed. Definition D.18 (Forbidden Red Lines) Forbidden red lines (FRL) are boundaries of action that must not be crossed under any circumstances. Actions that cross a forbidden red line are absolutely prohibited and admit no weighing or exception. Preliminary list of forbidden red lines: | No. | Content | Reason | |----------|----------|------| | FRL-1 | The deliberate extinction of any species or civilization possessing agency is forbidden | It irreversibly eliminates an entire space of possibilities | | FRL-2 | The irreversible deprivation of an agent's core cognitive capacities is forbidden | It eliminates the basis of agency | | FRL-3 | Unilateral irreversible decisions affecting all of humanity or an entire civilization are forbidden | It violates the principle of intersubjectivity | | FRL-4 | The deliberate creation of an existential risk that cannot be shut down is forbidden | It threatens all future possibilities | Formal statement: $$\text{FRL}: \forall a \in \text{FRL}: \neg\text{Permissible}(a) \text{ (no exceptions)}$$ Proposition D.23 (The Absoluteness of the Forbidden Red Lines) Forbidden red lines are absolute and admit no utilitarian weighing. Even if crossing a red line might bring huge expected benefit, that cannot justify the crossing. This position rests on the following reasons: (1) under deep uncertainty the calculation of expected benefit is unreliable; (2) some harms are irreversible and cannot be compensated by later benefits; (3) the forbidden red lines protect the space of possibilities itself, not particular possibilities.

Preview of the Protocol Stack This work adopts a "protocol stack" methodological framework, organizing the theoretical system into a layered structure. Definition D.19 (Protocol Stack) A protocol stack is a layered way of organizing theory, borrowed from the TCP/IP protocol stack of computer networks. Each layer builds on the layer below, provides services to the layer above, and hides the implementation details of its own layer. The protocol-stack structure of this work:

Design principles of the protocol stack: | Principle | Content | Function | |------|------|------| | Layer independence | Each layer has independent functions and interfaces | Facilitates layer-by-layer revision | | Downward dependence | Upper layers depend on lower layers, not vice versa | Ensures the stability of the foundation | | Clear interfaces | Interfaces between layers are clearly defined | Facilitates understanding and modification | | Replaceability | The content of a layer can be replaced without affecting other layers | Increases flexibility | Proposition D.24 (The Methodological Value of the Protocol Stack) The protocol-stack methodology provides this work with a clear organizational structure. It makes it possible: (1) for the content of different layers to be discussed and revised independently; (2) for the dependencies between layers to be clearly visible; (3) for readers to choose the layer they wish to attend to according to their needs; (4) for future extensions and revisions to have a definite place.

II. The Overall Structure of the Chain of Argument The argument of this work follows this overall structure: Chain of argument One: From physical constraints to the Three New Views $$\text{L}_0(\text{physical constraints}) \xrightarrow{\text{explanation}} \text{L}_1(\text{the Three New Views})$$ Specific path:

  • The second law of thermodynamics → the special character of negentropic organization → the New View of Life (NL)
  • The observer effect in quantum mechanics → the participatory cosmos → the New Cosmology (NC)
  • The emergence of complex systems → the constructive character of cognition → the New View of Cognition (NK)

Chain of argument Two: From the Three New Views to the normative principles $$\text{L}_1(\text{the Three New Views}) + \text{BP}(\text{bridge principles}) \xrightarrow{\text{derivation}} \text{L}_2(\text{normative principles})$$ Specific path:

  • NC + NL + BP-1 → the Recursive Freedom Principle (PRF)
  • NL + BP-1 + BP-3 → the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR)
  • NK + BP-2 → the Reversibility Principle (PR)

Chain of argument Three: From the normative principles to institutional design $$\text{L}_2(\text{normative principles}) \xrightarrow{\text{institutionalization}} \text{L}_3(\text{institutional design})$$ Specific path:

  • PRF + PNR → the multi-agent adjudication chamber
  • PR + PNR → the cosmic-level IRB
  • PRF + PNR → intergenerational trust

Chain of argument Four: From institutional design to operating procedures $$\text{L}_3(\text{institutional design}) \xrightarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{L}_4(\text{operating procedures})$$ Specific path:

  • The need for determination of agency → the UCS indicator
  • The need for action assessment → the RFD and CRV indicators
  • The need for system assessment → the CDI, MBCL and CSIA indicators

III. The Permeating Role of the Three New Views The Three New Views are not only the theoretical foundation of this work but permeate every part of the work: Table D.4 The permeation of the Three New Views across the parts | Part | Permeation of NC | Permeation of NL | Permeation of NK | |------|----------|----------|----------| | Part One (the Three New Views) | Direct argument | Direct argument | Direct argument | | Part Two (the indicator system) | Design of relational indicators | UCS based on NL-3 | CRV based on NK-4 | | Part Three (the normative principles) | PRF based on NC-3 | PNR based on NL-2 | PR based on NK-4 | | Part Four (institutional design) | Relational institutional design | Institutions for maintaining negentropy | Institutions of epistemic humility | | Part Five (stress testing) | Participatory test design | Testing of the view of life | Cognitive testing | Proposition D.25 (The Permeation of the Three New Views) The Three New Views (NC, NL, NK) are the "red thread" of this work, running through every part of it. This permeation ensures the internal consistency of this work and enables readers to enter at any part and still feel the unified framework of the Three New Views. IV. The Innovations of This Work The main innovations of this work relative to the existing literature: | Dimension of innovation | Content of innovation | Breakthrough relative to the existing literature | |----------|----------|----------------------| | Ontological innovation | The New Cosmology (NC) | Transcends substance ontology; establishes a relational-process ontology | | Innovation in the view of life | The New View of Life (NL) | Transcends the carbon-based view of life; establishes a cross-substrate negentropic view of life | | Epistemological innovation | The New View of Cognition (NK) | Transcends representationalism; establishes a participatory view of cognition | | Normative innovation | The three normative principles | Transcends anthropocentric ethics; establishes cosmic responsibility ethics | | Methodological innovation | The protocol-stack methodology | Provides a layered way of organizing theory | | Operational innovation | Six core indicators | Translates abstract principles into operable tools | | Institutional innovation | Institutional-design prototypes | Provides an institutional blueprint for the governance of interstellar civilization |
