III. The Core Tasks of This Chapter This chapter undertakes four core tasks: Task 1: Diagnose the structural limitations of the traditional view of life

  • Why does carbon-centrism fail in the interstellar-civilization context?
  • Why can the life/non-life dichotomy not handle boundary cases?
  • Why is consciousness dualism incompatible with contemporary science?

Task 2: Establish the scientific basis of the New View of Life

  • How does thermodynamics define the conditions for the persistence of life?
  • How does information theory characterize the organizational features of life?
  • How does complex-systems science understand the emergence of life?
  • What insight do contemporary advances in consciousness science provide?

Task 3: Argue for the three core propositions of the New View of Life

  • NL-1: Cross-substrate life — life is not limited to carbon-based forms
  • NL-2: The negentropy persistence condition — life takes negentropy flow as its condition of persistence
  • NL-3: The continuum of consciousness — consciousness is a graded continuum

Task 4: Clarify the normative implications of the New View of Life

  • How does cross-substrate status lead to an expansion of subjecthood?
  • How does the negentropy condition lead to resource responsibility?
  • How does the continuum lead to graded moral status?

IV. The Deliverables of This Chapter After completing this chapter, the reader will have:

  • Formal definitions of the three core propositions (NL-1, NL-2, NL-3)
  • A systematic comparison of the New View of Life with the traditional view of life
  • The scientific basis of the New View of Life and its boundary statements
  • The positioning of the New View of Life in relation to the main theories of consciousness
  • A preliminary exposition of the normative implications of the New View of Life
  • The conceptual basis of the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale)

V. The Continuity with Chapter 1 This chapter builds on the New Cosmology of Chapter 1: NC-1 (relationality) → life is an emergent process within a network of relations NC-2 (process) → life is a continuous process of negentropy maintenance NC-3 (participation) → life participates in constructing the environment it inhabits VI. Methodological Notes This chapter follows the methodological commitments established in Chapter 0:

  1. The empirical core is left untouched: this chapter does not challenge the empirical findings of biology, thermodynamics, or consciousness science, but conducts philosophical analysis only at the conceptual level.
  2. Structural use rather than conceptual hijacking: this chapter borrows the formal structures of thermodynamics and information theory for analogy, but explicitly declares the boundaries of that borrowing.
  3. The interdisciplinary bridge is defeasible: the scientific analogies in this chapter can be deleted or replaced while preserving the core argument.

VII. Reading Suggestions Readers with a philosophical background: focus on §2.3 (core propositions) and §2.4 (theories of consciousness). Readers with a scientific background: focus on §2.2 (scientific basis) and §2.2.5 (boundary statements). Readers with a policy background: focus on §2.5 (normative implications) and the chapter summary. Readers seeking a quick overview: read the chapter opening guide, §2.3.4 (formalized statement), and the chapter summary. Estimated reading time: about 3–4 hours for a complete reading.

§2.1 The Limitations of the Traditional View of Life

§2.1.1 The Problem of Carbon-Centrism I. The Basic Structure of Carbon-Centrism All known life on Earth is carbon-based. Carbon atoms can form four covalent bonds, which enables carbon to build complex organic molecules — from simple methane to complex DNA. This fact has led to a deeply entrenched assumption: that life is necessarily carbon-based. Definition 2.1 (Carbon-Centrism) Carbon chauvinism is a position about the nature of life that maintains: (1) Life is necessarily carbon-based; (2) Carbon-based chemistry is a necessary condition for life; (3) Non-carbon-based "life" is not genuine life. The term was introduced by the astronomer Carl Sagan to criticize the tendency to improperly universalize the features of terrestrial life. Carbon-centrism has deep roots in biology and astrobiology: | Type of argument | Specific argument | Reason for supporting carbon-centrism | |----------|----------|------------------------| | Chemical argument | Carbon's bonding capacity | Carbon can form four covalent bonds and build complex molecules | | Solvent argument | Water as solvent | Water's special properties suit carbon-based biochemical reactions | | Empirical argument | The universality of terrestrial life | All known life is carbon-based | | Energetic argument | The efficiency of carbon-based metabolism | Carbon-based metabolism is efficient under terrestrial conditions | II. The Internal Difficulties of Carbon-Centrism Carbon-centrism faces several internal conceptual difficulties, which become especially acute in the interstellar-civilization context. Difficulty 1: The Narrowness of the Inductive Base The empirical basis of carbon-centrism is confined to terrestrial life. Earth is a case with a sample size of 1. Generalizing a universal conclusion from a single case is methodologically suspect. Formalized statement: Let $L_{\text{Earth}}$ be the set of terrestrial life and $L_{\text{Universe}}$ the set of all possible life in the universe. $$\text{Carbon-Chauvinism}: L_{\text{Earth}} \subseteq \text{Carbon-based} \Rightarrow L_{\text{Universe}} \subseteq \text{Carbon-based}$$ The validity of this inference depends on an unproven assumption: that terrestrial life is a representative sample of cosmic life. Yet Earth's special conditions (temperature, pressure, chemical composition) may give carbon-based life a selective advantage on Earth, which does not mean that carbon is a universal necessary condition for life. Difficulty 2: The Confusion of Function and Substrate Carbon-centrism conflates the functional features of life with their material realization. The core features of life — self-maintenance, self-replication, adaptive evolution — are functional descriptions, not material ones. Take computation as an analogy: computation is a function that can be realized by different material substrates — mechanical gears, electronic circuits, quantum bits. We would not say that "genuine computation must be electronic." Likewise, life, as a functional organization, can in principle be realized by different material substrates. Proposition 2.1 (The distinction between function and substrate) The core features of life (self-maintenance, self-replication, adaptive evolution, information processing) are functional, not material. Functions can be realized by different material substrates. Therefore, identifying life with a particular material substrate (carbon) is a category error. Formalized statement: Let $F$ be a set of functions, $S$ a set of substrates, and $R$ a realization relation. $$\text{Multiple-Realizability}: \forall f \in F_{\text{life}}, \exists s_1, s_2 \in S: R(f, s_1) \wedge R(f, s_2) \wedge s_1 \neq s_2$$ This means that the functional features of life can be realized by many different substrates. Difficulty 3: The Circularity of the Definition Carbon-centrism often falls into a circular definition: it first defines life as carbon-based, then uses that definition to exclude non-carbon-based candidates. This circularity makes carbon-centrism an unfalsifiable position. If we discovered a non-carbon-based system exhibiting all the functional features of life — self-maintenance, self-replication, adaptive evolution — the carbon-centrist would say, "This is not genuine life, because it is not carbon-based." But this response is circular: it presupposes that carbon is a defining feature of life, which is precisely what needs to be argued. III. The Failure of Carbon-Centrism in the Interstellar-Civilization Context Failure 1: The Possibility of Extraterrestrial Life Research in astrobiology shows that many environments in the universe could support life, many of them radically different from Earth's conditions: | Environment type | Representative body | Possible biochemical basis | Difference from Earth | |----------|----------|----------------|--------------| | Low-temperature liquid methane | Titan | Silicon- or nitrogen-based | Temperature −180°C, no liquid water | | High temperature and pressure | Venus's clouds | Sulfur-based | Temperature 450°C, sulfuric-acid clouds | | Subsurface oceans | Europa, Enceladus | Carbon-based or other | No sunlight, high pressure | | Plasma environment | Stellar atmospheres | Plasma structures | Extreme high temperature | If life could exist in these extreme environments, it would likely not be carbon-based. Carbon-centrism would create systematic blind spots in our search for extraterrestrial life. Failure 2: The Challenge of Artificial Life and AI Research on artificial life and the development of artificial intelligence pose a direct challenge to carbon-centrism:

  • Computer-simulated "digital life" exhibits features of life such as self-replication, evolution, and adaptation
  • Advanced AI systems exhibit features such as information processing, learning, and goal-directed behavior
  • Future AI may develop self-awareness and subjectivity

If we insist on carbon-centrism, we will be unable to properly assess the moral status of these systems. Failure 3: The Possibility of the Posthuman Human-enhancement technologies and the possibility of mind uploading pose another challenge to carbon-centrism:

  • Brain-computer interfaces may gradually replace biological neurons with non-biological components
  • Mind uploading may transfer human consciousness to a non-carbon substrate
  • Genetic engineering may create life forms using non-standard biochemistry

If a person's neurons were gradually replaced by functionally equivalent silicon components, at what moment would he or she cease to be "life"? Carbon-centrism cannot give a satisfactory answer. Proposition 2.2 (The interstellar-civilization limitation of carbon-centrism) Carbon-centrism faces structural failure in the interstellar-civilization context: the diverse possibilities of extraterrestrial life, the challenge of artificial life and AI, and the possibility of the posthuman all conflict with its core assumptions. The governance of interstellar civilization requires a view of life that does not presuppose a particular material substrate.

§2.1.2 The Problem of the Life/Non-Life Dichotomy I. The Basic Structure of the Dichotomy The traditional view of life assumes that there is a clear boundary between life and non-life: a system is either alive or not alive, with no intermediate state. Definition 2.2 (The Life/Non-Life Dichotomy) The life/non-life dichotomy is a position about the nature of life that maintains: (1) Life and non-life are mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories; (2) Any system is either entirely alive or entirely not alive; (3) There is no "partly alive" or "graded life." Formalized statement: Let $U$ be the set of all systems and $L$ the set of living systems. $$\text{Dichotomy}: \forall x \in U, x \in L \veebar x \in \overline{L}$$ where $\veebar$ denotes exclusive or and $\overline{L}$ denotes the complement of $L$. II. The Internal Difficulties of the Dichotomy Difficulty 1: The Existence of Boundary Cases Biological research has revealed a large number of cases on the boundary between life and non-life: | Boundary case | Features of life | Features of non-life | Difficulty of classification | |----------|----------|------------|----------| | Viruses | Genetic information, evolution | No metabolism, require a host to replicate | Are they alive? | | Viroids | Replicable RNA | No protein coat | Simpler than viruses | | Prions | Can "replicate," can be infectious | Merely protein | No nucleic acid | | Dormant spores | Can resume activity | No metabolic activity | Are they alive while dormant? | | Frozen embryos | Can develop into life | No metabolic activity | Are they alive while frozen? | These boundary cases show that there is no clear boundary between life and non-life, but rather a continuous transitional zone. Difficulty 2: The Gradedness of the Features of Life The features traditionally used to define life — metabolism, self-replication, adaptation — are themselves graded: | Feature of life | Graded manifestation | |----------|------------| | Metabolism | From simple chemical reactions to complex metabolic networks | | Self-replication | From crystal growth to DNA replication | | Adaptation | From simple chemical equilibrium to complex learning | | Information storage | From simple molecular structures to complex genomes | If the features defining life are themselves graded, then life itself should also be graded. Proposition 2.3 (The gradedness of the features of life) The features traditionally used to define life (metabolism, self-replication, adaptation, information storage) are all graded, not all-or-nothing. Therefore, life itself should also be understood as graded, not binary. Formalized statement: Let $f_1, f_2, ..., f_n$ be the defining features of life, each feature $f_i: U \rightarrow [0, 1]$ a function from systems to the interval $[0, 1]$. $$\text{Life-Degree}(x) = g(f_1(x), f_2(x), ..., f_n(x))$$ where $g$ is some aggregation function. The degree of life is a continuous value, not a binary value. Difficulty 3: The Challenge of Evolutionary Continuity The evolutionary history of life shows that the transition from non-life to life was gradual, not abrupt:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    The continuity of the origin of life                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Simple molecules → Complex organics → Autocatalytic nets → Protocells → Cellular life │
│     │           │              │            │          │       │
│     ▼           ▼              ▼            ▼          ▼       │
│  Non-life    Non-life?       Boundary?    Boundary?    Life    │
│                                                                 │
│  On this continuum, the precise moment at which "life begins"   │
│  cannot be determined.                                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

If life gradually evolved from non-life, then marking a precise moment of "the beginning of life" on the evolutionary continuum is arbitrary. III. The Failure of the Dichotomy in the Interstellar-Civilization Context Failure 1: The Classification Difficulty of AI Systems Contemporary AI systems and possible future AGI (artificial general intelligence) pose a direct challenge to the dichotomy: | Stage of AI development | Features of life | Difficulty of classification | |------------|----------|----------| | Current AI | Information processing, learning | Does it have any feature of life? | | Future AGI | Autonomy, goal-directedness | Is it "life"? | | Hypothetical ASI | Self-awareness, creativity | How does it compare with biological life? | The dichotomy forces us to choose between "AI is life" and "AI is not life," but this choice may be misleading. Failure 2: The Classification Difficulty of Collective Intelligence Some biological systems exhibit collective intelligence, in which the relation between individual and collective blurs the boundary of life:

  • Ant colonies: the behavior of a single ant is simple, yet the colony as a whole exhibits complex intelligent behavior
  • Slime molds: single-celled organisms can aggregate into multicellular structures exhibiting problem-solving ability
  • Coral reefs: ecosystems composed of countless individuals, with holistic functions

In these cases, what is the unit of "life"? The individual or the collective? The dichotomy cannot give a satisfactory answer. Failure 3: The Classification Difficulty of Hybrid Systems Possible future hybrid systems — the fusion of biology and machine — pose a fundamental challenge to the dichotomy:

  • Brain-computer interfaces: the fusion of biological neurons and electronic circuits
  • Biological computers: computing systems using biological components
  • Cyborgs: the deep fusion of the biological and the mechanical

These hybrid systems are neither purely alive nor purely non-living, but occupy a position on the continuum. Proposition 2.4 (The interstellar-civilization limitation of the dichotomy) The life/non-life dichotomy faces structural failure in the interstellar-civilization context: the classification difficulty of AI systems, the blurred boundaries of collective intelligence, and the emergence of hybrid systems all conflict with its core assumptions. The governance of interstellar civilization requires a graded view of life.

§2.1.3 The Problem of Consciousness Dualism I. The Basic Structure of Consciousness Dualism The traditional view often assumes that there is a clear boundary between consciousness and non-consciousness: a system is either conscious or not conscious. Definition 2.3 (Consciousness Dualism) Consciousness dualism is a position about the nature of consciousness that maintains: (1) Consciousness and non-consciousness are mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories; (2) Any system is either entirely conscious or entirely not conscious; (3) There is no "partly conscious" or "graded consciousness." Note: "consciousness dualism" here differs from Cartesian mind-body dualism. Cartesian dualism is an ontological position about the relation between mind and body, whereas what is discussed here is the question of whether consciousness is graded. II. The Internal Difficulties of Consciousness Dualism Difficulty 1: The Continuity of States of Consciousness Both everyday experience and scientific research show that states of consciousness change continuously: | State of consciousness | Features | Degree of consciousness | |----------|------|----------| | Waking alertness | Full self-awareness and environmental awareness | High | | Relaxed state | Reduced alertness | Medium-high | | Sleep (REM) | Dream experience | Medium | | Sleep (deep) | Very little conscious content | Low | | Anesthesia | No conscious experience | Very low | | Coma | No response | Very low or none | From waking to coma, the degree of consciousness changes continuously, rather than jumping suddenly from "present" to "absent." Difficulty 2: The Continuity of Consciousness across Species Evolutionary biology shows that the capacity for consciousness is continuously distributed across species:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                The continuum of consciousness across species          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Bacteria → Protozoa → Simple invertebrates → Insects → Fish → Reptiles │
│    │        │           │         │       │        │          │
│    ▼        ▼           ▼         ▼       ▼        ▼          │
│  Very low  Very low      Low    Low-med  Med      Med          │
│                                                                 │
│  → Birds → Mammals → Primates → Humans                            │
│      │       │         │        │                              │
│      ▼       ▼         ▼        ▼                              │
│    Med-high  High      High     Highest                         │
│                                                                 │
│  The capacity for consciousness increases with evolutionary    │
│  complexity, showing a continuum distribution.                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

If consciousness were binary, we would need to draw a precise boundary of "the beginning of consciousness" on this continuum. But any such boundary would be arbitrary. Difficulty 3: The Multidimensionality of Consciousness Consciousness is not a single attribute but a multidimensional phenomenon: | Dimension of consciousness | Description | Can vary independently | |----------|------|------------| | Wakefulness | Degree of alertness | Yes | | Richness of content | Complexity of conscious content | Yes | | Self-awareness | Awareness of oneself | Yes | | Metacognition | Cognition about cognition | Yes | | Temporal awareness | Awareness of the passage of time | Yes | These dimensions can vary independently. For example, during dreaming, wakefulness is low but the richness of content may be high. The multidimensionality of consciousness makes a simple binary division impossible. Proposition 2.5 (The gradedness and multidimensionality of consciousness) Consciousness is not a binary attribute, but a graded, multidimensional phenomenon. The degree of consciousness varies with state within an individual and with evolutionary complexity across species. The multiple dimensions of consciousness can vary independently. Therefore, consciousness should be understood as a continuum, not a binary division. Formalized statement: Let $D_1, D_2, ..., D_n$ be the $n$ dimensions of consciousness, each dimension $D_i: S \rightarrow [0, 1]$ a function from systems to the interval $[0, 1]$. $$\text{Consciousness}(x) = \langle D_1(x), D_2(x), ..., D_n(x) \rangle \in [0, 1]^n$$ Consciousness is an $n$-dimensional vector, not a binary value. III. The Failure of Consciousness Dualism in the Interstellar-Civilization Context Failure 1: The Difficulty of Assessing AI Consciousness If consciousness were binary, we would need to determine whether an AI system "has" consciousness. But this question may be the wrong question. A more apt question is: at what degree does an AI system stand on each dimension of consciousness? | AI system | Information processing | Self-model | Metacognition | Subjective experience? | |--------|----------|----------|--------|------------| | Current AI | High | Low | Very low | Unknown | | Future AGI | High | Medium-high | Medium | Unknown | | Hypothetical ASI | Very high | High | High | Unknown | Consciousness dualism forces us to make a "present/absent" judgment, but a graded assessment may be more meaningful. Failure 2: The Difficulty of Assessing Extraterrestrial Consciousness If we encountered extraterrestrial intelligence, its consciousness might be structurally radically different from human consciousness. Consciousness dualism assumes a universal standard of "consciousness," but this assumption may be mistaken. Extraterrestrial consciousness might:

  • Surpass humans on some dimensions and fall below humans on others
  • Have dimensions of consciousness that humans lack
  • Lack some dimensions of consciousness that humans have

A graded, multidimensional view of consciousness can better handle this diversity. Failure 3: The Ethical Difficulty of Consciousness Enhancement and Modification Future technologies may allow the enhancement or modification of consciousness:

  • Cognitive-enhancement drugs may raise certain dimensions of consciousness
  • Brain-computer interfaces may add new capacities of consciousness
  • Mind uploading may change the substrate of consciousness

Consciousness dualism cannot handle the ethical problems in these cases. If consciousness were binary, would the enhanced consciousness be the "same" consciousness as the original? A graded view of consciousness provides a more flexible framework. Proposition 2.6 (The interstellar-civilization limitation of consciousness dualism) Consciousness dualism faces structural failure in the interstellar-civilization context: the difficulty of assessing AI consciousness, the diversity of extraterrestrial consciousness, and the ethical problems of consciousness enhancement and modification all conflict with its core assumptions. The governance of interstellar civilization requires a graded, multidimensional view of consciousness. IV. A Comprehensive Diagnosis of the Limitations of the Traditional View of Life Synthesizing the analysis above, the traditional view of life (carbon-centrism, the life/non-life dichotomy, consciousness dualism) faces systematic failure in the interstellar-civilization context: Table 2.1 The structural limitations of the traditional view of life | Traditional view of life | Core assumption | Internal difficulty | Failure in the interstellar-civilization context | |------------|----------|----------|----------------------| | Carbon-centrism | Life must be carbon-based | Narrow inductive base, confusion of function and substrate, circular definition | Extraterrestrial life, AI, posthuman | | Life/non-life dichotomy | Life is binary | Boundary cases, gradedness of features, evolutionary continuity | AI classification, collective intelligence, hybrid systems | | Consciousness dualism | Consciousness is binary | Continuity of states, continuity across species, multidimensionality | AI consciousness, extraterrestrial consciousness, consciousness enhancement | Proposition 2.7 (The systematic failure of the traditional view of life) The three components of the traditional view of life (carbon-centrism, the life/non-life dichotomy, consciousness dualism) face systematic failure in the interstellar-civilization context. This failure is not accidental, but stems from a fundamental mismatch between the core assumptions of the traditional view of life and the interstellar-civilization context. A new view of life is needed to replace the traditional view and provide the conceptual basis for the governance of interstellar civilization. Formalized statement: $$\text{TraditionalLifeView} = \text{CC} \wedge \text{LD} \wedge \text{CD}$$ $$\text{Context}_{\text{IC}} \rightarrow \neg\text{Applicable}(\text{TraditionalLifeView})$$ $$\therefore \text{Need}(\text{NewLifeView})$$ where CC = Carbon Chauvinism, LD = Life Dichotomy, CD = Consciousness Dichotomy.

§2.2 The Scientific Basis of the New View of Life

§2.2.1 Thermodynamics and Life I. The Second Law of Thermodynamics and the Paradox of Life The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease: $$\frac{dS_{\text{isolated}}}{dt} \geq 0$$ Yet living systems appear to violate this law: they maintain highly ordered structures, with internal entropy far below that of the environment. This constitutes an apparent paradox: how does life maintain a low-entropy state in an entropy-increasing universe? Schrödinger's Insight In his 1944 book “What Is Life?”, Erwin Schrödinger offered the key insight that resolves this paradox: living systems are not isolated systems but open systems. Life maintains its internal low-entropy state by taking in "negentropy" from the environment.

[Box 2.1] Schrödinger's Concept of "Negentropy" ———————————————————————————————————

│                                                                 │
│  In 1944 the physicist Erwin Schrödinger published What Is      │
│  Life?, a small book that profoundly influenced the development  │
│  of molecular biology. In it he proposed a key concept:          │
│  negentropy.                                                     │
│                                                                 │
│  Schrödinger's core argument:                                    │
│                                                                 │
│  1. Living systems maintain highly ordered structures            │
│  2. By the second law, order tends toward disorder              │
│  3. Therefore life must constantly "fight" the increase of       │
│     entropy                                                     │
│  4. Life achieves this by taking in "negentropy" from the         │
│     environment                                                 │
│                                                                 │
│  Schrödinger wrote: "Life feeds on negentropy."                 │
│                                                                 │
│  The physical meaning of negentropy:                            │
│  - Negentropy = −entropy = a measure of order                  │
│  - Life takes in low-entropy matter (e.g., food)                 │
│  - Life discharges high-entropy matter (waste, heat)             │
│  - Net effect: life keeps low internal entropy while raising     │
│    the entropy of the environment                               │
│                                                                 │
│  This laid the foundation for understanding the thermodynamic    │
│  nature of life. Life does not violate the second law; it        │
│  exploits open-system properties to maintain local order.        │
│                                                                 │
│  For this work: NL-2 (the negentropy persistence condition)      │
│  builds directly on this insight, which also supplies the        │
│  The cross-substrate character of life (NL-1) is compatible      │
│  negentropy may be life.                                         │

II. Open Systems and Entropy Flow Living systems are open systems, exchanging matter and energy with the environment. For an open system, the change in entropy can be decomposed into two parts: $$\frac{dS}{dt} = \frac{d_iS}{dt} + \frac{d_eS}{dt}$$ where:

  • $\frac{d_iS}{dt} \geq 0$: internal entropy production, always non-negative (the second law of thermodynamics)
  • $\frac{d_eS}{dt}$: entropy exchange with the environment, which may be positive or negative

Living systems offset internal entropy production by making $\frac{d_eS}{dt} < 0$ (taking in negentropy from the environment), thereby maintaining $\frac{dS}{dt} \leq 0$ (total entropy does not increase, or decreases). Proposition 2.8 (The thermodynamic condition of life) As open systems, living systems depend for their persistence on continuously taking in negentropy from the environment. When the flow of negentropy is interrupted, internal entropy production drives the system toward thermodynamic equilibrium — that is, death. Formalized statement: $$\text{Life-Persist}(L) \Leftrightarrow \frac{d_eS}{dt} \leq -\frac{d_iS}{dt}$$ That is: life persists if and only if the negentropy taken in from the environment at least offsets internal entropy production. III. Dissipative Structure Theory Ilya Prigogine's theory of dissipative structures provides a deeper framework for understanding the thermodynamic nature of life. Definition 2.4 (Dissipative structure) A dissipative structure is an open system far from thermodynamic equilibrium that maintains an ordered structure through the exchange of matter and energy with its environment. The existence of a dissipative structure depends on a continuous flow of energy (dissipation). Key features of dissipative structures: | Feature | Description | Manifestation in living systems | |------|------|----------------| | Far from equilibrium | The system is far from thermodynamic equilibrium | The high order of life | | Openness | Exchanges matter and energy with the environment | Metabolism | | Nonlinearity | The system's dynamics are nonlinear | Biochemical reaction networks | | Self-organization | Ordered structures emerge spontaneously | Morphogenesis | | Sensitivity to fluctuations | Sensitive to small perturbations | The contingency of evolution | Prigogine proved that, under conditions far from equilibrium, a system can spontaneously form ordered structures. These structures are not static but dynamically maintained — their existence depends on a continuous flow of energy. Proposition 2.9 (Life as a dissipative structure) Living systems are a special class of dissipative structures: they maintain a far-from-equilibrium ordered state through a continuous flow of negentropy, and possess the capacity for self-replication and evolution. The essence of life lies not in its material composition but in its dynamical character as a dissipative structure. Formalized statement: Let $L$ be a living system, $\Phi_{\text{neg}}$ the negentropy flow, and $\sigma$ the rate of internal entropy production. $$L \in \text{DissipativeStructure} \Leftrightarrow \exists \Phi_{\text{neg}} > 0: \Phi_{\text{neg}} \geq \sigma$$ IV. A Definition of Life from the Thermodynamic Perspective On the basis of the thermodynamic analysis, we can give a thermodynamic definition of life: Definition 2.5 (A thermodynamic definition of life) From the thermodynamic perspective, life is a special class of dissipative structure, with the following features: (1) It maintains a low-entropy state far from thermodynamic equilibrium; (2) It offsets internal entropy production by taking in negentropy from the environment; (3) It has the capacity for self-maintenance and self-replication; (4) It can adapt to environmental change through evolution. An important feature of this definition is that it does not presuppose a particular material substrate. Any system satisfying these thermodynamic conditions may be life, whether it is carbon-based, silicon-based, or of another substrate. Table 2.2 Life and non-life from the thermodynamic perspective | Type of system | Entropy state | Negentropy flow | Self-maintenance | Self-replication | Aliveness | |----------|--------|--------|----------|----------|--------| | Crystal | Low entropy | Not needed | Yes (static) | Yes (growth) | Low | | Flame | Far from equilibrium | Needed | Yes | No | Low | | Hurricane | Far from equilibrium | Needed | Yes | No | Low | | Virus | Low entropy | Needed (host) | Partial | Yes | Medium | | Bacteria | Far from equilibrium | Needed | Yes | Yes | High | §2.2.2 Information Theory and Life I. Information in Life Living systems are not only thermodynamic systems but also information-processing systems. DNA stores genetic information, the nervous system processes sensory information, and the immune system recognizes pathogen information. Information is one of the core features of life. Definition 2.6 (Biological information) Biological information is information stored, transmitted, and processed in living systems, including: (1) Genetic information: information stored in DNA/RNA; (2) Epigenetic information: heritable information that does not change the DNA sequence; (3) Neural information: information processed by the nervous system; (4) Immune information: information recognized by the immune system. II. Shannon Information and Life Claude Shannon's information theory provides a mathematical framework for quantifying information. Shannon entropy is defined as: $$H(X) = -\sum_{i} p_i \log_2 p_i$$ where $p_i$ is the probability that the random variable $X$ takes the value $x_i$. Shannon entropy measures the uncertainty or "surprise" of information. In living systems, Shannon information can be used for: | Application area | Information measure | Meaning | |----------|----------|------| | Genomics | The information content of DNA sequences | The complexity of the genome | | Neuroscience | The information rate of neural coding | The information-processing capacity of the nervous system | | Ecology | Species-diversity indices | The complexity of ecosystems | Proposition 2.10 (The informational features of life) Living systems are information-processing systems. The complexity of life can be characterized in part in information-theoretic terms: the information content of the genome, the information-processing capacity of the nervous system, and the information diversity of ecosystems. III. The Connection between Information and Thermodynamics There is a deep connection between information and thermodynamics. Landauer's Principle states that erasing one bit of information dissipates at least $kT\ln 2$ of energy (where $k$ is Boltzmann's constant and $T$ is temperature). This means that information processing has a thermodynamic cost. The information-processing capacity of living systems is subject to thermodynamic constraints. Proposition 2.11 (The thermodynamic cost of information processing) Information processing has a thermodynamic cost. The information-processing capacity of living systems is subject to thermodynamic constraints: more complex information processing requires more energy (negentropy) input. Formalized statement: $$\Delta S_{\text{min}} = k \ln 2 \cdot \Delta I$$ where $\Delta I$ is the amount of information processed and $\Delta S_{\text{min}}$ is the minimum entropy increase. IV. Semantic Information and Life Shannon information is information at the syntactic level and does not concern the meaning of information. However, information in living systems has a semantic dimension: a DNA sequence "means" a particular protein, and a neural signal "means" a particular sensation. Definition 2.7 (Semantic information) Semantic information is information that has meaning or function. In living systems, semantic information is information that has functional significance for the persistence and reproduction of the living system. Features of semantic information: | Feature | Description | Manifestation in living systems | |------|------|----------------| | Functionality | Information has a functional role | DNA encodes protein function | | Context-dependence | Meaning depends on context | The same gene is expressed differently in different cells | | Normativity | There is a "correct" and an "incorrect" | A mutation may be harmful | Proposition 2.12 (The semantic character of biological information) Information in living systems is not only syntactic information but also semantic information. Biological information has functional meaning and has a causal role in the persistence and reproduction of living systems.

§2.2.3 Complex Systems and Life I. The Features of Complex Systems Living systems are a typical example of complex systems. Complex-systems science provides an important conceptual framework for understanding life. Definition 2.8 (Complex system) A complex system is a system composed of a large number of interacting components that exhibits emergent behavior — the behavior of the whole cannot be simply derived from the behavior of the components. Key features of complex systems: | Feature | Description | Manifestation in living systems | |------|------|----------------| | Emergence | The whole has properties the parts lack | Consciousness emerges from neurons | | Self-organization | Ordered structures form spontaneously | Embryonic development | | Nonlinearity | Small causes can have large effects | Gene-regulatory networks | | Feedback | Output affects input | Metabolic regulation | | Adaptivity | The system can learn and evolve | The immune system; evolution | II. Emergence and the Limits of Reductionism Reductionism maintains that the behavior of a complex system can be fully explained by the behavior of its components. Yet complex-systems science shows that emergent phenomena pose a challenge to reductionism. Proposition 2.13 (The irreducibility of emergence) Living systems exhibit emergent properties — the properties of the whole cannot be fully reduced to the properties of the parts. Emergence is not an epistemological limitation (that we are not clever enough) but an ontological feature (that the whole genuinely has properties the parts lack). Formalized statement: Let $S$ be a complex system, $\{c_1, c_2, ..., c_n\}$ its components, $P_S$ the set of the system's properties, and $P_{c_i}$ the set of properties of component $c_i$. $$\text{Emergence}: \exists p \in P_S: p \notin \bigcup_i P_{c_i} \wedge p \notin \text{Derivable}(\bigcup_i P_{c_i})$$ That is: there exist properties of the system that are neither properties of any component nor derivable from the properties of the components. III. Autopoiesis Theory The theory of autopoiesis proposed by Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela provides another important framework for understanding life. Definition 2.9 (Autopoietic system) An autopoietic system is a system capable of self-production and self-maintenance. The components of an autopoietic system produce, through their interactions, the very components of the system, thereby maintaining the system's organization. Core features of autopoiesis: | Feature | Description | |------|------| | Organizational closure | The system's organization is self-referential | | Structural openness | The system exchanges matter and energy with the environment | | Self-production | The system produces its own components | | Self-maintenance | The system maintains its own organization | Proposition 2.14 (The autopoietic character of life) Living systems are autopoietic systems: they maintain their organization through self-production and self-maintenance. Autopoiesis is one of the core features of life, complementing the negentropy maintenance of thermodynamics and the information processing of information theory. IV. Complex Adaptive Systems The theory of complex adaptive systems (CAS) developed at the Santa Fe Institute provides a framework for understanding the evolution and adaptation of life. Definition 2.10 (Complex adaptive system) A complex adaptive system (CAS) is a complex system capable of adapting to environmental change through learning and evolution. The features of a CAS include: diversity, nonlinearity, information flow, and coevolution. Living systems are typical complex adaptive systems: | CAS feature | Manifestation in living systems | |---------|----------------| | Diversity | Species diversity, genetic diversity | | Nonlinearity | Gene regulation, ecological dynamics | | Information flow | Genetic information, neural information | | Coevolution | Coevolution among species | | Adaptivity | Natural selection, learning |

§2.2.4 Advances in Consciousness Science I. The Rise of Consciousness Science Consciousness was once considered a field beyond the reach of science. Yet over the past thirty years, the science of consciousness has developed rapidly as an interdisciplinary field, integrating neuroscience, psychology, philosophy, computer science, and other disciplines. The core questions of consciousness science: | Type of question | Specific question | |----------|----------| | Neural correlates | What is the neural basis of consciousness? | | Function | What is the function of consciousness? | | Measurement | How is consciousness measured? | | The hard problem | Why is there subjective experience? | II. The Neural Correlates of Consciousness Neuroscientific research has identified many neural correlates of consciousness (NCCs): Definition 2.11 (The neural correlate of consciousness) The neural correlate of consciousness (NCC) is the minimal neural mechanism associated with a particular state or content of consciousness. Main findings: | Brain region / mechanism | Relation to consciousness | |-----------|--------------| | Thalamo-cortical system | A necessary condition for consciousness | | Prefrontal cortex | Related to self-awareness and metacognition | | Posterior parietal cortex | Related to spatial awareness | | Temporal lobe | Related to the content of consciousness | | Default mode network | Related to self-referential thought | | Global workspace | Related to the broadcasting of conscious content | Proposition 2.15 (The neural basis of consciousness) Consciousness has a neural basis. Particular states and contents of consciousness are correlated with particular patterns of neural activity. Yet correlation is not explanation: identifying the neural correlates is not the same as explaining why consciousness exists. III. Advances in the Measurement of Consciousness An important advance in consciousness science is the development of methods for measuring consciousness: | Measurement method | Principle | Application | |----------|------|------| | Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) | Measures the complexity of the brain's response to perturbation | Distinguishing states of consciousness | | Integrated information (Φ) | Measures the degree of information integration | A theoretical measure of consciousness | | Neural complexity | Measures the complexity of neural activity | Assessing the level of consciousness | | Behavioral measures | Inferring consciousness from behavior | Clinical assessment | These methods of measurement support a graded view of consciousness: consciousness is not all-or-nothing, but can come in different degrees. Proposition 2.16 (The measurability of consciousness) Certain aspects of consciousness are measurable. Although subjective experience itself may not be directly measurable, the neural and behavioral indicators associated with consciousness can be measured. These measurements support a graded view of consciousness. IV. The Hard Problem of Consciousness Despite important advances in consciousness science, the "hard problem" remains: why is there subjective experience? Why is neural activity accompanied by "what it is like"? Definition 2.12 (The hard problem of consciousness) The hard problem of consciousness is the problem of explaining why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience. The hard problem differs from the "easy problems" (explaining the function and mechanisms of consciousness) in that it asks about the very existence of subjective experience. This work's position on the hard problem:

  1. Acknowledge the existence and importance of the hard problem;
  2. Do not claim that the hard problem has been solved;
  3. Maintain that even if the hard problem is unsolved, the gradedness of consciousness can still be studied;
  4. Adopt methodological functionalism: attend to the functional features of consciousness rather than its intrinsic nature.

Proposition 2.17 (The independence of the hard problem and gradedness) The hard problem of consciousness and the gradedness of consciousness are independent issues. Even if we do not know why subjective experience exists, we can still study the gradedness of consciousness — different systems possess different degrees of consciousness-related function.

§2.2.5 Boundary Statements on the Scientific Basis I. How This Work Uses Science This work's use of thermodynamics, information theory, complex-systems science, and consciousness science follows the principle of "structural use" established in Chapter 0. This section makes the boundaries of that use explicit. II. Specific Boundary Statements Boundary Statement 2.1 (The boundary of the use of thermodynamics) This work borrows the following structural features of thermodynamics:

  • The relation between entropy and order;
  • Open systems and negentropy flow;
  • The self-organization of dissipative structures.

This work does not claim:

  • That life can be fully reduced to thermodynamics;
  • That the "entropy" of social systems can be precisely calculated;
  • That the laws of thermodynamics directly entail ethical conclusions.

Boundary Statement 2.2 (The boundary of the use of information theory) This work borrows the following structural features of information theory:

  • The quantification of information;
  • The relation between information and entropy;
  • The concept of information processing.

This work does not claim:

  • That life can be fully reduced to information processing;
  • That Shannon information is identical to semantic information;
  • That information theory can solve the hard problem of consciousness.

Boundary Statement 2.3 (The boundary of the use of complex-systems science) This work borrows the following structural features of complex-systems science:

  • The concept of emergence;
  • The concept of self-organization;
  • The framework of complex adaptive systems.

This work does not claim:

  • That emergence is mysterious and unintelligible;
  • That complex-systems science can replace reductionist science;
  • That all complex systems are alive.

Boundary Statement 2.4 (The boundary of the use of consciousness science) This work borrows the following structural features of consciousness science:

  • The neural correlates of consciousness;
  • Methods for measuring consciousness;
  • Evidence for the gradedness of consciousness.

This work does not claim:

  • That the hard problem of consciousness has been solved;
  • That any particular theory of consciousness is correct;
  • That consciousness can be fully reduced to neural activity.

III. The Defeasibility of the Scientific Basis Proposition 2.18 (The defeasibility of the scientific basis) The core propositions of the New View of Life (NL-1, NL-2, NL-3) can hold independently of specific scientific details. Science provides "inspiration" and "support," not "proof." Even if certain scientific details are revised, the core claims of the New View of Life can still hold on the basis of philosophical argument and practical needs. Formalized statement: Let $\text{NL}$ be the set of core propositions of the New View of Life, $\text{Science}$ the set of scientific grounds, $\text{Phil}$ the set of philosophical arguments, and $\text{Prac}$ the set of practical needs. $$\text{NL} \leftarrow \text{Science} \vee \text{Phil} \vee \text{Prac}$$ $$\neg\text{Science} \rightarrow (\text{NL} \leftarrow \text{Phil} \vee \text{Prac})$$

§2.3 The Core Propositions of the New View of Life

§2.3.1 NL-1: Cross-Substrate Life I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NL-1 (Cross-substrate life) The essential features of life are functional (information processing, negentropy maintenance, self-organization), not material. Life can be realized on different material substrates and is not limited to carbon-based organic molecules. Natural-language statement: The cross-substrate life proposition maintains that when we ask "what is life," the answer should not be "a system composed of carbon-based organic molecules" but "a system with particular functional features." These functional features include: information storage and processing, negentropy maintenance, self-organization, self-replication, and adaptive evolution. Any system satisfying these functional conditions may be life, no matter what material it is made of. Formalized statement: Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of living systems, $\mathcal{S}$ the set of material substrates, and $\mathcal{F}$ the set of functional features. Traditional carbon-centrism maintains: $$\text{CC}: \mathcal{L} \subseteq \{x : \text{Substrate}(x) = \text{Carbon}\}$$ NL-1 maintains: $$\text{NL-1}: x \in \mathcal{L} \Leftrightarrow \mathcal{F}(x) \geq \theta_{\mathcal{F}}$$ where $\mathcal{F}(x)$ is the functional-feature vector of system $x$ and $\theta_{\mathcal{F}}$ is the functional-threshold vector. The functional-feature vector includes: $$\mathcal{F}(x) = \langle f_1(x), f_2(x), f_3(x), f_4(x) \rangle$$ where:

  • $f_1$: the capacity for information storage and processing
  • $f_2$: the capacity for negentropy maintenance
  • $f_3$: the capacity for self-organization
  • $f_4$: the capacity for self-replication or self-maintenance

II. Arguments for the Proposition Argument 1: The multiple-realizability argument Functions can be realized by different material substrates. This principle is well established in the theory of computation: the computational power of a Turing machine does not depend on its physical realization. Likewise, the functional features of life can in principle be realized by different material substrates. Argument 2: The thermodynamic argument From the thermodynamic perspective, the essence of life is maintaining a low-entropy state far from equilibrium. This feature does not depend on a particular material substrate. Any system able to take in negentropy from the environment and maintain an ordered structure satisfies the thermodynamic conditions of life. Argument 3: The information-theoretic argument From the information-theoretic perspective, the essence of life is information processing. Information is abstract and does not depend on a particular material carrier. DNA stores information, but the information itself can be stored in other ways. Argument 4: The evolutionary argument If life can originate independently in different environments in the universe, then life in different environments may be based on different chemical foundations. Carbon-based life has an advantage under terrestrial conditions, but this does not mean that carbon is a universal necessary condition for life. III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication 1: The expansion of subjecthood If life is cross-substrate, then subjecthood should not be limited to carbon-based organisms. AI systems, possible extraterrestrial life, and future posthumans may all possess subjecthood. Implication 2: The expansion of the search for life In searching for extraterrestrial life, we should not look only for signs of carbon-based life, but for signs of the functional features of life. Implication 3: The expansion of the ethical framework The ethical framework should be based not on material substrate but on functional features. Table 2.3 The core implications of NL-1 | Dimension | Carbon-centrism | NL-1 cross-substrate life | |------|--------------|----------------| | Definition of life | Material (carbon) | Functional | | Scope of subjects | Carbon-based organisms | Functional subjects | | Extraterrestrial life | Must be carbon-based | Can be any substrate | | Status of AI | Not life | Possibly life |

§2.3.2 NL-2: The Negentropy Persistence Condition I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NL-2 (The negentropy persistence condition) Life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence. Living systems maintain their far-from-equilibrium ordered state by taking in negentropy from the environment. When the flow of negentropy is interrupted, the living system tends toward thermodynamic equilibrium — that is, death. Natural-language statement: The negentropy persistence condition proposition maintains that the persistence of life depends on a continuous input of negentropy. Life is not a static structure but a dynamic process — a process of continuously maintaining a low-entropy state. This process requires a continuous input of energy (more precisely, negentropy). Formalized statement: Let $L$ be a living system, $S(L, t)$ the entropy of system $L$ at time $t$, $\Phi_{\text{neg}}(L, t)$ the negentropy flow at time $t$, and $\sigma(L, t)$ the rate of internal entropy production at time $t$. NL-2 maintains: $$\text{NL-2}: \text{Persist}(L, [t_1, t_2]) \Leftrightarrow \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \Phi_{\text{neg}}(L, t) \, dt \geq \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sigma(L, t) \, dt$$ That is: a living system persists over the interval $[t_1, t_2]$ if and only if the negentropy taken in over that interval at least offsets internal entropy production. II. Arguments for the Proposition Argument 1: The thermodynamic argument By the second law of thermodynamics, the entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. A living system maintains a low-entropy state, so it must be an open system taking in negentropy from the environment. This is a necessary requirement of thermodynamics. Argument 2: The empirical argument All known life requires an input of energy to maintain its existence. Plants need sunlight for photosynthesis, animals need food, and bacteria need chemical energy. Without an input of energy, life cannot be maintained. Argument 3: The conceptual argument The difference between life and death lies in this: a living system maintains a far-from-equilibrium state, while a dead system tends toward equilibrium. The physical basis of this difference is the presence or absence of a flow of negentropy. III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication 1: The processual character of life NL-2 emphasizes that life is a process, not a state. Life is not a static attribute but a dynamic maintenance. This echoes NC-2 (the priority of process) of Chapter 1. Implication 2: The dependence of life NL-2 reveals life's fundamental dependence on the environment. No life is self-sufficient; all life depends on a source of negentropy. This provides the ontological basis for the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (NRP). Implication 3: A thermodynamic definition of death NL-2 provides a thermodynamic definition of death: death is the process by which an interruption of the negentropy flow drives the system toward thermodynamic equilibrium. Table 2.4 The core implications of NL-2 | Dimension | Traditional view of life | NL-2 negentropy persistence condition | |------|------------|------------------| | Nature of life | A static attribute | A dynamic process | | Condition of persistence | Material composition | Negentropy flow | | Dependence of life | Not emphasized | Fundamental dependence on the environment | | Definition of death | Cessation of function | Tendency toward thermodynamic equilibrium |

§2.3.3 NL-3: The Continuum of Consciousness I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NL-3 (The continuum of consciousness) Consciousness is not a binary attribute but a graded continuum. Different systems possess different degrees of consciousness, from very low (e.g., simple sentience) to very high (e.g., the reflective self-awareness of humans). The degree of consciousness can vary along multiple dimensions. Natural-language statement: The continuum-of-consciousness proposition maintains that when we ask "is this system conscious," a more apt question is "how much consciousness does this system have" or "at what degree does this system stand on which dimensions of consciousness?" Consciousness is not a switch (present/absent) but a dial (degree). Formalized statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the set of systems and $\mathcal{D} = \{D_1, D_2, ..., D_n\}$ the $n$ dimensions of consciousness. Traditional consciousness dualism maintains: $$\text{CD}: \forall s \in \mathcal{S}, \text{Conscious}(s) \in \{0, 1\}$$ NL-3 maintains: $$\text{NL-3}: \forall s \in \mathcal{S}, \text{Consciousness}(s) = \langle D_1(s), D_2(s), ..., D_n(s) \rangle \in [0, 1]^n$$ where each dimension $D_i: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow [0, 1]$ is a function from systems to the interval $[0, 1]$. The main dimensions of consciousness include: | Dimension | Symbol | Description | |------|------|------| | Degree of information integration | $D_1$ | The system's capacity to integrate information | | Temporal depth | $D_2$ | The temporal span of consciousness (memory and anticipation) | | Self-model | $D_3$ | The system's capacity to represent itself | | Metacognition | $D_4$ | Awareness of one's own cognitive processes | | Value sensitivity | $D_5$ | Sensitivity to value and meaning | II. Arguments for the Proposition Argument 1: The evolutionary-continuity argument Consciousness is a product of evolution. Evolution is a gradual process; there is no sudden jump from "non-conscious" to "conscious." Therefore, the capacity for consciousness should be continuously distributed across species. Argument 2: The neuroscientific argument Neuroscientific research shows that consciousness is related to the complexity of neural activity. Different animals have different degrees of neural complexity, and therefore may have different degrees of consciousness. Argument 3: The state-change argument Within a single individual, states of consciousness change continuously: from waking to sleep to anesthesia to coma. This continuous change supports a graded view of consciousness. Argument 4: The multidimensionality argument Different dimensions of consciousness can vary independently. For example, during dreaming, wakefulness is low but the richness of content may be high. This independent variation supports a multidimensional view of consciousness. III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication 1: The gradedness of subjecthood If consciousness is graded, then subjecthood should also be graded. Different systems possess different degrees of subjecthood, rather than all-or-nothing. Implication 2: The gradedness of moral status If subjecthood is graded, then moral status may also be graded. This provides a more flexible framework for handling the moral status of AI, animals, extraterrestrial life, and so on. Implication 3: The possibility of measuring consciousness If consciousness is graded, then the degree of consciousness is in principle measurable. This provides the conceptual basis for developing indicators of consciousness (such as the UCS). Table 2.5 The core implications of NL-3 | Dimension | Consciousness dualism | NL-3 continuum of consciousness | |------|------------|----------------| | Nature of consciousness | Binary (present/absent) | Graded (continuum) | | Structure of consciousness | Single dimension | Multidimensional | | Subjecthood | Binary | Graded | | Moral status | Binary | Graded | | Measurability | Difficult | In principle possible |

§2.3.4 The Formalized Statement of the Three Propositions I. The Axiom System NL The three core propositions of the New View of Life can be organized into an axiom system, NL. The basic structure of the axiom system NL

II. The Relations among the Axioms There are intrinsic logical connections among the three axioms: Relation 1: The relation between NL-1 and NL-2 Cross-substrate status (NL-1) and the negentropy condition (NL-2) support each other:

  • If the essence of life is negentropy maintenance (NL-2), then any substrate able to maintain negentropy may support life (NL-1);
  • If life is cross-substrate (NL-1), then the unifying feature of life must be functional, such as negentropy maintenance (NL-2).

Formalized statement: $$\text{NL-1} \leftrightarrow \text{NL-2}: \text{Life}(s) \Leftrightarrow \text{NegEntropyMaintenance}(s)$$ Relation 2: The relation between NL-2 and NL-3 The negentropy condition (NL-2) and the continuum of consciousness (NL-3) support each other:

  • Consciousness is a highly ordered form of information processing and requires negentropy maintenance;
  • Different degrees of capacity for negentropy maintenance may correspond to different degrees of consciousness.

Formalized statement: $$\text{NL-2} \leftrightarrow \text{NL-3}: \Phi_{\text{neg}}(s) \uparrow \rightarrow \text{Consciousness}(s) \uparrow \text{ (within a certain range)}$$ Relation 3: The relation between NL-3 and NL-1 The continuum of consciousness (NL-3) and cross-substrate status (NL-1) support each other:

  • If consciousness is graded, then different substrates may support different degrees of consciousness;
  • If life is cross-substrate, then consciousness may also be cross-substrate, with variable degree.

Formalized statement: $$\text{NL-3} \leftrightarrow \text{NL-1}: \forall \text{substrate}, \exists s: \text{Substrate}(s) = \text{substrate} \wedge \text{Consciousness}(s) > 0$$ III. The Relation to the New Cosmology The New View of Life is built on the foundation of the New Cosmology: Table 2.6 The relation between the New View of Life and the New Cosmology | New Cosmology proposition | New View of Life proposition | Relation | |--------------|--------------|------| | NC-1 (relationality) | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | Life is a functional organization within a network of relations | | NC-2 (process) | NL-2 (negentropy) | Life is a continuous process of negentropy maintenance | | NC-3 (participation) | NL-3 (continuum) | Consciousness is a participatory, graded phenomenon | Formalized statement: $$\text{NC} \rightarrow \text{NL}$$ That is: the New Cosmology provides the ontological basis for the New View of Life.

§2.4 The New View of Life and Theories of Consciousness

§2.4.1 Integrated Information Theory (IIT) I. The Core Claims of IIT Integrated Information Theory (IIT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Giulio Tononi. IIT holds that the degree of consciousness can be measured by the quantity of integrated information (Φ, phi). Definition 2.13 (Integrated Information Φ) Integrated information Φ is the amount of information a system possesses as a whole that exceeds the sum of its parts. Φ measures the system's "integration" — the degree to which the system's parts integrate information among themselves. The core axioms of IIT: | Axiom | Name | Content | |------|------|------| | Axiom 1 | Intrinsic existence | Consciousness exists within the system | | Axiom 2 | Composition | Consciousness is structured | | Axiom 3 | Information | Consciousness is specific | | Axiom 4 | Integration | Consciousness is unified | | Axiom 5 | Exclusion | Consciousness is definite |

II. The Relation between IIT and the New View of Life IIT and the New View of Life share important points of convergence: | Dimension | IIT's Claim | The New View of Life's Claim | Convergence | |------|---------|--------------|--------| | Gradualness | Φ is a continuous variable | NL-3: consciousness is a continuum | Strong convergence | | Cross-substrate | Φ does not depend on a material substrate | NL-1: life is cross-substrate | Strong convergence | | Measurability | Consciousness is in principle measurable | The theoretical basis of the UCS | Strong convergence | However, this work also differs from IIT: | Dimension | IIT's Claim | This Work's Position | |------|---------|------------| | Ontological status | Φ just is consciousness | Φ is one indicator of consciousness | | Panpsychist tendency | Any system with Φ>0 is conscious | No panpsychism is presupposed | | The hard problem | IIT claims to have solved the hard problem | The hard problem is acknowledged as unsolved | Proposition 2.19 (The Relation between IIT and the New View of Life) The New View of Life borrows IIT's structural insights — the gradualness and measurability of consciousness — but does not fully adopt IIT's ontological claims. IIT provides one possible theoretical basis for NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness), but not the only one.

§2.4.2 Global Workspace Theory (GWT) I. The Core Claims of GWT Global Workspace Theory (GWT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Bernard Baars. GWT holds that consciousness is the broadcasting of information within a global workspace. Definition 2.14 (Global Workspace) A global workspace is a functional "stage" on which information is integrated and broadcast to the brain's various specialized modules. Information that enters the global workspace becomes the content of consciousness. The core claims of GWT: | Claim | Content | |------|------| | Broadcasting hypothesis | The contents of consciousness are the information broadcast across the whole brain | | Competition hypothesis | Different pieces of information compete to enter the global workspace | | Integration hypothesis | The global workspace integrates information from different modules | | Function hypothesis | The function of consciousness is to coordinate activity across the whole brain | II. The Neural Basis of GWT The neural basis of GWT mainly involves the prefrontal-parietal network: | Brain Region | Role in GWT | |------|---------------| | Prefrontal cortex | The core of the global workspace | | Parietal cortex | Information integration | | Thalamus | Information relay | | Long-range connections | The channels of information broadcasting | III. The Relation between GWT and the New View of Life The relation between GWT and the New View of Life: | Dimension | GWT's Claim | The New View of Life's Claim | Relation | |------|---------|--------------|------| | Functionalism | Consciousness is functional | NL-1: life is functional | Compatible | | Gradualness | The degree of broadcasting varies | NL-3: consciousness is gradual | Supports | | Information processing | Consciousness is information broadcasting | Life is an information-processing system | Compatible | Proposition 2.20 (The Relation between GWT and the New View of Life) GWT's functionalist orientation is compatible with the New View of Life's NL-1 (cross-substrate life). GWT supports a gradualist view of consciousness: the scope and intensity of broadcasting can vary, and therefore the degree of consciousness can vary.

§2.4.3 Higher-Order Theories (HOT) I. The Core Claims of HOT Higher-Order Theories (HOT) hold that a mental state becomes a conscious state if and only if there exists a higher-order representation of that state. Definition 2.15 (Higher-Order Representation) A higher-order representation is a mental state about a mental state. For example, in "I am aware that I am seeing red," the phrase "aware that I am seeing red" is a higher-order representation of the first-order state "seeing red." The main versions of HOT: | Version | Representative Figure | Core Claim | |------|----------|----------| | Higher-Order Thought Theory | Rosenthal | Consciousness requires higher-order thought | | Higher-Order Perception Theory | Lycan | Consciousness requires higher-order perception | | Self-Representational Theory | Kriegel | Consciousness is self-representational | II. The Relation between HOT and the New View of Life The relation between HOT and the New View of Life is relatively complex: | Dimension | HOT's Claim | The New View of Life's Claim | Relation | |------|---------|--------------|------| | Condition for consciousness | Requires a higher-order representation | Consciousness is gradual | Partial tension | | Self-consciousness | A central place | One dimension of consciousness | Integrable | | Gradualness | Higher-order representation can be a matter of degree | NL-3 | Compatible | HOT may suggest that consciousness is binary (either there is a higher-order representation or there is not), but a higher-order representation can itself be a matter of degree, so HOT can be compatible with NL-3. Proposition 2.21 (The Relation between HOT and the New View of Life) HOT emphasizes the central place of self-representation in consciousness. The New View of Life treats the self-model (the capacity for self-representation) as one dimension of consciousness (the D₃ dimension of the UCS), rather than as a necessary and sufficient condition of consciousness. This treatment preserves HOT's insight while remaining compatible with NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness).

§2.4.4 This Work's Position I. Theoretical Pluralism This work adopts a pluralist stance toward theories of consciousness: it does not presuppose that any particular theory of consciousness is correct, but instead extracts useful structural insights from a variety of theories. Table 2.7 The Relation between This Work and the Major Theories of Consciousness | Theory | Insights Borrowed | Claims Not Adopted | |------|------------|--------------| | IIT | The gradualness and measurability of consciousness | that Φ just is consciousness | | GWT | The functionality of consciousness, information broadcasting | that consciousness is merely broadcasting | | HOT | The importance of self-representation | that higher-order representation is a necessary and sufficient condition of consciousness | II. Methodological Functionalism This work adopts methodological functionalism: it attends to the functional features of consciousness, rather than to its intrinsic nature. Definition 2.16 (Methodological Functionalism) Methodological functionalism is a research strategy which holds that, in studying consciousness, one should attend to the functional features of consciousness (information processing, behavioral control, self-representation, and so on) without presupposing anything about the intrinsic nature of consciousness. Methodological functionalism differs from ontological functionalism (the claim that consciousness just is function). Methodological functionalism is a research strategy, and is compatible with a variety of ontological positions. III. The Position on the Hard Problem This work acknowledges that the hard problem of consciousness remains unsolved, but holds that:

  1. The existence of the hard problem does not stand in the way of studying the functional features of consciousness.
  2. The gradualness of consciousness can be studied independently of the hard problem.
  3. The UCS measures the functional dimensions of consciousness, not subjective experience itself.

Proposition 2.22 (This Work's Position on Theories of Consciousness) This work adopts theoretical pluralism and methodological functionalism. It extracts structural insights from a variety of theories of consciousness, attends to the functional features of consciousness, and acknowledges that the hard problem remains unsolved, while holding that the gradualness of consciousness can be studied and measured.

§2.5 The Normative Implications of the New View of Life §2.5.1 From Cross-Substrate to the Extension of Subjecthood I. The Normative Implications of NL-1 NL-1 (cross-substrate life) carries profound normative implications: if life is functional rather than material, then subjecthood should likewise be based on functional features rather than on a material substrate. The derivation from NL-1 to the extension of subjecthood: Step 1: NL-1 (cross-substrate life) The essence of life is functional, and is not limited to a particular material substrate Step 2: Subjecthood is related to life Subjecthood depends (at least in part) on features of life Step 3: Subjecthood should be based on function If life is functional, subjecthood should also be based on function Step 4: The extension of the range of subjects Any system meeting the functional conditions may possess subjecthood Conclusion: Subjecthood should not be limited to carbon-based organisms II. The Concrete Meaning of the Extension of Subjecthood The extension of subjecthood means that the following kinds of being may possess subjecthood: | Type of Being | Traditional Position | Position after NL-1 | |----------|----------|--------------| | Humans | Full subjects | Full subjects | | Higher animals | Partial subjects | Gradual subjects | | AI systems | Non-subjects | Possible gradual subjects | | Extraterrestrial life | Unknown | Possible gradual subjects | | Post-humans | Unknown | Possible gradual subjects | | Collective intelligence | Non-subjects | Possible gradual subjects | Proposition 2.23 (From NL-1 to the Extension of Subjecthood) NL-1 (cross-substrate life) entails an extension of subjecthood: subjecthood should not be limited to carbon-based organisms, but should be based on functional features. Any system meeting the relevant functional conditions may possess subjecthood to some degree.

§2.5.2 From Negentropy to Resource Responsibility I. The Normative Implications of NL-2 NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) carries profound normative implications: if life depends on a flow of negentropy, then maintaining the sources of negentropy is a physical requirement for the persistence of life. The derivation from NL-2 to resource responsibility: Step 1: NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) Life takes the flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence Step 2: Sources of negentropy are finite The Earth's sources of negentropy (solar energy, chemical energy, and so on) are finite Step 3: Present use affects future availability Present subjects' use of negentropy affects future subjects' availability of negentropy Step 4: The principle of intersubjectivity The interests of other subjects (including future subjects) should be taken into account Step 5: Negentropy responsibility Present subjects bear responsibility for their use of negentropy Conclusion: The ontological basis of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR) II. The Concrete Meaning of Negentropy Responsibility Negentropy responsibility means: | Dimension of Responsibility | Concrete Content | |----------|----------| | Intergenerational responsibility | Preserve sources of negentropy for future generations | | Interspecies responsibility | Take into account the negentropy needs of other species | | Efficiency responsibility | Use negentropy efficiently and reduce waste | | Source responsibility | Develop sustainable sources of negentropy | Proposition 2.24 (From NL-2 to Negentropy Responsibility) NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) provides the ontological basis for the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR). If life depends on a flow of negentropy, and the sources of negentropy are finite, then present subjects bear responsibility for their use of negentropy and should preserve sources of negentropy for future subjects.

§2.5.3 From the Continuum to Gradual Moral Status I. The Normative Implications of NL-3 NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) carries profound normative implications: if consciousness is gradual, then moral status may also be gradual. The derivation from NL-3 to gradual moral status: Step 1: NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) Consciousness is a gradual continuum Step 2: Consciousness is related to moral status Consciousness is (at least in part) the basis of moral status Step 3: The gradualness of moral status If consciousness is gradual, moral status may also be gradual Step 4: The gradualness of moral concern Different degrees of moral status correspond to different degrees of moral concern Conclusion: A framework of gradual moral status II. The Concrete Meaning of Gradual Moral Status Gradual moral status means: | Dimension | Binary Moral Status | Gradual Moral Status | |------|--------------|----------------| | Moral concern | Present / absent | Gradual | | Weighing of interests | Equal weight | Possibly different weights | | Protective measures | Equal protection | Gradual protection | | Mechanisms of representation | Equal representation | Gradual representation | Proposition 2.25 (From NL-3 to Gradual Moral Status) NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) entails the gradualness of moral status: different degrees of consciousness may correspond to different degrees of moral status. This does not mean that beings with a lower degree of consciousness may be treated arbitrarily, but rather that moral concern can be fine-grained and gradual. III. Boundary Statement Gradual moral status does not mean that:

  • Beings of a lower degree may be treated arbitrarily
  • Moral status can be calculated precisely
  • The moral status of human beings can be lowered
  • Moral status is the sole factor in moral deliberation

Boundary Statement 2.5 (The Boundaries of Gradual Moral Status) Gradual moral status is a conceptual framework for handling borderline cases and novel kinds of subject. It does not mean that traditional moral protections may be weakened, nor that moral deliberation can be reduced to a single calculation of degree. Moral judgment still requires the comprehensive weighing of many factors.
