│  VIII.  Preview of the Next Chapter                             │
│                                                                 │
│  Chapter 3 will establish the New View of Cognition (NK), and   │
│  will argue for the following core propositions:                │
│                                                                 │
│  NK-1 (participatory cognition): Cognition is not passive      │
│  reflection, but active participation in construction.          │
│                                                                 │
│  NK-2 (social knowledge): Knowledge is a social achievement,   │
│  not an individual possession.                                  │
│                                                                 │
│  NK-3 (normative cognition): Cognition has a normative         │
│  dimension, and involves questions of what ought to be.         │
│                                                                 │
│  NK-4 (negotiable standards): Standards of cognition are       │
│  negotiable, not fixed a priori.                                │
│                                                                 │
│  Chapter 3 will discuss:                                        │
│  - The limits of traditional epistemology                       │
│  - Advances in contemporary cognitive science (4E cognition,   │
│    predictive processing, and so on)                            │
│  - The core propositions of the New View of Cognition          │
│  - The relation between the New View of Cognition and social   │
│    epistemology                                                 │
│  - The normative implications of the New View of Cognition     │
│                                                                 │
│  Preview of key questions:                                      │
│  - Is cognition passive reflection or active construction?     │
│  - Is knowledge an individual possession or a social           │
│    achievement?                                                 │
│  - Are standards of cognition a priori or negotiable?          │
│  - What implications does the New View of Cognition have for   │
│    cross-civilizational cognition?                              │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 2 Appendix: UCS Conceptual Foundation Quick Reference

Table 2.F Conceptual Foundation of the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) | Attribute | Content | |------|------| | Full name | Universal Consciousness Scale | | Abbreviation | UCS | | Theoretical basis | NL-3 (consciousness continuum) | | Core function | Measuring the degree of consciousness of a subject | | Number of dimensions | 5 core dimensions | | Value range | Each dimension [0, 1], overall [0, 1]⁵ | | Detailed design | Chapter 7 | Formal definition of the UCS (preview): $$\text{UCS}(s) = \langle D_1(s), D_2(s), D_3(s), D_4(s), D_5(s) \rangle \in [0, 1]^5$$ Aggregation function of the UCS (optional): $$\text{UCS}_{\text{agg}}(s) = \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i \cdot D_i(s), \quad \text{where} \sum_{i=1}^{5} w_i = 1$$ Relation between the UCS and NL-3:

  • NL-3 provides the conceptual foundation: consciousness is a graded multidimensional continuum
  • The UCS provides an operationalization tool: converting NL-3 into measurable indices
  • The five dimensions of the UCS correspond to five core aspects of consciousness

Chapter 2 Supplementary Material: Case Studies of Cross-Substrate Life

Case One: Viruses—the Borderline Case of Life Viruses are the classic borderline case for traditional definitions of life. Analyzed from the perspective of the New View of Life: | Dimension | Features of viruses | NL Assessment | |------|------------|--------| | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | Carbon-based, but structurally simple | Satisfies the carbon-based condition | | NL-2 (negentropy) | Requires a host to supply negentropy | Partially satisfies (dependence) | | NL-3 (consciousness) | Non-conscious | D₁-D₅ are all 0 or extremely low | Judgment of the New View of Life: viruses lie at the lower end of the continuum of life, possessing some features of life (genetic information, evolvability) but lacking an independent capacity for negentropy maintenance. Viruses are "quasi-life" or "borderline life." Case Two: Current AI Systems Current AI systems (such as large language models), analyzed from the perspective of the New View of Life: | Dimension | Features of current AI | NL Assessment | |------|--------------|--------| | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | Silicon-based, non-carbon | Satisfies the cross-substrate condition | | NL-2 (negentropy) | Requires an electricity supply | Satisfies (dependence on external energy) | | NL-3 (consciousness) | Under dispute | D₁ moderate, D₂-D₅ low or unknown | Judgment of the New View of Life: current AI systems satisfy the conditions of NL-1 (cross-substrate) and NL-2 (negentropy dependence), but their assessment on the NL-3 (consciousness) dimension is disputed. From a functionalist perspective, current AI has certain features of life but may lack subjective experience. Case Three: Hypothetical Silicon-Based Extraterrestrial Life Suppose a silicon-based life form exists on some planet: | Dimension | Hypothetical features of silicon-based life | NL Assessment | |------|---------------------|--------| | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | Silicon-based, non-carbon | Satisfies the cross-substrate condition | | NL-2 (negentropy) | Draws negentropy from the environment | Satisfies | | NL-3 (consciousness) | May possess consciousness | Depends on the specific structure | Judgment of the New View of Life: silicon-based life fully conforms to the framework of the New View of Life. NL-1 explicitly permits the existence of non-carbon-based life. If silicon-based life satisfies NL-2 (negentropy maintenance) and possesses sufficient information-processing capacity, it may have subject status comparable to that of carbon-based life. Case Four: Collective Intelligence (Ant Colonies) The ant colony as a case of collective intelligence: | Dimension | Features of ant colonies | NL Assessment | |------|------------|--------| | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | Carbon-based (individuals), but the whole is an emergent structure | Complex case | | NL-2 (negentropy) | The whole maintains negentropy | Satisfies | | NL-3 (consciousness) | Low individual consciousness; does the whole have consciousness? | Under dispute | Judgment of the New View of Life: the ant colony challenges the traditional individualist view of life. From the perspective of the New View of Life, the ant colony as a whole may possess a certain degree of "collective life"—it maintains negentropy, processes information, and adapts to its environment. But whether the ant colony has "collective consciousness" is an open question.

III. The Core Tasks of This Chapter This chapter undertakes four core tasks: Task One: Diagnose the structural limits of the traditional view of cognition

  • Why does spectator epistemology fail under interstellar conditions?
  • Why can individualist epistemology not handle collective cognition?
  • Why does value-neutral epistemology not match cognitive practice?

Task Two: Establish the scientific basis of the New View of Cognition

  • What does research on embodied cognition reveal?
  • What insight does research on social cognition offer?
  • How does predictive processing theory reshape our understanding of cognition?

Task Three: Argue for the four core propositions of the New View of Cognition

  • NK-1: participatory cognition — cognition is participatory construction
  • NK-2: social knowledge — knowledge is a social achievement
  • NK-3: normative cognition — cognition has a normative dimension
  • NK-4: cognitive humility — standards of cognition are negotiable

Task Four: Clarify the normative implications of the New View of Cognition

  • How does participation lead to responsible cognition?
  • How does sociality lead to an obligation to negotiate?
  • How does normativity lead to reflective commitment?
  • How does humility lead to the Reversibility Principle?

IV. Deliverables of This Chapter After reading this chapter, the reader will obtain:

  • formal definitions of the four core propositions (NK-1, NK-2, NK-3, NK-4)
  • a systematic comparison of the New View of Cognition with the traditional view
  • the scientific basis of the New View of Cognition and its boundary statements
  • a positioning of the New View of Cognition in relation to contemporary epistemology
  • a preliminary exposition of the normative implications of the New View of Cognition
  • the conceptual basis of the CRV (Commitment-Validation Ratio)

V. Continuity with the Previous Two Chapters This chapter builds on Chapter 1's New Cosmology and Chapter 2's New View of Life: NC-1 (relationality) -> cognition is relational, depending on the relation between the cognizer and the world NC-2 (process) -> cognition is a process, a continuous construction rather than a static reflection NC-3 (participation) -> cognition is participatory; the cognizer participates in constructing the object of cognition NL-1 (cross-substrate) -> cognition can be realized by different substrates NL-2 (negentropy) -> cognition is part of the maintenance of negentropy NL-3 (continuum) -> cognitive capacity is a gradual continuum VI. Methodological Note This chapter follows the methodological commitments established in Chapter 0:

  1. The empirical core is left untouched: this chapter does not challenge the empirical findings of cognitive science, but carries out philosophical analysis at the conceptual level only.
  2. Structural use rather than conceptual hijacking: this chapter borrows the formal structures of cognitive science for analogy, but explicitly states the boundaries of that borrowing.
  3. Interdisciplinary bridging is truncatable: the scientific analogies in this chapter can be removed or replaced while preserving the core argument.

VII. Reading Advice Readers with a philosophical background: focus on §3.3 (the core propositions) and §3.4 (contemporary epistemology). Readers with a scientific background: focus on §3.2 (the scientific basis) and §3.2.4 (boundary statements). Readers with a policy background: focus on §3.5 (normative implications) and the chapter summary. Readers wanting a quick overview: read the chapter opening guide, §3.3.5 (the formalized statement), and the chapter summary. Estimated reading time: about 3-4 hours for a full read.

§3.1 The Limits of the Traditional View of Cognition

§3.1.1 The Problem of Spectator Epistemology I. The Basic Structure of Spectator Epistemology The mainstream tradition of Western epistemology understands cognition as a passive reflection of the external world. On this view, the cognizer is like a mirror, whose task is to reflect external reality as accurately as possible. This epistemological position may be called "spectator epistemology". Definition 3.1 (Spectator Epistemology) Spectator epistemology is a position about the nature of cognition which holds that: (1) cognition is a passive reflection of the external world; (2) the ideal cognizer is a neutral spectator who does not intervene in the object of cognition; (3) the goal of cognition is to obtain representations that correspond to external reality; (4) there is a clear boundary between the cognizer and the object of cognition. Spectator epistemology has deep philosophical roots: | Philosophical Tradition | Representative Figure | Core Claim | |----------|----------|----------| | Ancient Greek philosophy | Plato | Knowledge is the grasp of eternal Forms | | Early modern rationalism | Descartes | Clear and distinct ideas reflect reality | | Early modern empiricism | Locke | The mind is a blank slate on which experience is inscribed | | Logical positivism | Carnap | Scientific propositions are logical reflections of facts | John Dewey, in The Quest for Certainty, offered a profound critique of this epistemological tradition, calling it the "spectator theory of knowledge." Dewey pointed out that this epistemology treats the cognizer as ... II. The Internal Difficulties of Spectator Epistemology Difficulty One: The Theory-Ladenness of Observation Research in the philosophy of science shows that observation is not a purely passive reception, but is influenced by a theoretical framework. The work of Thomas Kuhn and Norwood Hanson revealed the "theory-ladenness" of observation ... Proposition 3.1 (The Theory-Ladenness of Observation) Observation is not a purely passive reception of the external world, but is influenced by the observer's theoretical framework, conceptual scheme, expectations, and background knowledge. There is no "pure" observation unaffected by theory. Formalized statement: Let $O$ be an observation, $W$ the state of the external world, $T$ a theoretical framework, and $B$ background knowledge. $$O = f(W, T, B)$$ Observation is a function of the external world, the theoretical framework, and background knowledge, and not merely of the external world. Difficulty Two: The Intervention of Measurement Quantum mechanics reveals the intervention of measurement: at the microscopic level, the act of measurement itself changes the system being measured. This finding challenges the core assumption of spectator epistemology — that the cognizer can observe the world without intervening. Chapter 1 has already discussed the quantum measurement problem. Here we emphasize its epistemological implications: $$\text{Measurement}(S) \rightarrow \Delta S$$ Measuring system $S$ brings about a change $\Delta S$ in the system's state. The cognizer is not a spectator, but a participant. Difficulty Three: The Embodiment of Cognition Research in contemporary cognitive science shows that cognition does not occur in a "mind" isolated from the world, but is embodied, embedded, extended, and enactive — the so-called "4E cognition". Proposition 3.2 (The Embodiment of Cognition) Cognition is not pure information processing occurring in a mind isolated from the world, but a process that is embodied, embedded in an environment, and interacting with the world. The cognizer's body, environment, and action are constitutive parts of cognition. III. The Failure of Spectator Epistemology under Interstellar Conditions Failure One: The Impossibility of Cross-Civilizational Cognition If cognition were passive reflection, then different civilizations should be able to obtain the same knowledge — so long as they observe the same world. Yet different civilizations may have fundamentally different conceptual frameworks, perceptual modes, and cognitive structures. Spectator epistemology cannot handle such fundamental cognitive difference. | Cognitive Dimension | Human Cognition | Possible Extraterrestrial Cognition | Source of Difference | |----------|----------|----------------|----------| | Perceptual mode | Mainly vision and hearing | Possibly entirely different | Evolutionary history | | Conceptual framework | Space-time, causality | Possibly fundamentally different | Cognitive structure | | Mode of reasoning | Logical reasoning | Possibly different | Cognitive architecture | | Value framework | Human values | Possibly incommensurable | Cultural evolution | Failure Two: The Difficulty of Evaluating AI Cognition Spectator epistemology assumes a clear boundary between the cognizer and the object of cognition. Yet AI systems blur this boundary: AI is both a cognizer (processing information and making judgments) and an object of cognition (studied and evaluated by humans). More complex still, AI may participate in constructing the human cognitive environment. Failure Three: The Cognitive Predicament under Deep Uncertainty Spectator epistemology assumes that there exists a determinate external world waiting to be known. Yet under conditions of deep uncertainty, the "external world" is itself indeterminate — future states depend on present decisions, and present decisions in turn depend on cognition of the future. The cognizer is not observing an independent world, but participating in ... Proposition 3.3 (The Interstellar Limits of Spectator Epistemology) Spectator epistemology faces structural failure under interstellar conditions: the fundamental difference of cross-civilizational cognition, the blurred boundaries of AI cognition, and the cognition-action loop under deep uncertainty. These features conflict with the core assumptions of spectator epistemology. The governance of interstellar civilizations needs a participatory view of cognition.

§3.1.2 The Problem of Individualist Epistemology I. The Basic Structure of Individualist Epistemology Traditional epistemology focuses mainly on the knowledge states of individual cognizers. Knowledge is defined as an individual's "justified true belief," and the core question of epistemology is how an individual acquires knowledge and how beliefs are justified. Definition 3.2 (Individualist Epistemology) Individualist epistemology is a position about the nature of knowledge which holds that: (1) the basic unit of knowledge is the belief state of an individual; (2) the justification of knowledge ultimately depends on the cognitive capacities of the individual; (3) the core question of epistemology is how an individual acquires and justifies knowledge; (4) social factors are secondary or merely instrumental in the constitution of knowledge. The classic formulation of individualist epistemology is the "JTB" definition of knowledge: $$K(S, p) \Leftrightarrow B(S, p) \wedge J(S, p) \wedge T(p)$$ Here $K(S, p)$ means that subject $S$ knows proposition $p$, $B(S, p)$ means that $S$ believes $p$, $J(S, p)$ means that $S$'s belief is justified, and $T(p)$ means that $p$ is true. II. The Internal Difficulties of Individualist Epistemology Difficulty One: The Sociality of Knowledge Research in contemporary social epistemology shows that knowledge is essentially social:

  • Most knowledge comes from testimony, rather than from an individual's direct experience.
  • Scientific knowledge is the collective achievement of a scientific community, rather than the discovery of an individual scientist.
  • The standards for justifying knowledge are social, depending on the norms of a cognitive community.

Proposition 3.4 (The Sociality of Knowledge) Knowledge is not merely an individual's belief state, but a social achievement. The acquisition, justification, and transmission of knowledge all depend on social structures, institutions, and norms. Individual knowledge is a node in a social knowledge system, not an independent unit. Formalized statement: Let $K_i$ be the knowledge of individual $i$, $K_C$ the knowledge of community $C$, and $S$ a social structure. $$K_i = f(K_C, S, i)$$ Individual knowledge is a function of community knowledge, social structure, and individual features. Difficulty Two: The Irreducibility of Collective Cognition Some cognitive achievements are collective, and cannot be reduced to a simple aggregation of individual cognition: | Type of Collective Cognition | Example | Irreducibility | |--------------|------|------------| | Scientific knowledge | Quantum mechanics | Exceeds any individual's understanding | | Institutional knowledge | The legal system | Distributed across institutions | | Cultural knowledge | Language | Exists in social practice | | Technical knowledge | The Internet | Embedded in technical systems | Proposition 3.5 (The Irreducibility of Collective Cognition) Some cognitive achievements are collective, and cannot be reduced to a simple aggregation of individual cognition. Collective cognition has emergent properties — the cognitive capacity of the whole exceeds the sum of its parts. Difficulty Three: The Division of Cognitive Labor Cognition in modern society is highly divided. No individual can master all relevant knowledge; we rely on experts, institutions, and technical systems to extend our cognitive capacities. Individualist epistemology cannot properly handle this division of cognitive labor. III. The Failure of Individualist Epistemology under Interstellar Conditions Failure One: The Problem of the Ownership of Cross-Civilizational Knowledge If human beings establish contact with an extraterrestrial civilization, to whom should the knowledge exchanged by the two sides belong? Individualist epistemology assumes that knowledge belongs to individuals, but cross-civilizational knowledge may be genuinely "shared knowledge" — belonging to no individual or single civilization. Failure Two: The Problem of the Ownership of AI Knowledge To whom should the knowledge produced by AI systems belong — to the AI itself, to the AI's designers, to the AI's users, or to the whole human-machine system? Individualist epistemology cannot handle this distributed ownership of knowledge. Failure Three: The Problem of the Transmission of Intergenerational Knowledge The timescales of interstellar civilization require considering the transmission of knowledge across many generations. Knowledge exists not only in the minds of present individuals, but also in cultural traditions, institutional structures, and technical systems. Individualist epistemology cannot properly handle this intergenerational existence of knowledge. Proposition 3.6 (The Interstellar Limits of Individualist Epistemology) Individualist epistemology faces structural failure under interstellar conditions: the problem of the ownership of cross-civilizational knowledge, the distributedness of AI knowledge, and the transmission of intergenerational knowledge. These features conflict with the core assumptions of individualist epistemology. The governance of interstellar civilizations needs a social view of knowledge.

§3.1.3 The Problem of Value-Neutral Epistemology I. The Basic Structure of Value-Neutral Epistemology Traditional epistemology assumes that cognition and value are separate: the goal of cognition is to obtain truth, and truth is value-neutral. The cognizer should exclude value bias and pursue objective knowledge. Definition 3.3 (Value-Neutral Epistemology) Value-neutral epistemology is a position about the relation between cognition and value which holds that: (1) the goal of cognition is to obtain truth, and truth is value-neutral; (2) value judgments should not influence factual judgments; (3) the ideal cognizer should exclude value bias; (4) science should be value-neutral. This position receives its clearest formulation in logical positivism: fact and value are sharply separate; science deals only with facts, and value belongs to a non-cognitive domain. II. The Internal Difficulties of Value-Neutral Epistemology Difficulty One: The Value Character of Cognitive Goals Cognition itself has goals — to obtain truth, understand the world, solve problems. These goals are themselves value-laden. To pursue truth rather than falsehood, and understanding rather than confusion, is a value choice. Proposition 3.7 (The Value Character of Cognitive Goals) Cognitive activity itself presupposes values: truth is better than falsehood, understanding is better than confusion, knowledge is better than ignorance. Cognition is not a value-neutral activity, but a value-oriented one. Difficulty Two: The Value-Ladenness of Research Agendas The choice of a scientific research agenda is value-laden: what problem we choose to study, what methods we use, and how we allocate resources all involve value judgments. | Type of Decision | Values Involved | |----------|------------| | Choice of problem | What problem is worth studying? | | Choice of method | What method is acceptable? | | Allocation of resources | How should limited research resources be allocated? | | Application of results | How should research results be applied? | Difficulty Three: The Value Character of Cognitive Norms Cognitive activity is constrained by norms: we should believe propositions supported by evidence, avoid logical contradiction, and remain open to refutation. These cognitive norms are themselves normative — they tell us how we ought to cognize. Proposition 3.8 (The Value Character of Cognitive Norms) Cognitive activity is constrained by norms that tell us how we ought to cognize. Cognitive norms are normative, not purely descriptive. Cognition therefore has a normative dimension. Formalized statement: Let $C$ be a cognitive activity and $N$ a set of cognitive norms. $$\text{Good-Cognition}(C) \Leftrightarrow \text{Conforms}(C, N)$$ Good cognition is cognition that conforms to cognitive norms. Cognitive norms are normative. III. The Failure of Value-Neutral Epistemology under Interstellar Conditions Failure One: Differences in the Norms of Cross-Civilizational Cognition Different civilizations may have different cognitive norms. If cognition were value-neutral, there should exist universal cognitive standards. Yet cognitive norms may be culturally relative. Value-neutral epistemology cannot handle this normative pluralism. Failure Two: The Ethical Dimension of Cognition Under interstellar conditions, cognitive activity has a profound ethical dimension:

  • Cognition of extraterrestrial life may affect how we treat it.
  • Cognition of AI may affect the rights and status of AI.
  • Cognition of the future may affect our responsibility toward future generations.

Cognition is not value-neutral, but has ethical consequences. Failure Three: Cognition as Intervention In a participatory universe (NC-3), cognition is itself a form of intervention. Our cognitive frameworks participate in shaping the world in which we are able to act. Cognition is not a passive reflection of an independent world, but an active construction of the world. Proposition 3.9 (The Interstellar Limits of Value-Neutral Epistemology) Value-neutral epistemology faces structural failure under interstellar conditions: differences in the norms of cross-civilizational cognition, the ethical dimension of cognition, and cognition as intervention. These features conflict with the core assumptions of value-neutral epistemology. The governance of interstellar civilizations needs a view of cognition that acknowledges its normativity. IV. A Comprehensive Diagnosis of the Limits of the Traditional View of Cognition Taking the above analysis together, the traditional view of cognition (spectator epistemology, individualist epistemology, and value-neutral epistemology) faces systematic failure under interstellar conditions: Table 3.1 The Structural Limits of the Traditional View of Cognition | Traditional View | Core Assumption | Internal Difficulty | Failure under Interstellar Conditions | |------------|----------|----------|----------------------| | Spectator epistemology | Cognition is passive reflection | Theory-ladenness, the intervention of measurement, embodiment | Cross-civilizational cognition, AI cognition, deep uncertainty | | Individualist epistemology | Knowledge belongs to individuals | The sociality of knowledge, collective cognition, the division of cognitive labor | Cross-civilizational knowledge, AI knowledge, intergenerational knowledge | | Value-neutral epistemology | Cognition is value-neutral | The value character of goals, the ladenness of agendas, normativity | Normative pluralism, the ethical dimension, cognition as intervention | Proposition 3.10 (The Systematic Failure of the Traditional View of Cognition) The three components of the traditional view of cognition (spectator epistemology, individualist epistemology, and value-neutral epistemology) face systematic failure under interstellar conditions. This failure is not accidental, but stems from a fundamental mismatch between the core assumptions of the traditional view and the interstellar situation. A new view of cognition is needed to replace the traditional one, in order to ... Formalized statement: $$\text{TraditionalCognitiveView} = \text{SE} \wedge \text{IE} \wedge \text{VNE}$$ $$\text{Context}_{\text{IC}} \rightarrow \neg\text{Applicable}(\text{TraditionalCognitiveView})$$ $$\therefore \text{Need}(\text{NewCognitiveView})$$ Here SE = Spectator Epistemology, IE = Individualist Epistemology, VNE = Value-Neutral Epistemology.

§3.2 The Scientific Basis of the New View of Cognition

§3.2.1 Research on Embodied Cognition I. The Core Claims of Embodied Cognition Embodied cognition is an important research paradigm in contemporary cognitive science, which challenges the traditional computationalist view of cognition. Its core claim is that cognition is not abstract information processing occurring in a "mind" isolated from the world, but a process that depends on the body, is embedded in an environment, and interacts with the world. Definition 3.4 (Embodied Cognition) Embodied cognition is a research paradigm about the nature of cognition which holds that: (1) cognition depends on the body — the body's structure and capacities shape cognition; (2) cognition is embedded in an environment — the environment is a constitutive part of cognition; (3) cognition is action-oriented — cognition serves action, not pure representation; (4) cognition is situated — cognition depends on the concrete situation. The main evidence from research on embodied cognition: | Type of Evidence | Concrete Finding | Challenge to the Traditional View | |----------|----------|---------------------| | Sensorimotor coupling | Perception and movement are tightly coupled | Challenges the separation of perception and action | | Bodily metaphor | Abstract concepts depend on bodily metaphors | Challenges purely abstract thought | | Situated cognition | Cognition depends on the concrete situation | Challenges de-situated cognition | | Gesture and thought | Gesture participates in the thought process | Challenges the mind-body separation | II. The 4E Cognition Framework Research on embodied cognition has developed the "4E cognition" framework, emphasizing four dimensions of cognition: Table 3.2 The 4E Cognition Framework | Dimension | English | Core Claim | Representative Researchers | |------|------|----------|------------| | Embodied | Embodied | Cognition depends on the body | Varela, Thompson, Rosch | | Embedded | Embedded | Cognition is embedded in an environment | Hutchins | | Extended | Extended | Cognition can extend beyond the body | Clark, Chalmers | | Enactive | Enactive | Cognition is the coupling of perception and action | Varela, Thompson |

III. Support from Embodied Cognition for the New View of Cognition Research on embodied cognition provides an important scientific basis for the New View of Cognition: Support One: The Participatory Character of Cognition Embodied cognition shows that cognition is not passive information reception, but an active process of interacting with the world. The cognizer participates in the world through action, rather than merely spectating it. This supports NK-1 (participatory cognition). Support Two: The Situatedness of Cognition Embodied cognition shows that cognition depends on the concrete situation. There is no "pure cognition" detached from a situation. This means that cognitive standards may be situation-relative, supporting NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability). Support Three: The Distributedness of Cognition The extended-mind argument shows that cognition can be distributed across the brain, body, and environment. This provides a basis for understanding social knowledge, supporting NK-2 (social knowledge). Proposition 3.11 (Support from Embodied Cognition for the New View of Cognition) Research on embodied cognition provides a scientific basis for the New View of Cognition: the participatory character of cognition supports NK-1, the situatedness of cognition supports NK-4, and the distributedness of cognition supports NK-2. Embodied cognition challenges the core assumptions of spectator epistemology.

§3.2.2 Research on Social Cognition I. The Core Findings of Social Cognition Research on social cognition reveals the social dimension of cognition: human cognition is essentially social, depending on social interaction, social structures, and social norms. Definition 3.5 (Social Cognition) Social cognition is the field of research on how human beings understand and interact with the social world, including: (1) theory of mind — the capacity to understand others' mental states; (2) social learning — the capacity to learn by observing others; (3) joint attention — the capacity to share a focus of attention with others; (4) social reasoning — the capacity to reason in social situations. The main findings of research on social cognition: | Field of Finding | Concrete Finding | Epistemological Implication | |----------|----------|------------| | Theory of mind | Humans can understand others' beliefs and intentions | Knowledge depends on social understanding | | Mirror neurons | Observing others' actions activates one's own motor system | Cognition has a social basis | | Joint attention | Infants develop the capacity for joint attention early | Cognitive development depends on social interaction | | Testimonial learning | Most knowledge comes from the testimony of others | Knowledge is socially acquired | II. Distributed Cognition Research on distributed cognition shows that many cognitive tasks are accomplished jointly by multiple individuals and tools, and that cognitive processes are distributed across social systems. Definition 3.6 (Distributed Cognition) Distributed cognition is a research paradigm in cognitive studies which holds that: (1) cognitive processes can be distributed across multiple individuals; (2) cognitive processes can be distributed between individuals and tools; (3) the boundaries of a cognitive system are not limited to an individual brain; (4) social organization is part of the cognitive system. Edwin Hutchins's study of maritime navigation is a classic case of distributed cognition. He found that maritime navigation is not accomplished by a single individual, but jointly by the whole crew and the navigational tools. The cognitive process is distributed across people, tools, and procedures. Proposition 3.12 (The Distributedness of Cognition) Many cognitive tasks are distributed, accomplished jointly by multiple individuals and tools. The boundaries of a cognitive system are not limited to an individual brain, but extend to social organizations and technical systems. Formalized statement: Let $T$ be a cognitive task, $A = \{a_1, a_2, ..., a_n\}$ a set of participants, and $I = \{i_1, i_2, ..., i_m\}$ a set of tools. $$\text{Cognition}(T) = f(A, I, S)$$ Here $S$ is a social structure. Cognition is a function of participants, tools, and social structure. III. Social Epistemology Social epistemology is an important branch of contemporary epistemology, studying the social dimension of knowledge. Table 3.3 The Main Topics of Social Epistemology | Topic | Core Question | Representative Scholars | |------|----------|----------| | Testimonial knowledge | How do we acquire knowledge through the testimony of others? | Coady, Lackey | | The division of cognitive labor | How is cognitive labor distributed in society? | Kitcher, Goldman | | Collective knowledge | Can groups possess knowledge? | Gilbert, List | | Epistemic justice | Questions of justice in cognitive practice | Fricker | Miranda Fricker's concept of "epistemic injustice" reveals questions of power and justice in cognitive practice:

  • Testimonial injustice: because of prejudice, some people's testimony is improperly devalued.
  • Hermeneutical injustice: because of a lack of conceptual resources, some experiences cannot be properly understood.

Proposition 3.13 (The Sociality of Knowledge) Knowledge is essentially social: the acquisition of knowledge depends on testimony, the validation of knowledge depends on social standards, and the transmission of knowledge depends on social institutions. Individual knowledge is a node in a social knowledge system. IV. Support from Social Cognition for the New View of Cognition Research on social cognition provides an important scientific basis for the New View of Cognition: Support One: The Sociality of Knowledge Research on social cognition shows that most knowledge comes from social sources (testimony, education, cultural transmission). This supports NK-2 (social knowledge). Support Two: The Normativity of Cognition Social epistemology reveals the normative dimension of cognitive practice — epistemic justice, testimonial responsibility, and so on. This supports NK-3 (normative cognition). Support Three: The Sociality of Cognitive Standards Social epistemology shows that cognitive standards are social, depending on the norms of a cognitive community. This supports NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability). Proposition 3.14 (Support from Social Cognition for the New View of Cognition) Research on social cognition provides a scientific basis for the New View of Cognition: the sociality of knowledge supports NK-2, the normativity of cognition supports NK-3, and the sociality of cognitive standards supports NK-4. Social cognition challenges the core assumptions of individualist epistemology.

§3.2.3 Predictive Processing Theory I. The Core Claims of Predictive Processing Predictive processing theory is an important theoretical framework in contemporary cognitive science and neuroscience, developed by Karl Friston, Andy Clark, Jakob Hohwy, and others. Definition 3.7 (Predictive Processing) Predictive processing is a theory of brain function which holds that: (1) the brain is a prediction machine — it continuously generates predictions about sensory input; (2) perception is prediction-error minimization — the goal of perception is to minimize the error between prediction and actual input; (3) cognition is active inference — cognition is not passive reception, but active inference; (4) action is the realization of prediction — action is the way of making the world conform to prediction. │         │                       ▼                                │
│         │              ┌─────────────┐                           │
│         └───────────── │  sensory    │                           │
│                        │  input      │                           │
│                        └─────────────┘                           │
│                                                                 │
│  Prediction error can be minimized in two ways:                   │
│  1. Update the internal model (perceptual learning)               │
│  2. Change the world so that it conforms to prediction (action)   │
│                                                                 │

II. The Free Energy Principle Friston's free energy principle is the mathematical basis of predictive processing theory.

[Box 3.2] Friston's Free Energy Principle ————————————————————————————————————

│                                                                 │
│  Karl Friston's free energy principle is a unified theoretical    │
│  framework that attempts to explain the basic operating            │
│  principles of living systems (including the brain).              │
│                                                                 │
│  Core claim:                                                      │
│  Any self-organizing system (including living systems) must       │
│  minimize its free energy in order to maintain its existence      │
│  and resist the entropic tendency of the second law of            │
│  thermodynamics.                                                  │

│                                                                 │

│  - q(s) is the approximate posterior distribution over the        │
│    hidden state s                                                 │

│    hidden state s                                                 │
│  - E_q denotes the expectation under q                             │
│                                                                 │
│  Free energy can be decomposed as:                                │
│  F = Complexity - Accuracy                                        │
│    = KL[q(s)||p(s)] - E_q[ln p(o|s)]                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Minimizing free energy means:                                    │
│  1. Maximizing accuracy (the match of prediction and observation) │
│  2. Minimizing complexity (the simplicity of the model)           │
│                                                                 │

│  The free energy principle is deeply connected with the second    │
│  law of thermodynamics. Living systems maintain a state far from  │

│  NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence).                  │
│                                                                 │
│  Implications for cognition:                                      │
│  - Perception is inference: perception is Bayesian inference      │
│    about the hidden states of the world                            │
│  - Action is inference: action is the way of making the world     │
│    conform to prediction                                          │
│  - Learning is model updating: learning is updating the internal  │
│    generative model                                               │
│                                                                 │

│  - Supports NK-1 (participatory cognition): cognition is active   │
│    inference, not passive reception                               │

│    maintenance of negentropy                                      │

III. Predictive Processing's Challenge to Spectator Epistemology Predictive processing theory fundamentally challenges spectator epistemology: Challenge One: Perception Is Not Passive Reception In the predictive processing framework, perception is not the passive reception of the external world, but a process in which the brain actively generates predictions and matches them against sensory input. The world we "see" is to a large extent the result of the brain's predictions. Proposition 3.15 (The Activeness of Perception) Perception is not the passive reception of the external world, but a process in which the brain actively generates predictions and matches them against sensory input. The content of perception is partly determined by the brain's predictions, not solely by the external world. Formalized statement: Let $P$ be the content of perception, $S$ sensory input, and $M$ the internal generative model. $$P = f(S, M)$$ Perception is a function of sensory input and the internal model. Challenge Two: The Unity of Cognition and Action In the predictive processing framework, cognition and action are not separate, but unified: both are ways of minimizing prediction error. The cognizer is not a spectator separate from the world, but an agent participating in the world through action. Challenge Three: The Constructive Character of Cognition Predictive processing shows that the world we experience is to a large extent constructed by the brain. This supports the participatory-construction view of cognition. Proposition 3.16 (Support from Predictive Processing for the New View of Cognition) Predictive processing theory provides a scientific basis for the New View of Cognition: the activeness of perception supports NK-1 (participatory cognition), the unity of cognition and action supports the practical character of cognition, and the constructive character of cognition supports the constructive role of cognitive frameworks.

§3.2.4 Boundary Statements on the Scientific Basis I. How This Work Uses Science This work's use of embodied cognition, social cognition, and predictive processing theory follows the principle of "structural use" established in Chapter 0. This section makes the boundaries of that use explicit. II. Concrete Boundary Statements Boundary Statement 3.1 (The Boundary of the Use of Embodied Cognition) This work borrows the following structural features of embodied cognition:

  • the participatory and situated character of cognition
  • the functionality of cognitive boundaries
  • the connection between cognition and action

This work does not claim:

  • that all cognition is embodied (abstract cognition may be partly independent of the body)
  • the strong version of the extended-mind argument (that external tools "really" are part of the mind)
  • that embodied cognition can entirely replace the computationalist view of cognition

Boundary Statement 3.2 (The Boundary of the Use of Social Cognition) This work borrows the following structural features of social cognition:

  • the sociality of knowledge
  • the distributedness of cognition
  • the sociality of cognitive norms

This work does not claim:

  • that all knowledge is socially constructed (there exist non-social sources of knowledge)
  • that cognition can be entirely reduced to social processes
  • that social epistemology can replace individual epistemology

Boundary Statement 3.3 (The Boundary of the Use of Predictive Processing) This work borrows the following structural features of predictive processing:

  • the activeness of perception
  • the unity of cognition and action
  • the constructive character of cognition

This work does not claim:

  • that predictive processing is a complete theory of cognition
  • that the free energy principle is a complete theory of life
  • that all cognition can be explained by prediction-error minimization

III. The Truncatability of the Scientific Basis Proposition 3.17 (The Truncatability of the Scientific Basis) The core propositions of the New View of Cognition (NK-1, NK-2, NK-3, NK-4) can hold independently of the concrete scientific details. Science provides "inspiration" and "support," not "proof." Even if certain scientific details were revised, the core claims of the New View of Cognition could still hold on the basis of philosophical argument and practical need. Formalized statement: Let $\text{NK}$ be the set of core propositions of the New View of Cognition, $\text{Science}$ the set of its scientific bases, $\text{Phil}$ the set of philosophical arguments, and $\text{Prac}$ the set of practical needs. $$\text{NK} \leftarrow \text{Science} \vee \text{Phil} \vee \text{Prac}$$ $$\neg\text{Science} \rightarrow (\text{NK} \leftarrow \text{Phil} \vee \text{Prac})$$

§3.3 The Core Propositions of the New View of Cognition

§3.3.1 NK-1: Participatory Cognition I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NK-1 (Participatory Cognition) Cognition is not the passive reflection of a pre-existing reality, but a participatory construction in which the cognizer and the environment interact. Cognitive frameworks participate in shaping the knowable reality. Natural-language statement: The proposition of participatory cognition holds that, when we ask "what is cognition," the answer should not be "a mirror reflection of the external world," but "a constructive process in which the cognizer and the world interact." The cognizer is not a spectator standing outside the world, but a participant embedded in the world and interacting with it. Cognitive frameworks — the ones we use to understand ... Formalized statement: Let $K$ be the cognizer, $E$ the environment, $C$ the content of cognition, and $F$ the cognitive framework. Spectator epistemology holds: $$C = f(E)$$ that is, the content of cognition is determined solely by the environment. NK-1 holds: $$C = g(K, E, F)$$ that is, the content of cognition is determined jointly by the cognizer, the environment, and the cognitive framework. More strongly: $$E' = h(E, K, F)$$ that is, the cognitive framework participates in shaping the knowable environment $E'$. II. The Argument for the Proposition Argument One: From NC-3 to NK-1 NC-3 (participation), established in Chapter 1, holds that the universe is participatory — the observer participates in constructing reality. NK-1 is the epistemological expression of NC-3: if the universe is participatory, then cognition, as a form of observation, is participatory too. $$\text{NC-3} \rightarrow \text{NK-1}$$ Argument Two: From Embodied Cognition to NK-1 Research on embodied cognition shows that cognition depends on the body and the environment, and that the cognizer participates in the world through action. This supports NK-1: cognition is not passive reflection, but active participation. Argument Three: From Predictive Processing to NK-1 Predictive processing theory shows that perception is a process in which the brain actively generates predictions and matches them against sensory input. The world we "see" is partly determined by the brain's predictions. This supports NK-1: the content of cognition is partly determined by the cognizer. Argument Four: From Theory-Ladenness to NK-1 Research in the philosophy of science shows that observation is theory-laden. What we see depends in part on what we believe. This supports NK-1: cognitive frameworks participate in shaping the content of cognition. Argument Five: From Quantum Measurement to NK-1 The measurement problem in quantum mechanics shows that, at the microscopic level, the act of measurement changes the system being measured. This is the physical-level manifestation of participatory cognition. III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication One: Cognitive Responsibility If cognition is participatory, then the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. Cognition is not something that happens to the cognizer, but something the cognizer does. The cognizer can choose different cognitive frameworks, and is therefore responsible for their choice. Implication Two: The Constructive Character of Cognition If cognitive frameworks participate in shaping knowable reality, then different cognitive frameworks may lead to different "realities." This is not to say that reality is arbitrary, but that the way reality presents itself depends on the cognitive framework. Implication Three: The Practical Character of Cognition If cognition is participatory, then cognition and action are unified. Cognition is not a purely theoretical activity, but part of practical activity. Table 3.4 The Core Implications of NK-1 | Dimension | Spectator Epistemology | NK-1 Participatory Cognition | |------|--------------|----------------| | Nature of cognition | Passive reflection | Participatory construction | | Role of the cognizer | Spectator | Participant | | Cognitive framework | A transparent window | A constructive tool | | Cognitive responsibility | None (cognition happens) | Yes (cognition is done) |

§3.3.2 NK-2: Social Knowledge I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NK-2 (Social Knowledge) Knowledge is not the private property of an individual mind, but a social achievement. The production, validation, and transmission of knowledge are all social processes, depending on social structures, institutions, and norms. Natural-language statement: The proposition of social knowledge holds that, when we ask "what is knowledge," the answer should not be "a correct belief in an individual mind," but "a social cognitive achievement." Knowledge is not the product of isolated individuals, but the collective achievement of a cognitive community. The acquisition of knowledge depends on testimony and education, and the validation of knowledge depends on peer review and ... Formalized statement: Let $K$ be knowledge, $S$ a subject, $C$ a cognitive community, and $I$ an institutional structure. Individualist epistemology holds: $$K(S, p) \Leftrightarrow B(S, p) \wedge J(S, p) \wedge T(p)$$ that is, knowledge is an individual's justified true belief. NK-2 holds: $$K(p) \Leftrightarrow \text{SocialValidation}(p, C, I)$$ that is, a proposition $p$ becomes knowledge if and only if it receives social validation by the cognitive community $C$ within the institutional structure $I$. More completely: $$K(S, p) \Leftrightarrow B(S, p) \wedge \text{SocialValidation}(p, C, I) \wedge T(p)$$ that is, an individual knows $p$ if and only if the individual believes $p$, $p$ receives social validation, and $p$ is true. II. The Argument for the Proposition Argument One: From NC-1 to NK-2 NC-1 (relationality), established in Chapter 1, holds that reality is relational. NK-2 is the epistemological expression of NC-1: if reality is relational, then knowledge, as the grasp of reality, is relational too — depending on the relation between the cognizer and the cognitive community. $$\text{NC-1} \rightarrow \text{NK-2}$$ Argument Two: From Testimonial Knowledge to NK-2 Research in social epistemology shows that most knowledge comes from the testimony of others, rather than from an individual's direct experience. Our knowledge of history, science, geography, and so on comes almost entirely from testimony. This supports NK-2: knowledge is socially acquired. Argument Three: From the Division of Cognitive Labor to NK-2 Cognition in modern society is highly divided. No individual can independently verify all knowledge. We rely on experts, institutions, and technical systems. This supports NK-2: knowledge is socially validated. Argument Four: From Scientific Knowledge to NK-2 Scientific knowledge is the collective achievement of a scientific community, not the discovery of an individual scientist. The validation of scientific knowledge depends on peer review, replicability checks, and the acceptance of the community. This supports NK-2: knowledge is a social achievement. Argument Five: From Distributed Cognition to NK-2 Research on distributed cognition shows that many cognitive tasks are accomplished jointly by multiple individuals and tools. Cognitive processes are distributed across social systems. This supports NK-2: knowledge is distributed and social. III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication One: The Public Character of Knowledge If knowledge is social, then knowledge is essentially public, not private. Knowledge is not the private property of individual minds, but the public resource of a cognitive community. Implication Two: The Importance of Cognitive Institutions If knowledge depends on social validation, then cognitive institutions (such as peer review, academic publishing, and educational systems) are crucial to the production of knowledge. Good cognitive institutions promote the production of knowledge; bad ones hinder it. Implication Three: Epistemic Justice If knowledge is social, then there are questions of justice in cognitive practice. Some groups may be systematically excluded from the production of knowledge, or their testimony improperly devalued. Epistemic justice requires correcting these injustices. Table 3.5 The Core Implications of NK-2 | Dimension | Individualist Epistemology | NK-2 Social Knowledge | |------|----------------|----------------| | Ownership of knowledge | Individual | Community | | Validation of knowledge | Individual justification | Social validation | | Transmission of knowledge | Individual to individual | Institutionalized transmission | | Cognitive responsibility | Individual responsibility | Collective responsibility |

§3.3.3 NK-3: Normative Cognition I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NK-3 (Normative Cognition) Cognition is not only descriptive (how we do cognize), but also normative (how we ought to cognize). Cognitive activity is constrained by norms, and the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. Natural-language statement: The proposition of normative cognition holds that cognition is not a value-neutral activity, but a normative one. Cognition admits of better and worse: some ways of cognizing are good (such as following evidence, remaining consistent, and being open to refutation), while others are bad (such as ignoring evidence, contradicting oneself, and being stubborn). The cognizer ought to pursue good ways of cognizing and avoid ... Formalized statement: Let $C$ be a cognitive activity, $N$ a set of cognitive norms, and $R$ cognitive responsibility. Value-neutral epistemology holds: $$\text{Cognition}(C) \rightarrow \neg\text{Normative}(C)$$ that is, cognitive activity has no normative character. NK-3 holds: $$\text{Cognition}(C) \rightarrow \text{Normative}(C)$$ that is, cognitive activity has a normative character. More concretely: $$\text{Good-Cognition}(C) \Leftrightarrow \text{Conforms}(C, N)$$ $$\text{Conforms}(C, N) \rightarrow R(S, C)$$ that is, good cognition is cognition that conforms to cognitive norms, and conformity to cognitive norms entails cognitive responsibility. II. The Argument for the Proposition Argument One: From Cognitive Goals to NK-3 Cognitive activity has goals — to obtain truth, understand the world, solve problems. These goals are themselves value-laden. To pursue truth rather than falsehood is a value choice. Therefore cognitive activity is value-oriented and has a normative character. Argument Two: From Cognitive Norms to NK-3 Cognitive activity is constrained by norms: we should believe propositions supported by evidence, avoid logical contradiction, and remain open to refutation. These norms tell us how we ought to cognize, and are therefore normative. Argument Three: From Cognitive Evaluation to NK-3 We routinely evaluate cognitive activity: someone's reasoning is good or bad, someone's belief is reasonable or unreasonable, someone's judgment is wise or foolish. Such evaluation presupposes the normativity of cognition. Argument Four: From Cognitive Responsibility to NK-3 We hold cognizers responsible for their cognitive activity: if someone believes a proposition unsupported by evidence, we criticize them; if someone ignores an obvious refutation, we blame them. This attribution of responsibility presupposes the normativity of cognition.

[Box 3.3] The "Normative Turn" in Cognitive Science ——————————————————————————————————

III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication One: Cognitive Virtues and Cognitive Vices If cognition is normative, then there exist cognitive virtues (such as openness, caution, and honesty) and cognitive vices (such as stubbornness, credulity, and self-deception). The cognizer should cultivate cognitive virtues and avoid cognitive vices. Implication Two: Cognitive Responsibility If cognition is normative, then the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. The cognizer can be praised or criticized for their cognitive activity. Implication Three: Cognitive Ethics If cognition is normative, then there exists a cognitive ethics — ethical norms governing cognitive activity. Cognitive ethics may include: the obligation to pursue truth, the obligation to be honest about evidence, and the obligation to be fair to the testimony of others. Table 3.6 The Core Implications of NK-3 | Dimension | Value-Neutral Epistemology | NK-3 Normative Cognition | |------|----------------|----------------| | Nature of cognition | Descriptive | Normative | | Cognitive evaluation | No better or worse | Better or worse | | Cognitive responsibility | None | Yes | | Cognitive ethics | Does not exist | Exists |

§3.3.4 NK-4: Cognitive Humility and Negotiability I. The Statement of the Proposition Proposition NK-4 (Cognitive Humility and Negotiability)

Cognitive standards are not given a priori, universal, and unchanging, but are negotiable and revisable. The cognizer should maintain cognitive humility, acknowledging the limits and fallibility of their own cognition.

Natural-language statement: The proposition of cognitive humility and negotiability holds that there exist no a priori, universal, unchanging cognitive standards. Cognitive standards are historical, cultural, and revisable. Different cognitive communities may adopt different cognitive standards, and these standards can be negotiated and adjusted among one another. The cognizer should remain humble, acknowledging the limits ... Formalized statement: Let $S$ be a cognitive standard, $C$ a cognitive community, and $t$ time. Traditional epistemology holds: $$\exists S^: \forall C, \forall t: \text{ValidStandard}(C, t) = S^$$ that is, there exists a universal, unchanging cognitive standard $S^$. NK-4 holds: $$\neg\exists S^: \forall C, \forall t: \text{ValidStandard}(C, t) = S^$$ that is, there exists no universal, unchanging cognitive standard. More positively: $$\text{ValidStandard}(C, t) = \text{Negotiate}(C, t, \text{Context})$$ that is, a valid cognitive standard is the result of negotiation by a cognitive community at a particular time and in a particular context. II. The Argument for the Proposition Argument One: From the History of Science to NK-4 The history of science shows that scientific cognitive standards have changed historically. Kuhn's theory of paradigms reveals the shift in cognitive standards during scientific revolutions. This supports NK-4: cognitive standards are revisable. Argument Two: From Cultural Diversity to NK-4 Different cultures may have different cognitive practices and cognitive standards. Such diversity shows that there exist no universal, a priori cognitive standards. This supports NK-4: cognitive standards are culturally relative. Argument Three: From Deep Uncertainty to NK-4 Under conditions of deep uncertainty, we cannot determine which cognitive standard is "correct." Different cognitive standards may each have advantages in different situations. This supports NK-4: cognitive standards need to be negotiated according to the situation. Argument Four: From the Fallibility of Cognition to NK-4 Human cognition is fallible. Cognitive standards we once took to be correct may later prove to be mistaken. This supports NK-4: cognitive standards are revisable, and the cognizer should remain humble. Argument Five: From the Cross-Civilizational Context to NK-4 Under interstellar conditions, we may encounter extraterrestrial civilizations with fundamentally different cognitive structures. We cannot assume that human cognitive standards are universally valid. This supports NK-4: cognitive standards need cross-civilizational negotiation. III. The Implications of the Proposition Implication One: Cognitive Humility If cognitive standards are negotiable, then the cognizer should remain humble, acknowledging the limits of their own cognition. Cognitive humility is not skepticism, but a proper assessment of one's own cognitive capacities. Implication Two: Cognitive Openness If cognitive standards are revisable, then the cognizer should remain open to different cognitive standards. Cognitive openness requires taking different cognitive traditions and practices seriously. Implication Three: Cognitive Negotiation If cognitive standards are negotiable, then different cognitive communities need to engage in cognitive negotiation. Cognitive negotiation is the path to building cross-civilizational cognitive consensus. Implication Four: The Epistemological Basis of the Reversibility Principle If cognition is fallible and cognitive standards are revisable, then the cognizer should leave room for correction of error. This provides the epistemological basis for the Reversibility Principle (PR). Table 3.7 The Core Implications of NK-4 | Dimension | Traditional Epistemology | NK-4 Cognitive Humility and Negotiability | |------|------------|------------------------| | Cognitive standards | A priori, universal, unchanging | Negotiable, revisable | | Cognitive attitude | Certainty | Humility | | Cross-cultural cognition | Universal standards | Negotiated standards | | Handling of error | Eliminating error | Leaving room for error |

§3.3.5 The Formalized Statement of the Four Propositions I. The Axiom System NK The four core propositions of the New View of Cognition can be organized into an axiom system NK. The basic structure of the axiom system NK
