II. The Relations among the Axioms There are intrinsic logical connections among the four axioms: Connection One: The Relation between NK-1 and NK-2 Participatory cognition (NK-1) and social knowledge (NK-2) support each other:

  • From NK-1 to NK-2: if cognition is participatory construction, then the constructive process necessarily involves social factors. Cognitive frameworks are social, cognitive tools are social, and cognitive practice is social.
  • From NK-2 to NK-1: if knowledge is a social achievement, then the production of knowledge necessarily involves the participation of multiple cognizers. Knowledge is collectively constructed, not individually discovered.

Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-1} \leftrightarrow \text{NK-2}: \text{Participatory}(C) \leftrightarrow \text{Social}(K)$$ Connection Two: The Relation between NK-1 and NK-3 Participatory cognition (NK-1) and normative cognition (NK-3) support each other:

  • From NK-1 to NK-3: if cognition is participatory, then the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. Responsibility presupposes normativity.
  • From NK-3 to NK-1: if cognition is normative, then the cognizer is an active agent, not a passive receiver.

Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-1} \leftrightarrow \text{NK-3}: \text{Participatory}(C) \leftrightarrow \text{Responsibility}(K)$$ Connection Three: The Relation between NK-2 and NK-4 Social knowledge (NK-2) and negotiability (NK-4) support each other:

  • From NK-2 to NK-4: if knowledge is social, then cognitive standards are social too, and therefore negotiable.
  • From NK-4 to NK-2: if cognitive standards are negotiable, then the process of negotiation is social, and the validation of knowledge depends on social processes.

Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-2} \leftrightarrow \text{NK-4}: \text{Social}(K) \leftrightarrow \text{Negotiable}(S)$$ Connection Four: The Relation between NK-3 and NK-4 Normative cognition (NK-3) and negotiability (NK-4) support each other:

  • From NK-3 to NK-4: if cognition is normative, then cognitive norms require justification. The process of justification is negotiable.
  • From NK-4 to NK-3: if cognitive standards are negotiable, then negotiation is itself a normative activity, constrained by norms.

Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-3} \leftrightarrow \text{NK-4}: \text{Normative}(C) \leftrightarrow \text{Revisable}(N)$$ III. The Relation to the New Cosmology and the New View of Life The New View of Cognition builds on the New Cosmology and the New View of Life: Table 3.8 The Relation between the New View of Cognition and the New Cosmology and New View of Life | Proposition of the New Cosmology / New View of Life | Proposition of the New View of Cognition | Relation | |----------------------|--------------|------| | NC-1 (relationality) | NK-2 (sociality) | Knowledge is a relational social achievement | | NC-2 (process) | NK-1 (participatory) | Cognition is processual participatory construction | | NC-3 (participation) | NK-1 (participatory) | Cognition is participatory | | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | NK-1 (participatory) | Cognition can be realized by different substrates | | NL-3 (continuum) | NK-4 (negotiable) | Cognitive capacity is gradual | Formalized statement: $$\text{NC} \wedge \text{NL} \rightarrow \text{NK}$$ that is, the New Cosmology and the New View of Life provide the ontological basis for the New View of Cognition.

§3.4 The New View of Cognition and Contemporary Epistemology

§3.4.1 The Relation to Social Epistemology I. The Core Claims of Social Epistemology Social epistemology is an important branch of contemporary epistemology, studying the social dimension of knowledge. Its main representatives include Alvin Goldman, Steve Fuller, Miranda Fricker, and others. Table 3.9 The Main Schools of Social Epistemology | School | Representative Figure | Core Claim | |------|----------|----------| | Reliabilist social epistemology | Goldman | Attends to the cognitive reliability of social practice | | Critical social epistemology | Fuller | Attends to the power relations in the production of knowledge | | Feminist epistemology | Harding, Longino | Attends to the gender dimension of knowledge production | | The theory of epistemic justice | Fricker | Attends to questions of justice in cognitive practice | II. What the New View of Cognition and Social Epistemology Share The New View of Cognition and social epistemology share the following core claims: Common Ground One: The Sociality of Knowledge Both hold that knowledge is essentially social, rather than a purely individual achievement. The acquisition, validation, and transmission of knowledge all depend on social processes. Common Ground Two: The Importance of Cognitive Institutions Both emphasize the importance of cognitive institutions (such as peer review, academic publishing, and educational systems) to the production of knowledge. Common Ground Three: The Sociality of Cognitive Norms Both acknowledge that cognitive norms are social, depending on the practices and standards of a cognitive community. III. Where the New View of Cognition and Social Epistemology Differ Difference One: Ontological Basis Social epistemology usually does not concern itself with ontological questions, whereas the New View of Cognition is built on the ontological basis of the New Cosmology (NC). The sociality claim of the New View of Cognition (NK-2) is not only epistemological, but also has ontological support (NC-1 relationality). Difference Two: The Participatory Dimension The New View of Cognition emphasizes the participatory character of cognition (NK-1), a dimension that is not a central concern of social epistemology. The New View of Cognition holds that cognitive frameworks participate in shaping knowable reality, which goes beyond the usual scope of social epistemology. Difference Three: The Interstellar Context The New View of Cognition is explicitly directed at the interstellar context, considering cross-civilizational cognition, AI cognition, and deep uncertainty. Social epistemology mainly concerns knowledge questions within human society. Proposition 3.18 (The Relation between the New View of Cognition and Social Epistemology) The New View of Cognition and social epistemology share the core claim of the sociality of knowledge, but the New View of Cognition has a deeper ontological basis (NC), a stronger participatory dimension (NK-1), and a broader scope of application (the interstellar context). The New View of Cognition can be seen as an extension and deepening of social epistemology under interstellar conditions.

§3.4.2 The Relation to Virtue Epistemology I. The Core Claims of Virtue Epistemology Virtue epistemology is another important branch of contemporary epistemology, shifting the focus of epistemology from belief to the character of the cognizer. Its main representatives include Ernest Sosa, Linda Zagzebski, and others. Definition 3.8 (Virtue Epistemology) Virtue epistemology is an epistemological position which holds that: (1) the central object of cognitive evaluation is the character of the cognizer, not merely belief; (2) knowledge is the manifestation of cognitive virtue; (3) there exist cognitive virtues (such as openness, caution, and honesty) and cognitive vices (such as stubbornness, credulity, and self-deception); (4) the cognizer should cultivate cognitive virtues. The two main branches of virtue epistemology: | Branch | Representative Figure | Core Claim | |------|----------|----------| | Reliabilist virtue epistemology | Sosa, Greco | Cognitive virtue is a reliable cognitive capacity | | Responsibilist virtue epistemology | Zagzebski, Code | Cognitive virtue is a trait of character | II. What the New View of Cognition and Virtue Epistemology Share Common Ground One: The Normativity of Cognition Both hold that cognition is normative, and that there are good and bad ways of cognizing. NK-3 (normative cognition) agrees with the core claim of virtue epistemology. Common Ground Two: Cognitive Responsibility Both hold that the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. The cognizer can be praised or criticized for their cognitive activity. Common Ground Three: The Importance of Cognitive Character Both emphasize the importance of cognitive character (cognitive virtue). A good cognizer not only holds correct beliefs, but also has a good cognitive character. III. Where the New View of Cognition and Virtue Epistemology Differ Difference One: The Social Dimension Virtue epistemology mainly concerns the character of individual cognizers, whereas the New View of Cognition emphasizes the sociality of knowledge (NK-2). The New View of Cognition holds that cognitive virtue is not only an individual trait of character, but also a social practical capacity. Difference Two: The Participatory Dimension The New View of Cognition emphasizes the participatory character of cognition (NK-1): the cognizer participates in constructing knowable reality. This dimension is not a central concern of virtue epistemology. Difference Three: The Negotiability Dimension The New View of Cognition emphasizes the negotiability of cognitive standards (NK-4), whereas virtue epistemology usually assumes that there exist universal standards of cognitive virtue. Proposition 3.19 (The Relation between the New View of Cognition and Virtue Epistemology) The New View of Cognition and virtue epistemology share the core claim of the normativity of cognition, but the New View of Cognition adds the social dimension (NK-2), the participatory dimension (NK-1), and the negotiability dimension (NK-4). The New View of Cognition can be seen as a socialized and situated extension of virtue epistemology.

§3.4.3 The Relation to Pragmatist Epistemology I. The Core Claims of Pragmatist Epistemology Pragmatist epistemology stems from the American pragmatist tradition; its main representatives include Charles Peirce, William James, and John Dewey. Definition 3.9 (Pragmatist Epistemology) Pragmatist epistemology is an epistemological position which holds that: (1) knowledge is a tool for action, not a mirror reflection of reality; (2) truth is "what works" — a belief that works in practice is true; (3) cognition is a process of problem-solving, not a purely theoretical activity; (4) cognition and action are unified. Dewey's critique of the "spectator theory of knowledge" is a central contribution of pragmatist epistemology. Dewey holds that cognition is not a passive reflection of a pre-existing reality, but an active inquiry interacting with the environment. II. What the New View of Cognition and Pragmatist Epistemology Share Common Ground One: Anti-Spectator Epistemology Both oppose spectator epistemology, holding that cognition is participatory and practical. NK-1 (participatory cognition) agrees with Dewey's critique. Common Ground Two: The Unity of Cognition and Action Both hold that cognition and action are unified, and that cognition serves practical ends. Common Ground Three: The Situatedness of Cognition Both emphasize the situatedness of cognition: cognition depends on the concrete problem situation. III. Where the New View of Cognition and Pragmatist Epistemology Differ Difference One: Ontological Basis The New View of Cognition is built on the ontological basis of the New Cosmology (NC), whereas pragmatist epistemology usually avoids ontological questions or takes an anti-ontological stance. Difference Two: The Degree of Emphasis on Sociality Although Dewey emphasizes the sociality of cognition, the New View of Cognition's emphasis on the sociality of knowledge is more systematic (NK-2). Difference Three: The Interstellar Context The New View of Cognition is explicitly directed at the interstellar context, considering cross-civilizational cognition, AI cognition, and so on. Pragmatist epistemology mainly concerns the context of human practice. Proposition 3.20 (The Relation between the New View of Cognition and Pragmatist Epistemology) The New View of Cognition and pragmatist epistemology share the core position of anti-spectator epistemology, but the New View of Cognition has a clearer ontological basis (NC), a more systematic emphasis on sociality (NK-2), and a broader scope of application (the interstellar context). The New View of Cognition can be seen as a development of pragmatist epistemology under interstellar conditions.

§3.4.4 The Distinctive Position of This Work I. Synthesis and Transcendence The New View of Cognition synthesizes the insights of social epistemology, virtue epistemology, and pragmatist epistemology, while transcending their respective limits: Table 3.10 A Comparison of the New View of Cognition with Contemporary Epistemological Schools | Dimension | Social Epistemology | Virtue Epistemology | Pragmatist Epistemology | The New View of Cognition | |------|------------|------------|----------------|----------| | Sociality of knowledge | Central | Secondary | Important | Central (NK-2) | | Normativity of cognition | Important | Central | Important | Central (NK-3) | | Participatory character of cognition | Secondary | Secondary | Central | Central (NK-1) | | Negotiability of standards | Partial | Less | Partial | Central (NK-4) | | Ontological basis | Less | Less | Avoided | Explicit (NC) | | Interstellar context | None | None | None | Central | II. The Distinctive Contributions of the New View of Cognition Contribution One: Ontological Basis The New View of Cognition is built on the ontological basis of the New Cosmology (NC), providing ontological support for its epistemological claims. This makes the New View of Cognition not only epistemological, but a unified ontological-epistemological framework. Contribution Two: The Integration of Four Dimensions The New View of Cognition integrates four dimensions — participation (NK-1), sociality (NK-2), normativity (NK-3), and negotiability (NK-4) — forming a systematic epistemological framework. Contribution Three: Applicability to the Interstellar Context The New View of Cognition is explicitly directed at the interstellar context, and can handle cross-civilizational cognition, AI cognition, and deep uncertainty — problems that traditional epistemology struggles to handle. Contribution Four: Normative Implications The New View of Cognition has clear normative implications, providing the epistemological basis for the Reversibility Principle (PR) and the CRV (Commitment-Validation Ratio). Proposition 3.21 (The Distinctive Position of the New View of Cognition) The New View of Cognition synthesizes the insights of social epistemology, virtue epistemology, and pragmatist epistemology, while making distinctive contributions: an ontological basis (NC), the integration of four dimensions (NK-1 through NK-4), applicability to the interstellar context, and clear normative implications. The New View of Cognition is an epistemological framework designed for the governance of interstellar civilizations.

§3.5 The Normative Implications of the New View of Cognition

§3.5.1 From Participation to Responsible Cognition I. The Normative Implications of NK-1 NK-1 (participatory cognition) carries profound normative implications: if cognition is participatory, then the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. The derivation from NK-1 to cognitive responsibility: Step 1: NK-1 (participatory cognition) Cognition is participatory construction; the cognitive framework participates in shaping knowable reality Step 2: The cognizer is active If cognition is participatory, then the cognizer is an active agent, not a passive receiver Step 3: Activeness entails responsibility An active agent bears responsibility for their actions Step 4: Cognitive responsibility The cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity Conclusion: Participatory cognition entails cognitive responsibility II. The Concrete Content of Cognitive Responsibility Cognitive responsibility includes the following dimensions: Table 3.11 The Dimensions of Cognitive Responsibility | Dimension of Responsibility | Concrete Content | Example | |----------|----------|------| | Responsibility for framework choice | Responsibility for the choice of cognitive framework | Choosing an appropriate theoretical framework | | Responsibility for evidence | Responsibility for the collection and assessment of evidence | Collecting relevant evidence comprehensively | | Responsibility for reasoning | Responsibility for the reasoning process | Avoiding logical fallacies | | Responsibility for transmission | Responsibility for the transmission of cognitive results | Not spreading information known to be false | | Responsibility for consequences | Responsibility for the consequences of cognitive activity | Considering the impact of cognitive activity | Proposition 3.22 (From NK-1 to Cognitive Responsibility) NK-1 (participatory cognition) entails cognitive responsibility: if cognition is participatory, then the cognizer bears responsibility for their cognitive activity. Cognitive responsibility includes responsibility for framework choice, evidence, reasoning, transmission, and consequences.

§3.5.2 From Sociality to the Obligation to Negotiate I. The Normative Implications of NK-2 NK-2 (social knowledge) carries profound normative implications: if knowledge is social, then the cognizer has an obligation to participate in cognitive negotiation. The derivation from NK-2 to the obligation to negotiate: Step 1: NK-2 (social knowledge) Knowledge is a social achievement, depending on social validation Step 2: Social validation requires participation Social validation requires the participation of cognizers Step 3: Participation is an obligation If knowledge depends on social validation, then participating in social validation is an obligation of the cognizer Step 4: The obligation to negotiate The cognizer has an obligation to participate in cognitive negotiation Conclusion: Social knowledge entails the obligation to negotiate II. The Concrete Content of the Obligation to Negotiate The obligation to negotiate includes the following dimensions: Table 3.12 The Dimensions of the Obligation to Negotiate | Dimension of Obligation | Concrete Content | Example | |----------|----------|------| | Obligation to participate | Participate in the discussions of the cognitive community | Participating in academic discussion | | Obligation to listen | Listen carefully to others' viewpoints | Remaining open to different viewpoints | | Obligation to respond | Respond to criticism and challenge | Responding to peer-review comments | | Obligation to revise | Revise one's views in light of the results of negotiation | Revising beliefs in light of new evidence | | Obligation to be fair | Treat different cognitive contributions fairly | Avoiding testimonial injustice | Proposition 3.23 (From NK-2 to the Obligation to Negotiate) NK-2 (social knowledge) entails the obligation to negotiate: if knowledge is social, then the cognizer has an obligation to participate in cognitive negotiation. The obligation to negotiate includes the obligation to participate, to listen, to respond, to revise, and to be fair.

§3.5.3 From Normativity to Reflective Commitment I. The Normative Implications of NK-3 NK-3 (normative cognition) carries profound normative implications: if cognition is normative, then the cognizer is committed to reflecting on their own cognitive activity. The derivation from NK-3 to reflective commitment: Step 1: NK-3 (normative cognition) Cognition is normative; there exist cognitive norms Step 2: Conformity to norms requires reflection Conforming to norms requires reflecting on whether one's activity conforms to the norms Step 3: Reflection is part of cognitive activity Reflecting on one's own cognitive activity is itself a cognitive activity Step 4: Reflective commitment The cognizer is committed to reflecting on their own cognitive activity Conclusion: Normative cognition entails reflective commitment II. The Concrete Content of Reflective Commitment Reflective commitment includes the following dimensions: Table 3.13 The Dimensions of Reflective Commitment | Dimension of Commitment | Concrete Content | Example | |----------|----------|------| | Self-monitoring | Monitor one's own cognitive processes | Checking whether reasoning is valid | | Bias identification | Identify one's own cognitive biases | Being aware of confirmation bias | | Norm assessment | Assess whether one conforms to cognitive norms | Checking whether one follows the evidence | | Metacognition | Cognition about one's own cognition | Assessing one's own cognitive capacities | | Continuous improvement | Continuously improve cognitive practice | Learning new methods of cognition | Proposition 3.24 (From NK-3 to Reflective Commitment) NK-3 (normative cognition) entails reflective commitment: if cognition is normative, then the cognizer is committed to reflecting on their own cognitive activity. Reflective commitment includes self-monitoring, bias identification, norm assessment, metacognition, and continuous improvement.

§3.5.4 From Humility to Reversibility I. The Normative Implications of NK-4 NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) carries profound normative implications: if cognition is fallible and cognitive standards are revisable, then the cognizer should leave room for the correction of error. This provides the epistemological basis for the Reversibility Principle (PR). The derivation from NK-4 to the Reversibility Principle: Step 1: NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) Cognition is fallible; cognitive standards are revisable Step 2: Fallibility requires room for correction If cognition is fallible, then room for the correction of error should be left Step 3: Correction requires reversibility Correcting an error requires that action be reversible Step 4: The Reversibility Principle Reversible actions should be preferred Conclusion: Cognitive humility entails the Reversibility Principle II. The Epistemological Basis of the Reversibility Principle The epistemological basis of the Reversibility Principle (PR) is cognitive humility: Table 3.14 The Epistemological Basis of the Reversibility Principle | Epistemological Premise | Normative Conclusion | |------------|------------| | Cognition is fallible | Room for the correction of error should be left | | Cognitive standards are revisable | One should remain open to the revision of standards | | Future cognition may surpass present cognition | Possibilities should be preserved for future cognition | | Different cognitive frameworks may each have advantages | One should avoid irreversibly excluding certain frameworks | Proposition 3.25 (From NK-4 to the Reversibility Principle) NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) provides the epistemological basis for the Reversibility Principle (PR): if cognition is fallible and cognitive standards are revisable, then reversible actions should be preferred, leaving room for the correction of error and the revision of standards. III. The Conceptual Basis of the CRV NK-4 also provides the conceptual basis for the CRV (Commitment-to-Reversibility Value). The CRV measures the relation between the degree of commitment of a decision and its reversibility. Definition 3.10 (The Conceptual Basis of the CRV) The CRV (Commitment-to-Reversibility Value) is an indicator measuring the relation between the degree of commitment of a decision and its reversibility. Its epistemological basis is NK-4: if cognition is fallible, then decisions with high commitment and low reversibility require stronger epistemological justification. Formalized statement: $$\text{CRV}(d) = \frac{\text{Commitment}(d)}{\text{Reversibility}(d)}$$ Here $d$ is a decision, $\text{Commitment}(d)$ the degree of commitment of the decision, and $\text{Reversibility}(d)$ the reversibility of the decision. The higher the CRV, the stronger the epistemological justification a decision requires.

Chapter 3 Appendix: Axiomatic System NK Quick Reference

Table 3.C Axiomatic System NK Quick-Reference Table | Axiom | Name | Formal Expression | Meaning | |------|------|------------|------| | NK-1a | Cognitive Content Determined | $C = g(K, E, F)$ | Cognitive content is jointly determined by the knower, the environment, and the framework | | NK-1b | Cognitive Change | $\text{Cognize}(k,e) \rightarrow \text{Change}(k) \vee \text{Change}(e)$ | Cognition changes the knower or the environment | | NK-1c | Framework Constitutivity | $F \in \text{Constitutive}(C)$ | The framework is a constitutive part of cognitive content | | NK-2a | Social Validation | $\text{Knowledge}(p) \rightarrow \text{SocialValidation}(p, \text{Com})$ | Knowledge requires social validation | | NK-2b | Community Dependence | $\text{Knowledge}(k,p) \rightarrow \exists \text{com}: \text{Member}(k,\text{com})$ | Individual knowledge depends on community membership | | NK-2c | Collective Knowledge | $\exists p: \text{Knowledge}(\text{Com},p) \wedge \neg\exists k: \text{Knowledge}(k,p)$ | There exists irreducible collective knowledge | | NK-3a | Cognitive Normativity | $\text{Cognition}(c) \rightarrow \text{Normative}(c)$ | Cognition is normative | | NK-3b | Definition of Good Cognition | $\text{Good-Cognition}(c) \leftrightarrow \text{Conforms}(c, N)$ | Good cognition conforms to cognitive norms | | NK-3c | Norms Imply Responsibility | $\text{Conforms}(c, N) \rightarrow \text{Responsibility}(k, c)$ | Conformity to norms implies responsibility | | NK-4a | No Universal Standard | $\neg\exists S^: \forall \text{Com},\forall t: \text{ValidStandard}(\text{Com},t) = S^$ | No universal and invariant cognitive standard exists | | NK-4b | Negotiated Standard | $\text{ValidStandard}(\text{Com},t) = \text{Negotiate}(\text{Com}, t, \text{Context})$ | Valid standards are the outcome of negotiation | | NK-4c | Standards Are Revisable | $\forall s \in S: \text{Revisable}(s)$ | All cognitive standards are revisable |

Chapter 3 Appendix: CRV Conceptual Foundations Quick Reference

Table 3.E Conceptual Foundations of CRV (Commitment-to-Reversibility Value) | Attribute | Content | |------|------| | Full name | Commitment-to-Reversibility Value | | Abbreviation | CRV | | Theoretical basis | NK-4 (Cognitive Humility and Negotiability) | | Core function | Measuring the relation between the degree of commitment and reversibility of a decision | | Basic formula | $\text{CRV}(d) = \frac{\text{Commitment}(d)}{\text{Reversibility}(d)}$ | | Normative implication | The higher the CRV, the stronger the epistemic justification a decision requires | | Detailed design | Chapter 8 | The relation between CRV and NK-4:

  • NK-4 provides the conceptual foundation: cognition is fallible and standards are revisable
  • CRV provides an operationalization tool: it translates NK-4 into a measurable indicator
  • The normative implication of CRV: decisions with high commitment and low reversibility require stronger justification

Chapter 3 Appendix: The Five Dimensions of Cognitive Responsibility Explained

Table 3.F The Five Dimensions of Cognitive Responsibility | Dimension | Definition | Specific Content | Consequence of Violation | |------|------|----------|------------| | Responsibility for framework choice | Responsibility for the choice of cognitive framework | Selecting appropriate theoretical frameworks, conceptual tools, and methods of analysis | Cognitive bias, misleading conclusions | | Evidential responsibility | Responsibility for the collection and assessment of evidence | Collecting all relevant evidence, assessing evidence impartially, not ignoring counterevidence | One-sided conclusions, confirmation bias | | Responsibility for reasoning | Responsibility for the process of reasoning | Following logical rules, avoiding fallacies, maintaining consistency | Invalid reasoning, self-contradiction | | Responsibility for dissemination | Responsibility for the dissemination of cognitive results | Communicating accurately, not exaggerating, not spreading information known to be false | Misleading others, spreading fallacies | | Responsibility for consequences | Responsibility for the consequences of cognitive activity | Considering the impact of cognitive activity and foreseeing possible consequences | Causing harm, irresponsibility |

The Unity and Interconnection of the Three ViewsChapter 4

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Place of This Chapter in the Book Chapter 4 is the synthesizing link in the argument for the Three New Views, and stands at the L1 layer of the protocol stack (the ontological-epistemological framework layer). Its task is to argue for the intrinsic unity among the New Cosmology (NC), the New View of Life (NL), and the New View of Cognition (NK), showing how the three views support one another and jointly constitute a coherent ontological-epistemological ... III. The Core Tasks of This Chapter This chapter undertakes four core tasks: Task One: Argue for the logical connections among the Three Views

  • How does the New Cosmology entail the New View of Life?
  • How does the New View of Life entail the New View of Cognition?
  • How does the New View of Cognition support the New Cosmology retrospectively?
  • How do the Three Views form a circular, mutually constituting whole?

Task Two: Reveal the common basis of the Three Views

  • How does relationality run through the Three Views?
  • How does process run through the Three Views?
  • How does participation run through the Three Views?

Task Three: Establish an integrative framework for the Three Views

  • What is the formalized statement of the integrative framework?
  • How is the integrative framework applied to concrete problems?

Task Four: Dialogue with traditional philosophy and acknowledge limits

  • What is the relation between the Three Views and the Western metaphysical tradition?
  • What is the relation between the Three Views and the Eastern philosophical tradition?
  • What open problems and limits do the Three Views have?

IV. Deliverables of This Chapter After reading this chapter, the reader will obtain:

  • a formalized argument for the logical connections among the Three Views
  • a systematic exposition of the common basis of the Three Views (relationality, process, participation)
  • a formalized statement and diagram of the integrative framework of the Three Views
  • a positioning of the dialogue between the Three Views and traditional philosophy
  • an honest acknowledgment of the limits and open problems of the Three Views

V. Continuity with the Previous Three Chapters This chapter builds on the previous three chapters: Output of Chapter 1: NC-1 (relationality), NC-2 (process), NC-3 (participation) Output of Chapter 2: NL-1 (cross-substrate), NL-2 (negentropy), NL-3 (continuum) Output of Chapter 3: NK-1 (participatory), NK-2 (sociality), NK-3 (normativity), NK-4 (negotiability) The task of this chapter: to argue how these ten propositions form a unified theoretical framework VI. Methodological Note This chapter follows the methodological commitments established in Chapter 0:

  1. Formalized argument: the relations among the Three Views are stated in a formalized way.
  2. Boundary statements: the boundaries and limits of the unity argument are made explicit.
  3. Open problems: unsolved problems are honestly acknowledged.
  4. Revisability: the unity framework is revisable, not a closed dogma.

VII. Reading Advice Readers with a philosophical background: focus on §4.4 (the dialogue with traditional philosophy). Readers with a formal background: focus on §4.3 (the formalized statement of the integrative framework). Critical readers: focus on §4.5 (limits and open problems). Readers wanting a quick overview: read the chapter opening guide, §4.3.2 (the diagram), and the chapter summary. Estimated reading time: about 3-4 hours for a full read.

§4.1 The Logical Connections among the Three Views

§4.1.1 From the New Cosmology to the New View of Life I. The Basic Structure of the Logical Connection There is a profound logical connection between the New Cosmology (NC) and the New View of Life (NL). The New Cosmology provides the ontological basis for the New View of Life, and the New View of Life is the concrete unfolding of the New Cosmology in the domain of life. Proposition 4.1 (The Entailment Relation from NC to NL) The three core propositions of the New Cosmology (NC-1, NC-2, NC-3) entail the three core propositions of the New View of Life (NL-1, NL-2, NL-3). This entailment is not a strict logical deduction, but a conceptual, natural extension. Formalized statement: $$\text{NC} \Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}} \text{NL}$$ Here $\Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}}$ denotes a relation of conceptual entailment. II. The Derivation from NC-1 to NL-1 NC-1 (relationality) holds that the basic unit of reality is relation, not substance. This ontological position has direct implications for the concept of life. The path of derivation: Step 1: NC-1 (relationality) The basic unit of reality is relation, not independently existing substance Step 2: Life is part of reality Life exists within the universe, and is a form of reality Step 3: The relational nature of life If reality is relational, then life is relational too Life is not an independently existing substance, but an organizational pattern in a network of relations Step 4: A functional definition If life is an organizational pattern in a network of relations, then the essence of life is functional Function can be realized by different material substrates Conclusion: NL-1 (cross-substrate life) The essence of life is functional, and is not limited to a particular material substrate Proposition 4.2 (From NC-1 to NL-1) NC-1 (relationality) entails NL-1 (cross-substrate life): if the basic unit of reality is relation rather than substance, then life, as a form of reality, is essentially relational and functional rather than material. Therefore life is not limited to a particular material substrate. Formalized statement: $$\text{NC-1} \wedge \text{Life} \subseteq \text{Reality} \Rightarrow \text{NL-1}$$ III. The Derivation from NC-2 to NL-2 NC-2 (process) holds that reality is processual: change and becoming are basic, and static existence is derivative. This ontological position has direct implications for the conditions of life's persistence. The path of derivation: Step 1: NC-2 (process) Reality is processual; change and becoming are basic Step 2: Life is a process Life is not static existence, but a continuous process Step 3: A process requires maintenance The continuation of any process requires the maintenance of conditions Step 4: Thermodynamic constraint In the physical universe, the maintenance of a process requires an input of energy/negentropy (This is a physical constraint at the L₀ layer.) Step 5: The negentropy condition of life Life, as a process, requires the maintenance of a flow of negentropy for its continuation Conclusion: NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) Life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence Proposition 4.3 (From NC-2 to NL-2) NC-2 (process) entails NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence): if reality is processual, then life, as a process, requires the maintenance of conditions for its continuation. In the physical universe, this condition is a flow of negentropy. Therefore life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence. Formalized statement: $$\text{NC-2} \wedge \text{Life} = \text{Process} \wedge \text{PhysicalConstraints} \Rightarrow \text{NL-2}$$ IV. The Derivation from NC-3 to NL-3 NC-3 (participation) holds that the universe is participatory: the observer participates in constructing reality. This ontological position has direct implications for the understanding of consciousness. The path of derivation: Step 1: NC-3 (participation) The universe is participatory; the observer participates in constructing reality Step 2: Consciousness is the basis of participation Participation requires some form of consciousness or perceptual capacity Step 3: The gradualness of participation If participation is a basic feature of the universe, then participation may be gradual Different systems may have different degrees of participatory capacity Step 4: The gradualness of consciousness If participatory capacity is gradual, then consciousness, as the basis of participation, is gradual too Conclusion: NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) Consciousness is a gradual, multidimensional continuum Proposition 4.4 (From NC-3 to NL-3) NC-3 (participation) entails NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness): if the universe is participatory, then participatory capacity may be gradual. Consciousness, as the basis of participation, is therefore gradual rather than binary. Formalized statement: $$\text{NC-3} \wedge \text{Participation} = \text{Graded} \Rightarrow \text{NL-3}$$ V. The Comprehensive Derivation from NC to NL Taking the above analysis together, the derivation from the New Cosmology to the New View of Life can be represented as: Table 4.1 The Derivation Relations from NC to NL | Proposition of the New Cosmology | Proposition of the New View of Life | Path of Derivation | |--------------|--------------|----------| | NC-1 (relationality) | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | relationality -> functionality -> cross-substrate | | NC-2 (process) | NL-2 (negentropy) | process -> conditions of maintenance -> negentropy | | NC-3 (participation) | NL-3 (continuum) | participation -> gradualness -> continuum | Formalized statement: $$\text{NC} = \{\text{NC-1}, \text{NC-2}, \text{NC-3}\}$$ $$\text{NL} = \{\text{NL-1}, \text{NL-2}, \text{NL-3}\}$$ $$\text{NC} \Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}} \text{NL}$$ Boundary Statement 4.1 (The Boundary of the Derivation from NC to NL) The derivation from NC to NL is a conceptual entailment, not a strict logical deduction. This means:

  • the derivation depends on certain background assumptions (such as that life is part of reality);
  • there may be other paths of derivation;
  • the validity of the derivation can be questioned and revised;
  • even if NC were revised, NL might still hold on other grounds.

§4.1.2 From the New View of Life to the New View of Cognition I. The Basic Structure of the Logical Connection There is a profound logical connection between the New View of Life (NL) and the New View of Cognition (NK). The New View of Life provides the conceptual basis for the subject in the New View of Cognition, and the New View of Cognition is the concrete unfolding of the New View of Life in the domain of cognition. Proposition 4.5 (The Entailment Relation from NL to NK) The three core propositions of the New View of Life (NL-1, NL-2, NL-3) entail the four core propositions of the New View of Cognition (NK-1, NK-2, NK-3, NK-4). This entailment is a conceptual, natural extension. Formalized statement: $$\text{NL} \Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}} \text{NK}$$ II. The Derivation from NL-1 to NK-1 NL-1 (cross-substrate life) holds that the essence of life is functional, and is not limited to a particular material substrate. This position has direct implications for the understanding of cognition. The path of derivation: Step 1: NL-1 (cross-substrate life) The essence of life is functional, and is not limited to a particular material substrate Step 2: Cognition is a function of life Cognition is a function of living systems Step 3: The functionality of cognition If life is functional, then cognition, as a function of life, is functional too Step 4: The constructive character of cognition Functional cognition is not passive reflection, but active construction The cognitive system participates in constructing the content of cognition through its functional organization Conclusion: NK-1 (participatory cognition) Cognition is participatory construction, rather than passive reflection Proposition 4.6 (From NL-1 to NK-1) NL-1 (cross-substrate life) entails NK-1 (participatory cognition): if the essence of life is functional, then cognition, as a function of life, is functional and constructive, rather than passive reflection. Formalized statement: $$\text{NL-1} \wedge \text{Cognition} \subseteq \text{LifeFunction} \Rightarrow \text{NK-1}$$ III. The Derivation from NL-2 to NK-2 and NK-3 NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) holds that life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence. This position has implications for the sociality and normativity of cognition. The path of derivation (to NK-2): Step 1: NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) Life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence Step 2: Cognition requires resources Cognitive activity requires energy and informational resources Step 3: The social acquisition of resources In complex living systems, the acquisition of cognitive resources is social The production, validation, and transmission of knowledge depend on social structures Conclusion: NK-2 (social knowledge) Knowledge is a social achievement, not an individual possession The path of derivation (to NK-3): Step 1: NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) Life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence Step 2: The maintenance of negentropy requires effective cognition Living systems require effective cognition to maintain negentropy Ineffective cognition may lead to the interruption of the flow of negentropy Step 3: The normativity of cognition The distinction between effective and ineffective is normative Cognitive activity therefore has a normative dimension Conclusion: NK-3 (normative cognition) Cognition has a normative dimension, and involves questions of what ought to be Proposition 4.7 (From NL-2 to NK-2 and NK-3) NL-2 (the negentropy condition of persistence) entails NK-2 (social knowledge) and NK-3 (normative cognition): if life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence, then cognition, as a means of maintaining negentropy, has a social mode of resource acquisition (NK-2) and a normative character of effectiveness (NK-3). Formalized statement: $$\text{NL-2} \wedge \text{Cognition} = \text{NegentropyMaintenance} \Rightarrow \text{NK-2} \wedge \text{NK-3}$$ IV. The Derivation from NL-3 to NK-4 NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) holds that consciousness is a gradual, multidimensional continuum. This position has direct implications for the understanding of cognitive standards. The path of derivation: Step 1: NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) Consciousness is a gradual, multidimensional continuum Step 2: The gradualness of cognitive capacity If consciousness is gradual, then cognitive capacity is gradual too Different systems have different degrees of cognitive capacity Step 3: The relativity of cognitive standards If cognitive capacity is gradual, then cognitive standards may be relative to cognitive capacity There exist no universal standards applicable to all cognitive systems Step 4: The negotiability of cognitive standards If cognitive standards are relative, then different cognitive systems need to negotiate cognitive standards Conclusion: NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) Cognitive standards are negotiable, rather than fixed a priori Proposition 4.8 (From NL-3 to NK-4) NL-3 (the continuum of consciousness) entails NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability): if consciousness is gradual, then cognitive capacity is gradual too, and cognitive standards are therefore relative and negotiable, rather than fixed a priori. Formalized statement: $$\text{NL-3} \wedge \text{CognitiveCapacity} = \text{Graded} \Rightarrow \text{NK-4}$$ V. The Comprehensive Derivation from NL to NK Taking the above analysis together, the derivation from the New View of Life to the New View of Cognition can be represented as: Table 4.2 The Derivation Relations from NL to NK | Proposition of the New View of Life | Proposition of the New View of Cognition | Path of Derivation | |--------------|--------------|----------| | NL-1 (cross-substrate) | NK-1 (participatory) | functionality -> constructiveness -> participatory | | NL-2 (negentropy) | NK-2 (sociality) | negentropy maintenance -> resource acquisition -> sociality | | NL-2 (negentropy) | NK-3 (normativity) | negentropy maintenance -> effectiveness -> normativity | | NL-3 (continuum) | NK-4 (negotiability) | gradualness -> relativity -> negotiability | Formalized statement: $$\text{NL} = \{\text{NL-1}, \text{NL-2}, \text{NL-3}\}$$ $$\text{NK} = \{\text{NK-1}, \text{NK-2}, \text{NK-3}, \text{NK-4}\}$$ $$\text{NL} \Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}} \text{NK}$$

§4.1.3 From the New View of Cognition Back to the New Cosmology I. The Basic Structure of the Logical Connection There is a relation of retrospective support between the New View of Cognition (NK) and the New Cosmology (NC). The New View of Cognition is not only a result of the New Cosmology, but also supports and deepens it in turn. Proposition 4.9 (The Retrospective Support from NK to NC) The four core propositions of the New View of Cognition (NK-1, NK-2, NK-3, NK-4) retrospectively support the three core propositions of the New Cosmology (NC-1, NC-2, NC-3). This support is a conceptual, mutual reinforcement. Formalized statement: $$\text{NK} \Rightarrow_{\text{support}} \text{NC}$$ II. The Retrospective Support from NK-1 to NC-3 NK-1 (participatory cognition) holds that cognition is participatory construction. This position retrospectively supports NC-3 (participation). The path of support: Step 1: NK-1 (participatory cognition) Cognition is participatory construction; the cognitive framework participates in shaping knowable reality Step 2: Cognition is part of the universe Cognitive activity occurs within the universe, and is part of cosmic processes Step 3: The participatory character of cognition entails the participatory character of the universe If cognition is participatory, then there exist at least participatory processes in the universe This supports the claim that the universe is participatory Conclusion: NK-1 supports NC-3 Participatory cognition provides a concrete instance and support for a participatory universe Proposition 4.10 (The Retrospective Support from NK-1 to NC-3) NK-1 (participatory cognition) retrospectively supports NC-3 (participation): participatory cognition is a concrete instance of a participatory universe. The participatory character of cognition provides an empirical basis and conceptual support for the participatory character of the universe. Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-1} \Rightarrow_{\text{support}} \text{NC-3}$$ III. The Retrospective Support from NK-2 to NC-1 NK-2 (social knowledge) holds that knowledge is a social achievement. This position retrospectively supports NC-1 (relationality). The path of support: Step 1: NK-2 (social knowledge) Knowledge is a social achievement, depending on social structures and relations Step 2: Knowledge is about reality Knowledge is a cognitive achievement about reality Step 3: The sociality of knowledge entails the relationality of reality If knowledge about reality is social and relational, then reality itself may also be relational (This is an inference from epistemology to ontology.) Conclusion: NK-2 supports NC-1 Social knowledge provides epistemological support for a relational reality Proposition 4.11 (The Retrospective Support from NK-2 to NC-1) NK-2 (social knowledge) retrospectively supports NC-1 (relationality): if knowledge is social and relational, then this provides epistemological support for the relationality of reality. The sociality of knowledge and the relationality of reality echo each other. Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-2} \Rightarrow_{\text{support}} \text{NC-1}$$ IV. The Retrospective Support from NK-4 to NC-2 NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) holds that cognitive standards are negotiable and revisable. This position retrospectively supports NC-2 (process). The path of support: Step 1: NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) Cognitive standards are negotiable and revisable, rather than fixed a priori Step 2: The historicity of cognitive standards If cognitive standards are revisable, then cognitive standards are historical and processual Step 3: The processual character of cognition entails the processual character of reality If cognition is processual, then reality, as the object of cognition, may also be processual A static reality would not require revisable cognitive standards Conclusion: NK-4 supports NC-2 The revisability of cognitive standards provides epistemological support for the processual character of reality Proposition 4.12 (The Retrospective Support from NK-4 to NC-2) NK-4 (cognitive humility and negotiability) retrospectively supports NC-2 (process): if cognitive standards are revisable and processual, then this provides epistemological support for the processual character of reality. The processual character of cognition and that of reality echo each other. Formalized statement: $$\text{NK-4} \Rightarrow_{\text{support}} \text{NC-2}$$ V. The Comprehensive Retrospective Support from NK to NC Taking the above analysis together, the retrospective support from the New View of Cognition to the New Cosmology can be represented as: Table 4.3 The Retrospective Support Relations from NK to NC | Proposition of the New View of Cognition | Proposition of the New Cosmology | Path of Support | |--------------|--------------|----------| | NK-1 (participatory) | NC-3 (participation) | participatory cognition -> participatory universe | | NK-2 (sociality) | NC-1 (relationality) | relationality of knowledge -> relationality of reality | | NK-4 (negotiability) | NC-2 (process) | processual character of cognition -> processual character of reality | Formalized statement: $$\text{NK} \Rightarrow_{\text{support}} \text{NC}$$ Boundary Statement 4.2 (The Boundary of the Retrospective Support from NK to NC) The retrospective support from NK to NC is a conceptual, mutual reinforcement, not a strict logical proof. This means:

  • retrospective support is not circular reasoning, but mutual coherence;
  • retrospective support enhances the overall credibility of the Three Views;
  • retrospective support can be questioned and revised;
  • even if some retrospective support were weakened, other parts of the Three Views might still hold.

§4.1.4 The Circular Mutual Constitution of the Three Views I. The Basic Structure of Circular Mutual Constitution The analysis of the previous three sections reveals the circular relation among the Three Views:

II. The Character of Circular Mutual Constitution Proposition 4.13 (The Circular Mutual Constitution of the Three Views) The Three New Views (NC, NL, NK) form a circular, mutually constituting whole: NC entails NL, NL entails NK, and NK retrospectively supports NC. This circle is not a vicious circle, but a mutually coherent whole. Formalized statement: $$\text{NC} \Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}} \text{NL} \Rightarrow_{\text{conceptual}} \text{NK} \Rightarrow_{\text{support}} \text{NC}$$ The character of circular mutual constitution: | Character | Explanation | |------|------| | Not a vicious circle | Not the circular argument of proving B by A and then A by B | | Mutual coherence | The Three Views support one another, forming a coherent whole | | The whole exceeds its parts | The overall credibility of the Three Views exceeds the sum of the parts | | Revisability | Any link in the circle can be revised | III. Circular Mutual Constitution and Coherentism The circular mutual constitution of the Three Views embodies the epistemological position of coherentism. Coherentism holds that the justification of a belief does not depend on basic beliefs, but on the overall coherence of a system of beliefs. Proposition 4.14 (The Coherence of the Three Views) The justification of the Three New Views does not depend on some "basic" proposition, but on the overall coherence of the Three Views. The Three Views support one another, forming a coherent network of beliefs. Formalized statement: Let $B = \{\text{NC-1}, \text{NC-2}, \text{NC-3}, \text{NL-1}, \text{NL-2}, \text{NL-3}, \text{NK-1}, \text{NK-2}, \text{NK-3}, \text{NK-4}\}$. Definition of coherence: $$\text{Coherent}(B) \Leftrightarrow \forall b_i, b_j \in B: \text{Support}(b_i, b_j) \vee \text{Consistent}(b_i, b_j)$$ that is, $B$ is coherent if and only if any two propositions in $B$ either support each other or are at least mutually consistent. Proposition 4.15 (The Coherence Argument for the Three Views) The set of propositions $B$ of the Three New Views is coherent: the propositions in $B$ support each other or are at least mutually consistent, and there is no internal contradiction. IV. The Epistemological Significance of Circular Mutual Constitution Circular mutual constitution has important epistemological significance: Significance One: Holistic Understanding The Three Views are not three independent theories, but three aspects of one whole. Understanding any one view requires understanding its relations to the other two. Significance Two: Mutual Testing The Three Views can test one another: if a revision of one view brings it into inconsistency with the other two, this is a problem to be solved. Significance Three: Gradual Revision The revision of the Three Views is gradual: when revising one view, one must consider the impact on the other two, maintaining the coherence of the whole. Proposition 4.16 (The Epistemological Significance of Circular Mutual Constitution) The circular mutual constitution of the Three Views has important epistemological significance: it requires holistic understanding, permits mutual testing, and supports gradual revision. This structure enhances the epistemological robustness of the Three Views.

§4.2 The Common Basis of the Three Views

§4.2.1 Relationality as a Common Basis I. The Manifestation of Relationality in the Three Views Relationality is the first common basis of the Three New Views. Relationality is manifested differently in each of the Three Views: Table 4.4 The Manifestation of Relationality in the Three Views | View | Manifestation of Relationality | Concrete Proposition | |------|--------------|----------| | The New Cosmology | The basic unit of reality is relation | NC-1 | | The New View of Life | Life is a functional organization in a network of relations | NL-1 | | The New View of Cognition | Knowledge is a social achievement, depending on relations | NK-2 | II. The Formalized Statement of Relationality Definition 4.1 (Relationality) Relationality is an ontological position which holds that: (1) the basic unit of reality is relation, not independently existing substance; (2) the properties of a substance are relational, depending on its relations to other substances; (3) the whole cannot be reduced to its parts, and relation has ontological priority. Formalized statement: Let $E$ be a set of entities, $R$ a set of relations, and $P$ a property function. Relationality holds: $$\forall e \in E: P(e) = f(R_e)$$ Here $R_e$ is the set of relations in which $e$ participates. That is, the properties of any entity are a function of the relations in which it participates. III. How Relationality Runs through the Three Views In the New Cosmology: NC-1 directly holds that reality is relational. This is the ontological-level expression of relationality. $$\text{NC-1}: \text{Reality} = \text{Relational}$$ In the New View of Life: NL-1 holds that life is functional, and is not limited to a particular substrate. Function is relational — function depends on the relation between a system and its environment. $$\text{NL-1}: \text{Life} = \text{Function} = f(\text{Relations})$$ In the New View of Cognition: NK-2 holds that knowledge is a social achievement. Sociality is relational — society is a network of relations. $$\text{NK-2}: \text{Knowledge} = \text{SocialAchievement} = f(\text{SocialRelations})$$ Proposition 4.17 (Relationality as a Common Basis) Relationality is a common basis of the Three New Views: the New Cosmology holds that reality is relational (NC-1), the New View of Life holds that life is a functional organization in a network of relations (NL-1), and the New View of Cognition holds that knowledge is an achievement of social relations (NK-2). Relationality runs through the Three Views and is the first basis of their unity. Formalized statement: $$\text{Relationality} \in \text{Foundation}(\text{NC}) \cap \text{Foundation}(\text{NL}) \cap \text{Foundation}(\text{NK})$$

§4.2.2 Process as a Common Basis I. The Manifestation of Process in the Three Views Process is the second common basis of the Three New Views. Process is manifested differently in each of the Three Views: Table 4.5 The Manifestation of Process in the Three Views | View | Manifestation of Process | Concrete Proposition | |------|--------------|----------| | The New Cosmology | Reality is processual; change is basic | NC-2 | | The New View of Life | Life is a continuous process of negentropy maintenance | NL-2 | | The New View of Cognition | Cognitive standards are revisable and historical | NK-4 | II. The Formalized Statement of Process Definition 4.2 (Processuality) Processuality is an ontological position which holds that: (1) reality is processual; change and becoming are basic; (2) static existence is derivative, a temporary stable state of a process; (3) time is a basic dimension of reality, not an external parameter. Formalized statement: Let $S(t)$ be the state of a system at time $t$, and $P(t_1, t_2)$ the process from $t_1$ to $t_2$. Processuality holds: $$S(t_2) = f(P(t_1, t_2), S(t_1))$$ that is, the state of the system is the result of the process, not the premise of the process. More strongly: $$\text{Ontological-Priority}(\text{Process}) > \text{Ontological-Priority}(\text{State})$$ III. How Process Runs through the Three Views In the New Cosmology: NC-2 directly holds that reality is processual. This is the ontological-level expression of process. $$\text{NC-2}: \text{Reality} = \text{Process}$$ In the New View of Life: NL-2 holds that life takes a flow of negentropy as its condition of persistence. A flow of negentropy is a process — life is a continuous process of negentropy maintenance. $$\text{NL-2}: \text{Life} = \text{NegentropyProcess}$$ In the New View of Cognition: NK-4 holds that cognitive standards are revisable. Revisability means that cognitive standards are historical and processual. $$\text{NK-4}: \text{CognitiveStandards} = \text{HistoricalProcess}$$ Proposition 4.18 (Process as a Common Basis) Process is a common basis of the Three New Views: the New Cosmology holds that reality is processual (NC-2), the New View of Life holds that life is a continuous process of negentropy maintenance (NL-2), and the New View of Cognition holds that cognitive standards are historical and revisable (NK-4). Process runs through the Three Views and is the second basis of their unity. Formalized statement: $$\text{Processuality} \in \text{Foundation}(\text{NC}) \cap \text{Foundation}(\text{NL}) \cap \text{Foundation}(\text{NK})$$

§4.2.3 Participation as a Common Basis I. The Manifestation of Participation in the Three Views Participation is the third common basis of the Three New Views. Participation is manifested differently in each of the Three Views: Table 4.6 The Manifestation of Participation in the Three Views | View | Manifestation of Participation | Concrete Proposition | |------|--------------|----------| | The New Cosmology | The observer participates in constructing reality | NC-3 | | The New View of Life | Life participates in constructing its environment | NL-1, NL-2 | | The New View of Cognition | Cognition is participatory construction | NK-1 | II. The Formalized Statement of Participation Definition 4.3 (Participatoriness) Participatoriness is an ontological-epistemological position which holds that: (1) the observer/cognizer is not a spectator separate from the world, but a participant; (2) the act of observation/cognition participates in constructing the observed/cognized reality; (3) subject and object are not sharply separate, but mutually constituting. Formalized statement: Let $O$ be an observer, $W$ the world, and $\text{Observe}(O, W)$ the act of observation. Participatoriness holds: $$\text{Observe}(O, W) \rightarrow \Delta W$$ that is, the act of observation changes the observed world. More strongly: $$W' = f(W, O, \text{Observe})$$ that is, the world after observation $W'$ is a function of the original world $W$, the observer $O$, and the act of observation. III. How Participation Runs through the Three Views In the New Cosmology: NC-3 directly holds that the universe is participatory. This is the ontological-level expression of participation. $$\text{NC-3}: \text{Universe} = \text{Participatory}$$ In the New View of Life: NL-1 and NL-2 entail that life participates in constructing its environment. Life changes its environment through the activity of maintaining negentropy. $$\text{NL-1} \wedge \text{NL-2} \Rightarrow \text{Life-Participates-In-Environment}$$ In the New View of Cognition: NK-1 directly holds that cognition is participatory construction. The cognitive framework participates in shaping knowable reality. $$\text{NK-1}: \text{Cognition} = \text{Participatory-Construction}$$ Proposition 4.19 (Participation as a Common Basis) Participation is a common basis of the Three New Views: the New Cosmology holds that the universe is participatory (NC-3), the New View of Life entails that life participates in constructing its environment (NL-1, NL-2), and the New View of Cognition holds that cognition is participatory construction (NK-1). Participation runs through the Three Views and is the third basis of their unity. Formalized statement: $$\text{Participatoriness} \in \text{Foundation}(\text{NC}) \cap \text{Foundation}(\text{NL}) \cap \text{Foundation}(\text{NK})$$ IV. The Relations among the Three Common Bases There are intrinsic connections among the three common bases of relationality, process, and participation: Proposition 4.20 (The Intrinsic Connections among the Three Common Bases) The three common bases of relationality, process, and participation mutually entail one another:

  • Relationality entails process: relations are dynamic, and the maintenance of a relation is a process.
  • Process entails participation: a process involves the interaction of multiple participants.
  • Participation entails relationality: participation establishes relations, and participants are mutually constituted through relations.

Formal expression: $$\text{Relationality} \leftrightarrow \text{Processuality} \leftrightarrow \text{Participatoriness}$$

§4.3 The Integrative Framework of the Three Views

§4.3.1 A Formal Expression of the Integrative Framework

  1. The Axiom System NTV

The Three New Views can be organized into a unified axiom system, NTV (New Triad of Views). Definition 4.4 (The Axiom System NTV) The axiom system NTV is the formal expression of the Three New Views, containing the following axioms: Foundational axioms (relationality, processuality, participatoriness): A1 (Axiom of Relationality): ∀x ∈ U: Properties(x) = f(Relations(x)) The properties of any entity are a function of the relations in which it participates A2 (Axiom of Processuality): ∀x ∈ U: State(x, t₂) = g(Process(x, t₁, t₂), State(x, t₁)) The state of any entity is the result of a process A3 (Axiom of Participatoriness): ∀o ∈ O, ∀e ∈ E: Observe(o, e) → Δe Any act of observation changes the object observed New Cosmology axioms: NC-1 (Relational Reality): Reality = RelationalNetwork Reality is a relational network NC-2 (Processual Reality): Reality = Process Reality is process NC-3 (Participatory Reality): Reality = Participatory Reality is participatory New View of Life axioms: NL-1 (Cross-Substrate Life): Life(x) ↔ Function(x) ∧ ¬∃s: Substrate(x) = s Life is functional and not limited to a particular substrate NL-2 (Negentropic Persistence): ∀l ∈ L: Persist(l) → NegentropyFlow(l) > 0 The persistence of life requires a positive negentropy flow NL-3 (Consciousness Continuum): Consciousness: E → [0, 1]ⁿ Consciousness is a function from entities to an n-dimensional unit hypercube New View of Cognition axioms: NK-1 (Participatory Cognition): ∀k ∈ K, ∀e ∈ E: Cognize(k, e) → Participate(k, e) Cognition entails participation NK-2 (Social Knowledge): ∀p: Knowledge(p) → SocialValidation(p) Knowledge requires social validation NK-3 (Normative Cognition): ∀c: Cognition(c) → Normative(c) Cognition has a normative character NK-4 (Negotiable Standards): ¬∃S: ∀C, ∀t: ValidStandard(C, t) = S There is no universally invariant standard of cognition

  1. Properties of the Axiom System

Theorem 4.1 (Consistency of NTV) The axiom system NTV is consistent: there are no logical contradictions among the axioms of NTV. Proof sketch: Construct a model $M$ such that $M$ satisfies all the axioms of NTV. If such a model exists, then NTV is consistent. Model construction:

  • Let $U$ be the set of relational networks
  • Let $L$ be the subset of $U$ that satisfies the negentropy condition
  • Let $K$ be the subset of $L$ that possesses cognitive capacity
  • Verify that all axioms hold in this model

Theorem 4.2 (Independence of the NTV Axioms) The core axioms of NTV are independent: none of the axioms can be derived from the others. Proof sketch: For each axiom $A_i$, construct a model $M_i$ such that $M_i$ satisfies all the axioms except $A_i$, but does not satisfy $A_i$. Theorem 4.3 (Coherence of NTV) NTV is coherent: the axioms of NTV support one another, forming a coherent whole. Proof sketch: Show the support relations among the axioms (as in §4.1), and thereby demonstrate that these support relations enhance the overall credibility of the axiom system.

  1. From Axioms to Theorems

A series of theorems can be derived from the axioms of NTV: Theorem 4.4 (Subject-Expansion Theorem) From NL-1 it can be derived that subjecthood is not limited to carbon-based organisms; any system that satisfies the functional conditions may possess subjecthood. Formal expression: $$\text{NL-1} \Rightarrow \forall x: [\text{Function}(x) \geq \theta] \rightarrow \text{PotentialSubject}(x)$$ Theorem 4.5 (Negentropy Responsibility Theorem) From NL-2 it can be derived that subjects dependent on a negentropy flow bear responsibility toward the sources of negentropy. Formal expression: $$\text{NL-2} \Rightarrow \forall l \in L: \text{Depend}(l, \text{Negentropy}) \rightarrow \text{Responsibility}(l, \text{Negentropy})$$ Theorem 4.6 (Epistemic Humility Theorem) From NK-4 it can be derived that cognizers should remain humble and open toward their own standards of cognition. Formal expression: $$\text{NK-4} \Rightarrow \forall k \in K: \text{Ought}(k, \text{CognitiveHumility})$$
