│  │  BP-2 (the Epistemic Humility Principle):                           │   │
│  │  - The fallibility of cognition requires that decisions preserve     │   │
│  │    reversibility                                                    │   │
│  │  - Connected with NK-4 (negotiable); derives PR                      │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  BP-3 (the Intersubjectivity Principle):                            │   │
│  │  - In multi-agent situations, adopt principles that can be           │   │
│  │    reasonably accepted by others                                    │   │
│  │  - Connected with NC-1 and NC-3; derives RFP                         │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Thesis Three: The justification of the bridge principles            │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The survival-conditions argument:                                    │   │
│  │  - The bridge principles are necessary conditions for maintaining    │   │
│  │    survival conditions                                              │   │
│  │  - An argument from instrumental rationality                         │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The reflective-equilibrium argument:                                 │   │
│  │  - The bridge principles are consistent with moral intuitions         │   │
│  │  - The bridge principles cohere with the Three New Views             │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The practical-reason argument:                                       │   │
│  │  - The bridge principles are requirements of practical reason         │   │
│  │  - Supported by a Kantian argument                                    │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The convergence of multiple arguments:                               │   │
│  │  - Three independent paths converge on the justification of the       │   │
│  │    bridge principles                                                │   │
│  │  - Strengthens the credibility and robustness of the conclusion      │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Thesis Four: This work’s metaethical position                      │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  Constrained weak realism:                                           │   │
│  │  - Objective normative constraints exist                             │   │
│  │  - Normative constraints depend on agents’ survival conditions        │   │
│  │  - The normative cannot be reduced to the descriptive                │   │
│  │  - The normative is derived from the descriptive through the bridge   │   │
│  │    principles                                                       │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  Relation to other positions:                                        │   │
│  │  - With moral realism: partially accepted (weak realism)              │   │
│  │  - With constructivism: partially accepted (constrained construction) │   │
│  │  - With naturalism: rejects reduction, but acknowledges a connection  │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Thesis Five: The derivation from the bridge principles to the        │   │
│  │  normative principles                                                │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  Derivation path one: NC-1 + NC-3 + BP-3 → RFP                     │   │
│  │  Derivation path two: NL-2 + BP-1 + BP-3 → PNR                     │   │
│  │  Derivation path three: NK-4 + BP-2 → PR                           │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The validity of the derivation:                                      │   │
│  │  - Follows valid logical rules                                       │   │
│  │  - The premises are explicit and the conclusion is derived from them  │   │
│  │  - Does not violate Hume’s problem                                  │   │
│  │                                                           │   │
│  │  The boundaries of the derivation:                                    │   │
│  │  - Applies to agents with rationality, a will to survive, and         │   │
│  │    cognitive capacity                                               │   │
│  │  - The derivation is revisable                                       │   │
│  │  - The derivation has limitations and cannot resolve all normative    │   │
│  │    problems                                                         │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                 │
│  II. Summary of core definitions                                     │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Definition | Name              | Core content                    │   │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │ Definition 5.1  | Hume’s Problem   | Ought cannot be derived from is  │   │
│  │ Definition 5.2  | Naturalistic Fallacy | Good cannot be defined by natural properties │   │
│  │ Definition 5.3  | Bridge Principle | A principle connecting description and norm │   │
│  │ Definition 5.4  | BP-1 Survival Rationality | Agents ought to maintain survival conditions │   │
│  │ Definition 5.5  | BP-2 Epistemic Humility | Decisions ought to be reversible or specially justified │   │
│  │ Definition 5.6  | BP-3 Intersubjectivity | Principles ought to be acceptable to others │   │
│  │ Definition 5.7  | Bridge-principle axiom system | The formalized formulation of BP │   │
│  │ Definition 5.8  | Reflective Equilibrium | Mutual adjustment of principles and intuitions │   │
│  │ Definition 5.9  | Practical Reason | The rational capacity that guides action │   │
│  │ Definition 5.10 | Convergence of Multiple Arguments | Multiple paths point to the same conclusion │   │
│  │ Definition 5.11 | Moral Realism | Objective moral facts exist │   │
│  │ Definition 5.12 | Weak Realism | Agent-relative objective normativity │   │
│  │ Definition 5.13 | Moral Constructivism | Principles are those rational agents would agree to │   │
│  │ Definition 5.14 | Ethical Naturalism | Morality can be reduced to nature │   │
│  │ Definition 5.15 | This work’s metaethical position | Constrained weak realism │   │

│    P3 (survival requires conditions of survival)                │
│  - Conclusion: rational agents should maintain their conditions of survival │
│  - Testability: if a rationality that does not pursue survival proves feasible, revision is required │

│  - Premises: P1 (cognitive agents are fallible), P2 (fallibility requires the capacity for error correction), │
│    P3 (the capacity for error correction requires reversibility) │
│  - Conclusion: cognitive agents should prefer reversible actions   │
│  - Testability: if infallible cognition proves feasible, revision is required │

│    P3 (negotiation requires principles acceptable to others)    │
│  - Conclusion: principles that can be reasonably accepted by others should be adopted │
│  - Testability: if purely individual norms prove feasible, revision is required │

§11.1 The Derivation of the Recursive Freedom Principle

§11.1.1 From the New Cosmology to Possibility Space I. Review of the Core Propositions of the New Cosmology Chapter 1 established three core propositions of the New Cosmology. Before deriving the Recursive Freedom Principle, it is necessary to review the core content of these propositions. Proposition NC-1 (relational reality): The basic units of reality are not independent entities but relations. Properties are functions of relations, not intrinsic features of entities. Formal statement: $$\forall x \in U: P(x) = f(R_x)$$ where $U$ is the set of existents in the universe, $P(x)$ is the property of $x$, $R_x$ is the relational network in which $x$ is situated, and $f$ is a function from relations to properties. Proposition NC-2 (processual reality): Reality is processual, not static. Existents are nodes of processes, not the substrate of processes. Formal statement: $$S(t_2) = g(P(t_1, t_2), S(t_1))$$ where $S(t)$ is the state at time $t$, $P(t_1, t_2)$ is the process from $t_1$ to $t_2$, and $g$ is a function from the process and the initial state to the final state. Proposition NC- (participatory reality): The universe is participatory. The observer is not a spectator of the universe but a participant in it. The act of observation participates in constructing the observed reality. Formal statement: $$\text{Observe}(o, e) \rightarrow \Delta e$$ where $o$ is the observer, $e$ is the observed event, and $\Delta e$ denotes the effect of the act of observation on $e$. II. From Relationality to Possibility Space NC-1 (relational reality) entails an important corollary: the properties of an existent depend on the relational network in which it is situated. This means that changing the relational network changes the properties of the existent. Definition 11.1 (Possibility Space) The Possibility Space is the set of all states that a system can attain under given constraints. For an agent $S$, its possibility space $PS(S)$ is the set of all states that $S$ can realize within its current relational network. Formal statement: $$PS(S) = \{s \in \Sigma : \text{Achievable}(S, s, R_S)\}$$ where $\Sigma$ is the set of all possible states, $R_S$ is the relational network in which $S$ is situated, and $\text{Achievable}(S, s, R_S)$ denotes that, under the relational network $R_S$, $S$ can attain state $s$. Proposition 11.1 (The link between relationality and possibility space) From NC-1 (relational reality), an agent's possibility space depends on the relational network in which it is situated. Changing the relational network will change the possibility space. Formal statement: $$\Delta R_S \rightarrow \Delta PS(S)$$ Argument 11.1 (From NC-1 to possibility space) Premise P1 (NC-1): properties are functions of relations, P(x) = f(R_x) Premise P2: the states an agent can attain depend on its properties Premise P: the possibility space is the set of states an agent can attain Step 1: by P1, an agent's properties depend on the relational network Step 2: by P2, the states an agent can attain depend on its properties Step : by Step 1 and Step 2, the states an agent can attain depend on the relational network Step 4: by P, the possibility space is the set of attainable states Conclusion: the possibility space depends on the relational network III. From Participatory Character to the Construction of Possibility Space NC- (participatory reality) entails another important corollary: an agent's action participates in constructing reality, including constructing the possibility spaces of other agents. Proposition 11.2 (The link between participatory character and the construction of possibility space) From NC- (participatory reality), an agent's action affects not only its own possibility space but also the possibility spaces of other agents. Agents are co-constructors of possibility space. Formal statement: $$\text{Act}(S_1, a) \rightarrow \Delta PS(S_2), \quad \forall S_2 \in \text{AffectedBy}(a)$$ where $\text{Act}(S_1, a)$ denotes that agent $S_1$ performs action $a$, and $\text{AffectedBy}(a)$ is the set of agents affected by action $a$. Argument 11.2 (From NC- to the construction of possibility space) Premise P1 (NC-): observation/action participates in constructing reality Premise P2: reality includes the relational network Premise P (Proposition 11.1): the possibility space depends on the relational network Step 1: by P1, an agent's action participates in constructing reality Step 2: by P2, an agent's action participates in constructing the relational network Step : by P, a change in the relational network leads to a change in the possibility space Conclusion: an agent's action participates in constructing possibility space (including the possibility spaces of others) IV. Structural Features of Possibility Space Possibility space has the following structural features, which are crucial for understanding the Recursive Freedom Principle. Definition 11.2 (Dimensions of Possibility Space) The Dimensions of Possibility Space are the independent directions along which the possibility space can vary. The more dimensions, the richer the possibility space. Formal statement: $$\text{Dim}(PS) = |\{d_i : d_i \text{ is an independent direction of variation}\}|$$ Definition 11. (Volume of Possibility Space) The Volume of Possibility Space is the "number" or "range" of attainable states in the possibility space. The larger the volume, the more possibilities there are. Formal statement: $$\text{Vol}(PS) = \int_{PS} d\mu$$ where $\mu$ is a suitable measure on the possibility space. Definition 11.4 (Connectivity of Possibility Space) The Connectivity of Possibility Space is the reachability among different states in the possibility space. The higher the connectivity, the easier it is to move from one state to another. Formal statement: $$\text{Conn}(PS) = \frac{|\{(s_1, s_2) : \text{Reachable}(s_1, s_2)\}|}{|PS|^2}$$ Table 11.1 Structural features of possibility space | Feature | Definition | Significance | Measurement | |------|------|------|----------| | Dimension | The number of independent directions of variation | The diversity of possibilities | Principal component analysis | | Volume | The range of attainable states | The richness of possibilities | Integral measure | | Connectivity | The reachability among states | The accessibility of possibilities | Graph-theoretic methods | V. The Dynamic Change of Possibility Space Possibility space is not static; it changes with time and action. This is consistent with NC-2 (processual reality). Definition 11.5 (Expansion of Possibility Space) The Expansion of Possibility Space is an increase in the dimensions, volume, or connectivity of the possibility space. Formal statement: $$\text{Expand}(PS, a) \Leftrightarrow \text{Dim}(PS') > \text{Dim}(PS) \vee \text{Vol}(PS') > \text{Vol}(PS) \vee \text{Conn}(PS') > \text{Conn}(PS)$$ where $PS'$ is the possibility space after action $a$. Definition 11.6 (Compression of Possibility Space) The Compression of Possibility Space is a decrease in the dimensions, volume, or connectivity of the possibility space. Formal statement: $$\text{Compress}(PS, a) \Leftrightarrow \text{Dim}(PS') < \text{Dim}(PS) \vee \text{Vol}(PS') < \text{Vol}(PS) \vee \text{Conn}(PS') < \text{Conn}(PS)$$ Definition 11.7 (Reversible and Irreversible Compression) Reversible Compression is compression that can be restored through subsequent action. Irreversible Compression is compression that cannot be restored through subsequent action. Formal statement: $$\text{ReversibleCompress}(PS, a) \Leftrightarrow \exists a': PS'' = PS$$ $$\text{IrreversibleCompress}(PS, a) \Leftrightarrow \neg\exists a': PS'' = PS$$ where $PS''$ is the possibility space after action $a'$. Proposition 11. (The special status of irreversible compression) Irreversible compression has a special normative status, because it permanently reduces the possibility space and deprives future agents of their opportunities for choice.

【Box 11.1】The Physics Analogy of Possibility Space —————————————————————————————————————————————————

│                                                                 │
│  1. The Phase-Space Analogy                                      │
│                                                                 │
│  In classical mechanics, phase space is the mathematical space   │
│  describing all possible states of a system. Each point repre-   │
│  sents one possible state of the system, determined by position  │
│  and momentum coordinates.                                        │
│                                                                 │
│  The analogy between possibility space and phase space:          │
│  - Dimensions of phase space ↔ dimensions of possibility space   │
│  - Volume of phase space ↔ volume of possibility space           │
│  - Trajectories in phase space ↔ evolutionary paths in possibility space │
│                                                                 │
│  2. The Lesson of Liouville's Theorem                            │
│                                                                 │
│  Liouville's Theorem states that, in a Hamiltonian system, the   │
│  volume of phase space remains constant under time evolution.     │
│  This means information is conserved.                             │
│                                                                 │
│  However, in open and dissipative systems, the effective volume  │
│  of phase space can decrease.                                    │
│                                                                 │
│  This is analogous to the compression of possibility space.      │
│                                                                 │
│  3. Entropy and Possibility Space                                │
│                                                                 │
│  In statistical mechanics, entropy is related to the volume of   │
│  phase space:                                                     │
│  S = k_B ln Ω                                                   │
│  where Ω is the number of accessible microstates in phase space.│
│                                                                 │
│  Similarly, the "entropy" of possibility space can be defined as: │
│  S_PS = ln |PS|                                                   │
│  The compression of possibility space corresponds to a decrease  │
│  in S_PS.                                                         │
│                                                                 │
│  4. Boundary Declaration                                         │
│                                                                 │
│  These analogies are heuristic, not strict isomorphisms. Possi-  │
│  bility space is a normative concept, while phase space is a      │
│  descriptive concept. This book does not claim that the two are   │
│  ontologically identical.                                         │

I. Review of the Bridge Principles Chapter 5 established three bridge principles, of which BP- (the intersubjectivity principle) is the key bridge for deriving the Recursive Freedom Principle. Bridge principle BP- (the intersubjectivity principle): In a multi-agent situation, agents should adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by other rational agents. Formal statement: $$BP\text{-}: \text{MultiAgent}(\text{Context}) \rightarrow O(\text{Acceptable}(\text{Principles}(S), \text{OtherRationalAgents}))$$ II. From Intersubjectivity to Possibility Protection BP- requires agents to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by other rational agents. The question now is: what kind of principles can be reasonably accepted by other rational agents? Proposition 11.4 (The unacceptability of possibility compression) A principle of action that irreversibly compresses the possibility space of others cannot be reasonably accepted by those others. Argument 11. (The argument for the unacceptability of possibility compression) Premise P1: rational agents value their possibility space (because the possibility space is the precondition for realizing any goal) Premise P2: actions that irreversibly compress the possibility space of others permanently reduce those others' opportunities for choice Premise P: actions that permanently reduce opportunities for choice harm the fundamental interests of others Premise P4: a principle of action that harms the fundamental interests of others cannot be reasonably accepted by those others Conclusion: a principle of action that irreversibly compresses the possibility space of others cannot be reasonably accepted by those others Proposition 11.5 (The acceptability of possibility protection) A principle of action that preserves or expands the possibility space of others can be reasonably accepted by those others. Argument 11.4 (The argument for the acceptability of possibility protection) Premise P1: rational agents value their possibility space Premise P2: actions that preserve or expand the possibility space of others maintain or increase those others' opportunities for choice Premise P: actions that maintain or increase opportunities for choice serve the interests of others Premise P4: a principle of action that serves the interests of others can be reasonably accepted by those others Conclusion: a principle of action that preserves or expands the possibility space of others can be reasonably accepted by those others III. Survival Rationality and Possibility Space BP-1 (the survival-rationality principle) is also related to possibility space. Survival requires possibility space, because survival means continuing to exist in the future, and continuing to exist requires that there be possible states that can be attained. Proposition 11.6 (The link between survival and possibility space) An agent's survival depends on the non-emptiness of its possibility space. If the possibility space is fully compressed (becoming the empty set), the agent cannot survive. Formal statement: $$\text{Survive}(S) \rightarrow PS(S) \neq \emptyset$$ Argument 11.5 (The argument for the link between survival and possibility space) Premise P1: survival means continuing to exist in the future Premise P2: continuing to exist requires that there be possible states that can be attained Premise P: the set of possible states is precisely the possibility space Premise P4: if the possibility space is empty, then no possible state can be attained Conclusion: survival depends on the non-emptiness of the possibility space IV. From Survival Rationality to Possibility Protection Combining BP-1 (the survival-rationality principle) and Proposition 11.6, it can be derived that agents have reason to protect possibility space. Proposition 11.7 (Survival rationality entails possibility protection) From BP-1 (the survival-rationality principle) and Proposition 11.6, rational agents with a will to survive should maintain their possibility space. Argument 11.6 (The argument that survival rationality entails possibility protection) Premise P1 (BP-1): rational agents with a will to survive should maintain their conditions of survival Premise P2 (Proposition 11.6): the non-emptiness of the possibility space is a necessary condition of survival Premise P: if X is a necessary condition of Y, and an agent should maintain Y, then the agent should maintain X Conclusion: rational agents with a will to survive should maintain their possibility space V. From Self-Protection to Mutual Protection So far, we have argued that agents have reason to protect their own possibility space. But the Recursive Freedom Principle requires mutual protection—protecting not only one's own possibility space but also the possibility space of others. Proposition 11.8 (From self-protection to mutual protection) From BP- (the intersubjectivity principle), agents should protect not only their own possibility space but also the possibility space of others. Argument 11.7 (The argument from self-protection to mutual protection) Premise P1 (Proposition 11.7): agents should maintain their own possibility space Premise P2 (BP-): agents should adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by other rational agents Premise P: if an agent protects only its own possibility space while compressing the possibility space of others, this principle cannot be reasonably accepted by those others Premise P4: if a principle cannot be reasonably accepted by others, then it violates BP- Intermediate conclusion C1: an agent should not protect only its own possibility space while compressing the possibility space of others Premise P5: a principle that protects the possibility space of others can be reasonably accepted by those others Premise P6: a principle that can be reasonably accepted by others conforms to BP- Conclusion: agents should protect the possibility space of others VI. The Recursiveness of Possibility Protection Possibility protection is recursive: the principle of protecting possibility space should itself remain open, so that it can be revised when necessary. Proposition 11.9 (The recursiveness of possibility protection) The principle of protecting possibility space should apply to the principle itself. That is, the application of the principle should not close off the possibility of revising the principle. Argument 11.8 (The argument for the recursiveness of possibility protection) Premise P1: possibility space includes cognitive possibility space (possible beliefs, principles, theories) Premise P2: if the application of a principle closes off the possibility of revising the principle, then it compresses the cognitive possibility space Premise P: compressing the cognitive possibility space violates the principle of possibility protection Conclusion: the principle of possibility protection should apply recursively to itself This recursiveness is one source of the name "the Recursive Freedom Principle." The principle requires protecting not only the possibility space of action but also the revisability of the principle itself.

§11.1.3 The Formal Statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle I. A Preliminary Statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle Based on the derivations of the preceding two sections, a preliminary statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle can now be given. Definition 11.8 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, preliminary statement) Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP): rational agents should preserve or expand possibility space, and avoid irreversibly compressing it. This principle applies recursively to the principle itself. II. The Formal Statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.9 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, formal statement) The formal statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle: $$RFP: \forall a \in A: O(\Delta PS(a) \geq 0) \vee O(\text{SpecialJustification}(a))$$ where:

  • $A$ is the set of actions
  • $PS$ is the possibility space
  • $\Delta PS(a)$ is the net effect of action $a$ on the possibility space
  • $O$ is the "ought" operator
  • $\text{SpecialJustification}(a)$ denotes that action $a$ has a special justification

Interpretation: for any action $a$, either the net effect of action $a$ on the possibility space is non-negative (that is, it preserves or expands the possibility space), or action $a$ requires a special justification. III. The Definition of the Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) To operationalize the Recursive Freedom Principle, a measurable indicator must be defined. Definition 11.10 (Recursive Freedom Degree, RFD) The Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) is an indicator measuring the effect of an action on the possibility space. Formal definition: $$\text{RFD}(a) = \frac{M(PS(s_1, T)) - M(PS(s_0, T))}{M(PS(s_0, T))}$$ where:

  • $s_0$ is the state before action $a$
  • $s_1$ is the state after action $a$
  • $T$ is the time horizon of evaluation
  • $M(PS)$ is a measure of the possibility space (which may be some combination of dimensions, volume, or connectivity)

Interpretation of RFD:

  • $\text{RFD}(a) > 0$: action $a$ expands the possibility space
  • $\text{RFD}(a) = 0$: action $a$ preserves the possibility space
  • $\text{RFD}(a) < 0$: action $a$ compresses the possibility space

IV. The Constraint Condition of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.11 (The constraint condition of the Recursive Freedom Principle) The constraint condition of the Recursive Freedom Principle: $$\text{RFD}(a) \geq \theta_{\min}$$ where $\theta_{\min}$ is the minimum acceptable Recursive Freedom Degree. Interpretation of the constraint condition:

  • When $\theta_{\min} = 0$, actions are required at least to preserve the possibility space
  • When $\theta_{\min} > 0$, actions are required to expand the possibility space
  • When $\theta_{\min} < 0$, a certain degree of possibility-space compression is permitted

Boundary Declaration 11.1 (The determination of $\theta_{\min}$) The specific value of $\theta_{\min}$ must be determined according to context, not fixed a priori. This book suggests a default value of $\theta_{\min} = 0$, that is, requiring actions at least to preserve the possibility space. But in specific contexts, this threshold may be adjusted through negotiation. V. The Recursive Clause of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.12 (The recursive clause) The recursive clause of the Recursive Freedom Principle: the application of the Recursive Freedom Principle should not close off the possibility of revising the Recursive Freedom Principle. Formal statement: $$\text{Apply}(RFP) \rightarrow \neg\text{Close}(\text{Revise}(RFP))$$ The significance of the recursive clause:

  • The Recursive Freedom Principle is not a dogma but a revisable principle
  • The application of the principle should preserve the revisability of the principle itself
  • This embodies the application of NK-4 (the negotiability of cognitive standards) at the normative level

VI. The Complete Formalization of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.1 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, complete formalization) The complete formal statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle: Axiom RFP-1 (the possibility-protection axiom): ∀a ∈ A: RFD(a) ≥ θ_min ∨ SpecialJustification(a) Axiom RFP-2 (the recursion axiom): Apply(RFP) → ¬Close(Revise(RFP)) Axiom RFP- (the intersubjectivity axiom): ∀S₁, S₂: Protect(S₁, PS(S₁)) → Protect(S₁, PS(S₂)) Auxiliary definition RFP-D1 (definition of RFD): RFD(a) = [M(PS(s₁, T)) - M(PS(s₀, T))] / M(PS(s₀, T)) Auxiliary definition RFP-D2 (the special-justification condition): SpecialJustification(a) ↔ [Necessity(a) ∧ Proportionality(a) ∧ MinimalCompression(a)] Table 11.2 The formal elements of the Recursive Freedom Principle | Element | Symbol | Meaning | Constraint | |------|------|------|------| | Set of actions | $A$ | All possible actions | - | | Possibility space | $PS$ | The set of attainable states | - | | Recursive Freedom Degree | $RFD$ | The effect of an action on the possibility space | $RFD \geq \theta_{\min}$ | | Minimum threshold | $\theta_{\min}$ | The minimum acceptable RFD | Defaults to 0 | | Special justification | $\text{SpecialJustification}$ | The justification for compressing the possibility space | Necessity + Proportionality + Minimality |

Validity Check of the Derivation Check 11.1 (The logical validity of the derivation) The logical validity of the derivation can be checked in the following ways:

  1. Acceptability of the premises: are NC-1, NC-, BP-1, and BP- acceptable?
  2. NC-1 and NC- were argued in Chapter 1
  3. BP-1 and BP- were argued in Chapter 5
  4. Therefore, the premises are acceptable
  5. Validity of the reasoning: is the reasoning from the premises to the conclusion valid?
  6. The reasoning steps of each argumentative node have been presented explicitly
  7. The reasoning follows standard logical rules
  8. Therefore, the reasoning is valid

. Coherence of the conclusion: is the conclusion coherent with other accepted propositions?

  • RFP is coherent with the other propositions of the Three New Views
  • RFP is coherent with the other two normative principles (PNR, PR)
  • Therefore, the conclusion is coherent

Boundary Declaration 11.2 (The boundaries of the derivation) The derivation of the Recursive Freedom Principle has the following boundaries:

  • The derivation depends on the acceptability of the New Cosmology (NC-1, NC-)
  • The derivation depends on the acceptability of the bridge principles (BP-1, BP-)
  • If these premises are revised, the conclusions of the derivation must also be revised accordingly
  • The derivation is revisable, not a closed proof

§11.2 The Content of the Recursive Freedom Principle

§11.2.1 The Meaning of "Recursive" I. The General Concept of Recursion "Recursion" is a concept originating in mathematics and computer science; it refers to a process or structure that refers to itself in its own definition. Definition 11.14 (Recursion) Recursion is the feature of a process, structure, or definition that refers to itself within itself. Recursive structures exhibit self-similarity: the structure of the whole reappears in the parts. Classic examples of recursion:

  • The factorial definition in mathematics: $n! = n \times (n-1)!$, where $0! = 1$
  • Recursive functions in computer science: a function that calls itself in its own definition
  • Fractal structures in nature: parts and whole share a similar structure

II. The Threefold Meaning of "Recursive" in the Recursive Freedom Principle In the Recursive Freedom Principle, "recursive" has a threefold meaning: Meaning One: the self-applicability of the principle The Recursive Freedom Principle applies to the principle itself. That is, the application of the principle should not close off the possibility of revising the principle. Formal statement: $$\text{Apply}(RFP) \rightarrow \neg\text{Close}(\text{Revise}(RFP))$$ This means that the Recursive Freedom Principle is not a dogma but a revisable principle. The principle itself is also located within possibility space and should remain open. Meaning Two: the nested structure of possibility space Possibility space has a nested structure: each state within the possibility space itself also corresponds to a possibility space. Formal statement: $$\forall s \in PS: \exists PS_s \text{ such that } PS_s \text{ is the possibility space at state } s$$ This means that protecting the possibility space is not only protecting current choices but also protecting the choice of future choices. Meaning Three: mutual protection among agents The Recursive Freedom Principle requires agents to mutually protect one another's possibility spaces. This mutual protection has a recursive structure: A protects B's possibility space, B protects C's possibility space, C protects A's possibility space… Formal statement: $$\forall S_i, S_j \in \text{Agents}: \text{Protect}(S_i, PS(S_j))$$ Table 11.4 The threefold meaning of "recursive" | Meaning | Description | Formalization | Significance | |------|------|--------|------| | Self-applicability | The principle applies to the principle itself | $\text{Apply}(RFP) \rightarrow \neg\text{Close}(\text{Revise}(RFP))$ | The revisability of the principle | | Nested structure | The nesting of possibility space | $\forall s \in PS: \exists PS_s$ | Protecting future choices | | Mutual protection | Mutual protection among agents | $\forall S_i, S_j: \text{Protect}(S_i, PS(S_j))$ | Reciprocity among agents | III. The Normative Significance of Recursiveness Recursiveness has important normative significance: Normative significance one: preventing dogmatization The self-applicability of the principle prevents the dogmatization of the principle. Any principle, including the Recursive Freedom Principle itself, should remain revisable. This is consistent with NK-4 (the negotiability of cognitive standards). Normative significance two: long-range responsibility The nested structure of possibility space means that current actions affect future possibility space. This provides the basis for long-range responsibility: present agents bear responsibility for the possibility space of future agents. Normative significance three: intersubjective justice Mutual protection among agents means that the Recursive Freedom Principle is not only an individual principle but also a social principle. It requires agents to mutually respect one another's possibility spaces, which is the basis of intersubjective justice.

§11.2.2 The Meaning of "Freedom" I. Review of Traditional Concepts of Freedom In the Western tradition of political philosophy, there are multiple concepts of freedom. Isaiah Berlin, in Two Concepts of Liberty (1958), distinguished negative freedom from positive freedom. Negative Freedom:

  • Definition: freedom from external interference
  • Core question: "To what extent am I not interfered with by others?"
  • Representative figures: Hobbes, Locke, Mill, Berlin

Positive Freedom:

  • Definition: freedom of self-realization and self-mastery
  • Core question: "Who is the master?"
  • Representative figures: Rousseau, Hegel, Green

Republican Freedom:

  • Definition: freedom from domination
  • Core question: "Am I subject to the arbitrary power of others?"
  • Representative figures: Machiavelli, Harrington, Pettit

II. The Difference between Recursive Freedom and Traditional Concepts of Freedom The "freedom" in the Recursive Freedom Principle differs importantly from traditional concepts of freedom. Definition 11.15 (Recursive freedom) Recursive freedom is the preservation and expansion of possibility space. Recursive freedom is not freedom from interference (negative freedom), not self-realization (positive freedom), and not freedom from domination (republican freedom), but rather the openness of possibility space. Table 11.5 A comparison of recursive freedom with traditional concepts of freedom | Dimension | Negative freedom | Positive freedom | Republican freedom | Recursive freedom | |------|----------|----------|--------------|----------| | Core concern | The absence of interference | Self-mastery | The absence of domination | Possibility space | | Core question | Am I free from interference? | Am I the master? | Am I dominated? | Is possibility open? | | Time dimension | The present | The present | The present | The long range | | Scope of agents | The individual | The individual | Individual/group | All agents | | Relation to others | Others are potential interferers | Others are conditions of self-realization | Others are potential dominators | Others are co-constructors of possibility space | III. The Distinctive Features of Recursive Freedom Recursive freedom has the following distinctive features: Feature one: oriented toward the future Recursive freedom concerns future possibilities rather than the present state. It requires keeping future choices open, not merely protecting present choices. Feature two: relationality Recursive freedom is relational. The possibility space depends on the relational network, so recursive freedom depends on relations among agents. This is consistent with NC-1 (relational reality). Feature three: gradability Recursive freedom is a matter of degree, not binary. The possibility space can expand or compress, so recursive freedom can increase or decrease. This is consistent with NL- (the continuum of consciousness/subjectivity). Feature four: recursiveness Recursive freedom is recursive. It concerns not only the current possibility space but also the future possibility space; not only one's own possibility space but also the possibility space of others. IV. The Relation between Recursive Freedom and the Capability Approach The Capability Approach developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum is akin to recursive freedom. Core concepts of the capability approach:

  • Functionings: the states and activities that an individual can realize
  • Capabilities: the set of functionings that an individual can choose

The relation between recursive freedom and the capability approach:

  • Similarity: both concern a set of possibilities rather than actual choices
  • Difference: recursive freedom places greater emphasis on the time dimension and recursive structure

Proposition 11.10 (The relation between recursive freedom and the capability approach) Recursive freedom can be understood as the temporal extension of the capability approach. The capability approach concerns the current set of capabilities, whereas recursive freedom concerns the long-range evolution of the set of capabilities.

§11.2.3 The Meaning of "Possibility Space" I. The Ontological Status of Possibility Space Possibility space is the core concept of the Recursive Freedom Principle. Its ontological status must be clarified. Definition 11.16 (The ontological status of possibility space) Possibility space is a modal concept; it refers to the set of states that can be realized under given constraints. Possibility space is not an actually existing physical space but an abstract space that describes the structure of possibility. Boundary Declaration 11. (The ontological status of possibility space) This book adopts a moderate realist stance toward possibility space: possibility space is real, but it is not physical reality. The reality of possibility space is manifested in its constraining and enabling effects on action. This book does not claim that possibility space is a "Platonic" reality independent of agents. II. The Constituent Elements of Possibility Space Possibility space is constituted by the following elements: Element one: the state space The state space is the set of all possible states. Each state is one possible configuration of the system. Formal statement: $$\Sigma = \{s_1, s_2, s_, ...\}$$ Element two: the constraints Constraints limit the range of attainable states. Constraints include physical constraints, resource constraints, cognitive constraints, and so on. Formal statement: $$C = \{c_1, c_2, c_, ...\}$$ Element three: the reachability relation The reachability relation defines the possible transitions from one state to another. Formal statement: $$R \subseteq \Sigma \times \Sigma$$ where $(s_i, s_j) \in R$ denotes that one can transition from state $s_i$ to state $s_j$. Element four: possibility space Possibility space is the set of states attainable under the constraints. Formal statement: $$PS = \{s \in \Sigma : \text{Reachable}(s, C, R)\}$$ Figure 11.2 The constituent elements of possibility space

III. Types of Possibility Space Possibility space can be classified along different dimensions. Table 11.6 Types of possibility space | Classification dimension | Type | Description | Example | |----------|------|------|------| | Scope of agents | Individual possibility space | The possibility space of a single agent | An individual's career choice | | | Group possibility space | The possibility space of a group | A society's development path | | | Civilizational possibility space | The possibility space of a civilization | The future of human civilization | | Domain of content | Physical possibility space | Physically possible states | The possibilities of technological development | | | Cognitive possibility space | Cognitively possible states | Possible beliefs and theories | | | Normative possibility space | Normatively possible states | Possible institutional arrangements | | Time range | Short-term possibility space | States attainable in the near term | Tomorrow's choices | | | Medium-term possibility space | States attainable in the medium term | Choices within a decade | | | Long-term possibility space | States attainable in the long term | Choices a century from now | IV. The Measurement of Possibility Space The measurement of possibility space is the key to operationalizing the Recursive Freedom Principle. Definition 11.17 (The measure of possibility space) The measure of possibility space $M(PS)$ is a quantification of the "size" of the possibility space. The measure can be based on dimensions, volume, connectivity, or a combination thereof. Measurement method one: a dimension-based measure $$M_{\text{dim}}(PS) = \text{Dim}(PS)$$ where $\text{Dim}(PS)$ is the effective dimension of the possibility space. Measurement method two: a volume-based measure $$M_{\text{vol}}(PS) = \int_{PS} d\mu$$ where $\mu$ is a suitable measure on the possibility space. Measurement method three: a connectivity-based measure $$M_{\text{conn}}(PS) = \frac{|\{(s_1, s_2) : \text{Reachable}(s_1, s_2)\}|}{|PS|^2}$$ Measurement method four: a composite measure $$M(PS) = \alpha \cdot M_{\text{dim}}(PS) + \beta \cdot M_{\text{vol}}(PS) + \gamma \cdot M_{\text{conn}}(PS)$$ where $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$ are weight coefficients. Boundary Declaration 11.4 (The limitations of measuring possibility space) The measurement of possibility space faces the following limitations:

  • Possibility space is usually high-dimensional and difficult to enumerate completely
  • Different types of possibility are difficult to compare
  • The measurement depends on an understanding of the constraints, which may not be fully known
  • Therefore, the measurement of possibility space is approximate, not exact

§11.2.4 The Complete Statement of the Principle I. The Core Statement of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.18 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, core statement) Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP): Actions should preserve or expand possibility space, and not irreversibly compress it. This principle applies recursively to the principle itself. II. Hierarchical Statements of the Recursive Freedom Principle The Recursive Freedom Principle can be stated at different levels: Table 11.7 Hierarchical statements of the Recursive Freedom Principle | Level | Statement | Formalization | |------|------|--------| | Individual level | Individual actions should preserve or expand possibility space | $\forall a \in A_{\text{ind}}: \text{RFD}(a) \geq 0$ | | Organizational level | Organizational actions should preserve or expand possibility space | $\forall a \in A_{\text{org}}: \text{RFD}(a) \geq 0$ | | Civilizational level | Civilizational actions should preserve or expand possibility space | $\forall a \in A_{\text{civ}}: \text{RFD}(a) \geq 0$ | | Institutional level | Institutional design should preserve or expand possibility space | $\forall i \in I: \text{RFD}(i) \geq 0$ | III. The Constraint Form of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.19 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, constraint form) The constraint form of the Recursive Freedom Principle: $$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in A: \text{RFD}(a) \geq \theta_{\min}$$ where $\theta_{\min}$ is the minimum acceptable Recursive Freedom Degree, with a default value of 0. IV. The Exception Clause of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.20 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, exception clause) The exception clause of the Recursive Freedom Principle: When the RFD of an action falls below $\theta_{\min}$, the action requires a special justification. A special justification must satisfy the following conditions:

  1. Necessity: the action is a necessary means to an important goal
  2. Proportionality: the benefits of the action are proportional to the compression of the possibility space
  3. Minimality: the action is the minimal-compression plan for realizing the goal

Formal statement: $$\text{SpecialJustification}(a) \Leftrightarrow \text{Necessity}(a) \wedge \text{Proportionality}(a) \wedge \text{MinimalCompression}(a)$$ V. The Recursive Clause of the Recursive Freedom Principle Definition 11.21 (The Recursive Freedom Principle, recursive clause) The recursive clause of the Recursive Freedom Principle: The application of the Recursive Freedom Principle should not close off the possibility of revising the Recursive Freedom Principle. Formal statement: $$\text{Apply}(RFP) \rightarrow \neg\text{Close}(\text{Revise}(RFP))$$ VI. The Complete Specification of the Recursive Freedom Principle Table 11.8 The complete specification of the Recursive Freedom Principle | Specification item | Content | |--------|------| | Principle number | RFP | | Principle name | Recursive Freedom Principle | | English name | Recursive Freedom Principle | | Core statement | Actions should preserve or expand possibility space, and not irreversibly compress it | | Formalization | $\forall a: \text{RFD}(a) \geq \theta_{\min}$ | | Default threshold | $\theta_{\min} = 0$ | | Exception conditions | Necessity + Proportionality + Minimality | | Recursive clause | The principle applies to the principle itself | | Theoretical anchoring | NC-1 (relationality), NC- (participatory character), BP- (intersubjectivity) | | Operational indicator | RFD (Recursive Freedom Degree) |
