§11.3 The Application of the Recursive Freedom Principle

§11.3.1 The General Procedure of Application I. The Overall Framework of the Application Procedure The application of the Recursive Freedom Principle follows this general procedure: Procedure 11.1 (The application procedure of the Recursive Freedom Principle) Step 1: Identify the action

  • Clarify what the action to be evaluated is
  • Determine the action's agent, object, and manner

Step 2: Delimit the possibility space

  • Determine the relevant possibility space
  • Clarify the boundaries and content of the possibility space

Step 3: Assess the possibility space before the action

  • Measure the possibility space before the action, PS(s₀, T)
  • Record features such as dimensions, volume, and connectivity

Step 4: Predict the possibility space after the action

  • Predict the possibility space after the action, PS(s₁, T)
  • Take into account uncertainty and multiple possible outcomes

Step 5: Compute the Recursive Freedom Degree

  • Compute RFD(a) = [M(PS(s₁, T)) - M(PS(s₀, T))] / M(PS(s₀, T))
  • Assess the confidence interval of the RFD

Step 6: Judge whether the principle is satisfied

  • If RFD(a) ≥ θ_min, the action satisfies the principle
  • If RFD(a) < θ_min, check whether there is a special justification

Step 7: If a special justification is needed, test the justification conditions

  • Test necessity: is the action necessary?
  • Test proportionality: are the benefits proportional to the compression?
  • Test minimality: is it the minimal-compression plan?

Step 8: Make a decision

  • If the principle is satisfied or there is a valid special justification, the action is acceptable
  • Otherwise, the action is unacceptable and needs to be modified or abandoned

II. The Formalization of the Application Procedure Definition 11.22 (The application function of the Recursive Freedom Principle) The application function of the Recursive Freedom Principle $\text{ApplyRFP}: A \rightarrow \{\text{Accept}, \text{Reject}, \text{Modify}\}$ is defined as follows: $$\text{ApplyRFP}(a) = \begin{cases} \text{Accept} & \text{if } \text{RFD}(a) \geq \theta_{\min} \\ \text{Accept} & \text{if } \text{RFD}(a) < \theta_{\min} \wedge \text{SpecialJustification}(a) \\ \text{Modify} & \text{if } \text{RFD}(a) < \theta_{\min} \wedge \neg\text{SpecialJustification}(a) \wedge \exists a': \text{RFD}(a') \geq \theta_{\min} \\ \text{Reject} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ III. Handling Uncertainty in Application In practical application, the measurement of possibility space and the computation of RFD usually face uncertainty. Definition 11.2 (RFD under uncertainty) Under uncertainty, RFD is a random variable rather than a determinate value. When applying the Recursive Freedom Principle, one should consider the distribution of RFD, not merely a point estimate. Formal statement: $$\text{RFD}(a) \sim \mathcal{D}(\mu, \sigma^2)$$ where $\mathcal{D}$ is some probability distribution, $\mu$ is the expected value, and $\sigma^2$ is the variance. Decision Rule 11.1 (Decision rules under uncertainty) Under uncertainty, the following decision rules apply:

  1. Expected-value rule: if $E[\text{RFD}(a)] \geq \theta_{\min}$, the action is acceptable
  2. Risk-aversion rule: if $P(\text{RFD}(a) < \theta_{\min}) < \epsilon$, the action is acceptable

. Worst-case rule: if $\min(\text{RFD}(a)) \geq \theta_{\min}$, the action is acceptable

§11.3.2 Application at the Individual Level I. Recursive Freedom Assessment of Individual Action At the individual level, the Recursive Freedom Principle requires individuals to consider the effect on possibility space when acting. Case 11.1 (Career choice) Situation: A young person faces a career choice and can choose A (stable but with limited room for development) or B (risky but with broad room for development). Applying the Recursive Freedom Principle: Step 1: Identify the action

  • Action: choose career A or B
  • Agent: the young person
  • Object: one's own future

Step 2: Delimit the possibility space

  • Relevant possibility space: the possibility space of career development
  • Including dimensions such as income, skills, social relations, and self-realization

Steps 3-4: Assess the possibility space

  • Possibility space after choosing A: fewer dimensions, smaller volume, but high certainty
  • Possibility space after choosing B: more dimensions, larger volume, but high uncertainty

Step 5: Compute the RFD

  • RFD(A) ≈ -0.2 (the possibility space is slightly compressed)
  • RFD(B) ≈ +0. (the possibility space expands, but with risk)

Steps 6-8: Judgment and decision

  • From the standpoint of the Recursive Freedom Principle, B is better
  • But one must consider the individual's risk preference and the specific situation
  • The Recursive Freedom Principle provides a reference, not a forced choice

II. The Recursive Freedom Checklist for Individual Decisions Table 11.9 The recursive freedom checklist for individual decisions | Decision type | Recursive freedom consideration | Key question | |----------|--------------|----------| | Educational choice | Does education expand future possibility space? | Does this educational path keep choices open? | | Career choice | Does the career preserve the possibilities of career development? | Does this career allow future transformation? | | Relationship choice | Does the relationship preserve the possibilities of personal development? | Does this relationship support the growth of both parties? | | Consumption choice | Does consumption affect future capacity to choose? | Does this consumption compress future financial freedom? | | Health choice | Do health behaviors preserve the body's possibilities? | Does this behavior maintain long-term health choices? |

§11.3.3 Application at the Organizational Level I. Recursive Freedom Assessment of Organizational Decisions At the organizational level, the Recursive Freedom Principle requires organizations to consider the effect of their decisions on the possibility spaces of members and stakeholders. Case 11.2 (Corporate strategic decision) Situation: A technology company faces a strategic choice and can choose A (focus on the existing business) or B (diversified development). Applying the Recursive Freedom Principle: Step 1: Identify the action

  • Action: choose strategy A or B
  • Agent: the company
  • Object: the company, employees, customers, society

Step 2: Delimit the possibility space

  • The company's possibility space: the possibilities of business development
  • Employees' possibility space: the possibilities of career development
  • Customers' possibility space: the possibilities of product choice
  • Society's possibility space: the possibilities of technological development

Steps 3-4: Assess the possibility space

  • Strategy A: the company's possibility space is compressed, employees' possibility space is stable
  • Strategy B: the company's possibility space expands; employees' possibility space may expand or compress

Step 5: Compute the RFD (considering all parties jointly)

  • RFD(A) ≈ -0.1 (the overall possibility space is slightly compressed)
  • RFD(B) ≈ +0.2 (the overall possibility space expands, but with risk)

Steps 6-8: Judgment and decision

  • From the standpoint of the Recursive Freedom Principle, B is better
  • But one must consider risk management and the specific circumstances of the stakeholders

II. The Recursive Freedom Principle in Organizational Institutional Design Proposition 11.11 (The Recursive Freedom Principle in organizational institutional design) Organizational institutional design should preserve or expand the possibility space of members. Institutions should not irreversibly compress members' opportunities for choice. Table 11.10 The recursive freedom checklist for organizational institutional design | Institution type | Recursive freedom consideration | Design principle | |----------|--------------|----------| | Employment system | Does it preserve employees' possibilities of career development? | Provide training, allow internal mobility | | Decision-making system | Does it preserve members' possibilities of participation? | Establish participatory mechanisms, maintain transparency | | Incentive system | Does it preserve the possibilities of diverse development? | Avoid single indicators, encourage innovation | | Exit system | Does it preserve post-exit possibilities? | Provide transition support, protect rights |

§11.3.4 Application at the Civilizational Level I. Recursive Freedom Assessment of Civilizational Decisions At the civilizational level, the Recursive Freedom Principle requires a civilization to consider the effect of major decisions on the possibility spaces of humanity as a whole and of future generations. Case 11. (Climate policy decision) Situation: Human civilization faces a climate policy choice and can choose A (maintain the status quo) or B (actively reduce emissions). Applying the Recursive Freedom Principle: Step 1: Identify the action

  • Action: choose climate policy A or B
  • Agent: human civilization
  • Object: the present generation, future generations, other species

Step 2: Delimit the possibility space

  • The present generation's possibility space: lifestyle, economic development
  • Future generations' possibility space: living environment, development choices
  • Other species' possibility space: survival and reproduction

Steps 3-4: Assess the possibility space

  • Policy A: the present generation's possibility space is preserved in the short term; future generations' possibility space is severely compressed
  • Policy B: the present generation's possibility space is slightly compressed in the short term; future generations' possibility space is preserved

Step 5: Compute the RFD (considering all parties and time jointly)

  • RFD(A) ≈ -0.5 (the long-term possibility space is severely compressed)
  • RFD(B) ≈ +0.1 (the long-term possibility space is preserved or expanded)

Steps 6-8: Judgment and decision

  • From the standpoint of the Recursive Freedom Principle, B is clearly better
  • Policy A does not satisfy the Recursive Freedom Principle and can hardly be given a special justification

II. The Recursive Freedom Principle for Civilization-Level Decisions Proposition 11.12 (The Recursive Freedom Principle for civilization-level decisions) Civilization-level decisions should pay particular attention to the effect on the possibility spaces of future generations and other species. Decisions that irreversibly compress civilization-level possibility space require extremely strict justification. Table 11.11 The recursive freedom checklist for civilization-level decisions | Decision type | Recursive freedom consideration | Key question | |----------|--------------|----------| | Environmental policy | Does it preserve the possibility space of ecosystems? | Does the policy maintain ecological diversity? | | Technological development | Does it preserve the possibility space of technological choice? | Does the technology cause irreversible lock-in? | | Resource use | Does it preserve the possibility space of resource use? | Is resource use sustainable? | | Space exploration | Does it preserve the possibility space of space development? | Do space activities keep choices open? |

§11.4 The Recursive Freedom Principle and Traditional Theories of Freedom

§11.4.1 The Relation to Negative Freedom I. The Core Claims of Negative Freedom Negative freedom is one of the concepts of freedom articulated by Isaiah Berlin in Two Concepts of Liberty. Definition 11.24 (Negative freedom) Negative freedom is freedom from external interference. A person is free if and only if no one prevents him from doing what he wants to do. Formal statement: $$\text{NegFree}(S) \Leftrightarrow \neg\exists O: \text{Interfere}(O, S)$$ II. A Comparison of Recursive Freedom and Negative Freedom Table 11.12 A comparison of recursive freedom and negative freedom | Dimension | Negative freedom | Recursive freedom | |------|----------|----------| | Core concern | The absence of interference | The openness of possibility space | | Time dimension | The present | The long range | | Scope of agents | The individual | All agents (including future agents) | | Relation to others | Others are potential interferers | Others are co-constructors of possibility space | | Responsibility dimension | Negative responsibility (non-interference) | Positive responsibility (maintaining possibility space) | III. The Extension of Negative Freedom by Recursive Freedom Proposition 11.1 (The extension of negative freedom by recursive freedom) Recursive freedom includes negative freedom but is not limited to it. Negative freedom concerns present interference; recursive freedom concerns long-range possibility space. Negative freedom requires non-interference; recursive freedom requires actively maintaining possibility space. Argument 11.9 (Recursive freedom includes negative freedom) Premise P1: interference usually compresses the possibility space of the interfered party Premise P2: the Recursive Freedom Principle requires not compressing the possibility space of others Conclusion: the Recursive Freedom Principle entails a requirement of non-interference (in cases where interference compresses possibility space) Boundary Declaration 11.5 (The boundary between recursive freedom and negative freedom) The relation between recursive freedom and negative freedom has the following boundaries:

  • Not all interference compresses possibility space (some interference may expand possibility space)
  • Not all compression of possibility space comes from interference (it may come from natural processes or one's own actions)
  • Therefore, recursive freedom and negative freedom are not in a simple relation of inclusion

§11.4.2 The Relation to Positive Freedom I. The Core Claims of Positive Freedom Positive freedom is the other concept of freedom distinguished by Berlin. Definition 11.25 (Positive freedom) Positive freedom is the freedom of self-realization and self-mastery. A person is free if and only if he is the master of his own life and can act according to his own rational will. Formal statement: $$\text{PosFree}(S) \Leftrightarrow \text{SelfMastery}(S) \wedge \text{SelfRealization}(S)$$ II. A Comparison of Recursive Freedom and Positive Freedom Table 11.1 A comparison of recursive freedom and positive freedom | Dimension | Positive freedom | Recursive freedom | |------|----------|----------| | Core concern | Self-mastery | The openness of possibility space | | Mode of realization | The realization of the rational will | The maintenance of possibility space | | View of the agent | A divided self (higher self vs. lower self) | A relational self | | Potential risk | Coercion in the name of freedom | Excessive conservatism | | Relation to others | Others may be conditions of or obstacles to self-realization | Others are co-constructors of possibility space | III. Recursive Freedom's Response to Positive Freedom Proposition 11.14 (Recursive freedom's response to positive freedom) Recursive freedom absorbs positive freedom's concern with self-realization, but avoids positive freedom's potential risks. Recursive freedom does not presuppose what "the true self" or "true freedom" is, but instead concerns the openness of possibility space, letting agents themselves decide how to realize themselves. Argument 11.10 (Recursive freedom avoids the risks of positive freedom) Premise P1: the risk of positive freedom lies in presupposing "true freedom" and coercing others on that basis Premise P2: recursive freedom does not presuppose the content of "true freedom" Premise P: recursive freedom only requires keeping the possibility space open Premise P4: keeping the possibility space open permits plural ways of self-realization Conclusion: recursive freedom avoids the risks of positive freedom

§11.4.3 The Relation to the Capability Approach I. The Core Claims of the Capability Approach The Capability Approach is a normative framework developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum. Definition 11.26 (The capability approach) The capability approach holds that the evaluation of individual well-being and social justice should focus on individuals' capabilities, that is, the set of functionings that individuals can choose. Core concepts:

  • Functionings: the states and activities that an individual can realize (such as being healthy, being educated, and participating in social life)
  • Capabilities: the set of functionings that an individual can choose

Formal statement: $$\text{Capability}(S) = \{f \in F : \text{Achievable}(S, f)\}$$ where $F$ is the set of all possible functionings. II. A Comparison of Recursive Freedom and the Capability Approach Table 11.14 A comparison of recursive freedom and the capability approach | Dimension | Capability approach | Recursive freedom | |------|----------|----------| | Core concept | Set of capabilities | Possibility space | | Focus | Current capabilities | The long-range evolution of capabilities | | Time dimension | Mainly the present | Emphasis on the long range and recursion | | Scope of agents | Mainly the individual | Includes all agents and future agents | | Normative requirement | Expand the set of capabilities | Keep the possibility space open | III. The Extension of the Capability Approach by Recursive Freedom Proposition 11.15 (The extension of the capability approach by recursive freedom) Recursive freedom can be understood as the temporal and recursive extension of the capability approach. The capability approach concerns the current set of capabilities, whereas recursive freedom concerns the long-range evolution of the set of capabilities and the capability to maintain capabilities. Argument 11.11 (Recursive freedom extends the capability approach) Premise P1: the capability approach concerns the set of functionings that an individual can choose Premise P2: recursive freedom concerns the openness of possibility space Premise P: possibility space includes the current set of capabilities and the future set of capabilities Premise P4: recursive freedom requires keeping the future set of capabilities open Conclusion: recursive freedom extends the capability approach by adding a time dimension and a recursive dimension Definition 11.27 (Meta-capability) Meta-capability is the capability to maintain and expand capabilities. The Recursive Freedom Principle requires protecting meta-capability, that is, protecting the capability to maintain capabilities. Formal statement: $$\text{MetaCapability}(S) = \text{Capability}(\text{Maintain}(\text{Capability}(S)))$$

§11.4.4 The Distinctive Contribution of This Book I. The Distinctive Features of the Recursive Freedom Principle Relative to traditional theories of freedom, the Recursive Freedom Principle has the following distinctive features: Feature one: the extension of the time dimension Traditional theories of freedom mainly concern the present state of freedom. The Recursive Freedom Principle extends the time dimension to the long-range future and concerns the effect of action on the future possibility space. Feature two: the introduction of recursive structure The Recursive Freedom Principle has a recursive structure: the principle applies to the principle itself, and possibility space contains possibility space. This recursive structure is lacking in traditional theories of freedom. Feature three: the extension of the scope of agents Traditional theories of freedom mainly concern the freedom of present agents. The Recursive Freedom Principle extends the scope of agents to all agents, including future agents and non-human agents (where the conditions of agenthood are satisfied). Feature four: the emphasis on relationality The Recursive Freedom Principle emphasizes the relationality of freedom. The possibility space depends on the relational network, and freedom is realized in relations. This is consistent with NC-1 (relational reality). Feature five: the enhancement of operability The Recursive Freedom Principle achieves operationalizability through the RFD indicator. This enables the principle to be applied in actual decision-making, rather than being merely an abstract ideal. II. The Theoretical Contributions of the Recursive Freedom Principle Table 11.15 The theoretical contributions of the Recursive Freedom Principle | Contribution domain | Specific contribution | Relation to traditional theories | |----------|----------|------------------| | Theories of freedom | Introduces a time dimension and recursive structure | Extends negative and positive freedom | | Theories of justice | Provides a basis for intergenerational justice | Supplements Rawls's A Theory of Justice | | Capability theory | Introduces the concept of meta-capability | Extends Sen and Nussbaum's capability approach | | Ethics | Provides a basis for long-range responsibility | Supplements traditional deontology and consequentialism | | Political philosophy | Provides principles for institutional design | Supplements liberalism and republicanism | III. The Relation between the Recursive Freedom Principle and the Three New Views Proposition 11.16 (The relation between the Recursive Freedom Principle and the Three New Views) The Recursive Freedom Principle is the embodiment of the Three New Views at the normative level. It starts from the New Cosmology (NC-1, NC-) and, passing through the bridge principle (BP-), derives normative conclusions. Table 11.16 The relation between the Recursive Freedom Principle and the Three New Views | Proposition of the Three New Views | Relation to the Recursive Freedom Principle | |------------|----------------------| | NC-1 (relationality) | The possibility space depends on the relational network | | NC-2 (processuality) | The possibility space evolves dynamically | | NC- (participatory character) | Action participates in constructing the possibility space | | NL- (continuum) | Recursive freedom is a matter of degree | | NK-4 (negotiability) | The Recursive Freedom Principle is revisable |

§11.5 The Boundaries and Exceptions of the Recursive Freedom Principle

§11.5.1 The Boundaries of the Principle's Application I. Boundaries of Agency Boundary Declaration 11.6 (Boundaries of agency) The Recursive Freedom Principle applies to entities that have agenthood. The determination of agenthood is based on the UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale). For entities whose UCS is below the threshold, the application of the Recursive Freedom Principle needs adjustment. Formal statement: $$\text{UCS}(S) > \theta_{\text{subject}} \Rightarrow \text{RFP applies to } S$$ Table 11.17 Specific provisions of the boundaries of agency | Agent type | UCS range | Applicability of RFP | Explanation | |----------|---------|-----------|------| | Human adults | High | Fully applicable | The standard case of application | | Human children | Medium-high | Applicable, but requires representation | Guardians consider on their behalf | | Higher animals | Medium | Partially applicable | Consider their possibility space | | AI systems | To be assessed | Depends on UCS | Requires specific assessment | | Simple organisms | Low | Indirectly applicable | Considered through ecosystems | II. Boundaries of Action Boundary Declaration 11.7 (Boundaries of action) The Recursive Freedom Principle mainly applies to actions that have a significant effect on possibility space. For everyday actions with minor effects, the binding force of the Recursive Freedom Principle is weaker. Formal statement: $$|\text{RFD}(a)| > \theta_{\text{action}} \Rightarrow \text{RFD strong constraint applies to } a$$ Table 11.18 Specific provisions of the boundaries of action | Action type | RFD effect | Strength of RFP constraint | Explanation | |----------|---------|-------------|------| | Civilization-level decisions | Extremely large | Extremely strong | Such as climate policy and nuclear weapons | | Organizational-level decisions | Large | Strong | Such as corporate strategy and policy-making | | Major personal decisions | Medium | Medium | Such as career choice and marriage | | Everyday decisions | Small | Weak | Such as daily consumption and leisure | III. Boundaries of Context Boundary Declaration 11.8 (Boundaries of context) The Recursive Freedom Principle has stronger normative force in contexts of deep uncertainty. In contexts of higher certainty, one may rely more on consequence assessment. Formal statement: $$\text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Context}) \Rightarrow \text{RFP has strong normative force}$$ IV. Boundaries of Time Boundary Declaration 11.9 (Boundaries of time) The Recursive Freedom Principle concerns long-range effects, but the time horizon of evaluation must be determined according to context. A time horizon that is too short may neglect important effects, while one that is too long may lead to excessive uncertainty. Formal statement: $$T_{\text{min}} \leq T \leq T_{\text{max}}$$ where $T$ is the time horizon of evaluation, and $T_{\text{min}}$ and $T_{\text{max}}$ are context-dependent boundaries.

§11.5.2 Possible Exceptions I. The General Framework of Exceptions Definition 11.28 (Exceptions) Exceptions are cases in which the RFD falls below $\theta_{\min}$ but the action is still acceptable. Exceptions must satisfy the special-justification conditions. Special-justification conditions:

  1. Necessity: the action is a necessary means to an important goal
  2. Proportionality: the benefits of the action are proportional to the compression of the possibility space
  3. Minimality: the action is the minimal-compression plan for realizing the goal

II. Specific Exceptions Exception one: necessity (emergency avoidance) In emergencies, it may be necessary to take actions that compress possibility space in order to avoid a greater loss. Case 11.4 (Emergency avoidance) Situation: A ship is about to sink, and the captain must decide whether to jettison part of the cargo to save the passengers' lives. Analysis:

  • Jettisoning the cargo compresses the possibility space of the cargo's owner
  • But not jettisoning the cargo would cause the passengers' death, compressing a greater possibility space
  • Therefore, jettisoning the cargo satisfies the special-justification conditions

Conclusion: emergency avoidance is an exception to the Recursive Freedom Principle Exception two: Pareto improvement If an action, although compressing some possibilities, expands more important possibilities, it may be acceptable. Case 11.5 (Pareto improvement) Situation: A technological innovation will eliminate some old technologies but open up more new possibilities. Analysis:

  • Eliminating the old technologies compresses the possibility space of those who depend on them
  • But the new technologies open up more new possibility space
  • If the net effect is an expansion of possibility space, the action is acceptable

Conclusion: Pareto improvement can be an exception to the Recursive Freedom Principle Exception three: negotiated consent If all affected agents agree to compress certain possibilities, it may be acceptable. Case 11.6 (Negotiated consent) Situation: A community decides to permanently protect a piece of land as a nature reserve, forgoing the possibility of development. Analysis:

  • Permanent protection compresses the possibility space of development
  • But the community members agreed to this decision through negotiation
  • The negotiated consent provides a special justification

Conclusion: negotiated consent can be an exception to the Recursive Freedom Principle Table 11.19 Summary of exceptions | Exception type | Condition | Basis of justification | Restriction | |----------|------|----------|------| | Emergency avoidance | Emergency | Avoid a greater loss | Must be genuinely urgent | | Pareto improvement | Net effect is positive | The overall possibility space expands | Requires reliable assessment | | Negotiated consent | All affected parties agree | Autonomous decision | Consent must be genuine |

§11.5.3 Handling Conflicts with Other Principles I. Potential Conflict with the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Conflict Scenario 11.1 Situation: A certain technology can expand possibility space but requires consuming a large amount of negentropy resources. Conflict analysis:

  • The Recursive Freedom Principle supports this technology (it expands possibility space)
  • The Negentropy Responsibility Principle may oppose this technology (it consumes negentropy resources)

Handling:

  1. Assess the net effect: does the expansion of possibility space exceed the cost of negentropy consumption?
  2. Seek alternatives: is there an alternative technology that consumes less negentropy?
  3. Time trade-off: does short-term negentropy consumption buy long-term expansion of possibility space?

II. Potential Conflict with the Reversibility Principle Conflict Scenario 11.2 Situation: A certain irreversible action can significantly expand possibility space. Conflict analysis:

  • The Recursive Freedom Principle supports this action (it expands possibility space)
  • The Reversibility Principle may oppose this action (it is irreversible)

Handling:

  1. Assess the degree of irreversibility: is it completely irreversible or partially reversible?
  2. Assess the certainty of the expansion of possibility space: is the expansion certain or uncertain?
  3. Risk assessment: if the expansion fails, what are the consequences?

III. A General Framework for Handling Principle Conflicts Definition 11.29 (A framework for handling principle conflicts) When the Recursive Freedom Principle conflicts with other principles, the following framework is adopted: Step 1: Identify the conflict

  • Clarify which principles are in conflict
  • Assess the nature and degree of the conflict

Step 2: Assess the weight of each principle

  • In the specific context, what is the relative importance of each principle?
  • Does any principle have priority?

Step : Seek a reconciliatory solution

  • Is there a solution that simultaneously satisfies each principle?
  • Can the conflict be reduced by modifying the action?

Step 4: If reconciliation is impossible, make a trade-off

  • Determine the priority according to context
  • Choose the overall optimal solution

Step 5: Record the reasons for the decision

  • Explicitly record why a particular solution was chosen
  • Provide a reference for similar situations in the future

Table 11.20 General guidance on the priority of principles | Context | Order of priority | Reason | |------|------------|------| | A taboo red line exists | Taboo red line > other principles | The taboo red line is an absolute constraint | | Deep uncertainty | Reversibility > recursive freedom > negentropy responsibility | Under uncertainty, prioritize maintaining reversibility | | Higher certainty | Recursive freedom ≈ negentropy responsibility > reversibility | One may rely more on consequence assessment | | Emergency | Survival > other principles | Survival is the precondition of everything else |

Footnotes

Chapter 11 Footnotes

[1] The Concept of Possibility Space: The concept of possibility space is related to, but not identical with, the concept of "possible worlds" in modal logic. Possible worlds are logically possible worlds, whereas a possibility space is the set of states reachable under given constraints. For discussion of possible worlds, see: Lewis, D. (1986). On the Plurality of Worlds. Blackwell. [2] Negative and Positive Liberty: For Berlin's classic distinction, see: Berlin, I. (1958). "Two Concepts of Liberty." In Four Essays on Liberty. Oxford University Press, 1969. For criticism and development of this distinction, see: MacCallum, G. C. (1967). "Negative and Positive Freedom." Philosophical Review, 76(), 12-4. [3] Republican Liberty: For a contemporary exposition of republican liberty, see: Pettit, P. (1997). Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government. Oxford University Press. Skinner, Q. (1998). Liberty before Liberalism. Cambridge University Press. [4] The Capability Approach: For Sen's capability approach, see: Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom. Oxford University Press. For Nussbaum's development of it, see: Nussbaum, M. C. (2011). Creating Capabilities: The Human Development Approach. Harvard University Press. [5] The Concept of Recursion: For the mathematical and computer-science foundations of recursion, see: Hofstadter, D. R. (1979). Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid. Basic Books. For applications of recursion in philosophy, see: Sider, T. (2011). Writing the Book of the World. Oxford University Press. [6] Intergenerational Justice: For discussion of intergenerational justice, see: Parfit, D. (1984). Reasons and Persons, Part IV. Oxford University Press. Gosseries, A., & Meyer, L. H. (Eds.) (2009). Intergenerational Justice. Oxford University Press. [7] Longtermism: For contemporary discussion of longtermism, see: MacAskill, W. (2022). What We Owe the Future. Basic Books. Ord, T. (2020). The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity. Hachette Books. [8] Phase Space and Liouville's Theorem: For the physical foundations of phase space and Liouville's theorem, see: Goldstein, H., Poole, C., & Safko, J. (2002). Classical Mechanics (rd ed.). Addison-Wesley, Chapter 9. [9] Deep Uncertainty: For the concept of deep uncertainty and decision methods under it, see: Walker, W. E., et al. (201). "Deep Uncertainty." In S. I. Gass & M. C. Fu (Eds.), Encyclopedia of Operations Research and Management Science (rd ed.). Springer. [10] Meta-capability: The concept of meta-capability is an innovation of this work. For related discussion, see the discussion of "capabilities of capabilities" in the capability-approach literature: Wolff, J., & de-Shalit, A. (2007). Disadvantage. Oxford University Press.

Chapter 11 Appendix: The Axiom System of the Recursive Freedom Principle

Axiom System 11.A (Recursive Freedom Principle Axiom System RFP-AX) 【Basic Definitions】 Definition D1 (Possibility Space): PS(S) = {s ∈ Σ : Achievable(S, s, R_S)} where Σ is the state space and R_S is the relational network in which S is situated Definition D2 (Measure of Possibility Space): M: PS → ℝ⁺ M(PS) = α·Dim(PS) + β·Vol(PS) + γ·Conn(PS) where α + β + γ = 1 Definition D (Recursive Freedom Degree): RFD: A → ℝ RFD(a) = [M(PS(s₁, T)) - M(PS(s₀, T))] / M(PS(s₀, T)) where s₀ is the pre-action state, s₁ is the post-action state, and T is the assessment time horizon Definition D4 (Special Justification): SpecialJustification(a) ↔ Necessity(a) ∧ Proportionality(a) ∧ MinimalCompression(a) 【Axioms】 Axiom A1 (Possibility Protection Axiom): ∀a ∈ A: O(RFD(a) ≥ θ_min) ∨ O(SpecialJustification(a)) Actions should maintain the possibility space, or have special justification Axiom A2 (Recursion Axiom): Apply(RFP) → ¬Close(Revise(RFP)) The application of a principle should not close off the possibility of revising the principle Axiom A (Intersubjectivity Axiom): ∀S₁, S₂ ∈ Agents: Protect(S₁, PS(S₁)) → Protect(S₁, PS(S₂)) Protecting one's own possibility space implies protecting others' possibility space Axiom A4 (Irreversible Compression Axiom): IrreversibleCompress(a, PS) → ¬Permissible(a) ∨ StrongJustification(a) Irreversible compression requires strong justification Axiom A5 (Temporal Extension Axiom): ∀t₁ < t₂: Protect(PS(t₁)) → Protect(PS(t₂)) Protecting the present possibility space implies protecting the future possibility space 【Inference Rules】 Rule R1 (RFD Assessment Rule): If RFD(a) ≥ θ_min, then a satisfies RFP Rule R2 (Special Justification Rule): If RFD(a) < θ_min and SpecialJustification(a), then a satisfies RFP Rule R (Non-Satisfaction Rule): If RFD(a) < θ_min and ¬SpecialJustification(a), then a does not satisfy RFP Rule R4 (Recursive Application Rule): RFP applies to the application of RFP itself 【Theorems】 Theorem T1 (Possibility Protection Theorem): ∀a: Permissible(a) → (RFD(a) ≥ θ_min ∨ SpecialJustification(a)) Proof: Follows directly from Axiom A1 Theorem T2 (Mutual Protection Theorem): ∀S₁, S₂: RFP(S₁) → Protect(S₁, PS(S₂)) Proof: Follows from Axiom A and the definition of RFP Theorem T (Recursivity Theorem): RFP applies to the revision of RFP Proof: Follows from Axiom A2

§12.1 The Derivation of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

§12.1.1 From the New View of Life to Negentropy Dependence I. A Review of the Core Propositions of the New View of Life Chapter 2 established three core propositions of the New View of Life. Before deriving the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, it is necessary to review the core content of these propositions, especially NL-2 (negentropy persistence). Proposition NL-1 (cross-substrate life): Life is not limited to carbon-based biological forms. The essence of life lies in its functional organization, not in a particular material substrate. Any system capable of maintaining its own organization, processing information, interacting with its environment, and exhibiting purposive behavior may be an instance of life. Formalized statement: $$\text{Life}(x) \Leftrightarrow \text{SelfMaintenance}(x) \wedge \text{InfoProcessing}(x) \wedge \text{EnvInteraction}(x) \wedge \text{Purposiveness}(x)$$ Proposition NL-2 (negentropy persistence): Life is a process of local reverse entropy. Living systems maintain their own ordered structure by acquiring negentropy (low-entropy energy and matter) from the environment, while exporting high-entropy waste to the environment. The persistence of life depends on a continuous flow of negentropy. Formalized statement: $$\text{Survive}(L) \Rightarrow \exists \text{NegFlow}(L, E) > 0$$ Here $L$ is the living system, $E$ is the environment, and $\text{NegFlow}(L, E)$ is the net flow of negentropy from the environment into the living system. Proposition NL- (the continuum of consciousness/subjectivity): Consciousness and subjectivity are not binary (present or absent) but a matter of degree. There exists a continuum of consciousness from simple to complex, and different life forms occupy different positions along this continuum. Formalized statement: $$\text{Consciousness}: \text{Entities} \rightarrow [0, 1]$$ II. The Physical Basis of Negentropy Dependence NL-2 (negentropy persistence) is grounded in the second law of thermodynamics. The second law states that in an isolated system, entropy always tends to increase. Living systems, however, are open systems: they maintain their own low-entropy state by exchanging matter and energy with the environment. Definition 12.1 (Entropy) Entropy is a measure of the degree of disorder of a system. In thermodynamics, entropy is defined as: $$S = k_B \ln \Omega$$ Here $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant and $\Omega$ is the number of possible microstates of the system. Definition 12.2 (Negentropy) Negentropy is the negative of entropy, that is, a measure of the degree of order of a system. Negentropy can also be understood as the degree to which a system deviates from the maximum-entropy state. $$N = S_{\max} - S$$ Here $S_{\max}$ is the maximum possible entropy of the system and $S$ is the actual entropy of the system. Proposition 12.1 (the negentropy dependence of life) The persistence of a living system depends on a continuous input of negentropy. If the negentropy input is interrupted, the living system will tend toward thermodynamic equilibrium (death). Formalized statement: $$\frac{dS_L}{dt} = \frac{dS_i}{dt} + \frac{dS_e}{dt}$$ Here $S_L$ is the entropy of the living system, $\frac{dS_i}{dt}$ is the internal entropy production rate (always positive), and $\frac{dS_e}{dt}$ is the rate of entropy flow exchanged with the environment (which may be negative). The condition under which a living system maintains a low-entropy state is: $$\frac{dS_e}{dt} < -\frac{dS_i}{dt}$$ That is, the negentropy acquired from the environment must exceed the internal entropy production. III. The Sources and Finitude of Negentropy Proposition 12.2 (the finitude of negentropy sources) In any finite environment, the available negentropy is finite. The main sources of negentropy include:

  • Stellar radiation (solar energy)
  • Chemical energy (fossil fuels, nuclear energy)
  • Gravitational potential energy
  • Ordered material structures

Formalized statement: $$N_{\text{available}}(E, t) < \infty$$ Here $N_{\text{available}}(E, t)$ is the total negentropy available to environment $E$ at time $t$. Proposition 12. (the irreversibility of negentropy consumption) The consumption of negentropy is usually irreversible. Once negentropy is consumed (converted into high-entropy waste), restoring it requires an additional input of negentropy. Formalized statement: $$\text{Consume}(N) \rightarrow \text{Irreversible}(\text{Consume}(N)) \vee \text{RequireMoreNeg}(\text{Restore}(N))$$ IV. From Negentropy Dependence to Negentropy Competition Proposition 12.4 (negentropy competition) In multi-agent situations, different living systems may compete for limited negentropy resources. One agent's consumption of negentropy may reduce the negentropy available to other agents. Formalized statement: $$\text{Consume}(L_1, N) \rightarrow \Delta N_{\text{available}}(L_2) < 0$$ Here $L_1$ and $L_2$ are different living systems. Proposition 12.5 (negentropy externalization) In the process of consuming negentropy, living systems produce high-entropy waste. If this waste is discharged into a shared environment, it constitutes the externalization of entropy costs. Formalized statement: $$\text{Consume}(L, N) \rightarrow \text{Produce}(L, S_{\text{waste}})$$ $$\text{Externalize}(L, S_{\text{waste}}, E) \rightarrow \Delta S(E) > 0$$ Here $S_{\text{waste}}$ is the entropy of the waste and $E$ is the shared environment.

【Column 12.1】Schrödinger's concept of “negentropy” —————————————————————————————————

│                                                                 │
│  I. Historical background                                       │
│                                                                 │
│  The concept of “negentropy” was first proposed by the physicist   │
│  Erwin Schrödinger in his 1944 work What Is Life?. Schrödinger    │
│  sought to understand the essence of life from the standpoint of  │
│  physics.                                                         │
│                                                                 │
│  II. Schrödinger's core thesis                                   │
│                                                                 │
│  Schrödinger pointed out that living systems appear to violate   │
│  the second law of thermodynamics—they maintain highly ordered    │
│  structures rather than tending toward disorder. His explanation  │
│  is that living systems are open systems that maintain their own   │
│  ordered state by “feeding on negative entropy”.                  │
│                                                                 │
│  Schrödinger's original words:                                   │
│  “Life feeds on negative entropy.”                               │
│                                                                 │
│  III. Subsequent development                                     │
│                                                                 │
│  Schrödinger's concept was later developed by Ilya Prigogine and  │
│  others into the theory of dissipative structures. Dissipative     │
│  structures are open systems far from thermodynamic equilibrium    │
│  that maintain their own ordered structure by exchanging matter    │
│  and energy with the environment.                                 │
│                                                                 │
│  IV. Use in this work                                             │
│                                                                 │
│  This work adopts Schrödinger's concept of “negentropy” but gives │
│  it a normative extension:                                        │
│  - Descriptive level: life depends on negentropy (Schrödinger's  │
│    original meaning)                                             │
│  - Normative level: life bears responsibility for negentropy      │
│    (this work's extension)                                       │
│                                                                 │
│  V. Boundary declaration                                         │
│                                                                 │
│  This work's use of the concept of “negentropy” is heuristic rather │
│  than a strict physical definition. In some contexts, “free       │
│  energy” may be a more precise concept. This work does not claim   │
│  that the concept of “negentropy” can be applied directly to all   │
│  physical contexts.                                              │

§12.1.2 From Intersubjectivity to the Distribution of Responsibility I. A Review of the Bridge Principles Chapter 5 established three bridge principles, among which BP-1 (the principle of survival rationality) and BP- (the principle of intersubjectivity) are the key bridges for deriving the Negentropy Responsibility Principle. Bridge principle BP-1 (the principle of survival rationality): A rational agent with a will to survive ought to maintain its conditions of survival. Formalized statement: $$BP\text{-}1: \text{Rational}(S) \wedge \text{WillToSurvive}(S) \rightarrow O(\text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions}(S)))$$ Bridge principle BP- (the principle of intersubjectivity): In multi-agent situations, agents ought to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by other rational agents. Formalized statement: $$BP\text{-}: \text{MultiAgent}(\text{Context}) \rightarrow O(\text{Acceptable}(\text{Principles}(S), \text{OtherRationalAgents}))$$ II. From Survival Rationality to Negentropy Maintenance Combining NL-2 (negentropy persistence) and BP-1 (the principle of survival rationality), it can be derived that agents have reason to maintain the sources of negentropy. Proposition 12.6 (survival rationality implies negentropy maintenance) From BP-1 (the principle of survival rationality) and NL-2 (negentropy persistence), a rational agent with a will to survive ought to maintain its sources of negentropy. Argument 12.1 (the argument that survival rationality implies negentropy maintenance) Premise P1 (BP-1): a rational agent with a will to survive ought to maintain its conditions of survival Premise P2 (NL-2): the persistence of life depends on a continuous flow of negentropy Premise P: the flow of negentropy depends on the availability of negentropy sources Premise P4: if X is a necessary condition of Y, and the agent ought to maintain Y, then the agent ought to maintain X Step 1: from P2, the flow of negentropy is a necessary condition of survival Step 2: from P, the negentropy source is a necessary condition of the flow of negentropy Step : from Step 1 and Step 2, the negentropy source is a necessary condition of survival Step 4: from P1 and P4, the agent ought to maintain the negentropy source Conclusion: a rational agent with a will to survive ought to maintain its sources of negentropy III. From Intersubjectivity to Negentropy Responsibility So far we have argued that agents have reason to maintain their own sources of negentropy. But the Negentropy Responsibility Principle requires a broader responsibility—not only maintaining one's own sources of negentropy, but also not harming the sources of negentropy of others, and not externalizing entropy costs. Proposition 12.7 (the externality of negentropy consumption)

  • In a shared environment, one agent's consumption of negentropy may produce negative externalities:
  • reducing the negentropy available to other agents
  • increasing the entropy of the shared environment (pollution)

Formalized statement: $$\text{Consume}(S_1, N, E) \rightarrow \text{NegativeExternality}(S_2, E)$$ Proposition 12.8 (the unacceptability of externalization) From BP- (the principle of intersubjectivity), a principle of action that externalizes entropy costs onto others cannot be reasonably accepted by others. Argument 12.2 (the argument for the unacceptability of externalization) Premise P1 (BP-): agents ought to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by others Premise P2: externalizing entropy costs onto others harms their conditions of survival Premise P: a principle of action that harms others' conditions of survival cannot be reasonably accepted by others Conclusion: a principle of action that externalizes entropy costs onto others cannot be reasonably accepted by others Proposition 12.9 (the intersubjective basis of negentropy responsibility) From BP- (the principle of intersubjectivity), agents ought not only to maintain their own sources of negentropy but also to:

  • not over-consume shared negentropy resources
  • not externalize entropy costs onto others
  • contribute to the sustainability of shared negentropy resources

Argument 12. (the intersubjective argument for negentropy responsibility) Premise P1 (Proposition 12.6): agents ought to maintain their own sources of negentropy Premise P2 (BP-): agents ought to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by others Premise P (Proposition 12.8): a principle that externalizes entropy costs cannot be reasonably accepted by others Premise P4: a principle that maintains shared negentropy resources can be reasonably accepted by others Step 1: from P1, agents have reason to maintain sources of negentropy Step 2: from P2 and P, agents ought not to externalize entropy costs Step : from P2 and P4, agents ought to maintain shared negentropy resources Conclusion: agents ought to maintain sources of negentropy, not externalize entropy costs, and maintain shared negentropy resources IV. Principles of the Distribution of Responsibility How is negentropy responsibility distributed among different agents? This requires considering several factors. Proposition 12.10 (the multi-factor principle of responsibility distribution) The distribution of negentropy responsibility ought to consider the following factors:

  • Consumption: agents that consume more negentropy bear more responsibility
  • Capability: agents with greater capability to maintain negentropy bear more responsibility
  • Benefit: agents that benefit more from negentropy consumption bear more responsibility
  • History: agents that have historically consumed more negentropy bear more responsibility

Formalized statement: $$R(S) = f(\text{Consumption}(S), \text{Capability}(S), \text{Benefit}(S), \text{History}(S))$$ Here $R(S)$ is the negentropy responsibility of agent $S$, and $f$ is a function that takes all factors into account. Definition 12. (the proportionality-of-consumption principle) Principle of proportional consumption: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to its negentropy consumption. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{consumption}}(S) \propto \text{Consumption}(S)$$ Definition 12.4 (the capability principle) Capability principle: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to its capability to maintain negentropy. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{capability}}(S) \propto \text{Capability}(S)$$ Definition 12.5 (the benefit principle) Benefit principle: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to the benefit it obtains from negentropy consumption. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{benefit}}(S) \propto \text{Benefit}(S)$$ Definition 12.6 (the historical principle) Historical principle: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to its historical negentropy consumption. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{history}}(S) \propto \int_0^t \text{Consumption}(S, \tau) d\tau$$

§12.1.3 The Formalized Statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle I. A Preliminary Statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Based on the derivations of the preceding two sections, a preliminary statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle can now be given. Definition 12.7 (the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, preliminary statement) Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR): living agents ought to maintain their sources of negentropy and ought not to externalize entropy costs onto others or onto the shared environment. II. The Formalized Statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Definition 12.8 (the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, formalized statement) The formalized statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle: $$PNR: \forall S \in L: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}(S))) \wedge O(\neg\text{Externalize}(\text{EntropyCost}(S)))$$ Here:

  • $L$ is the set of living agents
  • $\text{NegSource}(S)$ is the source of negentropy of agent $S$
  • $\text{EntropyCost}(S)$ is the entropy cost of agent $S$
  • $O$ is the “ought” operator
  • $\text{Externalize}$ denotes externalizing costs

Interpretation: for any living agent $S$, $S$ ought to maintain its sources of negentropy, and $S$ ought not to externalize entropy costs. III. The Constraint Forms of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Definition 12.9 (the negentropy balance constraint) Negentropy balance constraint: an agent's negentropy consumption ought not to exceed its negentropy contribution (or the regenerative capacity of its negentropy sources). Formalized statement: $$\dot{N}_{\text{consume}}(S) \leq \dot{N}_{\text{contribute}}(S) + \dot{N}_{\text{regenerate}}(\text{Source}(S))$$ Here:

  • $\dot{N}_{\text{consume}}(S)$ is the negentropy consumption rate of agent $S$
  • $\dot{N}_{\text{contribute}}(S)$ is the negentropy contribution rate of agent $S$
  • $\dot{N}_{\text{regenerate}}(\text{Source}(S))$ is the regeneration rate of the negentropy source

Definition 12.10 (the entropy externalization constraint) Entropy externalization constraint: the entropy an agent emits into the shared environment ought not to exceed the environment's entropy absorption capacity. Formalized statement: $$\dot{S}_{\text{emit}}(S) \leq \dot{S}_{\text{absorb}}(E) \cdot \frac{\text{Share}(S)}{\sum_i \text{Share}(S_i)}$$ Here:

  • $\dot{S}_{\text{emit}}(S)$ is the entropy emission rate of agent $S$
  • $\dot{S}_{\text{absorb}}(E)$ is the entropy absorption capacity of environment $E$
  • $\text{Share}(S)$ is the fair share of agent $S$

IV. The Allocation Formula of Negentropy Responsibility Definition 12.11 (the negentropy responsibility allocation formula) Negentropy responsibility allocation formula: the negentropy responsibility $R(S)$ of agent $S$ is determined by the following formula: $$R(S) = \alpha \cdot \frac{\text{Consumption}(S)}{\sum_i \text{Consumption}(S_i)} + \beta \cdot \frac{\text{Capability}(S)}{\sum_i \text{Capability}(S_i)} + \gamma \cdot \frac{\text{Benefit}(S)}{\sum_i \text{Benefit}(S_i)} + \delta \cdot R_{\text{baseline}}$$ Here:

  • $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ are weight coefficients, with $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 1$
  • $R_{\text{baseline}}$ is the baseline responsibility (the minimum responsibility of all agents)

Table 12.1 Suggested weights for the allocation of negentropy responsibility | Situation | $\alpha$ (consumption) | $\beta$ (capability) | $\gamma$ (benefit) | $\delta$ (baseline) | |------|------------------|-----------------|------------------|------------------| | Default situation | 0. | 0. | 0. | 0.1 | | Large capability differences | 0.2 | 0.4 | 0. | 0.1 | | Historical injustice | 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.4 | 0.2 | | Emergency situation | 0.4 | 0. | 0.2 | 0.1 | Boundary declaration 12.1 (the determination of weights) The specific values of the weights $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ need to be determined through negotiation according to the situation; they are not fixed a priori. This work provides suggested values, not mandatory values. Different situations may require different weight configurations. V. The Complete Formalization of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Definition 12.12 (the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, complete formalization) The complete formalized statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle: Axiom PNR-1 (maintenance axiom): ∀S ∈ L: O(Maintain(NegSource(S))) Living agents ought to maintain their sources of negentropy Axiom PNR-2 (no-externalization axiom): ∀S ∈ L: O(¬Externalize(EntropyCost(S), SharedEnv)) Living agents ought not to externalize entropy costs onto the shared environment Axiom PNR- (responsibility-allocation axiom): ∀S ∈ L: R(S) = f(Consumption(S), Capability(S), Benefit(S), Baseline) Negentropy responsibility is allocated according to consumption, capability, benefit, and baseline Axiom PNR-4 (intergenerational responsibility axiom): ∀S ∈ L: O(¬Externalize(EntropyCost(S), FutureGenerations)) Living agents ought not to externalize entropy costs onto future generations Auxiliary definition PNR-D1 (negentropy balance constraint): Ṅ_consume(S) ≤ Ṅ_contribute(S) + Ṅ_regenerate(Source(S)) Auxiliary definition PNR-D2 (entropy externalization constraint): Ṡ_emit(S) ≤ Ṡ_absorb(E) · Share(S) / Σ Share(S_i) Table 12.2 The formalized elements of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle | Element | Symbol | Meaning | Constraint | |------|------|------|------| | Set of living agents | $L$ | all living agents | - | | Negentropy source | $\text{NegSource}$ | the agent's source of negentropy | - | | Entropy cost | $\text{EntropyCost}$ | the entropy produced by the agent | - | | Negentropy responsibility | $R$ | the agent's negentropy responsibility | $R \geq R_{\text{baseline}}$ | | Negentropy consumption rate | $\dot{N}_{\text{consume}}$ | negentropy consumption per unit time | $\leq$ regeneration rate | | Entropy emission rate | $\dot{S}_{\text{emit}}$ | entropy emission per unit time | $\leq$ share of absorption capacity |

A Validity Check of the Derivation Check 12.1 (the logical validity of the derivation) The logical validity of the derivation can be checked in the following ways:

  1. Acceptability of the premises: are NL-2, BP-1, and BP- acceptable?
  2. NL-2 has been argued for in Chapter 2
  3. BP-1 and BP- have been argued for in Chapter 5
  4. Therefore, the premises are acceptable
  5. Validity of the reasoning: is the reasoning from the premises to the conclusion valid?
  6. The inferential steps of each argument node have been presented explicitly
  7. The reasoning follows standard logical rules
  8. Therefore, the reasoning is valid

. Coherence of the conclusion: is the conclusion coherent with other accepted propositions?

  • PNR is coherent with the other propositions of the Three New Views
  • PNR is coherent with RFP (the Recursive Freedom Principle)
  • Therefore, the conclusion is coherent

Boundary declaration 12.2 (the boundaries of the derivation) The derivation of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle has the following boundaries:

  • The derivation depends on the acceptability of the New View of Life (NL-2)
  • The derivation depends on the acceptability of the bridge principles (BP-1, BP-)
  • If these premises are revised, the conclusions of the derivation must be revised accordingly
  • The derivation is revocable, not a closed proof

§12.2 The Content of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

§12.2.1 The Meaning of “Negentropy” I. The Thermodynamic Definition of Negentropy Definition 12.1 (thermodynamic negentropy) Thermodynamic negentropy is the negative of entropy, expressing the degree to which a system deviates from the maximum-entropy state. Formalized statement: $$N = S_{\max} - S = -k_B \ln \frac{\Omega}{\Omega_{\max}}$$ Here $\Omega$ is the current number of microstates of the system, and $\Omega_{\max}$ is the maximum possible number of microstates of the system. The features of thermodynamic negentropy:

  • Negentropy is a measure of the degree of order of a system
  • The higher the negentropy, the more ordered the system
  • Maintaining negentropy requires an input of energy
  • The consumption of negentropy is usually irreversible

II. The Information-Theoretic Definition of Negentropy Definition 12.14 (information-theoretic negentropy) Information-theoretic negentropy is the negative of information entropy, expressing a system's information content or degree of certainty. Formalized statement: $$N_I = -H(X) = \sum_i p_i \log p_i$$ Here $H(X)$ is the Shannon entropy and $p_i$ is the probability of state $i$. The features of information-theoretic negentropy:

  • Negentropy is positively correlated with the amount of information
  • Acquiring information is equivalent to reducing uncertainty
  • Information processing requires the consumption of negentropy (Landauer's principle)

III. The Unification of Thermodynamic and Information-Theoretic Negentropy Proposition 12.11 (the unity of negentropy) Thermodynamic negentropy and information-theoretic negentropy are unified at a deep level. Landauer's Principle shows that erasing one bit of information requires consuming at least $k_B T \ln 2$ of energy. Formalized statement: $$\Delta E \geq k_B T \ln 2 \cdot \Delta I$$ Here $\Delta E$ is the energy consumed and $\Delta I$ is the amount of information erased (in bits). Table 12.4 A comparison of thermodynamic and information-theoretic negentropy | Dimension | Thermodynamic negentropy | Information-theoretic negentropy | |------|------------|------------| | Definition | $S_{\max} - S$ | $-H(X)$ | | Unit | joule/kelvin | bit | | Physical meaning | degree of order | information content | | Relation | unified through Landauer's principle | unified through Landauer's principle | IV. The Extended Meaning of Negentropy in This Work Definition 12.15 (normative negentropy) In this work, negentropy is not only a physical concept but also a normative concept. Normative negentropy refers to the resources and conditions that maintain ordered structures and support the persistence of life and the development of civilization. The scope of normative negentropy:

  • Energy resources (solar energy, fossil fuels, nuclear energy)
  • Material resources (minerals, water, air)
  • Ecosystem services (the carbon cycle, the water cycle, biodiversity)
  • Social order (institutions, knowledge, culture)

Boundary declaration 12. (the boundaries of the concept of negentropy) This work's use of the concept of “negentropy” is extensional, going beyond the strict definition of physics. In some contexts, “free energy”, “available energy”, or “resources” may be more precise concepts. This work does not claim that all contexts can be precisely described with the concept of “negentropy”.

§12.2.2 The Meaning of “Responsibility” I. The General Concept of Responsibility Definition 12.16 (responsibility) Responsibility refers to an agent's obligation to answer for something or for some action. Responsibility can be retrospective (accountability for past actions) or prospective (accountability for future actions). Types of responsibility:

  • Causal responsibility: because the agent's action caused a certain outcome, the agent is responsible for that outcome
  • Role responsibility: because the agent occupies a certain role, the agent is responsible for the duties of that role
  • Capacity responsibility: because the agent has the capacity to do something, the agent has a responsibility to do it
  • Benefit responsibility: because the agent benefits from something, the agent is responsible for that thing

II. The Particularity of Negentropy Responsibility Proposition 12.12 (the particularity of negentropy responsibility) Negentropy responsibility is a special kind of responsibility that combines several types of responsibility:

  • Causal responsibility: the agent consumes negentropy, and is therefore responsible for the consequences of negentropy consumption
  • Capacity responsibility: the agent has the capacity to maintain negentropy, and is therefore responsible for maintaining it
  • Benefit responsibility: the agent benefits from negentropy consumption, and is therefore responsible for the negentropy source
  • Survival responsibility: the agent's survival depends on negentropy, and it is therefore responsible for the negentropy source

Table 12.5 The relation of negentropy responsibility to traditional types of responsibility | Type of responsibility | Manifestation in negentropy responsibility | Weight | |----------|-------------------|------| | Causal responsibility | consuming negentropy causes a reduction of negentropy | medium | | Capacity responsibility | having the capacity to maintain the negentropy source | high | | Benefit responsibility | benefiting from negentropy consumption | high | | Survival responsibility | survival depends on negentropy | highest | III. The Temporal Dimension of Negentropy Responsibility Proposition 12.1 (the temporal dimension of negentropy responsibility) Negentropy responsibility has an important temporal dimension:

  • Retrospective responsibility: responsibility for past negentropy consumption
  • Present responsibility: responsibility for current negentropy use
  • Prospective responsibility: responsibility for the future availability of negentropy

Definition 12.17 (intergenerational negentropy responsibility) Intergenerational negentropy responsibility refers to the responsibility borne by present-day agents for the future availability of negentropy to future generations. Present-day agents ought not to over-consume negentropy to the point of harming the conditions of survival of future generations. Formalized statement: $$O(\text{Preserve}(N_{\text{available}}(t_{\text{future}})) \geq N_{\text{threshold}})$$ Here $N_{\text{available}}(t_{\text{future}})$ is the negentropy available at a future time, and $N_{\text{threshold}}$ is the minimum negentropy threshold for maintaining the persistence of life.

§12.2.3 The Principles of the Distribution of Responsibility I. The Basic Problem of Responsibility Distribution How is negentropy responsibility distributed among different agents? This is a complex problem involving several dimensions, such as fairness, efficiency, and feasibility. Question 12.1 (the problem of responsibility distribution) Given limited negentropy resources and multiple agents that consume negentropy, how can negentropy responsibility be distributed fairly and effectively? II. Three Principles of Distribution Principle 1: the principle of proportional consumption Definition 12.18 (the principle of proportional consumption) Principle of proportional consumption: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to its negentropy consumption. Agents that consume more negentropy bear more responsibility. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{consumption}}(S_i) = \frac{\text{Consumption}(S_i)}{\sum_j \text{Consumption}(S_j)} \cdot R_{\text{total}}$$ The case for the principle of proportional consumption:

  • Causal relation: agents that consume more negentropy make a greater causal contribution to the reduction of negentropy
  • Fairness: it is fair that agents that consume more bear more responsibility
  • Incentive effect: it encourages a reduction in negentropy consumption

Principle 2: the capability principle Definition 12.19 (the capability principle) Capability principle: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to its capability to maintain negentropy. Agents with greater capability bear more responsibility. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{capability}}(S_i) = \frac{\text{Capability}(S_i)}{\sum_j \text{Capability}(S_j)} \cdot R_{\text{total}}$$ The case for the capability principle:

  • Efficiency: capable agents can maintain negentropy more effectively
  • Fairness: with greater capability comes greater responsibility
  • Feasibility: only capable agents can bear responsibility

Principle 3: the benefit principle Definition 12.20 (the benefit principle) Benefit principle: an agent's negentropy responsibility is proportional to the benefit it obtains from negentropy consumption. Agents that benefit more bear more responsibility. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{benefit}}(S_i) = \frac{\text{Benefit}(S_i)}{\sum_j \text{Benefit}(S_j)} \cdot R_{\text{total}}$$ The case for the benefit principle:

  • Fairness: it is fair that agents that benefit more bear more responsibility
  • Compensatory character: beneficiaries ought to compensate the negentropy source
  • Incentive effect: it encourages the fair sharing of benefits

III. The Synthesis of the Three Principles Definition 12.21 (the synthetic allocation formula) Synthetic allocation formula: an agent's negentropy responsibility is determined synthetically by the three principles. Formalized statement: $$R(S_i) = \alpha \cdot R_{\text{consumption}}(S_i) + \beta \cdot R_{\text{capability}}(S_i) + \gamma \cdot R_{\text{benefit}}(S_i) + \delta \cdot R_{\text{baseline}}$$ Here $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 1$. Proposition 12.14 (the relation among the three principles) The three principles of distribution are mutually complementary, not mutually exclusive. In different situations, the weights of the three principles can be adjusted. Table 12.6 Weight configurations in different situations | Situation | Weight of the consumption principle | Weight of the capability principle | Weight of the benefit principle | Baseline weight | |------|--------------|--------------|--------------|----------| | Resource scarcity | high | medium | medium | low | | Large capability differences | low | high | medium | medium | | Historical injustice | medium | low | high | high | | Emergency | high | high | low | low | IV. Handling Conflicts among the Distribution Principles Proposition 12.15 (the potential conflict among the distribution principles) The three distribution principles may come into conflict. For example, an agent may consume a great deal of negentropy but have limited capability, or may benefit greatly but consume very little. Methods for handling conflicts:

  1. Priority ordering: determine the priority of the principles in a specific situation
  2. Negotiated settlement: determine the allocation scheme through intersubjective negotiation
  3. Minimization principle: choose the allocation scheme that minimizes conflict

§12.2.4 The Complete Statement of the Principle I. The Core Statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Definition 12.22 (the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, core statement) Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR): Living agents ought to maintain their sources of negentropy and ought not to externalize entropy costs onto others, onto the shared environment, or onto future generations. Negentropy responsibility is allocated according to consumption, capability, and benefit. II. The Tiered Statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Table 12.7 The tiered statement of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle | Tier | Statement | Formalization | |------|------|--------| | Individual tier | individuals ought to maintain the sources of negentropy they use | $\forall s \in S_{\text{ind}}: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}(s)))$ | | Organizational tier | organizations ought to maintain the sources of negentropy they use | $\forall o \in S_{\text{org}}: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}(o)))$ | | Civilizational tier | civilizations ought to maintain cosmic-scale sources of negentropy | $\forall c \in S_{\text{civ}}: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}(c)))$ | | Institutional tier | institutions ought to incentivize the maintenance of negentropy sources | $\forall i \in I: O(\text{Incentivize}(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource})))$ | III. The Complete Specification of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Table 12.8 The complete specification of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle | Specification item | Content | |--------|------| | Principle number | PNR | | Principle name | the Negentropy Responsibility Principle | | English name | Principle of Negentropic Responsibility | | Core statement | maintain the negentropy source, do not externalize entropy costs | | Formalization | $O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource})) \wedge O(\neg\text{Externalize}(\text{EntropyCost}))$ | | Allocation formula | $R(S) = \alpha \cdot R_{\text{consumption}} + \beta \cdot R_{\text{capability}} + \gamma \cdot R_{\text{benefit}} + \delta \cdot R_{\text{baseline}}$ | | Theoretical anchoring | NL-2 (negentropy persistence), BP-1 (survival rationality), BP- (intersubjectivity) | | Operationalization indicators | CDI (Civilizational Development Index), the D₃ dimension of CSIA | | Applicable boundary | all living agents | | Exceptional conditions | emergency survival, negotiated consent |
