§12.3 The Application of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

§12.3.1 The General Procedure of Application I. The Overall Framework of the Application Procedure The application of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle follows this general procedure: Procedure 12.1 (the application procedure of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle) Step 1: Identify the negentropy system

  • clarify what the negentropy source involved is
  • determine the boundaries and features of the negentropy source

Step 2: Identify the relevant agents

  • determine which agents consume this negentropy source
  • determine which agents are affected by this negentropy source

Step : Assess the negentropy situation

  • assess the total amount and regenerative capacity of the negentropy source
  • assess the negentropy consumption of each agent
  • assess the degree of externalization of entropy costs

Step 4: Allocate negentropy responsibility

  • allocate responsibility according to the principles of consumption, capability, and benefit
  • determine the share of responsibility of each agent

Step 5: Formulate a maintenance plan

  • formulate a plan for maintaining the negentropy source
  • formulate a plan for internalizing entropy costs

Step 6: Monitor and adjust

  • monitor changes in the negentropy situation
  • adjust the allocation of responsibility and the maintenance plan according to those changes

II. The Formalization of the Application Procedure Definition 12.2 (the application function of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle) The application function of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, $\text{ApplyPNR}: \text{Situation} \rightarrow \text{ResponsibilityAllocation}$, is defined as follows: $$\text{ApplyPNR}(\text{Sit}) = \langle R(S_1), R(S_2), ..., R(S_n), \text{MaintenancePlan}, \text{InternalizationPlan} \rangle$$ Here:

  • $\text{Sit}$ is the description of the situation
  • $R(S_i)$ is the share of responsibility of agent $S_i$
  • $\text{MaintenancePlan}$ is the maintenance plan
  • $\text{InternalizationPlan}$ is the internalization plan

III. Handling Uncertainty in Application In practical application, the assessment of the negentropy situation and the allocation of responsibility usually face uncertainty. Definition 12.24 (responsibility allocation under uncertainty) Under uncertainty, the allocation of responsibility ought to take the degree of uncertainty into account and adopt a conservative principle. Formalized statement: $$R(S_i) = R_{\text{expected}}(S_i) + k \cdot \sigma(R(S_i))$$ Here $R_{\text{expected}}(S_i)$ is the expected responsibility, $\sigma(R(S_i))$ is the standard deviation of responsibility, and $k$ is the conservatism coefficient. Decision rule 12.1 (the decision rule under uncertainty) Under uncertainty, the following decision rules apply:

  1. Precautionary principle: when uncertainty is high, adopt a more conservative strategy of negentropy use
  2. Reversibility principle: give priority to reversible modes of negentropy use
  3. Monitoring principle: strengthen the monitoring of the negentropy situation and adjust strategies in a timely manner

§12.3.2 The Responsibility of Resource Use I. Resources as Sources of Negentropy Natural resources are important sources of negentropy. The use of resources involves the consumption of negentropy and the production of entropy costs. Definition 12.25 (the negentropy value of resources) The negentropy value of a resource refers to the ordered structure and available energy contained in that resource. Formalized statement: $$N_{\text{resource}}(R) = N_{\text{structure}}(R) + N_{\text{energy}}(R)$$ Here $N_{\text{structure}}(R)$ is the structural negentropy of the resource and $N_{\text{energy}}(R)$ is the energy negentropy of the resource. Table 12.9 The negentropy features of different resources | Type of resource | Structural negentropy | Energy negentropy | Regenerative capacity | Entropy cost | |----------|----------|----------|----------|--------| | Fossil fuels | low | high | extremely low | high | | Solar energy | none | high | high | low | | Mineral resources | high | low | extremely low | medium | | Biological resources | high | medium | medium | medium | | Water resources | low | low | high | low | II. The Negentropy Responsibility of Resource Use Proposition 12.16 (the negentropy responsibility of resource use) Users of resources bear negentropy responsibility for the resources they use, including:

  • maintaining the regenerative capacity of resources (for renewable resources)
  • using non-renewable resources sparingly
  • internalizing the entropy costs of resource use

Case 12.1 (the negentropy responsibility of fossil fuel use) Situation: a country uses fossil fuels heavily as an energy source. Negentropy responsibility analysis: Step 1: Identify the negentropy system

  • negentropy source: fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas)
  • features: high energy negentropy, extremely low regenerative capacity

Step 2: Identify the relevant agents

  • consuming agents: the country's firms, residents, and government
  • affected agents: all agents worldwide (climate change), future generations

Step : Assess the negentropy situation

  • fossil fuel reserves are limited and are being consumed rapidly
  • the entropy cost (CO₂ emissions) is externalized onto the global environment and future generations

Step 4: Allocate negentropy responsibility

  • the country bears primary responsibility for fossil fuel consumption
  • responsibility is proportional to consumption, capability, and benefit

Step 5: Formulate a maintenance plan

  • reduce fossil fuel consumption
  • develop renewable energy
  • carbon capture and storage

Step 6: Internalize entropy costs

  • a carbon tax or carbon trading
  • compensate the affected agents

III. The Distribution of Responsibility for Resource Use Table 12.10 An example of distributing responsibility for resource use | Type of agent | Share of consumption | Share of capability | Share of benefit | Share of responsibility | |----------|----------|----------|----------|----------| | Developed countries | high | high | high | high | | Developing countries | medium | medium | medium | medium | | Least developed countries | low | low | low | low + baseline | | Future generations | none | none | none | borne on their behalf by the present generation |

§12.3.3 The Responsibility of Environmental Protection I. The Environment as a Negentropy System The environment is a complex negentropy system that provides a variety of negentropy services. Definition 12.26 (the negentropy services of the environment) The negentropy services of the environment refer to the functions provided by environmental systems that maintain ordered structures and support the persistence of life. Types of environmental negentropy services:

  • Provisioning services: providing negentropy resources such as food, water, and raw materials
  • Regulating services: regulating the climate, purifying air and water, decomposing waste
  • Supporting services: soil formation, nutrient cycling, photosynthesis
  • Cultural services: providing aesthetic, spiritual, and educational value

Proposition 12.17 (the entropy absorption capacity of the environment) The environment has a certain entropy absorption capacity and can absorb and process a certain amount of entropy costs (waste, pollution). But this capacity is finite. Formalized statement: $$\dot{S}_{\text{absorb}}(E) < \infty$$ Here $\dot{S}_{\text{absorb}}(E)$ is the entropy absorption capacity of environment $E$. II. The Negentropy Responsibility of Environmental Protection Proposition 12.18 (the negentropy responsibility of environmental protection) All agents that benefit from environmental negentropy services bear negentropy responsibility for environmental protection, including:

  • maintaining the negentropy service capacity of the environment
  • not emitting waste in excess of the environment's entropy absorption capacity
  • repairing damaged environmental negentropy systems

Case 12.2 (the negentropy responsibility of ecosystem protection) Situation: a tract of tropical rainforest faces the threat of logging. Negentropy responsibility analysis: Step 1: Identify the negentropy system

  • negentropy source: the tropical rainforest ecosystem
  • negentropy services: carbon storage, biodiversity, regulation of the water cycle, oxygen production

Step 2: Identify the relevant agents

  • direct beneficiaries: local residents, timber companies
  • indirect beneficiaries: all agents worldwide (climate regulation)
  • those harmed: forest organisms, future generations

Step : Assess the negentropy situation

  • the rainforest provides a large amount of negentropy services
  • logging would cause an irreversible loss of negentropy services
  • the entropy cost (carbon release, loss of biodiversity) is externalized

Step 4: Allocate negentropy responsibility

  • timber companies: high consumption, high benefit → high responsibility
  • consuming countries: high benefit → high responsibility
  • local communities: low capability → low responsibility but with baseline responsibility
  • global society: indirect benefit → shared responsibility

Step 5: Formulate a maintenance plan

  • establish protected areas
  • sustainable forestry management
  • ecological compensation mechanisms

Step 6: Internalize entropy costs

  • carbon credit trading
  • payments for ecosystem services
  • international transfer payments

III. The Intergenerational Dimension of Environmental Responsibility Proposition 12.19 (the intergenerational dimension of environmental responsibility) The negentropy responsibility of environmental protection has an important intergenerational dimension. The present generation bears responsibility toward future generations and ought not to over-consume the negentropy service capacity of the environment. Definition 12.27 (intergenerational environmental responsibility) Intergenerational environmental responsibility refers to the responsibility borne by the present generation for the availability of environmental negentropy services to future generations. Formalized statement: $$O(\text{Preserve}(\text{EnvNegService}(t_{\text{future}})) \geq \text{EnvNegService}(t_{\text{now}}))$$ That is, the present generation has an obligation to keep future environmental negentropy services no lower than the current level.

§12.3.4 The Responsibility of Intergenerational Transmission I. Intergenerational Justice and Negentropy Responsibility Proposition 12.20 (the negentropy basis of intergenerational justice) Intergenerational justice can be understood from the perspective of negentropy responsibility: the present generation bears negentropy responsibility toward future generations, ought not to over-consume negentropy resources, and ought not to externalize entropy costs onto future generations. Definition 12.28 (intergenerational negentropy transmission) Intergenerational negentropy transmission refers to the process by which the present generation transmits negentropy resources and negentropy service capacity to future generations. Formalized statement: $$\text{Transfer}(N, t_{\text{now}}, t_{\text{future}}) = N_{\text{available}}(t_{\text{future}}) - N_{\text{consumed}}(t_{\text{now}}, t_{\text{future}})$$ Here $N_{\text{available}}(t_{\text{future}})$ is the negentropy available in the future, and $N_{\text{consumed}}(t_{\text{now}}, t_{\text{future}})$ is the negentropy consumed from now into the future. II. The Principles of Intergenerational Negentropy Responsibility Principle 1: the non-declining principle Definition 12.29 (the non-declining principle) Non-declining principle: the present generation ought to keep the negentropy resources it transmits to future generations no lower than the negentropy resources it inherited from previous generations. Formalized statement: $$N_{\text{transfer}}(t_{\text{now}} \rightarrow t_{\text{future}}) \geq N_{\text{inherit}}(t_{\text{past}} \rightarrow t_{\text{now}})$$ Principle 2: the sustainability principle Definition 12.0 (the sustainability principle) Sustainability principle: the negentropy consumption of the present generation ought not to exceed the regenerative capacity of the negentropy source. Formalized statement: $$\dot{N}_{\text{consume}}(t) \leq \dot{N}_{\text{regenerate}}(t)$$ Principle 3: the compensation principle Definition 12.1 (the compensation principle) Compensation principle: if the present generation consumes non-renewable negentropy resources, it ought to compensate future generations by other means. Formalized statement: $$\text{Consume}(N_{\text{non-renewable}}) \rightarrow O(\text{Compensate}(\text{FutureGenerations}))$$ III. The Institutionalization of Intergenerational Negentropy Responsibility Proposition 12.21 (the institutionalization of intergenerational negentropy responsibility) Intergenerational negentropy responsibility needs to be realized through institutionalization, including:

  • intergenerational trust mechanisms
  • a system of representatives for future generations
  • long-term negentropy accounts
  • intergenerational impact assessment

Table 12.11 Institutionalization schemes for intergenerational negentropy responsibility | Institution | Function | Relation to PNR | |------|------|-------------| | Intergenerational trust | hold negentropy resources in trust for future generations | realizes the non-declining principle | | Representatives of future generations | represent the interests of future generations in decision-making | realizes intersubjectivity | | Long-term negentropy accounts | record and monitor negentropy transmission | realizes the sustainability principle | | Intergenerational impact assessment | assess the impact of decisions on future generations | realizes the compensation principle |

§12.4 The Negentropy Responsibility Principle and Traditional Theories of Responsibility

§12.4.1 The Relation to Causal Responsibility I. The Core Claim of Causal Responsibility Definition 12.2 (causal responsibility) Causal responsibility means that because an agent's action caused a certain outcome, the agent is responsible for that outcome. The core of causal responsibility is the causal relation. Formalized statement: $$\text{Cause}(S, a, r) \rightarrow \text{Responsible}(S, r)$$ Here $S$ is the agent, $a$ is the action, and $r$ is the outcome. II. A Comparison of Negentropy Responsibility and Causal Responsibility Table 12.12 A comparison of negentropy responsibility and causal responsibility | Dimension | Causal responsibility | Negentropy responsibility | |------|----------|----------| | Core focus | the causal relation | negentropy consumption and maintenance | | Basis of responsibility | action caused the outcome | consumption, capability, benefit | | Temporal dimension | mainly retrospective | retrospective + prospective | | Scope of agents | the actor | all living agents | | Collective responsibility | difficult to handle | can be handled | III. How Negentropy Responsibility Extends Causal Responsibility Proposition 12.22 (negentropy responsibility extends causal responsibility) Negentropy responsibility includes causal responsibility but is not limited to it. Negentropy responsibility extends causal responsibility:

  • from individual action to collective action
  • from direct causation to indirect causation
  • from the retrospective to the prospective
  • from the actor to the beneficiary

Argument 12.4 (negentropy responsibility includes causal responsibility) Premise P1: consuming negentropy is the cause of the reduction of negentropy Premise P2: causal responsibility requires being responsible for the outcomes caused by one's action Premise P: negentropy responsibility requires being responsible for negentropy consumption Conclusion: negentropy responsibility includes causal responsibility (in the case of negentropy consumption)

§12.4.2 The Relation to Role Responsibility I. The Core Claim of Role Responsibility Definition 12. (role responsibility) Role responsibility means that because an agent occupies a certain role, the agent is responsible for the duties of that role. The core of role responsibility is role obligation. Formalized statement: $$\text{Role}(S, r) \wedge \text{Duty}(r, d) \rightarrow \text{Responsible}(S, d)$$ Here $S$ is the agent, $r$ is the role, and $d$ is the duty. II. A Comparison of Negentropy Responsibility and Role Responsibility Table 12.1 A comparison of negentropy responsibility and role responsibility | Dimension | Role responsibility | Negentropy responsibility | |------|----------|----------| | Core focus | role obligation | negentropy consumption and maintenance | | Basis of responsibility | occupying a role | consumption, capability, benefit | | Source of responsibility | social construction | conditions of survival | | Universality | role-specific | universally applicable | | Variability | changes with the role | relatively stable | III. The Relation of Negentropy Responsibility to Role Responsibility Proposition 12.2 (the relation of negentropy responsibility to role responsibility) Negentropy responsibility can be understood as a kind of universal role responsibility: all living agents occupy the role of “negentropy user” and are therefore responsible for maintaining negentropy. Definition 12.4 (the role of negentropy user) The role of negentropy user is a role occupied by all living agents. As negentropy users, agents are responsible for maintaining sources of negentropy and for not externalizing entropy costs. Formalized statement: $$\forall S \in L: \text{Role}(S, \text{NegentropyUser}) \wedge \text{Duty}(\text{NegentropyUser}, \text{MaintainNegSource})$$

§12.4.3 The Relation to Capacity Responsibility I. The Core Claim of Capacity Responsibility Definition 12.5 (capacity responsibility) Capacity responsibility means that because an agent has the capacity to do something, the agent has a responsibility to do it. The core of capacity responsibility is “with greater capability comes greater responsibility”. Formalized statement: $$\text{Capability}(S, a) \rightarrow \text{Responsible}(S, a)$$ Here $S$ is the agent and $a$ is the action. II. A Comparison of Negentropy Responsibility and Capacity Responsibility Table 12.14 A comparison of negentropy responsibility and capacity responsibility | Dimension | Capacity responsibility | Negentropy responsibility | |------|----------|----------| | Core focus | capability | negentropy consumption and maintenance | | Basis of responsibility | having the capacity to do something | consumption, capability, benefit | | Degree of responsibility | proportional to capability | a synthesis of multiple factors | | Scope of application | those with capability | all living agents | III. How Negentropy Responsibility Integrates Capacity Responsibility Proposition 12.24 (negentropy responsibility integrates capacity responsibility) Negentropy responsibility integrates capacity responsibility: capability is one of the important factors in the allocation of negentropy responsibility. Agents with greater capability to maintain negentropy bear more responsibility. Definition 12.6 (capability-weighted negentropy responsibility) Capability-weighted negentropy responsibility refers to adjusting an agent's negentropy responsibility according to its capability. Formalized statement: $$R_{\text{capability-weighted}}(S) = R_{\text{base}}(S) \cdot \frac{\text{Capability}(S)}{\text{Capability}_{\text{average}}}$$

§12.4.4 The Distinctive Contribution of This Work I. The Distinctive Features of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Relative to traditional theories of responsibility, the Negentropy Responsibility Principle has the following distinctive features: Feature 1: making the material basis explicit Traditional theories of responsibility usually do not make the material basis of responsibility explicit. The Negentropy Responsibility Principle makes explicit the material basis of responsibility—negentropy. This makes responsibility quantifiable and operationalizable. Feature 2: the integration of multi-factor allocation Traditional theories of responsibility usually focus on a single factor (causation, role, or capability). The Negentropy Responsibility Principle integrates multiple factors (consumption, capability, benefit) and provides a more comprehensive framework for allocating responsibility. Feature 3: emphasis on the intergenerational dimension Traditional theories of responsibility mainly focus on responsibility among present-day agents. The Negentropy Responsibility Principle emphasizes the intergenerational dimension and makes explicit the responsibility of the present generation toward future generations. Feature 4: the connection to the conditions of survival The Negentropy Responsibility Principle connects responsibility to the conditions of survival. This makes responsibility not an abstract moral requirement but a practical requirement directly related to the persistence of life. Feature 5: the enhancement of operability The Negentropy Responsibility Principle achieves operationalizability through the concept of negentropy. Negentropy can be measured (at least approximately), and responsibility can be allocated quantitatively. II. The Theoretical Contribution of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Table 12.15 The theoretical contribution of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle | Domain of contribution | Specific contribution | Relation to traditional theories | |----------|----------|------------------| | Theory of responsibility | provides a material basis | supplements causal, role, and capacity responsibility | | Environmental ethics | provides a unified framework | integrates resource ethics and ecological ethics | | Intergenerational justice | provides an operationalizable scheme | supplements Rawls and Parfit | | Distributive justice | provides a multi-factor framework | supplements utilitarianism and egalitarianism | | Global justice | provides a scheme for allocating responsibility | supplements cosmopolitanism and statism | III. The Connection of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle to the Three New Views Proposition 12.25 (the connection of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle to the Three New Views) The Negentropy Responsibility Principle is the manifestation of the Three New Views at the normative level. Starting from the New View of Life (NL-2) and passing through the bridge principles (BP-1, BP-), it derives a normative conclusion. Table 12.16 The connection of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle to the Three New Views | Proposition of the Three New Views | Connection to the Negentropy Responsibility Principle | |------------|----------------------| | NC-1 (relationality) | negentropy responsibility is relational and depends on intersubjective relations | | NC-2 (processuality) | negentropy consumption and maintenance are processual | | NL-2 (negentropy persistence) | the direct basis of negentropy responsibility | | NL- (continuum) | negentropy responsibility is a matter of degree | | NK-4 (negotiability) | the allocation of negentropy responsibility is negotiable |

§12.5 The Boundaries and Exceptions of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

§12.5.1 The Applicable Boundaries of the Principle I. The Boundary of Agents Boundary declaration 12.4 (the boundary of agents) The Negentropy Responsibility Principle applies to all living agents. The determination of agent status is based on NL-1 (cross-substrate life) and UCS (the Universal Consciousness Scale). Formalized statement: $$\text{Life}(S) \rightarrow \text{PNR applies to }S$$ Table 12.17 Specific provisions on the boundary of agents | Type of agent | Qualification for life | Applicability of PNR | Explanation | |----------|----------|-----------|------| | Humans | yes | fully applicable | the standard case of application | | Higher animals | yes | applicable | lower degree of responsibility | | Simple organisms | yes | indirectly applicable | through ecosystem considerations | | AI systems | to be assessed | depends on qualification for life | requires specific assessment | | Organizations/states | derived agents | applicable | as aggregates of individuals | | Civilizations | derived agents | applicable | as aggregates of organizations | II. The Boundary of Action Boundary declaration 12.5 (the boundary of action) The Negentropy Responsibility Principle mainly applies to actions that have a significant impact on negentropy systems. For everyday actions with a negligible impact, the binding force of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle is weaker. Formalized statement: $$|\Delta N(a)| > \theta_{\text{action}} \Rightarrow \text{PNR strongly binds }a$$ Table 12.18 Specific provisions on the boundary of action | Type of action | Impact on negentropy | Strength of PNR binding | Explanation | |----------|----------|-------------|------| | Civilization-level resource development | extremely large | extremely strong | such as large-scale mining, deforestation | | Industrial production | large | strong | such as manufacturing, energy production | | Everyday consumption | medium | medium | such as transportation, diet | | Personal behavior | small | weak | such as personal choices | III. The Boundary of Situation Boundary declaration 12.6 (the boundary of situation) The Negentropy Responsibility Principle has a stronger normative force in situations of resource scarcity. In situations of resource abundance, its binding force is relatively weaker. Formalized statement: $$\text{Scarcity}(N) \uparrow \Rightarrow \text{PNR normative force} \uparrow$$ IV. The Boundary of Time Boundary declaration 12.7 (the boundary of time) The Negentropy Responsibility Principle is concerned with long-range impacts, but the temporal scope of assessment needs to be determined according to the situation. For non-renewable resources, the temporal scope ought to be longer; for renewable resources, it can be shorter. Formalized statement: $$T_{\text{evaluation}} = f(\text{Renewability}(N), \text{Scarcity}(N), \text{Impact}(a))$$

§12.5.2 Possible Exceptions I. The General Framework of Exceptional Cases Definition 12.7 (exceptional cases) Exceptional cases are cases in which the binding force of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle may be temporarily relaxed or waived. Exceptional cases need to satisfy specific conditions. The general framework of exceptional conditions:

  1. Urgency: is the situation urgent?
  2. Necessity: is the exception necessary?
  3. Proportionality: is the degree of the exception proportional to the urgency?
  4. Temporariness: is the exception temporary?

II. Specific Exceptional Cases Exceptional case 1: emergency survival In cases of emergency survival, agents may temporarily relax the binding force of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle. Case 12. (the emergency survival exception) Situation: a community faces famine, and the only source of food is overfishing an endangered fish species. Analysis:

  • Urgency: the community faces a threat to its survival
  • Necessity: there is no other source of food
  • Proportionality: the catch should be limited to what is needed for survival
  • Temporariness: alternatives should be sought as quickly as possible

Conclusion: emergency survival is an exceptional case for the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, but it ought to satisfy the conditions of proportionality and temporariness Exceptional case 2: basic needs Negentropy consumption that satisfies basic needs may be exempted from part of the responsibility. Definition 12.8 (the basic-needs exception) Basic-needs exception: negentropy consumption that satisfies basic survival needs may be exempted from part of negentropy responsibility. Formalized statement: $$\text{Consumption}(S) \leq \text{BasicNeeds}(S) \Rightarrow R(S) = R_{\text{baseline}}$$ Exceptional case 3: technological limits The externalization of entropy costs that cannot be avoided under current technological conditions may be temporarily exempted. Definition 12.9 (the technological-limits exception) Technological-limits exception: the externalization of entropy costs that cannot be avoided under current technological conditions may be temporarily exempted, but the agent has an obligation to develop alternative technologies. Formalized statement: $$\neg\exists \text{Tech}: \text{Avoid}(\text{Externalize}(S_{\text{cost}})) \Rightarrow \text{TemporaryExemption}(S) \wedge O(\text{DevelopAlternative}(S))$$ Exceptional case 4: negotiated consent If all affected agents consent to a certain mode of negentropy use, it may serve as an exception. Case 12.4 (the negotiated-consent exception) Situation: the residents of a region negotiate and consent to the development of local mineral resources, even though this consumes non-renewable negentropy. Analysis:

  • all directly affected agents participated in the negotiation
  • the negotiation was voluntary and informed
  • the outcome of the negotiation took the interests of future generations into account (through representative mechanisms)

Conclusion: negotiated consent can be an exceptional case for the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, but it needs to satisfy the conditions of procedural justice Table 12.19 Summary of exceptional cases | Type of exception | Condition | Basis of justification | Limitation | |----------|------|----------|------| | Emergency survival | threat to survival | survival takes priority | proportionality, temporariness | | Basic needs | satisfaction of basic needs | basis in human rights | limited to basic needs | | Technological limits | no alternative technology | feasibility | obligation to develop alternatives | | Negotiated consent | consent of all agents | autonomous decision | procedural justice |

§12.5.3 Handling Conflicts with Other Principles I. Potential Conflicts with the Recursive Freedom Principle Conflict situation 12.1 Situation: a certain technology can greatly expand the space of possibilities (in accordance with RFP), but it requires the consumption of a large amount of negentropy resources (which may violate PNR). Conflict analysis:

  • the Recursive Freedom Principle supports the technology (expanding the space of possibilities)
  • the Negentropy Responsibility Principle may oppose the technology (consuming negentropy resources)

Ways of handling:

  1. Assess the net effect: does the expansion of the space of possibilities exceed the cost of negentropy consumption?
  2. Seek alternatives: is there an alternative technology that consumes less negentropy?
  3. Temporal trade-off: does the short-term negentropy consumption buy a long-term expansion of the space of possibilities?
  4. Distributional consideration: who bears the cost of the negentropy consumption?

Proposition 12.26 (the relation between RFP and PNR) The Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP) and the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR) are usually complementary rather than conflicting. Maintaining the space of possibilities requires the support of negentropy resources; maintaining negentropy resources is also for the sake of preserving the future space of possibilities. Formalized statement: $$\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}) \rightarrow \text{Support}(\text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace}))$$ II. Potential Conflicts with the Reversibility Principle Conflict situation 12.2 Situation: a certain irreversible action can significantly maintain a negentropy source (in accordance with PNR), but it violates the Reversibility Principle (PR). Conflict analysis:

  • the Negentropy Responsibility Principle supports the action (maintaining the negentropy source)
  • the Reversibility Principle may oppose the action (irreversibility)

Ways of handling:

  1. Assess the degree of irreversibility: is it completely irreversible or partially reversible?
  2. Assess the urgency of negentropy maintenance: is there an urgent negentropy crisis?
  3. Risk assessment: if the action fails, what are the consequences?
  4. Alternatives: is there a reversible alternative?

III. A General Framework for Handling Conflicts among Principles Definition 12.40 (the framework for handling conflicts among principles) When the Negentropy Responsibility Principle conflicts with other principles, the following framework is adopted: Step 1: Identify the conflict

  • clarify which principles are in conflict
  • assess the nature and degree of the conflict

Step 2: Assess the weight of each principle

  • in the specific situation, what is the relative importance of each principle?
  • does any principle have priority?

Step : Seek a reconciliatory scheme

  • is there a scheme that satisfies all principles at once?
  • can the conflict be reduced by modifying the action?

Step 4: If reconciliation is impossible, make a trade-off

  • determine the priority according to the situation
  • choose the overall optimal scheme

Step 5: Record the reasons for the decision

  • explicitly record why a particular scheme was chosen
  • provide a reference for similar future situations

Table 12.20 General guidance on the priority of principles | Situation | Order of priority | Reason | |------|------------|------| | Presence of a taboo red line | taboo red line > other principles | the taboo red line is an absolute constraint | | Emergency survival crisis | PNR > RFP > PR | survival is the precondition of everything else | | Deep uncertainty | PR > RFP > PNR | under uncertainty, give priority to maintaining reversibility | | Extreme resource scarcity | PNR > RFP > PR | negentropy maintenance is an urgent task | | Ordinary situations | RFP ≈ PNR ≈ PR | balanced consideration of the three principles |

Footnotes

Chapter 12 Footnotes

[1] Schrödinger and the Concept of Negentropy: In What is Life? (1944), Schrödinger first introduced the concept of negentropy into the life sciences. He wrote: "Life feeds on negative entropy." This concept was subsequently widely discussed and developed. See: Schrödinger, E. (1944). What is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell. Cambridge University Press. [2] The Second Law of Thermodynamics: The second law states that in an isolated system, entropy always tends to increase. This law is one of the fundamental laws of physics. For philosophical discussion of the second law, see: Callender, C. (2001). "Thermodynamic Asymmetry in Time." Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. [3] Dissipative Structure Theory: The theory of dissipative structures developed by Ilya Prigogine explains how open systems far from equilibrium maintain ordered structures. See: Prigogine, I., & Stengers, I. (1984). Order Out of Chaos: Man's New Dialogue with Nature. Bantam Books. [4] Landauer's Principle: Landauer's Principle states that erasing one bit of information requires dissipating at least $k_B T \ln 2$ of energy. This principle establishes a connection between information and thermodynamics. See: Landauer, R. (1961). "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process." Chapter 12 Appendix: The Axiom System of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

Axiom System 12.A (Principle of Negentropy Responsibility Axiom System PNR-AX) 【Basic Definitions】 Definition D1 (Negentropy): N = S_max - S where S_max is the maximum possible entropy of the system and S is the actual entropy of the system Definition D2 (Negentropy Flow): Ṅ(L, E) = dN/dt the net negentropy transfer rate from the environment E to the living system L Definition D (Negentropy Source): NegSource(S) = {R : ∃Ṅ(S, R) > 0} the negentropy sources of an agent S are the set of all resources that provide a positive negentropy flow to S Definition D4 (Entropy Cost): EntropyCost(S) = Ṡ_produce(S) the rate of entropy increase produced by the activities of an agent S Definition D5 (Entropy Externalization): Externalize(S, E) ↔ Ṡ_emit(S, E) > 0 ∧ ¬Compensate(S, E) an agent S discharges entropy into the environment E without compensation 【Axioms】 Axiom A1 (Maintenance Axiom): ∀S ∈ L: O(Maintain(NegSource(S))) Living agents should maintain their negentropy sources Axiom A2 (Prohibition of Externalization Axiom): ∀S ∈ L, ∀E ∈ SharedEnv: O(¬Externalize(S, E)) Living agents should not externalize entropy costs onto the shared environment Axiom A (Intergenerational Responsibility Axiom): ∀S ∈ L, ∀G ∈ FutureGen: O(¬Externalize(S, G)) Living agents should not externalize entropy costs onto future generations Axiom A4 (Responsibility Allocation Axiom): ∀S ∈ L: R(S) = f(Consumption(S), Capability(S), Benefit(S), Baseline) Negentropy responsibility is allocated according to consumption, capability, benefit, and baseline Axiom A5 (Balance Axiom): ∀S ∈ L: Ṅ_consume(S) ≤ Ṅ_contribute(S) + Ṅ_regenerate(Source(S)) Negentropy consumption should not exceed contribution plus regeneration 【Inference Rules】 Rule R1 (Maintenance Inference Rule): If NegSource(S) is threatened, then S is obligated to take maintenance action Rule R2 (Externalization Inference Rule): If Externalize(S, E), then S is obligated to stop externalizing or to compensate E Rule R (Responsibility Allocation Inference Rule): R(S) = α·(Consumption(S)/Σ_i Consumption(S_i))

  • β·(Capability(S)/Σ_i Capability(S_i))
  • γ·(Benefit(S)/Σ_i Benefit(S_i))
  • δ·R_baseline

where α + β + γ + δ = 1 Rule R4 (Exception Inference Rule): EmergencySurvival(S) ∨ BasicNeeds(S) ∨ TechLimitation(S) ∨ NegotiatedConsent(S) → TemporaryExemption(S) 【Theorems】 Theorem T1 (Negentropy Maintenance Theorem): ∀S ∈ L: Survive(S) → O(Maintain(NegSource(S))) Proof: Follows directly from NL-2 and Axiom A1 Theorem T2 (Prohibition of Externalization Theorem): ∀S ∈ L, ∀E: Externalize(S, E) → ¬Permissible(Action(S)) Proof: Follows from Axioms A2 and A Theorem T (Responsibility Proportion Theorem): ∀S₁, S₂ ∈ L: Consumption(S₁) > Consumption(S₂) → R(S₁) > R(S₂) Proof: Follows from Axiom A4 and Rule R (other things being equal)

The core of this chapter is to establish the “Reversibility Principle” (Principle of Reversibility, PR), which is the third and last of the three normative principles of this work. II.   • Via the bridge principle (BP-2 epistemic humility)
  • Deriving the Reversibility Principle (PR)

§13.1 The Derivation of the Reversibility Principle

§13.1.1 From the New View of Cognition to Epistemic Humility I. Review of the Core Propositions of the New View of Cognition Chapter 3 established the four core propositions of the New View of Cognition. Before deriving the Reversibility Principle, it is necessary to review the core content of these propositions, especially NK-1 (participatory construction) and NK-4 (negotiability). Proposition NK-1 (participatory construction): Cognition is not a passive reflection of an external world independent of the cognizer, but a product of the interaction between the cognizer and the world. The cognitive process participates in constructing its object of cognition. Formal statement: $$\text{Know}(S, p) \Leftrightarrow \text{Participate}(S, \text{Construction}(p))$$ Proposition NK-2 (sociality): Cognition is a social achievement. The production, validation, and dissemination of knowledge depend on the social practices of an epistemic community. Formal statement: $$\text{Knowledge}(p) \Rightarrow \exists C: \text{SocialValidation}(C, p)$$ Proposition NK-3 (normativity): Cognitive activity is intrinsically normative. Cognition concerns not only “what is” but also “how one ought to cognize.” Formal statement: $$\text{Cognition}(S) \Rightarrow \text{NormativeCommitment}(S)$$ Proposition NK-4 (negotiability): Cognitive results are negotiable and revisable. No cognitive result is absolutely certain or unrevisable. Formal statement: $$\forall p: \text{Know}(S, p) \Rightarrow \text{Revisable}(p)$$ II. The Concept of Epistemic Humility Definition 13.1 (epistemic humility) Epistemic Humility is the attitude of recognizing the limits of one’s own cognitive capacities and acknowledging that one’s beliefs may be mistaken, incomplete, or in need of revision. Formal statement: $$\text{EpistemicHumility}(S) \Leftrightarrow \text{Acknowledge}(S, \text{Fallibility}(S)) \wedge \text{Acknowledge}(S, \text{Incompleteness}(\text{Knowledge}(S)))$$ Proposition 13.1 (the New View of Cognition entails epistemic humility) From the core propositions of the New View of Cognition, especially NK-1 (participatory construction) and NK-4 (negotiability), it can be derived that epistemic humility is an attitude that a rational agent ought to have. Argument 13.1 (the argument that the New View of Cognition entails epistemic humility) Premise P1 (NK-1): cognition is participatory construction, not a passive reflection of an external world Premise P2 (NK-4): all cognitive results are revisable Premise P3: if cognition is participatory construction, then cognitive results depend on the cognizer’s perspective and method Premise P4: if cognitive results depend on perspective and method, then different perspectives and methods may produce different results Premise P5: if all cognitive results are revisable, then no cognitive result is absolutely certain Step 1: from P1 and P3, cognitive results depend on the cognizer’s perspective and method Step 2: from Step 1 and P4, different perspectives and methods may produce different results Step 3: from P2 and P5, no cognitive result is absolutely certain Step 4: from Step 2 and Step 3, the cognizer ought to acknowledge the limits of their own cognition Step 5: from Step 4, epistemic humility is an attitude that a rational agent ought to have Conclusion: the New View of Cognition entails epistemic humility III. Deep Uncertainty and Epistemic Humility Definition 13.2 (deep uncertainty) Deep Uncertainty is uncertainty that cannot be described by a probability distribution. Under deep uncertainty, we not only do not know what the outcomes are, but we do not even know what the space of possible outcomes is, nor can we assign probabilities to the possible outcomes. Formal statement: $$\text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Situation}) \Leftrightarrow \neg\exists P: \text{ProbabilityDistribution}(P, \text{Outcomes}(\text{Situation}))$$ Proposition 13.2 (the ubiquity of deep uncertainty) In situations involving complex systems, long time scales, and multi-agent interaction, deep uncertainty is ubiquitous. Sources of deep uncertainty:

  • System complexity: the behavior of complex systems is hard to predict
  • Time scale: prediction over long time scales faces cumulative error
  • Multi-agent interaction: the decisions of multiple agents influence one another, producing unpredictable emergent behavior
  • Cognitive limits: inherent limits of human cognitive capacity
  • Model uncertainty: the models we use to understand the world may themselves be wrong

Proposition 13.3 (deep uncertainty reinforces epistemic humility) The existence of deep uncertainty further reinforces the necessity of epistemic humility. Under deep uncertainty, we ought to acknowledge not only that we may be wrong, but also that we do not even know where we may be wrong. Argument 13.2 (the argument that deep uncertainty reinforces epistemic humility) Premise P1: under deep uncertainty, we cannot assign probabilities to possible outcomes Premise P2: if we cannot assign probabilities, then we cannot use the standard method of maximizing expected utility Premise P3: if we cannot use the standard decision method, then an alternative decision principle is needed Premise P4: epistemic humility requires acknowledging the limits of one’s own cognition Premise P5: deep uncertainty is an extreme manifestation of cognitive limitation Step 1: from P1 and P5, deep uncertainty indicates the severity of cognitive limitation Step 2: from P4 and Step 1, deep uncertainty reinforces the necessity of epistemic humility Step 3: from P2 and P3, deep uncertainty requires an alternative decision principle Conclusion: deep uncertainty reinforces epistemic humility and requires an alternative decision principle IV. Review of the Bridge Principle BP-2 Chapter 5 established three bridge principles, among which BP-2 (the epistemic humility principle) is the key bridge for deriving the Reversibility Principle. Bridge principle BP-2 (the epistemic humility principle): Under deep uncertainty, a rational agent ought to act cautiously and avoid irreversible catastrophic consequences. Formal statement: $$BP\text{-}2: \text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Situation}) \rightarrow O(\text{Cautious}(S) \wedge \text{Avoid}(\text{IrreversibleCatastrophe}))$$

| | | Column 13.1: A Typology of Deep Uncertainty | | ————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————— | | | | I. Levels of Uncertainty | | | | Uncertainty can be divided into several levels, from shallow to deep: | | | | Level 1: Risk | | - The outcome space is known | | - The probability distribution is known | | - Expectation-utility maximization can be used | | - Example: rolling dice | | | | Level 2: Uncertainty | | - The outcome space is known | | - The probability distribution is unknown | | - The maximin principle, etc. can be used | | - Example: the market reaction to a new product | | | | Level 3: Deep Uncertainty | | - The outcome space is unknown or incomplete | | - No probability distribution can be assigned | | - Alternative decision principles are needed | | - Example: the long-term effects of climate change | | | | Level 4: Ignorance | | - Not knowing what one does not know | | - Unable to identify the relevant uncertainties | | - Extreme caution is required | | - Example: unknown unknowns | | | | II. Characteristics of Deep Uncertainty | | | | Deep uncertainty has the following characteristics: | | | | 1. Model uncertainty: not knowing which model is correct | | 2. Parameter uncertainty: even if the model is correct, the parameters | | are uncertain | | 3. Structural uncertainty: not knowing the structure of the system | | 4. Emergent uncertainty: the system may produce unexpected emergent | | behavior | | 5. Reflexive uncertainty: the decision itself changes the system being | | decided upon | | | | III. The Decision Challenge of Deep Uncertainty | | | | Under deep uncertainty, traditional decision methods face challenges: | | | | - Expectation-utility maximization: expected utility cannot be computed | | - Bayesian updating: there is no prior probability to update | | - Cost-benefit analysis: costs and benefits cannot be quantified | | | | This is why the Reversibility Principle is needed as an alternative | | decision principle. | | | |_____________________________________________________________________________|

Conclusion: reversible actions preserve the value of acquiring new information Defense Path Three: the intersubjectivity path Proposition 13.8 (the intersubjective basis of reversibility) By BP-3 (the intersubjectivity principle), actions that irrevocably affect others cannot be reasonably accepted by those others. Reversibility preserves the others’ space of choice. Argument 13.6 (the intersubjectivity argument) Premise P1 (BP-3): principles should be adopted that can be reasonably accepted by others Premise P2: irrevocably affecting others reduces their space of choice Premise P3: actions that reduce others’ space of choice cannot be reasonably accepted by those others Premise P4: reversible actions preserve the others’ space of choice Conclusion: reversible actions can be reasonably accepted by others IV. The Preference for Reversibility and the Possibility Space Proposition 13.9 (the relation between reversibility and the possibility space) Reversibility is closely related to the possibility space. Reversible actions keep the possibility space open; irreversible actions compress the possibility space. Formal statement: $$\text{Reversible}(a) \Rightarrow \text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace})$$ $$\text{Irreversible}(a) \Rightarrow \text{Compress}(\text{PossibilitySpace})$$ Proposition 13.10 (the relation between the Reversibility Principle and the Recursive Freedom Principle) The Reversibility Principle and the Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP) support each other. RFP requires maintaining the possibility space; the Reversibility Principle provides procedural guidance for maintaining the possibility space.

§13.1.3 The Formal Statement of the Reversibility Principle I. A Preliminary Statement of the Reversibility Principle Based on the derivations of the preceding two sections, a preliminary statement of the Reversibility Principle can now be given. Definition 13.4 (the Reversibility Principle, preliminary statement) The Reversibility Principle (Principle of Reversibility, PR): under deep uncertainty, a rational agent ought to give priority to reversible actions and avoid irreversible actions, especially irreversible catastrophic consequences. II. The Formal Statement of the Reversibility Principle Definition 13.5 (the Reversibility Principle, formal statement) The formal statement of the Reversibility Principle: $$PR: \text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Sit}) \rightarrow O(\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a)) \wedge \text{Avoid}(\text{IrreversibleCatastrophe}))$$ Where:

  • $\text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Sit})$ denotes that the situation is under deep uncertainty
  • $O$ is the “ought” operator
  • $\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a))$ denotes preferring reversible actions
  • $\text{Avoid}(\text{IrreversibleCatastrophe})$ denotes avoiding irreversible catastrophic consequences

Reading: under deep uncertainty, a rational agent ought to prefer reversible actions and avoid irreversible catastrophic consequences. III. The Complete Formalization of the Reversibility Principle Definition 13.6 (the reversibility function) The reversibility function $\text{Rev}: A \rightarrow [0, 1]$ maps an action to its degree of reversibility. $$\text{Rev}(a) = P(\text{Restore}(s_0) | \text{Execute}(a, s_0) \rightarrow s_1, \text{Reverse}(a))$$ Where:

  • $s_0$ is the state before the action
  • $s_1$ is the state after the action
  • $\text{Reverse}(a)$ is the reverse action
  • $P(\text{Restore}(s_0) | ...)$ is the probability of restoring the initial state after performing the reverse action

Definition 13.7 (the reversibility-preference rule) The reversibility-preference rule: other things being equal, the action with higher reversibility should be chosen. Formal statement: $$\text{OtherEqual}(a_1, a_2) \wedge \text{Rev}(a_1) > \text{Rev}(a_2) \Rightarrow a_1 \succ a_2$$ Where $a_1 \succ a_2$ denotes that $a_1$ is preferred to $a_2$. Definition 13.8 (the justification threshold for irreversible actions) The justification threshold for irreversible actions: irreversible actions require stronger justification. The higher the irreversibility, the higher the justification threshold. Formal statement: $$\text{JustificationThreshold}(a) \propto 1 - \text{Rev}(a)$$ Definition 13.9 (the Reversibility Principle, complete formalization) The complete formal statement of the Reversibility Principle: Axiom PR-1 (the reversibility-preference axiom): ∀a₁, a₂ ∈ A: OtherEqual(a₁, a₂) ∧ Rev(a₁) > Rev(a₂) → a₁ ≻ a₂ Other things being equal, the action with higher reversibility should be chosen Axiom PR-2 (the justification-threshold axiom): ∀a ∈ A: Rev(a) < θ_rev → RequireStrongJustification(a) Actions whose reversibility is below the threshold require strong justification Axiom PR-3 (the catastrophic-consequence axiom): ∀a ∈ A: IrreversibleCatastrophe(a) → ¬Permissible(a) ∨ ExtremeJustification(a) Irreversible catastrophic consequences require extreme justification Axiom PR-4 (the rollback-obligation axiom): ∀a ∈ A: Execute(a) ∧ NegativeConsequence(a) ∧ Reversible(a) → O(Rollback(a)) If an action produces a negative consequence and is reversible, then there is an obligation to roll back Auxiliary definition PR-D1 (the reversibility threshold): θ_rev ∈ [0, 1], default value 0.5 Auxiliary definition PR-D2 (catastrophic consequence): IrreversibleCatastrophe(a) ↔ Rev(a) < 0.1 ∧ Severity(a) > θ_severity Table 13.1 Formal elements of the Reversibility Principle | Element | Symbol | Meaning | Constraint | |------|------|------|------| | Action set | $A$ | All possible actions | - | | Reversibility function | $\text{Rev}$ | The degree of reversibility of an action | $\text{Rev}: A \rightarrow [0, 1]$ | | Reversibility threshold | $\theta_{\text{rev}}$ | The threshold requiring strong justification | Default 0.5 | | Severity threshold | $\theta_{\text{severity}}$ | The threshold for catastrophic consequences | Context-dependent | | Preference relation | $\succ$ | The priority relation between actions | Transitivity | | Justification threshold | $\text{JustificationThreshold}$ | The strength of justification an action requires | Negatively correlated with reversibility | Boundary declaration 13.1 (determination of the reversibility threshold) The specific value of the reversibility threshold $\theta_{\text{rev}}$ must be determined according to the situation; it is not fixed a priori. The default value of 0.5 offered by this work is a suggested value, not a mandatory one. In high-risk situations the threshold may need to be raised; in low-risk situations it may be possible to lower it.

Validity Check of the Derivation Check 13.1 (the logical validity of the derivation) The logical validity of the derivation can be checked in the following ways:

  1. Acceptability of the premises: are NK-1, NK-4, and BP-2 acceptable?
  2. NK-1 and NK-4 were argued in Chapter 3
  3. BP-2 was argued in Chapter 5
  4. Therefore, the premises are acceptable
  5. Validity of the inference: is the inference from premises to conclusion valid?
  6. The inferential steps of each argument node are presented explicitly
  7. The inferences follow standard logical rules
  8. Therefore, the inferences are valid
  9. Coherence of the conclusion: is the conclusion coherent with other accepted propositions?
  10. PR is coherent with the other propositions of the Three New Views
  11. PR is coherent with RFP (the Recursive Freedom Principle) and PNR (the Negentropy Responsibility Principle)
  12. Therefore, the conclusion is coherent

Boundary declaration 13.2 (the boundaries of the derivation) The derivation of the Reversibility Principle has the following boundaries:

  • The derivation depends on the acceptability of the New View of Cognition (NK-1, NK-4)
  • The derivation depends on the acceptability of the bridge principle (BP-2)
  • If these premises are revised, the conclusion of the derivation must be revised accordingly
  • The derivation is revisable, not a closed proof

Auxiliary definition PR-D1 (the reversibility threshold): θ_rev ∈ [0, 1], default value 0.5 Auxiliary definition PR-D2 (catastrophic consequence): IrreversibleCatastrophe(a) ↔ Rev(a) < 0.1 ∧ Severity(a) > θ_severity Table 13.1 Formal elements of the Reversibility Principle | Element | Symbol | Meaning | Constraint | |------|------|------|------| | Action set | $A$ | All possible actions | - | | Reversibility function | $\text{Rev}$ | The degree of reversibility of an action | $\text{Rev}: A \rightarrow [0, 1]$ | | Reversibility threshold | $\theta_{\text{rev}}$ | The threshold requiring strong justification | Default 0.5 | | Severity threshold | $\theta_{\text{severity}}$ | The threshold for catastrophic consequences | Context-dependent | | Preference relation | $\succ$ | The priority relation between actions | Transitivity | | Justification threshold | $\text{JustificationThreshold}$ | The strength of justification an action requires | Negatively correlated with reversibility | Boundary declaration 13.1 (determination of the reversibility threshold) The specific value of the reversibility threshold $\theta_{\text{rev}}$ must be determined according to the situation; it is not fixed a priori. The default value of 0.5 offered by this work is a suggested value, not a mandatory one. In high-risk situations the threshold may need to be raised; in low-risk situations it may be possible to lower it.
