  • The derivation is revisable, not a closed proof

§13.2 The Content of the Reversibility Principle

§13.2.1 The Meaning of “Reversibility” I. Reversibility in Physics Definition 13.10 (physical reversibility) Physical reversibility means that a physical process can proceed backwards along time without violating the laws of physics. Formal statement: $$\text{PhysicallyReversible}(P) \Leftrightarrow \exists P^{-1}: P^{-1}(P(s)) = s \wedge \text{LawsOfPhysics}(P^{-1})$$ Characteristics of physical reversibility:

  • Microscopic physical processes are usually reversible (the unitary evolution of quantum mechanics)
  • Macroscopic physical processes are usually irreversible (the second law of thermodynamics)
  • Physical reversibility is an idealized concept

Table 13.3 Levels of physical reversibility | Level | Reversibility | Example | Note | |------|--------|------|------| | Microscopic quantum | High | Evolution of quantum states | Unitary evolution is reversible | | Microscopic classical | High | Elastic collision | Newtonian mechanics is time-reversal symmetric | | Macroscopic thermodynamic | Low | Heat conduction | Entropy-increasing processes are irreversible | | Macroscopic complex systems | Extremely low | Ecosystem change | Involves multi-scale coupling | II. Reversibility in Decision Theory Definition 13.11 (decision reversibility) Decision reversibility means that a decision can be revoked or modified, restoring the system to the state prior to the decision or close to it. Formal statement: $$\text{DecisionReversible}(d) \Leftrightarrow \exists d^{-1}: \text{Execute}(d^{-1}, \text{Execute}(d, s)) \approx s$$ Characteristics of decision reversibility:

  • Decision reversibility is a matter of degree, not binary
  • Decision reversibility depends on time, cost, and technology
  • Decision reversibility may change over time

III. Institutional Reversibility Definition 13.12 (institutional reversibility) Institutional reversibility means that an institutional arrangement can be modified or abolished, restoring the social system to the state prior to the institution’s establishment or steering it to a new state. Formal statement: $$\text{InstitutionallyReversible}(I) \Leftrightarrow \exists \text{Process}: \text{Modify}(I) \vee \text{Abolish}(I)$$ Characteristics of institutional reversibility:

  • Institutional reversibility depends on institutional design
  • Some institutions are path-dependent and hard to reverse
  • Institutional reversibility is an important feature of democratic governance

IV. Cognitive Reversibility Definition 13.13 (cognitive reversibility) Cognitive reversibility means that a cognitive state can be revised, enabling the cognizer to change their beliefs, theories, or worldview. Formal statement: $$\text{CognitivelyReversible}(B) \Leftrightarrow \exists \text{Evidence}: \text{Revise}(B, \text{Evidence})$$ Characteristics of cognitive reversibility:

  • Cognitive reversibility is a core feature of rationality
  • Some cognitive states may have inertia and be hard to revise
  • Cognitive reversibility depends on openness and reflective capacity

V. A Unified Understanding of Reversibility Proposition 13.11 (a unified understanding of reversibility) Although reversibility has different specific meanings in different domains, they share one core feature: the capacity to return to a prior state or to transition to a new state. Formal statement: $$\text{Reversibility}(X) \Leftrightarrow \text{Capacity}(\text{Return}(X, s_0) \vee \text{Transition}(X, s_{\text{new}}))$$ Table 13.4 Comparison of the multi-layered meanings of reversibility | Type | Core meaning | Dependent factors | Degree-like | |------|----------|----------|--------| | Physical reversibility | The process can proceed backwards along time | Laws of physics | Yes | | Decision reversibility | The decision can be revoked | Time, cost, technology | Yes | | Institutional reversibility | The institution can be modified | Institutional design, political conditions | Yes | | Cognitive reversibility | The belief can be revised | Evidence, openness | Yes |

§13.2.2 The Degree of Reversibility I. Reversibility Is Degree-Like Proposition 13.12 (the degree-like character of reversibility) Reversibility is not binary (reversible or irreversible) but a matter of degree. Actions can have different degrees of reversibility, from fully reversible to fully irreversible. Definition 13.14 (degree of reversibility) The degree of reversibility $\text{Rev}(a) \in [0, 1]$ denotes the degree of reversibility of action $a$.

  • $\text{Rev}(a) = 1$: fully reversible
  • $\text{Rev}(a) = 0$: fully irreversible
  • $0 < \text{Rev}(a) < 1$: partially reversible

II. Determinants of the Degree of Reversibility Proposition 13.13 (determinants of the degree of reversibility) The degree of reversibility is determined by the following factors:

  • Possibility of restoration: can it be restored to the prior state?
  • Cost of restoration: how much does restoration cost?
  • Time of restoration: how long does restoration take?
  • Completeness of restoration: how close to the prior state can it be restored?

Formal statement: $$\text{Rev}(a) = f(\text{Possibility}, \text{Cost}, \text{Time}, \text{Completeness})$$ Definition 13.15 (the formula for the degree of reversibility) The formula for the degree of reversibility: $$\text{Rev}(a) = P_{\text{restore}} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + C_{\text{restore}}/C_{\text{ref}}} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + T_{\text{restore}}/T_{\text{ref}}} \cdot Q_{\text{completeness}}$$ Where:

  • $P_{\text{restore}}$ is the probability of restoration
  • $C_{\text{restore}}$ is the cost of restoration, $C_{\text{ref}}$ is the reference cost
  • $T_{\text{restore}}$ is the time of restoration, $T_{\text{ref}}$ is the reference time
  • $Q_{\text{completeness}}$ is the completeness of restoration (0 to 1)

III. Grading of the Degree of Reversibility Definition 13.16 (grading of the degree of reversibility) The degree of reversibility can be divided into the following grades: Table 13.5 Grading of the degree of reversibility | Grade | Reversibility range | Description | Example | |------|------------|------|------| | Fully reversible | $\text{Rev} = 1$ | Can be fully restored to the prior state | Undoing a document edit | | Highly reversible | $0.8 \leq \text{Rev} < 1$ | Can be mostly restored | Demolishing a temporary structure | | Moderately reversible | $0.5 \leq \text{Rev} < 0.8$ | Can be partially restored | Restoring a degraded ecosystem | | Lowly reversible | $0.2 \leq \text{Rev} < 0.5$ | Restoration is difficult | Cleaning up large-scale pollution | | Extremely lowly reversible | $0 < \text{Rev} < 0.2$ | Restoration is nearly impossible | Restoration after species extinction | | Fully irreversible | $\text{Rev} = 0$ | Cannot be restored | Species extinction |

§13.2.3 The Assessment of Reversibility I. A General Framework for Reversibility Assessment Procedure 13.1 (reversibility assessment procedure) Step 1: identify the consequences of the action

  • Make explicit what consequences the action will produce
  • Identify the various dimensions of the consequences

Step 2: assess the possibility of restoration

  • For each consequence, assess whether it can be restored
  • Identify the obstacles to restoration

Step 3: assess the cost of restoration

  • Estimate the resources required for restoration
  • Include economic cost, time cost, and social cost

Step 4: assess the time of restoration

  • Estimate the time required for restoration
  • Consider the uncertainty of the time

Step 5: assess the completeness of restoration

  • Assess how close to the prior state it can be restored
  • Identify the elements that cannot be restored

Step 6: compute the composite degree of reversibility

  • Use the formula of Definition 13.15
  • Or use a simplified assessment method

Step 7: determine the reversibility grade

  • Determine the grade according to Table 13.5
  • Record the uncertainty of the assessment

II. Dimensions of Reversibility Assessment Definition 13.17 (dimensions of reversibility assessment) Reversibility assessment should consider the following dimensions: Table 13.6 Dimensions of reversibility assessment | Dimension | Assessment content | Assessment method | |------|----------|----------| | Physical dimension | Whether the physical state can be restored | Physical analysis | | Ecological dimension | Whether the ecosystem can be restored | Ecological assessment | | Social dimension | Whether the social structure can be restored | Sociological analysis | | Economic dimension | Whether the economic state can be restored | Economic analysis | | Cognitive dimension | Whether the cognitive state can be restored | Psychological analysis | | Institutional dimension | Whether the institutional arrangement can be restored | Institutional analysis | III. The Uncertainty of Reversibility Assessment Proposition 13.14 (the uncertainty of reversibility assessment) Reversibility assessment itself faces uncertainty. We may not know:

  • all the consequences of the action
  • all the obstacles to restoration
  • the true cost and time of restoration
  • whether future technological developments will change the reversibility

Definition 13.18 (the confidence interval of reversibility assessment) Reversibility assessment should include a confidence interval, representing the uncertainty of the assessment. Formal statement: $$\text{Rev}(a) = \text{Rev}_{\text{point}} \pm \Delta\text{Rev}$$ Where $\text{Rev}_{\text{point}}$ is the point estimate and $\Delta\text{Rev}$ is the range of uncertainty. Decision rule 13.1 (reversibility decision under uncertainty) When there is uncertainty in the reversibility assessment, a conservative principle should be adopted: use the lower bound of the reversibility estimate for decision-making. Formal statement: $$\text{Rev}_{\text{decision}}(a) = \text{Rev}_{\text{point}}(a) - \Delta\text{Rev}(a)$$

§13.2.4 The Complete Statement of the Principle I. The Core Statement of the Reversibility Principle Definition 13.19 (the Reversibility Principle, core statement) The Reversibility Principle (Principle of Reversibility, PR): Under deep uncertainty, a rational agent ought to give priority to reversible actions, set a higher justification threshold for irreversible actions, and establish rollback mechanisms so as to correct errors when they are discovered. II. The Tiered Statements of the Reversibility Principle Table 13.7 Tiered statements of the Reversibility Principle | Tier | Statement | Formalization | |------|------|--------| | Individual tier | Individuals ought to give priority to reversible actions | $\forall s \in S_{\text{ind}}: O(\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a)))$ | | Organizational tier | Organizations ought to establish rollback mechanisms | $\forall o \in S_{\text{org}}: O(\text{Establish}(\text{RollbackMechanism}))$ | | Civilizational tier | Civilizations ought to avoid irreversible catastrophic decisions | $\forall c \in S_{\text{civ}}: O(\text{Avoid}(\text{IrreversibleCatastrophe}))$ | | Institutional tier | Institutions ought to maintain revisability | $\forall i \in I: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{Revisability}(i)))$ | III. The Complete Specification of the Reversibility Principle Table 13.8 Complete specification of the Reversibility Principle | Specification item | Content | |--------|------| | Principle number | PR | | Principle name | The Reversibility Principle | | English name | Principle of Reversibility | | Core statement | Under deep uncertainty, give priority to reversible actions and preserve error-correction capacity | | Formalization | $\text{DeepUncertainty} \rightarrow O(\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}) \wedge \text{Avoid}(\text{IrreversibleCatastrophe}))$ | | Reversibility function | $\text{Rev}: A \rightarrow [0, 1]$ | | Theoretical anchoring | NK-1 (participatory construction), NK-4 (negotiability), BP-2 (epistemic humility) | | Operationalization indicators | CRV (commitment-validation ratio), the D₄ dimension of CSIA | | Scope of application | Situations of deep uncertainty | | Exceptional conditions | Emergencies, unavoidable irreversibility |

§13.3 The Application of the Reversibility Principle

§13.3.1 The General Procedure of Application I. The Overall Framework of the Application Procedure The application of the Reversibility Principle follows this general procedure: Procedure 13.2 (the application procedure of the Reversibility Principle) Step 1: identify the decision situation

  • Make explicit the content and scope of the decision
  • Assess the degree of uncertainty of the situation

Step 2: identify the available actions

  • List all available courses of action
  • Include the “no action” option

Step 3: assess the reversibility of each action

  • Use Procedure 13.1 to assess the reversibility of each action
  • Record the uncertainty of the assessment

Step 4: identify irreversible catastrophic consequences

  • For each action, identify whether there are irreversible catastrophic consequences
  • Assess the severity of the catastrophic consequences

Step 5: apply the reversibility-preference rule

  • Other things being equal, choose the action with higher reversibility
  • If an action with lower reversibility is chosen, justification must be provided

Step 6: design a rollback mechanism

  • Design a rollback mechanism for the chosen action
  • Make explicit the triggering conditions and procedure for rollback

Step 7: monitoring and adjustment

  • Monitor the consequences of the action
  • Activate the rollback mechanism when problems are found

II. The Formalization of the Application Procedure Definition 13.20 (the application function of the Reversibility Principle) The application function of the Reversibility Principle $\text{ApplyPR}: \text{Situation} \times \text{Actions} \rightarrow \text{Decision}$ is defined as follows: $$\text{ApplyPR}(\text{Sit}, A) = \arg\max_{a \in A} \text{Score}(a)$$ Where: $$\text{Score}(a) = \begin{cases} -\infty & \text{if } \text{IrreversibleCatastrophe}(a) \wedge \neg\text{ExtremeJustification}(a) \\ w_1 \cdot \text{Rev}(a) + w_2 \cdot \text{Benefit}(a) - w_3 \cdot \text{Cost}(a) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Where $w_1, w_2, w_3$ are weight coefficients. III. Trade-offs in Application Proposition 13.15 (the trade-off between reversibility and other factors) The Reversibility Principle does not require absolutely prioritizing the action with the highest reversibility. In practical application, reversibility must be weighed against other factors such as benefit, cost, and urgency. Definition 13.21 (determination of the reversibility weight) The reversibility weight $w_1$ should be determined according to the following factors:

  • Degree of uncertainty: the higher the uncertainty, the larger $w_1$
  • Severity of consequences: the more severe the consequences, the larger $w_1$
  • Time horizon: the longer the time horizon, the larger $w_1$

Formal statement: $$w_1 = f(\text{Uncertainty}, \text{Severity}, \text{TimeHorizon})$$

§13.3.2 Application to Technological Decisions I. Characteristics of Technological Decisions Technological decisions usually have the following characteristics, which make the Reversibility Principle especially applicable:

  • High uncertainty: the long-term effects of new technologies are hard to predict
  • Potential large-scale impact: a technology may affect a large population
  • Path dependence: technological choices may produce lock-in effects
  • Rapid development: technology develops quickly and decision windows are short

II. Reversibility Assessment in Technological Decisions Case 13.1 (reversibility assessment of deploying an AI system) Situation: an organization considers deploying a large-scale artificial intelligence system. Reversibility assessment: Step 1: identify the consequences of the action

  • Direct consequences: the AI system begins to operate and produces outputs
  • Indirect consequences: effects on user behavior, market structure, employment, etc.
  • Long-term consequences: may change the social structure and cognitive patterns

Step 2: assess the possibility of restoration

  • The system can be shut down: high possibility
  • User behavior can be restored: medium possibility
  • Market structure can be restored: low possibility
  • Social structure can be restored: extremely low possibility

Step 3: assess the cost of restoration

  • Shutting down the system: low cost
  • Restoring user behavior: medium cost
  • Restoring market structure: high cost
  • Restoring social structure: extremely high cost

Step 4: assess the time of restoration

  • Shutting down the system: immediate
  • Restoring user behavior: months
  • Restoring market structure: years
  • Restoring social structure: decades

Step 5: assess the completeness of restoration

  • Shutting down the system: complete
  • Restoring user behavior: partial
  • Restoring market structure: partial
  • Restoring social structure: minimal

Step 6: compute the composite degree of reversibility

  • Short-term reversibility: high (0.8)
  • Medium-term reversibility: medium (0.5)
  • Long-term reversibility: low (0.3)

Step 7: determine the reversibility grade

  • Composite assessment: moderately reversible (0.5)
  • A rollback mechanism needs to be designed

Recommendations:

  • Adopt gradual deployment, starting on a small scale
  • Establish a monitoring mechanism to detect problems in time
  • Design shutdown and rollback procedures
  • Retain alternatives

III. Reversibility Design Principles for Technological Decisions Proposition 13.16 (reversibility design principles for technological decisions) In technological decisions, the following reversibility design principles should be followed:

  1. Gradual deployment: start on a small scale and expand step by step
  2. Modular design: enable the system to be partially rolled back
  3. Monitoring mechanisms: establish an early-warning system
  4. Kill switches: design reliable shutdown mechanisms
  5. Alternatives: retain alternative technological paths
  6. Version control: record system states to support rollback

Table 13.9 Reversibility design checklist for technological decisions | Design element | Purpose | Implementation method | |----------|------|----------| | Gradual deployment | Limit the initial scope of impact | Staged deployment, A/B testing | | Modular design | Support partial rollback | Loose coupling architecture, microservices | | Monitoring mechanisms | Detect problems in time | Logs, metrics, alerts | | Kill switches | Emergency stop | Hardware switches, software switches | | Alternatives | Retain options | Multiple technological paths, backup systems | | Version control | Support rollback | Version management, snapshots |

§13.3.3 Application to Policy Decisions I. Characteristics of Policy Decisions Policy decisions usually have the following characteristics:

  • Broad impact: policies affect a large population
  • Long-term effects: policy effects may last for decades
  • Path dependence: policies may produce institutional lock-in
  • Political constraints: modifying policies faces political obstacles

II. Reversibility Assessment in Policy Decisions Case 13.2 (reversibility assessment of climate policy) Situation: a country considers implementing a carbon tax policy. Reversibility assessment: Step 1: identify the consequences of the action

  • Direct consequences: the cost of carbon emissions increases
  • Indirect consequences: industrial restructuring, energy transition
  • Long-term consequences: the trajectory of climate change is altered

Step 2: assess the possibility of restoration

  • Abolishing the carbon tax: high possibility (the policy can be repealed)
  • Restoring the industrial structure: medium possibility
  • Restoring the climate trajectory: extremely low possibility (climate change itself is irreversible)

Step 3: assess the cost of restoration

  • Abolishing the carbon tax: low cost
  • Restoring the industrial structure: high cost
  • Restoring the climate trajectory: extremely high cost (possibly impossible)

Step 4: assess the time of restoration

  • Abolishing the carbon tax: immediate
  • Restoring the industrial structure: years to decades
  • Restoring the climate trajectory: centuries to millennia

Step 5: assess the completeness of restoration

  • Abolishing the carbon tax: complete
  • Restoring the industrial structure: partial
  • Restoring the climate trajectory: minimal

Step 6: compute the composite degree of reversibility

  • Reversibility of the policy itself: high (0.9)
  • Reversibility of the policy’s effects: low (0.3)

Step 7: determine the reversibility grade

  • The policy itself: highly reversible
  • The policy’s effects: lowly reversible

Analysis:

  • The carbon tax policy itself is highly reversible
  • But the consequences of not implementing the carbon tax (climate change) are irreversible
  • This is a case of “the irreversibility of inaction”
  • The Reversibility Principle supports implementing the carbon tax, since the consequences of inaction are more irreversible

Recommendations:

  • Implement the carbon tax policy
  • Design a gradual implementation plan
  • Establish monitoring and assessment mechanisms
  • Retain flexibility for policy adjustment

III. Reversibility Design Principles for Policy Decisions Proposition 13.17 (reversibility design principles for policy decisions) In policy decisions, the following reversibility design principles should be followed:

  1. Sunset clauses: set an automatic expiration date for the policy, requiring re-deliberation for extension
  2. Pilot first: pilot on a small scale and expand after assessing the effects
  3. Gradual implementation: implement in stages, deciding whether to continue after assessment at each stage
  4. Assessment mechanisms: establish regular assessment mechanisms and adjust the policy according to the assessment results
  5. Exit mechanisms: design an explicit policy exit procedure
  6. Compensation mechanisms: provide compensation to those affected by policy changes

Table 13.10 Reversibility design checklist for policy decisions | Design element | Purpose | Implementation method | |----------|------|----------| | Sunset clauses | Force re-deliberation | Set an expiration date | | Pilot first | Limit the initial impact | Select pilot regions | | Gradual implementation | Preserve room for adjustment | Staged implementation | | Assessment mechanisms | Detect problems in time | Regular assessment reports | | Exit mechanisms | Support policy termination | Explicit exit procedure | | Compensation mechanisms | Reduce political resistance | Transition-period compensation |

§13.3.4 Application to Institutional Design I. Characteristics of Institutional Design Institutional design has the following characteristics:

  • Long-term character: institutions are usually designed to operate over the long term
  • Path dependence: once an institution is established, the cost of modification is high
  • Emergent effects: institutions may produce unexpected emergent effects
  • Multi-agent interaction: institutions involve the interaction of multiple agents

II. The Reversibility Principle in Institutional Design Proposition 13.18 (the Reversibility Principle in institutional design) In institutional design, the Reversibility Principle requires:

  • institutions should be revisable
  • institutions should include self-correction mechanisms
  • institutions should avoid producing irreversible lock-in effects

Definition 13.22 (elements of institutional reversibility) Institutional reversibility includes the following elements:

  • Revision procedures: institutions should include explicit revision procedures
  • Assessment mechanisms: institutions should include regular assessment mechanisms
  • Exit mechanisms: institutions should include exit or abolition mechanisms
  • Version control: institutions should record historical versions to support rollback

III. A Case of Reversibility in Institutional Design Case 13.3 (reversibility design of an international treaty) Situation: designing an international climate treaty. Reversibility design elements:

  1. Revision procedures
  2. Regular conferences of the parties
  3. Revision proposal procedures
  4. Revision ratification procedures
  5. Assessment mechanisms
  6. Regular global stocktakes
  7. Independent scientific assessment
  8. Compliance review mechanisms
  9. Exit mechanisms
  10. An explicit exit procedure
  11. An exit notification period
  12. Obligations after exit
  13. Flexibility mechanisms
  14. Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC)
  15. A mechanism of progressively increasing ambition
  16. Differentiated responsibilities
  17. Version control
  18. Records of treaty amendments
  19. Records of resolutions and decisions
  20. Archiving of historical versions

Analysis:

  • The Paris Agreement embodies many reversibility design principles
  • The Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) mechanism provides flexibility
  • Regular global stocktakes provide opportunities for assessment and adjustment
  • But the exit mechanism (e.g., the United States’ withdrawal) also brings challenges

Table 13.11 Reversibility checklist for institutional design | Design element | Purpose | Implementation method | |----------|------|----------| | Revision procedures | Support institutional updating | Explicit revision rules | | Assessment mechanisms | Identify problems | Regular assessment, independent review | | Exit mechanisms | Support exit | Explicit exit procedure | | Flexibility mechanisms | Adapt to change | Differentiation, gradualness | | Version control | Support rollback | Historical records, archiving | | Self-correction | Automatic adjustment | Triggering conditions, adjustment rules |

§13.4 The Reversibility Principle and the Precautionary Principle

§13.4.1 Review of the Precautionary Principle I. The Definition of the Precautionary Principle Definition 13.23 (the precautionary principle) The Precautionary Principle means that in the face of potential serious or irreversible harm, even in the absence of full scientific certainty, this shall not be used as a reason to postpone cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation. The classic statement of the precautionary principle (Article 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration): “In order to protect the environment, the precautionary approach shall be widely applied by States according to their capabilities. Where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost-effective measures to prevent environmental degradation.” II. The Core Elements of the Precautionary Principle Proposition 13.19 (the core elements of the precautionary principle) The precautionary principle contains the following core elements:

  • Threat condition: there is a threat of serious or irreversible harm
  • Uncertainty condition: there is a lack of full scientific certainty
  • Action requirement: precautionary measures ought to be taken
  • Cost consideration: the measures ought to be cost-effective

Formal statement: $$\text{PP}: (\text{SeriousThreat} \vee \text{IrreversibleThreat}) \wedge \text{ScientificUncertainty} \rightarrow O(\text{PreventiveMeasures})$$ III. Controversies over the Precautionary Principle In practice the precautionary principle faces the following controversies:

  1. Vague triggering conditions: what degree of threat counts as “serious”?
  2. Unclear action requirement: what kind of precautionary measures ought to be taken?
  3. Cost-benefit trade-off: how should the cost of precaution be weighed against the potential benefit?
  4. Burden of proof: who ought to prove safety or danger?
  5. Risk of excessive caution: could it lead to excessive caution and hinder innovation?

§13.4.2 The Relation between the Reversibility Principle and the Precautionary Principle I. Common Ground of the Two Principles Proposition 13.20 (the common ground of the two principles) The Reversibility Principle and the precautionary principle share the following common ground:

  • Both are concerned with decision-making under uncertainty
  • Both are concerned with potentially serious consequences
  • Both require acting cautiously
  • Both emphasize the importance of irreversibility

Table 13.12 Common ground of the two principles | Common ground | Precautionary principle | Reversibility Principle | |--------|----------|------------| | Focus on uncertainty | Scientific uncertainty | Deep uncertainty | | Focus on consequences | Serious or irreversible harm | Irreversible consequences | | Action requirement | Take precautionary measures | Give priority to reversible actions | | Cautious attitude | Do not use uncertainty as an excuse for inaction | Preserve error-correction capacity | II. Differences between the Two Principles Proposition 13.21 (the differences between the two principles) The Reversibility Principle and the precautionary principle differ as follows:

  • Focus: the precautionary principle focuses on avoiding harm; the Reversibility Principle focuses on preserving error-correction capacity
  • Action guidance: the precautionary principle requires taking precautionary measures; the Reversibility Principle requires giving priority to reversible actions
  • Scope of application: the precautionary principle is mainly used in the environmental and health domains; the Reversibility Principle applies to all decision domains
  • Degree of operationalization: the precautionary principle is rather vague in its operationalization; the Reversibility Principle provides clearer operational guidance

Table 13.13 Differences between the two principles | Difference | Precautionary principle | Reversibility Principle | |------|----------|------------| | Focus | Avoiding harm | Preserving error-correction capacity | | Action guidance | Take precautionary measures | Give priority to reversible actions | | Scope of application | Environment, health | All decision domains | | Operationalization | Rather vague | Fairly clear (reversibility measure) | | Theoretical basis | Risk aversion | Epistemic humility | | Attitude toward inaction | May require action | Assess the reversibility of inaction | III. The Complementarity of the Two Principles Proposition 13.22 (the complementarity of the two principles) The Reversibility Principle and the precautionary principle are complementary, not substitutive. The two principles can be used in combination to provide more comprehensive decision guidance. Manifestations of complementarity:

  • The precautionary principle provides the motivation for action (avoiding harm)
  • The Reversibility Principle provides the manner of action (giving priority to reversible actions)
  • Together the two principles support a cautious decision-making attitude

§13.4.3 The Advantages of the Reversibility Principle I. Operationalization Advantages Proposition 13.23 (the operationalization advantages of the Reversibility Principle) The Reversibility Principle has operationalization advantages over the precautionary principle:

  • Reversibility can be measured (a continuous value from 0 to 1)
  • The reversibility-preference rule is explicit
  • The justification threshold is correlated with the degree of reversibility
  • The rollback mechanism provides concrete action guidance

Table 13.14 Comparison of operationalization | Operationalization element | Precautionary principle | Reversibility Principle | |------------|----------|------------| | Measurement of the core concept | Threat severity (hard to measure) | Degree of reversibility (measurable) | | Action rule | Take precautionary measures (unclear) | Give priority to reversible actions (clear) | | Threshold setting | Unclear | Correlated with the degree of reversibility | | Follow-up action | Unclear | Rollback mechanism | II. Theoretical-Basis Advantages Proposition 13.24 (the theoretical-basis advantages of the Reversibility Principle) The Reversibility Principle has a more solid theoretical basis:

  • It is derived from the New View of Cognition
  • It is directly related to epistemic humility
  • It has multiple independent paths of defense
  • It is coherent with the Recursive Freedom Principle and the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

III. Scope-of-Application Advantages Proposition 13.25 (the scope-of-application advantages of the Reversibility Principle) The Reversibility Principle has a broader scope of application:

  • It is not limited to the environmental and health domains
  • It applies to all decision domains such as technology, policy, and institutions
  • It applies to all tiers such as individuals, organizations, and civilizations

§13.4.4 Integrated Use of the Two Principles I. The Framework for Integrated Use Procedure 13.3 (the procedure for integrated use of the two principles) Step 1: identify the decision situation

  • Assess the degree of uncertainty
  • Identify potential serious or irreversible harm

Step 2: apply the precautionary principle

  • If there is a threat of serious or irreversible harm, initiate precautionary consideration
  • Determine whether precautionary measures need to be taken

Step 3: apply the Reversibility Principle

  • Assess the reversibility of each course of action
  • Give priority to the action with higher reversibility

Step 4: integrate the decision

  • Choose an action that both satisfies the precautionary requirement and has higher reversibility
  • If there is a conflict, weigh it according to the situation

Step 5: design a rollback mechanism

  • Design a rollback mechanism for the chosen action
  • Make explicit the triggering conditions and procedure for rollback

Step 6: monitoring and adjustment

  • Monitor the consequences of the action
  • Adjust the decision according to new information

II. A Case of Integrated Use Case 13.4 (integrated decision on gene-editing technology) Situation: consider whether to permit human embryo gene editing. Step 1: identify the decision situation

  • Uncertainty: high (long-term effects unknown)
  • Potential harm: serious (may affect future generations)

Step 2: apply the precautionary principle

  • There is a threat of serious harm: yes
  • Scientific uncertainty: yes
  • Requirement of the precautionary principle: take precautionary measures

Step 3: apply the Reversibility Principle

  • Reversibility of gene editing: extremely low (genetic changes are hard to reverse)
  • Requirement of the Reversibility Principle: set a high justification threshold

Step 4: integrate the decision

  • Both principles support a cautious attitude
  • Recommendation: suspend the clinical application of human embryo gene editing
  • Allow: controlled basic research

Step 5: design a rollback mechanism

  • For basic research: strict ethical review and regulation
  • For clinical application: suspend and await more evidence

Step 6: monitoring and adjustment

  • Continuously monitor scientific progress
  • Periodically reassess the policy

Table 13.15 Decision matrix for the integrated use of the two principles | Situation | Guidance from the precautionary principle | Guidance from the Reversibility Principle | Integrated decision | |------|--------------|----------------|----------| | High threat + low reversibility | Strong precaution | High threshold | Extreme caution | | High threat + high reversibility | Strong precaution | Acceptable | Cautious but can be attempted | | Low threat + low reversibility | Weak precaution | High threshold | Careful assessment | | Low threat + high reversibility | Weak precaution | Acceptable | Can proceed |

§13.5 The Boundaries and Exceptions of the Reversibility Principle

§13.5.1 The Boundaries of the Principle’s Application I. The Uncertainty Boundary Boundary declaration 13.3 (the uncertainty boundary) The Reversibility Principle mainly applies to situations of deep uncertainty. In low-uncertainty situations, the binding force of the Reversibility Principle is weaker, and the standard expectation-utility maximization method can be used. Formal statement: $$\text{Uncertainty}(\text{Sit}) < \theta_U \Rightarrow \text{PR weakly applies}$$ Table 13.16 Degree of uncertainty and applicability of the Reversibility Principle | Degree of uncertainty | Applicability of the Reversibility Principle | Decision method | |--------------|------------------|----------| | Risk (probability known) | Weak | Expectation-utility maximization | | Uncertainty (probability unknown) | Medium | Maximin principle | | Deep uncertainty | Strong | The Reversibility Principle | | Ignorance | Extremely strong | Extreme caution | II. The Impact Boundary Boundary declaration 13.4 (the impact boundary) The Reversibility Principle mainly applies to decisions with relatively large impact. For everyday decisions with negligible impact, the binding force of the Reversibility Principle is weaker. Formal statement: $$\text{Impact}(a) < \theta_I \Rightarrow \text{PR weakly applies}$$ III. The Time Boundary Boundary declaration 13.5 (the time boundary) The Reversibility Principle mainly applies to decisions with long-term impact. For decisions with short-term impact, the binding force of the Reversibility Principle is weaker. Formal statement: $$\text{Duration}(a) < \theta_T \Rightarrow \text{PR weakly applies}$$ IV. The Agent Boundary Boundary declaration 13.6 (the agent boundary) The Reversibility Principle applies to all rational agents. But for different types of agents, the specific requirements of the Reversibility Principle may differ. Formal statement: $$\text{PR}(S) = f(\text{Type}(S), \text{Capability}(S), \text{Context}(S))$$ Table 13.17 Applicability of the Reversibility Principle to different agents | Agent type | Applicability | Specific requirements | |----------|--------|----------| | Individual | Applies | Give priority to reversible options in personal decisions | | Organization | Applies | Establish organization-level rollback mechanisms | | State | Applies | Incorporate reversibility considerations into policy design | | Civilization | Strongly applies | Avoid civilization-level irreversible decisions | | AI system | To be assessed | Depends on the AI system’s agent status |

§13.5.2 Possible Exceptional Cases I. A General Framework for Exceptional Cases Definition 13.24 (exceptional cases) Exceptional cases are cases in which the constraints of the Reversibility Principle may be temporarily relaxed or exempted. Exceptional cases must satisfy specific conditions. The general framework for exceptional conditions:

  1. Urgency: is the situation urgent?
  2. Necessity: is the exception necessary?
  3. Proportionality: is the degree of the exception proportional to the urgency?
  4. Temporariness: is the exception temporary?

II. Specific Exceptional Cases Exceptional case one: emergencies In an emergency, there may be no time to assess reversibility or to choose the action with higher reversibility. Definition 13.25 (the emergency exception) The emergency exception: in an emergency, if waiting to assess reversibility would lead to greater harm, the constraints of the Reversibility Principle may be temporarily relaxed. Formal statement: $$\text{Emergency}(\text{Sit}) \wedge \text{Delay}(\text{Assessment}) \rightarrow \text{GreaterHarm} \Rightarrow \text{TemporaryExemption}$$ Case 13.5 (the emergency exception) Situation: a sudden epidemic requires immediate action. Analysis:

  • Urgency: extremely high (the epidemic spreads rapidly)
  • Necessity: yes (delaying action would lead to more infections)
  • Proportionality: the irreversibility of the action should be proportional to the urgency
  • Temporariness: emergency measures should be reassessed once the emergency is over

Conclusion: an emergency is an exceptional case of the Reversibility Principle, but it must satisfy the conditions of proportionality and temporariness Exceptional case two: unavoidable irreversibility Some actions are inherently irreversible, and no reversible alternative can be chosen. Definition 13.26 (the unavoidable-irreversibility exception) The unavoidable-irreversibility exception: when all available actions are irreversible, or inaction itself is also irreversible, the constraints of the Reversibility Principle need to be adjusted. Formal statement: $$\forall a \in A: \neg\text{Reversible}(a) \Rightarrow \text{AdjustedApplication}(\text{PR})$$ Case 13.6 (the unavoidable-irreversibility exception) Situation: in the face of climate change, both inaction and action may produce irreversible consequences. Analysis:

  • Inaction: climate change continues, producing irreversible environmental damage
  • Action (e.g., geoengineering): may produce irreversible side effects
  • Both are irreversible

Adjusted application:

  • Compare the degrees of irreversibility of different actions
  • Choose the action with a lower degree of irreversibility
  • Or choose the action with lighter irreversible consequences

Conclusion: when irreversibility is unavoidable, one should compare the degrees of irreversibility of different actions and choose the relatively better one Exceptional case three: negotiated consent If all affected agents consent to a certain irreversible action, it may serve as an exception. Definition 13.27 (the negotiated-consent exception) The negotiated-consent exception: if all affected agents, after being fully informed, consent to a certain irreversible action, the constraints of the Reversibility Principle may be relaxed. Formal statement: $$\forall S \in \text{AffectedParties}: \text{InformedConsent}(S, a) \Rightarrow \text{Exemption}(a)$$ Restricting conditions:

  • Consent must be informed
  • Consent must be voluntary
  • It must include all affected agents (including representatives of future generations)

Exceptional case four: the requirement of a higher principle When the Reversibility Principle conflicts with a principle at a higher tier (such as a taboo red line), the higher principle takes priority. Definition 13.28 (the higher-principle exception) The higher-principle exception: when complying with the Reversibility Principle would violate a principle at a higher tier, the higher principle takes priority. Formal statement: $$\text{Conflict}(\text{PR}, P_{\text{higher}}) \Rightarrow \text{Priority}(P_{\text{higher}})$$ Table 13.18 Summary of exceptional cases | Exception type | Condition | Basis of justification | Restriction | |----------|------|----------|------| | Emergency | Delay would cause greater harm | Harm minimization | Proportionality, temporariness | | Unavoidable irreversibility | All options are irreversible | Relative optimization | Choose the better option | | Negotiated consent | All agents give informed consent | Autonomous decision | Procedural justice | | Higher principle | Conflict with a higher principle | Principle hierarchy | Only genuine conflicts |

§13.5.3 Handling Conflicts with Other Principles I. Potential Conflict with the Recursive Freedom Principle Conflict situation 13.1 Situation: a certain technology can greatly expand the possibility space (consistent with RFP), but the deployment of that technology is irreversible (possibly violating PR). Conflict analysis:

  • The Recursive Freedom Principle supports the technology (expanding the possibility space)
  • The Reversibility Principle may oppose the technology (irreversible)

Way of handling:

  1. Assess the degree of expansion of the possibility space
  2. Assess the degree of irreversibility
  3. Weigh the two: is the expansion of the possibility space sufficient to justify the irreversibility?
  4. Look for alternatives: is there an alternative technology with higher reversibility?
  5. Design mitigation measures: can the irreversibility be reduced through design?

Proposition 13.26 (the relation between PR and RFP) The Reversibility Principle (PR) and the Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP) are usually complementary rather than conflicting. Reversibility keeps the possibility space open; irreversible actions may compress the possibility space. Formal statement: $$\text{Reversible}(a) \Rightarrow \text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace})$$ II. Potential Conflict with the Negentropy Responsibility Principle Conflict situation 13.2 Situation: a certain action can significantly maintain a negentropy source (consistent with PNR), but the action is irreversible (possibly violating PR). Conflict analysis:

  • The Negentropy Responsibility Principle supports the action (maintaining a negentropy source)
  • The Reversibility Principle may oppose the action (irreversible)

Way of handling:

  1. Assess the urgency of negentropy maintenance
  2. Assess the degree of irreversibility
  3. Weigh the two: is the urgency of negentropy maintenance sufficient to justify the irreversibility?
  4. Look for alternatives: is there an alternative with higher reversibility?
  5. Risk assessment: if the action fails, what are the consequences?

Proposition 13.27 (the relation between PR and PNR) The Reversibility Principle (PR) and the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR) are usually complementary. Reversibility preserves error-correction capacity and helps to maintain negentropy sources over the long term. III. A General Framework for Handling Principle Conflicts Definition 13.29 (framework for handling principle conflicts) When the Reversibility Principle conflicts with other principles, the following framework is used: Step 1: identify the conflict

  • Make explicit which principles are in conflict
  • Assess the nature and degree of the conflict

Step 2: assess the weight of each principle

  • In the specific situation, how important is each principle relatively?
  • Does any principle have priority status?

Step 3: look for a reconciling solution

  • Is there a solution that satisfies all the principles at once?
  • Can the conflict be reduced by modifying the action?

Step 4: if reconciliation is impossible, weigh

  • Determine the priority according to the situation
  • Choose the solution that is overall optimal

Step 5: record the reasons for the decision

  • Explicitly record why a particular solution was chosen
  • Provide a reference for similar situations in the future

Table 13.19 General guidance on principle priority | Situation | Priority order | Reason | |------|------------|------| | A taboo red line exists | Taboo red line > other principles | The taboo red line is an absolute constraint | | Emergency survival crisis | PNR > RFP > PR | Survival is the precondition for everything else | | Deep uncertainty | PR > RFP > PNR | Under uncertainty, prioritize preserving reversibility | | Sharp compression of the possibility space | RFP > PR > PNR | Protect the possibility space | | Ordinary situations | RFP ≈ PNR ≈ PR | Balanced consideration of the three principles |

Footnotes

Chapter 13 Footnotes

[1] Epistemic Humility: Epistemic humility is an important concept in contemporary epistemology. See: Whitcomb, D., Battaly, H., Baehr, J., & Howard-Snyder, D. (2017). "Intellectual Humility: Owning Our Limitations." Philosophy and Phenomenological Research, 94(3), 509-539. On the relation between epistemic humility and decision-making, see: Kruger, J., & Dunning, D. (1999). "Unskilled and Unaware of It: How Difficulties in Recognizing One's Own Incompetence Lead to Inflated Self-Assessments." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121-1134. [2] Deep Uncertainty: The concept of deep uncertainty is widely discussed in decision theory and risk management. See: Walker, W. E., Lempert, R. J., & Kwakkel, J. H. (2013). "Deep Uncertainty." In S. I. Gass & M. C. Fu (Eds.), Encyclopedia of Operations Research and Management Science (3rd ed.). Springer. On decision-making under deep uncertainty, see: Marchau, V. A., Walker, W. E., Bloemen, P. J., & Roelofs, K. J. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty: From Theory to Practice. Springer. [3] The Precautionary Principle: For philosophical discussion of the precautionary principle, see: Sunstein, C. R. (2005). Laws of Fear: Beyond the Precautionary Principle. Cambridge University Press. For a defense of the precautionary principle, see: Steel, D. (2014). Philosophy and the Precautionary Principle: Science, Evidence, and Environmental Policy. Cambridge University Press. [4] Reversibility and Decision Theory: On the role of reversibility in decision theory, see: Dixit, A. K., & Pindyck, R. S. (1994). Investment Under Uncertainty. Princeton University Press. On the distinctive character of irreversible decisions, see: Henry, C. (1974). "Investment Decisions Under Uncertainty: The Irreversibility Effect." American Economic Review, 64(6), 1006-1012. [5] Thermodynamic Reversibility: For discussion of thermodynamic reversibility, see: Callen, H. B. (1985). Thermodynamics and an Introduction to Thermostatistics (2nd ed.). Wiley. On the relation between microscopic reversibility and macroscopic irreversibility, see: Lebowitz, J. L. (1993). "Boltzmann's Entropy and Time's Arrow." Physics Today, 46(9), 32-38. [6] Institutional Reversibility: For discussion of institutional reversibility and path dependence, see: Pierson, P. (2000). "Increasing Returns, Path Dependence, and the Study of Politics." American Political Science Review, 94(2), 251-267. On reversibility considerations in institutional design, see: Goodin, R. E. (Ed.). (1996). The Theory of Institutional Design. Cambridge University Press. [7] Technological Decisions and Reversibility: On reversibility considerations in technological decisions, see: Collingridge, D. (1980). The Social Control of Technology. Frances Pinter. On reversible design of AI systems, see: Amodei, D., et al. (2016). "Concrete Problems in AI Safety." arXiv preprint arXiv:1606.06565. [8] Climate Policy and Reversibility: On reversibility considerations in climate policy, see: Stern, N. (2007). The Economics of Climate Change: The Stern Review. Cambridge University Press. On the irreversibility of climate change, see: Lenton, T. M., et al. (2008). "Tipping Elements in the Earth's Climate System." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(6), 1786-1793. [9] Rollback Mechanisms: On rollback mechanisms in software engineering, see: Humble, J., & Farley, D. (2010). Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation. Addison-Wesley. For discussion of policy rollback, see: Patashnik, E. M. (2008). Reforms at Risk: What Happens After Major Policy Changes Are Enacted. Princeton University Press. [10] Evolutionary Stability: For discussion of evolutionarily stable strategies, see: Maynard Smith, J. (1982). Evolution and the Theory of Games. Cambridge University Press. On the relation between adaptability and reversibility, see: Holland, J. H. (1992). Adaptation in Natural and Artificial Systems. MIT Press.

Chapter 13 Appendix: The Axiom System of the Principle of Reversibility

Axiom System 13.A (Principle of Reversibility Axiom System PR-AX) 【Basic Definitions】 Definition D1 (Reversibility Function): Rev: A → [0, 1] Rev(a) = P(Restore(s₀) | Execute(a, s₀) → s₁, Reverse(a)) Reversibility is the probability of restoring the initial state after performing the inverse action Definition D2 (Deep Uncertainty): DeepUncertainty(Sit) ↔ ¬∃P: ProbabilityDistribution(P, Outcomes(Sit)) Deep uncertainty is a situation in which a probability distribution cannot be assigned to outcomes Definition D3 (Catastrophic Consequence): IrreversibleCatastrophe(a) ↔ Rev(a) < 0.1 ∧ Severity(a) > θ_severity An irreversible catastrophic consequence is one with extremely low reversibility and extremely high severity Definition D4 (Error-Correction Capacity): ErrorCorrection(S, a) ↔ Reversible(a) ∧ Detect(S, Error(a)) → Correct(S, a) Error-correction capacity is the capacity to correct an error once it is discovered 【Axioms】 Axiom A1 (Reversibility Preference Axiom): ∀a₁, a₂ ∈ A: OtherEqual(a₁, a₂) ∧ Rev(a₁) > Rev(a₂) → a₁ ≻ a₂ Other things being equal, one should choose the more reversible action Axiom A2 (Justification Threshold Axiom): ∀a ∈ A: Rev(a) < θ_rev → RequireStrongJustification(a) Actions whose reversibility is below the threshold require strong justification Axiom A3 (Catastrophic Consequence Axiom): ∀a ∈ A: IrreversibleCatastrophe(a) → ¬Permissible(a) ∨ ExtremeJustification(a) Irreversible catastrophic consequences require extreme justification Axiom A4 (Rollback Obligation Axiom): ∀a ∈ A: Execute(a) ∧ NegativeConsequence(a) ∧ Reversible(a) → O(Rollback(a)) If an action produces negative consequences and is reversible, there is an obligation to roll back Axiom A5 (Epistemic Humility Axiom): ∀S ∈ RationalAgents: O(Acknowledge(Fallibility(S))) Rational agents should acknowledge their own fallibility 【Inference Rules】 Rule R1 (Reversibility Comparison Rule): If Rev(a₁) > Rev(a₂) and other things are equal, then choose a₁ Rule R2 (Justification Threshold Rule): JustificationThreshold(a) = f(1 - Rev(a)) The justification threshold is proportional to irreversibility Rule R3 (Rollback Trigger Rule): NegativeConsequence(a) ∧ Rev(a) > θ_rollback → Trigger(Rollback(a)) Rollback is triggered when there are negative consequences and reversibility is above the threshold Rule R4 (Exception Handling Rule): Emergency(Sit) ∨ UnavoidableIrreversibility(a) ∨ InformedConsent(All) ∨ HigherPrinciple → AdjustedApplication(PR) 【Theorems】 Theorem T1 (Reversibility Preserves Error-Correction Capacity Theorem): ∀a ∈ A: Reversible(a) → Maintain(ErrorCorrectionCapacity) Proof: Follows directly from Definition D4 and Axiom A4 Theorem T2 (Deep Uncertainty Reinforces Reversibility Preference Theorem): DeepUncertainty(Sit) → Strengthen(ReversibilityPreference) Proof: Follows from Axiom A5 and BP-2 Theorem T3 (Reversibility and Possibility Space Theorem): ∀a ∈ A: Reversible(a) → Maintain(PossibilitySpace) Proof: Reversible actions preserve the ability to return to a previous state, thereby preserving the possibility space

Chapter 13 Appendix: Guide to Designing Rollback Mechanisms

Table 13.H Guide to Designing Rollback Mechanisms | Design Element | Description | Implementation Method | Checklist | |----------|------|----------|----------| | State Recording | Record the state before the action | Snapshots, logs, backups | □ Are key states recorded? | | Monitoring Mechanism | Monitor the consequences of the action | Metrics, alerts, audits | □ Is a monitoring mechanism established? | | Trigger Condition | Define the conditions that trigger rollback | Thresholds, rules, human judgment | □ Are the trigger conditions clearly specified? | | Rollback Procedure | Define the concrete steps of rollback | Procedure documents, automation scripts | □ Is there a clear rollback procedure? | | Responsibility Allocation | Specify who is responsible for rollback | Role definitions, authorization mechanisms | □ Is the responsible party clearly specified? | | Resource Provision | Ensure the resources required for rollback | Budget, personnel, technology | □ Are there sufficient resources? | | Testing and Verification | Test the effectiveness of the rollback mechanism | Drills, simulations, reviews | □ Has the rollback mechanism been tested? | | Documentation | Record the process and results of rollback | Reports, retrospectives, knowledge base | □ Is there documentation? |

Procedure 13.4 (Procedure for Designing a Rollback Mechanism)

Step 1: Identify key states

  • Determine the key state variables that need to be recorded
  • Determine the frequency and manner of state recording

Step 2: Design a monitoring mechanism

  • Determine the metrics that need to be monitored
  • Design alert rules and thresholds

Step 3: Define trigger conditions

  • Specify under what circumstances rollback is triggered
  • Distinguish automatic triggering from manual triggering

Step 4: Design the rollback procedure

  • Formulate detailed rollback steps
  • Consider partial rollback and full rollback

Step 5: Allocate responsibility

  • Specify who has the authority to decide on rollback
  • Specify who is responsible for executing rollback

Step 6: Secure resources

  • Ensure that the resources required for rollback are available
  • Establish emergency resource reserves

Step 7: Test and verify

  • Test the rollback mechanism regularly
  • Improve it in light of test results

Step 8: Document

  • Record the design of the rollback mechanism
  • Record the process and results of each rollback

§14.1 The Integration Framework of the Three Principles

§14.1.1 The Logical Relations among the Three Principles I. A Review of the Three Principles Before integrating the Three Principles, it is necessary to review the core content and derivational basis of each principle. Table 14.1 A review of the core content of the Three Principles | Principle | Code | Core Statement | Derivational Basis | Operationalization Indicator | |------|------|----------|----------|------------| | Recursive Freedom Principle | RFP | Maintain or expand the space of possibilities | NC-2, NL-, BP-1 | RFD | | Negentropy Responsibility Principle | PNR | Maintain negentropy sources; do not externalize entropy costs | NL-2, BP-1, BP- | CDI | | Reversibility Principle | PR | Give priority to reversible actions; preserve the capacity for error correction | NK-1, NK-4, BP-2 | CRV | Review of the formalized statements of the Three Principles: $$RFP: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace}) \vee \text{Expand}(\text{PossibilitySpace}))$$ $$PNR: O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}) \wedge \neg\text{Externalize}(\text{EntropyCost}))$$ $$PR: \text{DeepUncertainty} \rightarrow O(\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}) \wedge \text{Avoid}(\text{IrreversibleCatastrophe}))$$ II. Types of Logical Relations among the Three Principles There exist multiple logical relations among the Three Principles, which must be analyzed one by one. Definition 14.1 (Types of logical relations among principles) The logical relations among principles can be divided into the following types:

  • Entailment relation: one principle entails another principle
  • Complementary relation: two principles supplement each other and jointly cover a broader domain
  • Independent relation: two principles are mutually independent and each applies to a different domain
  • Conflict relation: two principles come into conflict in certain situations

Proposition 14.1 (The principal relation among the Three Principles is complementarity) The principal relation among the Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP), the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR), and the Reversibility Principle (PR) is a complementary relation, not an entailment relation or a conflict relation. The Three Principles regulate action from different angles and jointly constitute a complete normative framework. Argument 14.1 (Argument for the complementary relation among the Three Principles) Premise P1: RFP concerns the maintenance and expansion of the space of possibilities Premise P2: PNR concerns the maintenance of negentropy sources and the distribution of entropy costs Premise P: PR concerns the reversibility of actions and the capacity for error correction Premise P4: The space of possibilities, negentropy sources, and reversibility are distinct but related concepts Premise P5: The Three Principles regulate action from different angles respectively Step 1: From P1–P, the Three Principles concern different normative dimensions Step 2: From P4, these dimensions are related but not identical Step : From P5 and Steps 1–2, the Three Principles supplement each other Step 4: Together the Three Principles cover multiple dimensions of the normativity of action Conclusion: The principal relation among the Three Principles is a complementary relation III. The Specific Relations among the Three Principles (1) The relation between RFP and PNR Proposition 14.2 (The complementarity of RFP and PNR) RFP and PNR are complementary. The maintenance of the space of possibilities depends on the maintenance of negentropy sources; the maintenance of negentropy sources helps to preserve the space of possibilities. Formalized statement: $$\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}) \rightarrow \text{Support}(\text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace}))$$ $$\text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace}) \rightarrow \text{Support}(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}))$$ Explanation:

  • Negentropy is the material basis for sustaining complexity; without negentropy there is no space of possibilities
  • The openness of the space of possibilities helps to discover new sources of negentropy

(2) The relation between RFP and PR Proposition 14. (The complementarity of RFP and PR) RFP and PR are complementary. Reversibility preserves the openness of the space of possibilities; the openness of the space of possibilities provides the condition for reversibility. Formalized statement: $$\text{Reversible}(a) \rightarrow \text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace})$$ $$\text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace}) \rightarrow \text{Enable}(\text{Reversibility})$$ Explanation:

  • A reversible action preserves the possibility of returning to a previous state, thereby preserving the space of possibilities
  • The openness of the space of possibilities provides the condition for the reversibility of actions

(3) The relation between PNR and PR Proposition 14.4 (The complementarity of PNR and PR) PNR and PR are complementary. Reversibility helps to maintain negentropy sources; the maintenance of negentropy sources provides the material basis for reversibility. Formalized statement: $$\text{Reversible}(a) \rightarrow \text{Support}(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}))$$ $$\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}) \rightarrow \text{Enable}(\text{Reversibility})$$ Explanation:

  • Reversible actions reduce irreversible damage to negentropy sources
  • The maintenance of negentropy sources provides the material basis for the reversibility of actions

IV. The Unifying Basis of the Three Principles Proposition 14.5 (The unifying basis of the Three Principles) The Three Principles share a single unifying basis: maintaining the conditions for the survival of complex organization. This basis derives from the Three New Views, especially NL-2 (negentropy dependence) and NC-2 (processuality). Argument 14.2 (Argument for the unifying basis of the Three Principles) Premise P1 (NL-2): Life depends on the continuous acquisition of negentropy flow Premise P2 (NC-2): The universe is processual; existence is continuous becoming Premise P (BP-1): Survival rationality requires maintaining the conditions of survival Premise P4: RFP maintains the space of possibilities, which is one of the conditions of survival Premise P5: PNR maintains negentropy sources, which is the material basis of survival Premise P6: PR maintains the capacity for error correction, which is the epistemic condition of survival Step 1: From P1–P, survival requires the maintenance of multiple conditions Step 2: From P4–P6, the Three Principles respectively maintain different conditions of survival Step : From Steps 1–2, the Three Principles share the unifying basis of “maintaining the conditions of survival” Conclusion: The unifying basis of the Three Principles is maintaining the conditions for the survival of complex organization Figure 14.1 Diagram of the logical relations among the Three Principles
