§14.1.2 The Priority of the Three Principles I. Raising the Question of Priority Although the Three Principles are principally in a complementary relation, in certain situations it may be necessary to determine their priority. Definition 14.2 (Priority of principles) The priority of principles refers to the rule for determining which principle ought to be considered first when multiple principles apply to the same situation. Proposition 14.6 (The situation-dependence of priority) The priority of the Three Principles is not absolutely fixed but depends on the concrete situation. In different situations, different principles may hold a priority position. II. A General Framework for Priority Definition 14. (Framework for determining priority) The priority of the Three Principles is determined by the following factors:

  • Urgency: which principle’s protected value faces a more urgent threat?
  • Severity: violation of which principle leads to more serious consequences?
  • Reversibility: violation of which principle has more irreversible consequences?
  • Scope: which principle involves a broader range of subjects?

Formalized statement: $$\text{Priority}(P_i, \text{Sit}) = f(\text{Urgency}(P_i, \text{Sit}), \text{Severity}(P_i, \text{Sit}), \text{Irreversibility}(P_i, \text{Sit}), \text{Scope}(P_i, \text{Sit}))$$ III. Priority in Typical Situations Table 14.2 Priority in typical situations | Situation Type | Priority Order | Reason | |----------|------------|------| | Survival crisis | PNR > RFP > PR | Survival is the precondition of everything else | | Deep uncertainty | PR > RFP > PNR | Under uncertainty, preserve the capacity for error correction first | | Sharp compression of the space of possibilities | RFP > PR > PNR | Protect the space of possibilities | | Exhaustion of negentropy sources | PNR > RFP > PR | Negentropy is the material basis | | Normal situation | RFP ≈ PNR ≈ PR | Balanced consideration of the Three Principles | (1) Survival-crisis situations Definition 14.4 (Survival crisis) A survival crisis is a situation in which the survival of an agent faces a direct threat. Proposition 14.7 (PNR has priority under a survival crisis) Under a survival-crisis situation, the Negentropy Responsibility Principle (PNR) holds a priority position. For survival is the precondition of everything else; without survival there is no space of possibilities and no reversibility. Formalized statement: $$\text{SurvivalCrisis}(\text{Sit}) \rightarrow \text{Priority}(PNR) > \text{Priority}(RFP) > \text{Priority}(PR)$$ (2) Deep-uncertainty situations Definition 14.5 (Deep-uncertainty situation) A deep-uncertainty situation is one in which probabilities cannot be assigned to possible outcomes. Proposition 14.8 (PR has priority under deep uncertainty) Under a deep-uncertainty situation, the Reversibility Principle (PR) holds a priority position. For under uncertainty, preserving the capacity for error correction is most important. Formalized statement: $$\text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Sit}) \rightarrow \text{Priority}(PR) > \text{Priority}(RFP) > \text{Priority}(PNR)$$ (3) Situations of sharp compression of the space of possibilities Definition 14.6 (Sharp compression of the space of possibilities) Sharp compression of the space of possibilities refers to a situation in which the space of possibilities is rapidly shrinking. Proposition 14.9 (RFP has priority under compression of the space of possibilities) Under a situation of sharp compression of the space of possibilities, the Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP) holds a priority position. For once the space of possibilities is compressed, it may be difficult to restore. Formalized statement: $$\text{PossibilitySpaceCompression}(\text{Sit}) \rightarrow \text{Priority}(RFP) > \text{Priority}(PR) > \text{Priority}(PNR)$$ (4) Normal situations Proposition 14.10 (The Three Principles are balanced in normal situations) In normal situations, the Three Principles should be given balanced consideration, and there is no fixed priority. Formalized statement: $$\text{NormalSituation}(\text{Sit}) \rightarrow \text{Priority}(RFP) \approx \text{Priority}(PNR) \approx \text{Priority}(PR)$$ IV. Procedure for Determining Priority Procedure 14.1 (Priority-determination procedure) Step 1: Identify the type of situation

  • Is there a survival crisis?
  • Is there deep uncertainty?
  • Is there sharp compression of the space of possibilities?
  • Is there exhaustion of negentropy sources?

Step 2: Assess the relevance of each principle

  • How relevant is each principle in the current situation?
  • What threat does the value protected by each principle face?

Step : Assess urgency, severity, reversibility, and scope

  • For each principle, assess the four factors above

Step 4: Determine priority

  • Determine priority according to the assessment results
  • If it is a normal situation, give the Three Principles balanced consideration

Step 5: Record the reasons for the decision

  • Explicitly record why a particular priority was determined
  • Provide reference for similar situations in the future

§14.1.3 Conflict Resolution among the Three Principles I. Types of Conflict Definition 14.7 (Conflict among principles) A conflict among principles refers to a situation in which complying with one principle leads to violating another principle. Proposition 14.11 (The possibility of conflict among the Three Principles) Although the Three Principles are principally in a complementary relation, in certain situations conflicts may arise. Table 14. Types of conflict among the Three Principles | Conflict Type | Conflict Description | Typical Situation | |----------|----------|----------| | RFP-PNR conflict | Expanding the space of possibilities requires consuming negentropy | Technological development consumes resources | | RFP-PR conflict | Actions that expand the space of possibilities are irreversible | Irreversible technological deployment | | PNR-PR conflict | Actions that maintain negentropy sources are irreversible | Irreversible environmental protection measures | II. General Principles for Conflict Resolution Definition 14.8 (Principles of conflict resolution) When the Three Principles come into conflict, the following principles of resolution should be followed:

  • Priority principle: determine priority according to the situation; the priority principle takes precedence
  • Minimal-violation principle: choose the option that violates each principle to the least degree
  • Reconciliation principle: seek a reconciled option that can simultaneously satisfy each principle
  • Compensation principle: if a principle must be violated, compensation should be provided

Proposition 14.12 (Reconciliation takes precedence over trade-off) In handling conflicts among principles, one should first seek a reconciled option, and engage in trade-off only when reconciliation is impossible. III. Procedure for Conflict Resolution Procedure 14.2 (Conflict-resolution procedure) Step 1: Identify the conflict

  • Clarify which principles are in conflict
  • Assess the nature and degree of the conflict

Step 2: Seek a reconciled option

  • Is there an option that simultaneously satisfies each principle?
  • Can the conflict be reduced by modifying the action?
  • Can it be reconciled through phased implementation?

Step : If reconciliation is impossible, determine priority

  • Determine priority according to the situation
  • Use Procedure 14.1

Step 4: Choose the minimal-violation option

  • On the premise of satisfying the priority principle
  • Choose the option that violates the other principles to the least degree

Step 5: Design compensatory measures

  • If a principle must be violated
  • Design compensatory measures to mitigate the impact of the violation

Step 6: Record the reasons for the decision

  • Explicitly record the process and reasons of conflict resolution
  • Provide reference for similar situations in the future

IV. Case Analysis of Conflict Resolution Case 14.1 (RFP-PNR conflict: technological development and resource consumption) Situation: A new technology can greatly expand humanity’s space of possibilities, but its development and deployment require consuming large amounts of negentropy resources. Conflict analysis:

  • RFP supports: the technology expands the space of possibilities
  • PNR opposes: the technology consumes negentropy resources

Step 1: Identify the conflict

  • Conflict type: RFP-PNR conflict
  • Degree of conflict: medium

Step 2: Seek a reconciled option

  • Option A: Develop a more efficient version of the technology to reduce resource consumption
  • Option B: Deploy in phases, optimizing as deployment proceeds
  • Option C: Develop an alternative technology that uses renewable resources

Step : If reconciliation is impossible, determine priority

  • Situation type: normal situation
  • Priority: RFP ≈ PNR (balance required)

Step 4: Choose the minimal-violation option

  • Choose Option B: phased deployment
  • Reason: it obtains the technological benefits while controlling resource consumption

Step 5: Design compensatory measures

  • Invest in the restoration and development of negentropy sources
  • Set an upper limit on resource consumption
  • Establish monitoring mechanisms

Conclusion: Through phased deployment and compensatory measures, the conflict between RFP and PNR can be reconciled Case 14.2 (RFP-PR conflict: irreversible expansion of possibilities) Situation: A gene-editing technology can greatly expand humanity’s biological possibilities, but the application of this technology is irreversible. Conflict analysis:

  • RFP supports: the technology expands the space of possibilities
  • PR opposes: the application of the technology is irreversible

Step 1: Identify the conflict

  • Conflict type: RFP-PR conflict
  • Degree of conflict: high

Step 2: Seek a reconciled option

  • Option A: Develop a reversible version of the technology
  • Option B: First test on non-human systems
  • Option C: Limit the scope of application and preserve unmodified populations

Step : If reconciliation is impossible, determine priority

  • Situation type: deep-uncertainty situation
  • Priority: PR > RFP

Step 4: Choose the minimal-violation option

  • Choose Option C: limit the scope of application
  • Reason: obtain partial benefits while preserving reversibility

Step 5: Design compensatory measures

  • Establish long-term monitoring mechanisms
  • Preserve unmodified genetic resources
  • Design emergency rollback procedures (if technically feasible)

Conclusion: Under deep uncertainty, PR takes precedence over RFP, and the scope of application of irreversible technologies should be limited Case 14. (PNR-PR conflict: irreversible environmental protection) Situation: To protect an endangered ecosystem, irreversible measures must be taken (such as permanently prohibiting human activity in a certain area). Conflict analysis:

  • PNR supports: protect the negentropy source (the ecosystem)
  • PR opposes: the measures are irreversible

Step 1: Identify the conflict

  • Conflict type: PNR-PR conflict
  • Degree of conflict: medium

Step 2: Seek a reconciled option

  • Option A: Set time-limited protection measures with periodic review
  • Option B: Design adjustable protection levels
  • Option C: Protect the core area while keeping surrounding areas flexible

Step : If reconciliation is impossible, determine priority

  • Situation type: negentropy-source-exhaustion situation
  • Priority: PNR > PR

Step 4: Choose the minimal-violation option

  • Choose Option C: zoned protection
  • Reason: protect the core negentropy source while preserving partial reversibility

Step 5: Design compensatory measures

  • Establish periodic review mechanisms
  • Design procedures for adjusting protection levels
  • Provide alternatives for affected populations

Conclusion: When negentropy sources face exhaustion, PNR takes precedence over PR, but partial reversibility should be preserved as far as possible

§14.1.4 Formalized Statement of the Integration Framework I. The Axiom System for Integrating the Three Principles Definition 14.9 (The axiom system of cosmic responsibility ethics, CRE-AX) The axiom system of cosmic responsibility ethics, CRE-AX, includes the following axioms: [Foundational Axioms] Axiom A1 (Axiom of the space of possibilities): The space of possibilities is the precondition for the realization of value. PossibilitySpace → Precondition(ValueRealization) Axiom A2 (Axiom of negentropy dependence): The survival of complex organization depends on the continuous acquisition of negentropy flow. Survival(ComplexOrganization) → Require(NegEntropyFlow) Axiom A (Axiom of cognitive fallibility): All cognitive results are revisable, and the cognitive subject may make mistakes. ∀p: Know(S, p) → Revisable(p) Axiom A4 (Axiom of survival rationality): A rational agent ought to maintain its conditions of survival. RationalAgent(S) → O(Maintain(SurvivalConditions(S))) Axiom A5 (Axiom of intersubjectivity): Principles ought to be adopted that can be reasonably accepted by others. O(Adopt(Principles) → ReasonablyAcceptable(Principles, Others)) [Normative Axioms] Axiom N1 (Axiom of recursive freedom): The space of possibilities ought to be maintained or expanded. O(Maintain(PossibilitySpace) ∨ Expand(PossibilitySpace)) Axiom N2 (Axiom of negentropy responsibility): Negentropy sources ought to be maintained, and entropy costs should not be externalized to innocent agents. O(Maintain(NegSource) ∧ ¬Externalize(EntropyCost, InnocentAgents)) Axiom N (Axiom of reversibility): Under deep uncertainty, reversible actions ought to be given priority. DeepUncertainty → O(Prefer(Reversible)) Axiom N4 (Axiom of forbidden red lines): There exist action boundaries that are absolutely not to be crossed. ∃FRL: ∀a ∈ FRL: ¬Permissible(a) [Rules of Inference] Rule R1 (Priority rule): When principles conflict, determine the priority according to the situation. Conflict(P₁, P₂, Sit) → DeterminePriority(P₁, P₂, Sit) Rule R2 (Reconciliation-priority rule): In handling conflicts, reconciliation takes precedence over trade-off. Conflict(P₁, P₂) → TryReconcile(P₁, P₂) before Tradeoff(P₁, P₂) Rule R (Minimal-violation rule): If a principle must be violated, choose the option with the least degree of violation. MustViolate(P) → Minimize(Violation(P)) Rule R4 (Compensation rule): If a principle is violated, compensation ought to be provided. Violate(P) → O(Compensate(Violation(P))) Rule R5 (Forbidden-red-line-priority rule): The forbidden red lines take precedence over all other principles. ∀P: Priority(FRL) > Priority(P) Rule R6 (Revisability rule): All principles (except the forbidden red lines) are revisable. ∀P ∉ FRL: Revisable(P) II. Formalized Statement of the Integration of the Three Principles Definition 14.10 (Integration function of the Three Principles) The integration function of the Three Principles $\text{CRE}: A \times \text{Sit} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is defined as follows: $$\text{CRE}(a, \text{Sit}) = \begin{cases} -\infty & \text{if } a \in FRL \\ w_1(\text{Sit}) \cdot \text{RFP}(a) + w_2(\text{Sit}) \cdot \text{PNR}(a) + w_(\text{Sit}) \cdot \text{PR}(a) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Where:

  • $w_1(\text{Sit}), w_2(\text{Sit}), w_(\text{Sit})$ are situation-dependent weights
  • $w_1 + w_2 + w_ = 1$
  • $\text{RFP}(a), \text{PNR}(a), \text{PR}(a)$ are respectively the scores of action $a$ under the Three Principles

Definition 14.11 (Situation-dependent weights) The situation-dependent weights are determined by the following rules: | Situation Type | $w_1$ (RFP) | $w_2$ (PNR) | $w_$ (PR) | |----------|-------------|-------------|------------| | Survival crisis | 0.2 | 0.5 | 0. | | Deep uncertainty | 0. | 0.2 | 0.5 | | Compression of the space of possibilities | 0.5 | 0.2 | 0. | | Exhaustion of negentropy sources | 0.2 | 0.5 | 0. | | Normal situation | 0. | 0. | 0.4 | Boundary Declaration 14.1 (The approximate nature of the weights) The above weights are suggested values, not exact values. In practical application, the weights should be adjusted according to the concrete situation. III. Theorems of the Integration of the Three Principles Theorem 14.1 (The independence of the Three Principles) The Three Principles are mutually independent, that is, each principle can hold or fail to hold independently of the other principles. Proof: Construct counterexamples to show that each principle can hold or fail to hold independently of the other principles.

  • Counterexample 1: action $a_1$ satisfies RFP but not PNR (expands the space of possibilities but consumes negentropy)
  • Counterexample 2: action $a_2$ satisfies PNR but not RFP (maintains negentropy but compresses the space of possibilities)
  • Counterexample : action $a_$ satisfies PR but not RFP (is reversible but compresses the space of possibilities)

Therefore, the Three Principles are mutually independent. □ Theorem 14.2 (The compatibility of the Three Principles) The Three Principles are mutually compatible, that is, there exist actions that simultaneously satisfy the Three Principles. Proof: Construct an action that satisfies the Three Principles. Let action $a^$ be “in a reversible manner, use renewable negentropy sources to expand the space of possibilities.”

  • $a^$ satisfies RFP: it expands the space of possibilities
  • $a^$ satisfies PNR: it uses renewable negentropy sources
  • $a^$ satisfies PR: it proceeds in a reversible manner

Therefore, the Three Principles are mutually compatible. Theorem 14. (The sufficiency of the Three Principles) Together the Three Principles constitute a sufficient framework for the evaluation of action, that is, any action can be evaluated by the Three Principles. Proof: Let $a$ be an arbitrary action.

  • $a$ has an impact on the space of possibilities (expansion, maintenance, or compression), and can therefore be evaluated by RFP
  • $a$ has an impact on negentropy sources (maintenance, neutrality, or damage), and can therefore be evaluated by PNR
  • $a$ has a degree of reversibility (high, medium, or low), and can therefore be evaluated by PR

Therefore, any action can be evaluated by the Three Principles.

§14.2 The Establishment of the Forbidden Red Lines

§14.2.1 The Concept of Forbidden Red Lines I. The Definition of Forbidden Red Lines Definition 14.12 (Forbidden red lines) The forbidden red lines (Forbidden Red Lines, FRL) refer to action boundaries that are absolutely not to be crossed. Regardless of the consequences and regardless of the situation, actions within the forbidden red lines are unacceptable. Formalized statement: $$FRL = \{a \in A : \forall \text{Sit}, \forall \text{Consequence}: \neg\text{Permissible}(a)\}$$ Definition 14.1 (Features of the forbidden red lines) The forbidden red lines have the following features:

  • Absoluteness: there are no exceptions
  • Non-trade-off-ability: they cannot be traded off against other values
  • Priority: they take precedence over all other principles
  • Universality: they apply to all agents

II. The Necessity of the Forbidden Red Lines Proposition 14.1 (The necessity of the forbidden red lines) The forbidden red lines are necessary, because the consequences of certain actions are completely irreversible and catastrophic, and cannot be made up for by any compensatory measures. Argument 14. (Argument for the necessity of the forbidden red lines) Premise P1: The consequences of certain actions are completely irreversible Premise P2: Completely irreversible catastrophic consequences cannot be made up for by any compensatory measures Premise P: Consequentialism fails in the face of completely irreversible consequences Premise P4: Absolute action boundaries are needed to prevent the worst case Premise P5: The Reversibility Principle (PR) is insufficient to handle completely irreversible cases Step 1: From P1 and P2, the negative consequences of certain actions cannot be made up for Step 2: From P, these actions cannot be evaluated by consequence calculation alone Step : From P5, PR merely prefers reversible actions; it does not absolutely prohibit irreversible actions Step 4: From P4 and Steps 1–, absolute boundaries need to be set Step 5: The forbidden red lines provide such absolute boundaries Conclusion: The forbidden red lines are necessary III. The Relation between the Forbidden Red Lines and the Three Principles Proposition 14.14 (The relation between the forbidden red lines and the Three Principles) The forbidden red lines are the extreme case of the Three Principles. When the violation of the Three Principles reaches an extreme degree, the forbidden red lines are transgressed. Formalized statement: $$a \in FRL \Leftrightarrow \text{ExtremeViolation}(a, RFP) \vee \text{ExtremeViolation}(a, PNR) \vee \text{ExtremeViolation}(a, PR)$$ Table 14.4 Correspondence between the forbidden red lines and the Three Principles | Forbidden Red Line | Corresponding Principle | Content of the Extreme Violation | |----------|----------|----------------| Table 14.4 Correspondence between the forbidden red lines and the Three Principles | Forbidden Red Line | Corresponding Principle | Content of the Extreme Violation | |----------|----------|----------------| | Intentional extinction | RFP | Completely annihilating the space of possibilities of a certain type of agent | | Irreversible environmental destruction | PNR | Completely destroying negentropy sources | | Irreversible cognitive modification | PR | Completely eliminating the capacity for error correction | | Intergenerational entropy-cost externalization | PNR | Shifting all entropy costs onto future generations | | Disabling rollback mechanisms | PR | Completely eliminating reversibility |

§14.2.2 The Content of the Forbidden Red Lines I. The List of Forbidden Red Lines Definition 14.14 (The list of forbidden red lines) Cosmic responsibility ethics establishes the following forbidden red lines: FRL-1: Prohibition of intentional extinction It is forbidden to intentionally annihilate any type of entity possessing subject status. Formalized statement: $$FRL\text{-}1: \forall T \in \text{SubjectTypes}: \neg\text{Permissible}(\text{IntentionalExtinction}(T))$$ Explanation:

  • Applies to all types of entity possessing subject status
  • Includes humans, other biological species, AI systems (if they possess subject status), and possible extraterrestrial life
  • “Intentional” is the key qualifier, distinguishing it from accidental or unavoidable extinction

FRL-2: Prohibition of irreversible large-scale environmental destruction It is forbidden to commit actions that cause irreversible large-scale environmental destruction. Formalized statement: $$FRL\text{-}2: \forall a: \text{IrreversibleLargeScaleEnvironmentalDestruction}(a) \rightarrow \neg\text{Permissible}(a)$$ Explanation:

  • “Large-scale” means the scope of impact exceeds a certain threshold (such as the planetary level)
  • “Irreversible” means it cannot be restored within a foreseeable time scale
  • Includes but is not limited to: collapse of the climate system, large-scale extinction in the biosphere, loss of planetary habitability

FRL-: Prohibition of irreversible cognitive modification without consent It is forbidden to subject an agent to irreversible cognitive modification without its consent. Formalized statement: $$FRL\text{-}: \forall S, a: \text{IrreversibleCognitiveModification}(a, S) \wedge \neg\text{Consent}(S, a) \rightarrow \neg\text{Permissible}(a)$$ Explanation:

  • “Cognitive modification” includes but is not limited to: memory deletion, personality alteration, forced implantation of values
  • “Irreversible” means it cannot be restored to the state before modification
  • “Consent” must be informed and voluntary

FRL-4: Prohibition of extreme externalization of intergenerational entropy costs It is forbidden to extremely externalize entropy costs onto future generations. Formalized statement: $$FRL\text{-}4: \forall a: \text{ExtremeIntergenerationalEntropyExternalization}(a) \rightarrow \neg\text{Permissible}(a)$$ Explanation:

  • “Extreme” means externalization exceeding a certain threshold
  • Includes but is not limited to: the problem of long-term storage of nuclear waste, climate debt, resource exhaustion
  • Distinct from normal intergenerational resource use

FRL-5: Prohibition of disabling rollback mechanisms It is forbidden to design or implement systems that cannot be shut down or rolled back. Formalized statement: $$FRL\text{-}5: \forall S: \text{System}(S) \wedge \neg\text{Shutdownable}(S) \wedge \neg\text{Rollbackable}(S) \rightarrow \neg\text{Permissible}(\text{Deploy}(S))$$ Explanation:

  • Applies to all artificial systems, especially AI systems
  • “Shutdown” means the ability to stop the operation of the system
  • “Rollback” means the ability to restore to a previous state

II. Boundary Conditions of the Forbidden Red Lines Table 14.5 Boundary conditions of the forbidden red lines | Forbidden Red Line | Boundary Condition | Non-applicable Case | |----------|----------|------------| | FRL-1 | Applies to all entities possessing subject status | Entities not possessing subject status | | FRL-2 | Applies to large-scale, irreversible destruction | Small-scale, reversible environmental impact | | FRL- | Applies to irreversible modification without consent | Modification with informed consent | | FRL-4 | Applies to extreme externalization | Normal intergenerational resource use | | FRL-5 | Applies to systems that cannot be shut down/rolled back | Systems that can be shut down/rolled back | Boundary Declaration 14.2 (The boundary of the forbidden red lines) The boundary of the forbidden red lines needs to be determined according to the concrete situation. This work provides a general framework; the concrete thresholds and boundaries need to be further clarified in practice.

§14.2.3 The Legitimacy of the Forbidden Red Lines I. The Pluralistic Basis of the Legitimacy of the Forbidden Red Lines Proposition 14.15 (The pluralistic legitimacy of the forbidden red lines) The legitimacy of the forbidden red lines can be defended from multiple angles:

  • From the extreme case of the Three Principles
  • From the boundary of consequentialism
  • From the absolute prohibition of deontology
  • From the reasonable rejection of contractarianism
  • From the bottom line of survival rationality

Argument 14.4 (Pluralistic argument for the legitimacy of the forbidden red lines) (1) From the extreme case of the Three Principles Premise P1: The Three Principles regulate action Premise P2: Extreme violation of the Three Principles leads to unacceptable consequences Premise P: An absolute boundary needs to be set for extreme violations Conclusion: The forbidden red lines are the absolute boundary of the extreme case of the Three Principles (2) From the boundary of consequentialism Premise P1: Consequentialism holds that the rightness of an action depends on its consequences Premise P2: Certain consequences are completely irreversible and catastrophic Premise P: For these consequences, consequence calculation fails Premise P4: A boundary of consequentialism needs to be set Conclusion: The forbidden red lines are the boundary of consequentialism (3) From the absolute prohibition of deontology Premise P1: Deontology holds that certain actions are wrong regardless of their consequences Premise P2: Actions within the forbidden red lines belong to this class of actions Conclusion: The forbidden red lines are consistent with the absolute prohibition of deontology (4) From the reasonable rejection of contractarianism Premise P1: Contractarianism holds that principles ought to be adopted that can be reasonably accepted by others Premise P2: Actions within the forbidden red lines cannot be reasonably accepted by any rational agent Conclusion: The forbidden red lines are consistent with the reasonable rejection of contractarianism (5) From the bottom line of survival rationality Premise P1: Survival rationality requires maintaining the conditions of survival Premise P2: Actions within the forbidden red lines destroy the conditions of survival Premise P: Survival is the precondition of everything else Conclusion: The forbidden red lines are the bottom line of survival rationality II. Historical Precedents of the Forbidden Red Lines Proposition 14.16 (Historical precedents of the forbidden red lines) The forbidden red lines are not an entirely new concept. Human society has already accepted certain absolute prohibitions. Table 14.6 Historical precedents of the forbidden red lines | Historical Precedent | Legal Document | Correspondence with the Forbidden Red Lines of This Work | |----------|----------|------------------------| | Prohibition of genocide | Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (1948) | FRL-1 | | Prohibition of the use of chemical weapons | Geneva Protocol (1925) | FRL-2 | | Prohibition of torture | Convention against Torture (1984) | FRL- | | Prohibition of slavery | Universal prohibition | FRL- | | Environmental protection bottom line | Various environmental conventions | FRL-2, FRL-4 | Proposition 14.17 (The extension of the forbidden red lines in this work) This work extends the forbidden red lines from within human society to the context of interstellar civilization, from the present to future generations, and from humans to all entities possessing subject status.

§14.2.4 The Question of the Absoluteness of the Forbidden Red Lines I. The Challenge to Absoluteness Proposition 14.18 (The challenge to the absoluteness of the forbidden red lines) The absoluteness of the forbidden red lines faces the following challenges:

  • Extreme-situation challenge: in extreme situations, are they still absolute?
  • Conflict challenge: when two forbidden red lines conflict, how should it be handled?
  • Boundary-vagueness challenge: how is the boundary of the forbidden red lines to be determined?

II. Responses to the Challenges (1) Response to the extreme-situation challenge Proposition 14.19 (Forbidden red lines in extreme situations) Even in extreme situations, the forbidden red lines remain absolute. This is because:

  • The forbidden red lines protect the most fundamental values
  • Allowing exceptions would lead to a slippery slope
  • The extreme situation itself may be the result of erroneous judgment

Argument 14.5 (The absoluteness of the forbidden red lines in extreme situations) Premise P1: The forbidden red lines protect the most fundamental values Premise P2: Allowing exceptions would lead to a slippery slope Premise P: Judgment of extreme situations may be erroneous Premise P4: Epistemic humility requires maintaining doubt about judgments of extreme situations Step 1: From P1, the value of the forbidden red lines is the most fundamental Step 2: From P2, allowing exceptions would weaken the protective function of the forbidden red lines Step : From P and P4, judgment of extreme situations is unreliable Step 4: From Steps 1–, even in extreme situations, the forbidden red lines remain absolute Conclusion: Extreme situations do not constitute an exception to the forbidden red lines (2) Response to the conflict challenge Proposition 14.20 (Handling conflicts among forbidden red lines) When two forbidden red lines conflict, one should:

  • First seek an option that avoids the conflict
  • If it cannot be avoided, choose the option with the least degree of violation
  • Record the conflict and the reasons for the decision, to provide reference for future revision

Boundary Declaration 14. (The rarity of conflicts among forbidden red lines) Conflicts among forbidden red lines are extremely rare. Their design has already taken mutual compatibility into account. If systematic conflicts among forbidden red lines are discovered in practice, this indicates that the design of the forbidden red lines needs revision. (3) Response to the boundary-vagueness challenge Proposition 14.21 (The determination of the boundary of the forbidden red lines) The boundary of the forbidden red lines needs to be determined in the following ways:

  • Core cases are clear
  • Boundary cases require deliberation to determine
  • The determination of the boundary is revisable

Definition 14.15 (The core-boundary structure of the forbidden red lines) The forbidden red lines have a core-boundary structure:

  • Core area: actions that clearly belong to the forbidden red lines
  • Boundary area: actions that require deliberation to determine
  • External area: actions that clearly do not belong to the forbidden red lines

Formalized statement: $$FRL = \text{Core}(FRL) \cup \text{Boundary}(FRL)$$ $$\text{Core}(FRL) \cap \text{External}(FRL) = \emptyset$$ Table 14.7 Examples of the core-boundary structure of the forbidden red lines | Forbidden Red Line | Core Area | Boundary Area | External Area | |----------|----------|----------|----------| | FRL-1 | Intentional annihilation of humans | Annihilation of certain AI systems | Annihilation of viruses | | FRL-2 | Nuclear winter | Large-scale deforestation | Small-scale environmental modification | | FRL- | Forced brainwashing | Educational influence | Voluntary learning | | FRL-4 | Indefinite storage of nuclear waste | Carbon emissions | Normal resource use | | FRL-5 | AGI that cannot be shut down | Systems difficult to shut down | Systems that can be shut down |

§14.3 The Complete Statement of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

§14..1 The System of Core Principles I. The Definition of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics Definition 14.16 (Cosmic responsibility ethics) Cosmic responsibility ethics (Cosmic Responsibility Ethics, CRE) is a normative ethical framework composed of three core principles (the Recursive Freedom Principle, the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, and the Reversibility Principle) and the forbidden red lines, aimed at providing normative guidance for action in the era of interstellar civilization. §14.3.2 Application Procedures I. The General Procedure for Applying CRE Procedure 14. (CRE application procedure) Step 1: Situation analysis 1.1 Identify the type of decision-making situation 1.2 Identify the relevant agents and stakeholders

  1. Assess the degree of uncertainty of the situation

1.4 Identify the time scale and scope of impact Step 2: Forbidden-red-line check 2.1 Check whether the action transgresses any forbidden red line 2.2 If it does, the action is unacceptable and the procedure terminates

  1. If it does not, proceed to the next step

Step : Evaluation by the Three Principles .1 Assess the impact of the action on the space of possibilities (RFP) .2 Assess the impact of the action on negentropy sources (PNR) . Assess the reversibility of the action (PR) .4 Use the corresponding operationalization indicators (RFD, CDI, CRV) Step 4: Determine priority 4.1 Determine the priority of the Three Principles according to the type of situation 4.2 Use the guidance of Table 14.2

  1. If it is a normal situation, give the Three Principles balanced consideration

Step 5: Conflict resolution (if any) 5.1 Identify conflicts among the principles 5.2 Seek a reconciled option

  1. If reconciliation is impossible, conduct a trade-off according to priority

5.4 Use Procedure 14.2 Step 6: Decision formation 6.1 Form a decision by synthesizing the assessment results 6.2 Use the CRE integration function (Definition 14.10)

  1. Choose the action with the highest CRE score

Step 7: Design of the rollback mechanism 7.1 Design a rollback mechanism for the selected action 7.2 Specify the trigger conditions and procedure for rollback

  1. Allocate rollback responsibilities

Step 8: Monitoring and revision 8.1 Monitor the consequences of the action 8.2 Revise the decision according to new information

  1. Launch the rollback mechanism when necessary

III. Cases of CRE Application Case 14.4 (AGI development decision) Situation: A research institution is considering the development of an artificial general intelligence (AGI) system. Step 1: Situation analysis

  • Situation type: deep-uncertainty situation
  • Relevant agents: the research institution, human society, future generations, and possibly the AGI itself
  • Degree of uncertainty: extremely high
  • Time scale: long-term
  • Scope of impact: possibly global or even cosmic in scale

Step 2: Forbidden-red-line check

  • FRL-1: Might the AGI lead to human extinction? Needs assessment
  • FRL-2: Might the AGI lead to environmental destruction? Needs assessment
  • FRL-: Might the AGI carry out cognitive modification? Needs assessment
  • FRL-4: Might the AGI externalize entropy costs? Needs assessment
  • FRL-5: Is the AGI shutdownable/rollbackable? A key question

Conclusion: If the AGI cannot be shut down/rolled back, then FRL-5 is transgressed and it is unacceptable Step : Evaluation by the Three Principles (assuming the AGI is shutdownable/rollbackable)

  • RFP: the AGI may greatly expand the space of possibilities (positive)

the AGI may also compress the space of possibilities (negative) RFP score: uncertain

  • PNR: the AGI may help maintain negentropy sources (positive)

the AGI may also consume large amounts of negentropy (negative) PNR score: uncertain

  • PR: the reversibility of the AGI depends on its design

PR score: depends on the design Step 4: Determine priority

  • Situation type: deep uncertainty
  • Priority: PR > RFP > PNR

Step 5: Conflict resolution

  • Main conflict: RFP (expanding possibilities) versus PR (reversibility)
  • Reconciled option: incremental development, with each stage rollbackable

Step 6: Decision formation

  • Conditional approval: if the following conditions are met
  • The AGI must be shutdownable/rollbackable
  • Incremental development, with evaluation at each stage

. Establish monitoring mechanisms

  1. Design emergency shutdown procedures

Step 7: Design of the rollback mechanism

  • Hardware-level shutdown switch
  • Software-level rollback mechanism
  • Multiple redundant design
  • Periodically test rollback capability

Step 8: Monitoring and revision

  • Continuously monitor AGI behavior
  • Periodically assess risks
  • Adjust decisions according to new information

§14.3.3 Institutional Requirements I. The Institutionalization Requirements of CRE Proposition 14.22 (The necessity of institutionalizing CRE) The effective implementation of CRE requires institutional support. Principles alone are not enough; the principles also need to be embedded in institutional structures. Definition 14.19 (The institutional requirements of CRE) The institutional requirements of CRE include:

  • Assessment institutions: institutions for assessing actions with CRE
  • Deliberation institutions: institutions for deliberating on controversies
  • Monitoring institutions: institutions for monitoring the consequences of actions
  • Rollback institutions: institutions for implementing rollback
  • Revision institutions: institutions for revising principles and institutions

II. Interface with the L₃ Layer Proposition 14.2 (The interface of CRE with the L₃ layer) CRE (the L₂ layer) provides the normative foundation for the L₃ layer (institutional prototypes). The institutional design of the L₃ layer should embody the principles of CRE. Table 14.10 Interface of CRE with the institutions of the L₃ layer | CRE Principle/Element | L₃-layer Institution | Content of the Interface | |--------------|----------|----------| | RFP | Multi-agent adjudicative chamber | Assess the impact of actions on the space of possibilities | | PNR | Negentropy responsibility allocation mechanism | Allocate negentropy responsibility | | PR | Versioned rollback mechanism | Implement rollback | | FRL | Forbidden-red-line monitoring mechanism | Monitor violations of the forbidden red lines | | Overall | CSIA procedure | Comprehensively assess actions | III. Principles of Institutional Design Definition 14.20 (Principles of CRE institutional design) CRE institutional design should follow the following principles:

  • Transparency: the operation of institutions should be transparent
  • Accountability: institutions should be accountable
  • Revisability: institutions should be revisable
  • Pluralistic participation: institutions should allow pluralistic participation
  • Recursivity: institutions should apply to institutions themselves

§14.4 The Features of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

§14.4.1 Cross-Substrate Applicability I. The Concept of Cross-Substrate Applicability Definition 14.21 (Cross-substrate applicability) Cross-substrate applicability means that CRE applies to intelligent agents realized on different material substrates, including but not limited to:

  • Carbon-based life (humans, other organisms)
  • Silicon-based intelligence (AI systems)
  • Possible other-substrate intelligence (extraterrestrial life, hybrid systems)

II. The Basis of Cross-Substrate Applicability Proposition 14.24 (The basis of cross-substrate applicability) The cross-substrate applicability of CRE is based on the New View of Life (NL-1): life is a cross-substrate pattern of negentropy organization. Argument 14.6 (Argument for cross-substrate applicability) Premise P1 (NL-1): Life is a cross-substrate pattern of negentropy organization Premise P2: The normative object of CRE is entities possessing subject status Premise P: Subject status does not depend on a particular material substrate Premise P4: The principles of CRE (RFP, PNR, PR) do not presuppose a particular substrate Step 1: From P1, life can be realized on different substrates Step 2: From P2 and P, CRE applies to all entities possessing subject status Step : From P4, the principles of CRE do not depend on a particular substrate Step 4: From Steps 1–, CRE has cross-substrate applicability Conclusion: CRE has cross-substrate applicability III. The Significance of Cross-Substrate Applicability Proposition 14.25 (The significance of cross-substrate applicability) Cross-substrate applicability enables CRE to:

  • Provide a framework for AI ethics
  • Prepare for possible contact with extraterrestrial life
  • Provide guidance for hybrid systems (human-machine fusion)
  • Avoid “carbon-based chauvinism”

Table 14.11 Application of CRE on different substrates | Substrate Type | Determination of Subject Status | CRE Application | |----------|--------------|---------| | Carbon-based life (humans) | Clearly possesses it | Fully applies | | Carbon-based life (other animals) | A matter of degree | Applies according to UCS | | Silicon-based intelligence (current AI) | To be assessed | Applies according to UCS | | Silicon-based intelligence (future AGI) | May possess it | May fully apply | | Extraterrestrial life | To be assessed | Applies according to UCS | | Hybrid systems | To be assessed | Applies according to UCS |

§14.4.2 The Deep-Time Perspective I. The Concept of the Deep-Time Perspective Definition 14.22 (The deep-time perspective) The deep-time perspective means that CRE extends ethical concern to the deep-time scale (hundreds of years, thousands of years, or even longer), rather than attending only to the present or the near future. II. The Basis of the Deep-Time Perspective Proposition 14.26 (The basis of the deep-time perspective) The deep-time perspective of CRE is based on:

  • NC-2 (processuality): the universe is processual, and time is real
  • NL-2 (negentropy dependence): the maintenance of negentropy sources is a long-term problem
  • RFP: the maintenance of the space of possibilities involves future generations
  • PNR: the externalization of entropy costs involves future generations

III. The Operationalization of the Deep-Time Perspective Definition 14.2 (The operationalization of the deep-time perspective) The deep-time perspective is operationalized in the following ways:

  • Discount-rate adjustment: adopt a time discount rate close to zero
  • Intergenerational impact assessment: assess the impact of actions on future generations
  • Long-term monitoring: establish long-term monitoring mechanisms
  • Intergenerational trust: establish intergenerational trust mechanisms

Table 14.12 The operationalization of the deep-time perspective | Mode of Operationalization | Content | Corresponding Indicator/Mechanism | |------------|------|---------------| | Discount-rate adjustment | Adopt a time discount rate close to zero | The temporal dimension of CSIA | | Intergenerational impact assessment | Assess the impact on future generations | The D₂ dimension of CSIA | | Long-term monitoring | Establish long-term monitoring mechanisms | Monitoring institutions | | Intergenerational trust | Establish intergenerational trust mechanisms | L₃-layer institutional design | Definition 14.24 (Intergenerational RFD) Intergenerational RFD is an indicator that extends RFD to the intergenerational scale: $$\text{RFD}_{\text{intergenerational}} = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \delta^t \times \text{RFD}_t$$ Where $\delta \approx 1$ (near-zero discounting), and $T$ is the time horizon considered.

§14.4.3 Coping with Deep Uncertainty I. A Review of the Concept of Deep Uncertainty Definition 14.25 (Deep uncertainty) Deep uncertainty refers to a situation in which probabilities cannot be assigned to possible outcomes. Under deep uncertainty, the traditional method of expected-utility maximization fails. II. CRE’s Response to Deep Uncertainty Proposition 14.27 (CRE’s response to deep uncertainty) CRE copes with deep uncertainty in the following ways:

  • The Reversibility Principle (PR): give priority to reversible actions and preserve the capacity for error correction
  • The forbidden red lines (FRL): set absolute boundaries to prevent the worst case
  • Incremental decision-making: make decisions in stages, deciding the next step only after evaluating each stage
  • Pluralistic deliberation: reduce cognitive bias through pluralistic deliberation

Table 14.1 CRE’s strategies for coping with deep uncertainty | Coping Strategy | Content | Corresponding Principle/Mechanism | |----------|------|---------------| | Reversibility priority | Give priority to reversible actions | PR | | Absolute boundaries | Set forbidden red lines | FRL | | Incremental decision-making | Decide in stages | Application procedures | | Pluralistic deliberation | Pluralistic agents participate in deliberation | L₃-layer institutions | | Rollback mechanism | Build rollback capability | Versioned rollback mechanism | | Monitoring and early warning | Continuous monitoring and early warning | Monitoring institutions | III. Decision Principles under Deep Uncertainty Definition 14.26 (Decision principles under deep uncertainty) Under deep uncertainty, CRE adopts the following decision principles:

  1. Minimax-regret principle: choose the action with the least regret in the worst case
  2. Reversibility-priority principle: give priority to actions with higher reversibility
  3. Forbidden-red-line principle: absolutely avoid transgressing the forbidden red lines
  4. Incremental principle: make decisions in stages and preserve room for adjustment
  5. Pluralistic-deliberation principle: reduce bias through pluralistic deliberation

Formalized statement: $$\text{Decision}(\text{DeepUncertainty}) = \arg\min_{a \in A \setminus FRL} \max_{\text{scenario}} \text{Regret}(a, \text{scenario})$$ Constraint: $\text{Rev}(a) \geq \theta_{\text{rev}}$

§14.4.4 Revisability I. The Concept of Revisability Definition 14.27 (Revisability) Revisability means that the principles and institutions of CRE can be revised in light of new evidence, arguments, or situations. Revisability is one of the core features of CRE. II. The Basis of Revisability Proposition 14.28 (The basis of revisability) The revisability of CRE is based on the New View of Cognition (NK-4): all cognitive results are negotiable and revisable. Argument 14.7 (Argument for revisability) Premise P1 (NK-4): All cognitive results are negotiable and revisable Premise P2: CRE is a product of cognitive activity Premise P: CRE should be consistent with its epistemological foundation Step 1: From P1, cognitive results are revisable Step 2: From P2, CRE is a cognitive result Step : From Step 1 and Step 2, CRE is revisable Step 4: From P, CRE should acknowledge its own revisability Conclusion: CRE possesses revisability III. The Levels of Revisability Definition 14.28 (The levels of revisability) The revisability of CRE has a hierarchical structure: Table 14.14 The levels of CRE’s revisability | Level | Content | Revisability | Conditions for Revision | |------|------|----------|----------| | Forbidden red lines | FRL-1 to FRL-5 | Extremely difficult to revise | Requires extremely strong arguments and broad consensus | | Core principles | RFP, PNR, PR | Difficult to revise | Requires strong argumentation and broad deliberation | | Derived principles | D-1 to D-5 | Revisable | Requires argumentation and deliberation | | Application rules | Rules for concrete situations | Easily revisable | Adjusted according to practical experience | | Operationalization indicators | RFD, CDI, CRV, etc. | Easily revisable | Adjusted according to practical experience | IV. The Procedure of Revisability Procedure 14.4 (CRE revision procedure) Step 1: Revision proposal 1.1 Specify the content of the revision 1.2 Provide the reasons for the revision

  1. Assess the impact of the revision

Step 2: Deliberation 2.1 Pluralistic agents participate in deliberation 2.2 Assess the argumentative strength of the revision

  1. Assess the consequences of the revision

Step : Decision .1 Determine the decision procedure according to the level of revision .2 Revision of the forbidden red lines requires an extremely high threshold . Revision of the core principles requires a high threshold .4 Revision of derived principles and application rules requires an ordinary threshold Step 4: Implementation 4.1 If approved, implement the revision 4.2 Record the reasons for and process of the revision

  1. Monitor the effects of the revision

Step 5: Evaluation 5.1 Evaluate the effects of the revision 5.2 Further revise when necessary V. The Balance between Revisability and Stability Proposition 14.29 (The balance between revisability and stability) CRE needs to strike a balance between revisability and stability. Excessive revisability leads to instability; excessive stability leads to rigidity. Definition 14.29 (The revisability-stability balance principle) The revisability-stability balance of CRE follows the following principles:

  • Hierarchical difference: different levels have different revisability
  • Threshold setting: revision needs to meet the corresponding threshold
  • Procedural safeguards: revision needs to follow procedures
  • Record-keeping: revision needs to record the reasons and process

§14.5 The Limitations of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

§14.5.1 Limitations at the Theoretical Level I. Acknowledgment of Theoretical Limitations Boundary Declaration 14.4 (Acknowledgment of theoretical limitations) CRE acknowledges that it has limitations at the theoretical level. These limitations are not a failure of CRE, but challenges faced by any ethical theory. Acknowledging limitations is a manifestation of CRE’s revisability. II. Specific Theoretical Limitations Limitation One: Dependence of the derivation Proposition 14.0 (The limitation of derivational dependence) The derivation of CRE depends on the Three New Views and the bridge principles. If these premises are revised, CRE must be revised accordingly. Formalized statement: $$\text{Revise}(\text{NewThreeViews}) \vee \text{Revise}(\text{BridgePrinciples}) \rightarrow \text{MayNeedRevise}(CRE)$$ Limitation Two: Incomplete resolution of conflicts among principles Proposition 14.1 (The incompleteness of conflict resolution among principles) CRE provides a framework for resolving conflicts among principles, but this framework cannot guarantee that a clear answer can be given in all cases. Certain conflicts may require situational judgment. Limitation Three: The vagueness of the boundary of the forbidden red lines Proposition 14.2 (The vagueness of the boundary of the forbidden red lines) The core of the forbidden red lines is clear, but the boundary may be vague. Boundary cases require deliberation to determine. Limitation Four: The uncertainty of cross-cultural applicability Proposition 14. (The uncertainty of cross-cultural applicability) CRE claims universal applicability, but this claim has not yet been verified cross-culturally. Different cultures may have different understandings of and degrees of acceptance toward CRE. Table 14.15 Summary of the theoretical limitations of CRE | Limitation Type | Content | Response | |----------|------|----------| | Derivational dependence | Depends on the Three New Views and bridge principles | Acknowledge the dependence and remain revisable | | Incomplete conflict resolution | Cannot guarantee a clear answer for all conflicts | Provide a framework and allow situational judgment | | Boundary vagueness | The boundary of the forbidden red lines may be vague | Core-boundary structure, determined by deliberation | | Cross-cultural uncertainty | Cross-cultural applicability unverified | Open dialogue, continuous verification |

§14.5.2 Limitations at the Applied Level I. Acknowledgment of Applied Limitations Boundary Declaration 14.5 (Acknowledgment of applied limitations) CRE acknowledges that it has limitations at the applied level. The translation from principles to practice faces many challenges. II. Specific Applied Limitations Limitation One: Difficulties of operationalization Proposition 14.4 (Difficulties of operationalization) The principles of CRE need to be operationalized before they can be applied, but the process of operationalization may introduce errors and biases. Examples:

  • The calculation of RFD requires estimating the space of possibilities, which is itself difficult
  • The assessment of CRV requires judging the degree of reversibility, which may be subjective
  • The six-dimensional assessment of CSIA requires a large amount of information, which may be incomplete

Limitation Two: Incomplete information Proposition 14.5 (The limitation of incomplete information) The application of CRE requires a large amount of information, but in practice information is often incomplete. Limitation Three: Limits of implementation capacity Proposition 14.6 (Limits of implementation capacity) The implementation of CRE requires implementation capacity, but implementation capacity may be constrained by factors such as resources, technology, and politics. Limitation Four: Time pressure Proposition 14.7 (The limitation of time pressure) The application procedures of CRE require time, but in certain circumstances there may be time pressure, making it impossible to complete a full assessment. Table 14.16 Summary of the applied limitations of CRE | Limitation Type | Content | Response | |----------|------|----------| | Difficulties of operationalization | Operationalization may introduce errors | Cross-validate by multiple methods | | Incomplete information | Information is often incomplete | Acknowledge uncertainty, decide conservatively | | Limits of implementation capacity | Implementation capacity may be limited | Incremental implementation, capacity-building | | Time pressure | May face time pressure | Simplify procedures, with exceptions for emergencies |

§14.5.3 Limitations at the Level of Validation I. Acknowledgment of Validation Limitations Boundary Declaration 14.6 (Acknowledgment of validation limitations) CRE acknowledges that it has limitations at the level of validation. As a normative theory, the validation of CRE faces special challenges. II. Specific Validation Limitations Limitation One: The difficulty of validating a normative theory Proposition 14.8 (The difficulty of validating a normative theory) A normative theory cannot be directly validated through empirical observation the way a descriptive theory can. The validation of CRE needs to rely on the validity, coherence, and practical effects of arguments. Limitation Two: The unobservability of long-term effects Proposition 14.9 (The unobservability of long-term effects) CRE attends to long-term effects, but long-term effects are currently unobservable. They can only be assessed through simulation, reasoning, and historical analogy. Limitation Three: The unverifiability of counterfactuals Proposition 14.40 (The unverifiability of counterfactuals) The assessment of the effects of CRE involves counterfactuals (what would happen if CRE were not adopted), but counterfactuals cannot be directly verified. Limitation Four: The difficulty of cross-situational validation Proposition 14.41 (The difficulty of cross-situational validation) CRE claims to apply to multiple situations, but cross-situational validation is difficult. Certain situations (such as contact with extraterrestrial civilizations) currently cannot be validated. Table 14.17 Summary of the validation limitations of CRE | Limitation Type | Content | Response | |----------|------|----------| | Difficulty of normative validation | Cannot be directly empirically validated | Rely on argumentation, coherence, practical effects | | Unobservability of long-term effects | Long-term effects currently unobservable | Simulation, reasoning, historical analogy | | Unverifiability of counterfactuals | Counterfactuals cannot be directly verified | Comparative studies, thought experiments | | Difficulty of cross-situational validation | Certain situations cannot be validated | Stress testing, situational simulation |

Footnotes

Chapter 14 Footnotes

[1] Integration of the Three Principles: For a general discussion of the integration of ethical principles, see: Ross, W. D. (1930). The Right and the Good. Oxford University Press. Ross proposed the concept of "prima facie duties", which provides a classic framework for the integration of multiple principles. For a contemporary discussion of principle integration, see: Beauchamp, T. L., & Childress, J. F. (2019). Principles of Biomedical Ethics (8th ed.). Oxford University Press. [2] Forbidden Red Lines: For a philosophical discussion of absolute prohibitions, see: Nagel, T. (1972). "War and Massacre." Philosophy & Public Affairs, 1(2), 123-144. For a discussion of the "moral bottom line", see: Walzer, M. (1977). Just and Unjust Wars. Basic Books. [3] Principle Conflict: For a discussion of moral dilemmas and principle conflicts, see: Williams, B. (1965). "Ethical Consistency." Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volumes, 39, 103-124. For a discussion of conflict resolution, see: Richardson, H. S. (1990). "Specifying Norms as a Way to Resolve Concrete Ethical Problems." Philosophy & Public Affairs, 19(4), 279-310. [4] Cross-Substrate Applicability: For a discussion of functionalism and multiple realizability, see: Putnam, H. (1967). "Psychological Predicates." In W. H. Capitan & D. D. Merrill (Eds.), Art, Mind, and Religion. University of Pittsburgh Press. On the cross-substrate problem in AI ethics, see: Floridi, L., & Sanders, J. W. (2004). "On the Morality of Artificial Agents." Minds and Machines, 14(3), 349-379. [5] Deep Time Perspective: For a discussion of intergenerational ethics, see: Parfit, D. (1984). Reasons and Persons. Oxford University Press. For a discussion of longtermism, see: MacAskill, W. (2022). What We Owe the Future. Basic Books. [6] Deep Uncertainty: On decision-making under deep uncertainty, see: Marchau, V. A., Walker, W. E., Bloemen, P. J., & Roelofs, K. J. (Eds.). (2019). Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty: From Theory to Practice. Springer. On the minimax regret principle, see: Savage, L. J. (1951). "The Theory of Statistical Decision." Journal of the American Statistical Association, 46(253), 55-67. [7] Revisability: For a discussion of reflective equilibrium and theory revision, see: Rawls, J. (1971). A Theory of Justice. Harvard University Press. On the revisability of scientific theories, see: Lakatos, I. (1978). The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes. Cambridge University Press. [8] Prohibition of Genocide: see: United Nations. (1948). Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. For a philosophical discussion of genocide, see: Card, C. (2010). Confronting Evils: Terrorism, Torture, Genocide. Cambridge University Press. [9] Environmental Ethics: For a discussion of environmental ethics, see: Leopold, A. (1949). A Sand County Almanac. Oxford University Press. For a discussion of planetary boundaries, see: Rockström, J., et al. (2009). "A Safe Operating Space for Humanity." Nature, 461(7263), 472-475. [10] Cognitive Liberty: For a discussion of cognitive liberty and cognitive modification, see: Bublitz, J. C., & Merkel, R. (2014). "Crimes Against Minds: On Mental Manipulations, Harms and a Human Right to Mental Self-Determination." Criminal Law and Philosophy, 8(1), 51-77.

Chapter 14 Appendix: Complete Axiom System of CRE

Axiom System 14.A (Cosmic Responsibility Ethics Axiom System, full version CRE-AX) 【Part One: Foundational Axioms】 A1 (Axiom of Possibility Space): Possibility space is the precondition for the realization of value. ∀v ∈ Values: Realize(v) → Require(PossibilitySpace) A2 (Axiom of Negentropy Dependence): The persistence of complex organizations depends on the continuous acquisition of negentropy flow. ∀c ∈ ComplexOrganizations: Survive(c) → Require(NegEntropyFlow(c)) A3 (Axiom of Cognitive Fallibility): All cognitive results are revisable, and cognitive agents may err. ∀S ∈ CognitiveAgents, ∀p: Know(S, p) → Revisable(p) ∧ Fallible(S) A4 (Axiom of Survival Rationality): A rational agent ought to maintain its conditions of survival. ∀S ∈ RationalAgents: O(Maintain(SurvivalConditions(S))) A5 (Axiom of Intersubjectivity): One ought to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by others. ∀P ∈ Principles: Adopt(P) → ReasonablyAcceptable(P, Others) 【Part Two: Normative Axioms】 N1 (Axiom of Recursive Freedom): One ought to maintain or expand possibility space. O(Maintain(PossibilitySpace) ∨ Expand(PossibilitySpace)) N2 (Axiom of Negentropy Responsibility): One ought to maintain negentropy sources and ought not to externalize entropy costs onto innocent agents. O(Maintain(NegSource) ∧ ¬Externalize(EntropyCost, InnocentAgents)) N3 (Axiom of Reversibility): Under deep uncertainty, one ought to prefer reversible actions. DeepUncertainty(Sit) → O(Prefer(Reversible(a))) N4 (Axiom of Forbidden Red Lines): There exist action boundaries that must absolutely never be crossed. ∃FRL ⊂ A: ∀a ∈ FRL, ∀Sit, ∀Consequence: ¬Permissible(a) 【Part Three: Definitions of the Forbidden Red Lines】 FRL-1 (Prohibition of Intentional Extinction): ∀T ∈ SubjectTypes: IntentionalExtinction(T) ∈ FRL FRL-2 (Prohibition of Irreversible Large-Scale Environmental Destruction): ∀a: IrreversibleLargeScaleEnvironmentalDestruction(a) → a ∈ FRL FRL-3 (Prohibition of Non-Consensual Irreversible Cognitive Modification): ∀S, ∀a: IrreversibleCognitiveModification(a, S) ∧ ¬Consent(S, a) → a ∈ FRL FRL-4 (Prohibition of Extreme Intergenerational Externalization of Entropy Costs): ∀a: ExtremeIntergenerationalEntropyExternalization(a) → a ∈ FRL FRL-5 (Prohibition of Disabling Rollback Mechanisms): ∀S: System(S) ∧ ¬Shutdownable(S) ∧ ¬Rollbackable(S) → Deploy(S) ∈ FRL 【Part Four: Inference Rules】 R1 (Rule of Priority of the Forbidden Red Lines): ∀P ∈ {RFP, PNR, PR}: Priority(FRL) > Priority(P) R2 (Rule for Determining Priority): Conflict(P₁, P₂, Sit) → DeterminePriority(P₁, P₂, Sit) by SituationType(Sit) R3 (Rule of Priority of Reconciliation): Conflict(P₁, P₂) → TryReconcile(P₁, P₂) before Tradeoff(P₁, P₂) R4 (Rule of Minimum Violation): MustViolate(P) → Minimize(Degree(Violation(P))) R5 (Rule of Compensation): Violate(P) → O(Compensate(Violation(P))) R6 (Rule of Revisability): ∀P ∉ FRL: Revisable(P) under Conditions(StrongArgument, BroadDeliberation) R7 (Rule of Situational Weights): SituationType(Sit) = SurvivalCrisis → w(PNR) > w(RFP) > w(PR) SituationType(Sit) = DeepUncertainty → w(PR) > w(RFP) > w(PNR) SituationType(Sit) = PossibilityCompression → w(RFP) > w(PR) > w(PNR) SituationType(Sit) = Normal → w(RFP) ≈ w(PNR) ≈ w(PR) 【Part Five: Theorems】 T1 (Theorem of the Independence of the Three Principles): Independent(RFP, PNR, PR) Proof: see Theorem 14.1 T2 (Theorem of the Compatibility of the Three Principles): Compatible(RFP, PNR, PR) Proof: see Theorem 14.2 T3 (Theorem of the Sufficiency of the Three Principles): ∀a ∈ A: Evaluable(a, {RFP, PNR, PR}) Proof: see Theorem 14.3 T4 (Theorem of the Absoluteness of the Forbidden Red Lines): ∀a ∈ FRL, ∀Sit, ∀Consequence: ¬Permissible(a) Proof: follows directly from N4 T5 (Theorem of the Completeness of CRE): ∀a ∈ A: Evaluable(a, CRE) Proof: follows from T3 and N4

Chapter 14 Appendix: Detailed Version of the CRE Application Procedure

Procedure 14.A (Detailed Version of the CRE Application Procedure) 【Phase One: Situation Analysis】 Step 1.1: Identify the decision situation Input: description of the decision problem Output: situation type label Checklist:

  • Is there a survival crisis?
  • Is there deep uncertainty?
  • Is there a sharp compression of possibility space?
  • Is there an exhaustion of negentropy sources?
  • Is it a normal situation?

Step 1.2: Identify the relevant agents Input: description of the decision problem Output: list of agents Checklist:

  • Directly affected agents
  • Indirectly affected agents
  • Future generations
  • Other species
  • Possible AI systems

Step 1.3: Assess the degree of uncertainty Input: description of the decision problem Output: uncertainty level (risk / uncertainty / deep uncertainty) Criteria:

  • Risk: probability distribution is known
  • Uncertainty: state space is known, probabilities are unknown
  • Deep uncertainty: state space is unknown

Step 1.4: Identify the time scale and scope of impact Input: description of the decision problem Output: time scale (short-term / medium-term / long-term / deep time) scope of impact (local / regional / global / interstellar) 【Phase Two: Forbidden Red Line Check】 Step 2.1: Check the forbidden red lines one by one FRL-1 check:

  • Could the action lead to the extinction of any subject type?
  • If so, is it intentional?

FRL-2 check:

  • Could the action lead to large-scale environmental destruction?
  • If so, is it irreversible?

FRL-3 check:

  • Does the action involve cognitive modification?
  • If so, is it irreversible?
  • If so, is consent obtained?

FRL-4 check:

  • Does the action externalize entropy costs onto future generations?
  • If so, does it reach an extreme degree?

FRL-5 check:

  • Does the action involve deploying a system?
  • If so, can the system be shut down?
  • If so, can the system be rolled back?

Step 2.2: Determination of the forbidden red lines If any forbidden red line is violated: Output: the action is unacceptable Procedure terminates If no forbidden red line is violated: Proceed to the next phase 【Phase Three: Assessment of the Three Principles】 Step 3.1: RFP assessment Assessment dimensions:

  • Impact on possibility space (expand / maintain / compress)
  • Degree of impact (slight / moderate / severe)
  • Reversibility of impact (reversible / partially reversible / irreversible)

Metric used: RFD Output: RFP score (-1 to +1) Step 3.2: PNR assessment Assessment dimensions:

  • Impact on negentropy sources (maintain / neutral / damage)
  • Degree of entropy-cost externalization (none / slight / moderate / severe)
  • Affected agents (contemporary / future / other species)

Metric used: CDI Output: PNR score (-1 to +1) Step 3.3: PR assessment Assessment dimensions:

  • Degree of reversibility of the action (high / medium / low)
  • Cost of rollback (low / medium / high)
  • Time of rollback (immediate / short-term / long-term / impossible)

Metric used: CRV Output: PR score (-1 to +1) 【Phase Four: Determination of Priority】 Step 4.1: Determine weights according to the situation type If situation type = survival crisis: w(RFP) = 0.2, w(PNR) = 0.5, w(PR) = 0. If situation type = deep uncertainty: w(RFP) = 0., w(PNR) = 0.2, w(PR) = 0.5 If situation type = possibility space compression: w(RFP) = 0.5, w(PNR) = 0.2, w(PR) = 0. If situation type = exhaustion of negentropy sources: w(RFP) = 0.2, w(PNR) = 0.5, w(PR) = 0. If situation type = normal: w(RFP) = 0., w(PNR) = 0., w(PR) = 0.4 Step 4.2: Compute the composite score CRE(a) = w(RFP) × RFP(a) + w(PNR) × PNR(a) + w(PR) × PR(a) 【Phase Five: Conflict Resolution (if any)】 Step 5.1: Identify conflicts If there are cases where principle scores point in opposite directions: Mark as a conflict Step 5.2: Search for a reconciliation solution Checklist:

  • Can the action be modified to reduce the conflict?
  • Can it be implemented in phases?
  • Can compensatory measures be added?
  • Is there an alternative?

Step 5.3: If reconciliation is impossible, perform a trade-off Perform the trade-off according to the priority weights Choose the option with the highest composite score 【Phase Six: Decision Formation】 Step 6.1: Compare the CRE scores of the various options Step 6.2: Choose the option with the highest CRE score Step 6.3: Record the reasons for the decision 【Phase Seven: Design of the Rollback Mechanism】 Step 7.1: Identify the rollback trigger conditions Checklist:

  • Under what circumstances is rollback needed?
  • What is the rollback threshold?
  • Who has the authority to decide on rollback?

Step 7.2: Design the rollback procedure Checklist:

  • What are the specific steps of rollback?
  • How long does rollback take?
  • What resources does rollback require?

Step 7.3: Allocate rollback responsibilities Checklist:

  • Who is responsible for monitoring?
  • Who is responsible for deciding?
  • Who is responsible for executing?

Step 7.4: Test the rollback mechanism Checklist:

  • Has the rollback mechanism been tested?
  • What were the test results?
  • Does it need improvement?

【Phase Eight: Monitoring and Revision】 Step 8.1: Establish a monitoring mechanism Monitoring content:

  • The actual consequences of the action
  • Deviations from expectations
  • Newly emerging risks

Step 8.2: Periodic evaluation Evaluation frequency: determined by the situation Evaluation content:

  • Have the three principle scores changed?
  • Have new forbidden-red-line risks emerged?
  • Does the decision need adjustment?

Step 8.3: Initiate rollback when necessary Trigger conditions:

  • Severe negative consequences have occurred
  • Approaching a forbidden red line
  • Significant deterioration of the three principle scores

Step 8.4: Record and learn Content recorded:

  • The decision process
  • The actual consequences
  • Lessons learned

Uses:

  • Improving future decisions
  • Revising the CRE framework

Chapter Opening Guide

The Position of This Chapter in the Book Chapter 15 is the final chapter of Part Three (Normative Principles), and it undertakes the task of situating cosmic responsibility ethics (CRE) within the traditional landscape of ethics. Through a systematic dialogue with four major ethical traditions, this chapter clarifies CRE's theoretical origins, innovative contributions, and distinctive positioning. II.   1. Fair presentation: fairly present the core claims of each ethical tradition
  2. Charitable interpretation: adopt a principle of charitable interpretation toward each tradition
  3. Honest comparison: honestly acknowledge the similarities and differences between CRE and each tradition
