§15.1 Dialogue with Utilitarianism

§15.1.1 The Core Claims of Utilitarianism I. The Definition of Utilitarianism Definition 15.1 (Utilitarianism) Utilitarianism is a theory of normative ethics that holds that the moral rightness of an action depends on its consequences—specifically, on its contribution to overall well-being or utility. Formal statement: $$\text{Utilitarianism}: \text{Right}(a) \Leftrightarrow \max_{a \in A} \sum_{i} U_i(a)$$ where $U_i(a)$ is the utility contribution of action $a$ to subject $i$. Readers with a background in ethics: read sequentially, noting comparisons with familiar traditions Readers with a background in the history of philosophy: focus on the sections on the core claims of each tradition Policymakers: focus on §15.5 (distinctive positioning) Readers wanting a quick overview: read the chapter opening guide, §15.5, and the chapter summary Estimated reading time: about 4-5 hours for a complete read

§15.1 Dialogue with Utilitarianism

§15.1.1 The Core Claims of Utilitarianism I. The Definition of Utilitarianism Definition 15.1 (Utilitarianism) Utilitarianism is a theory of normative ethics that holds that the moral rightness of an action depends on its consequences—specifically, on its contribution to overall well-being or utility. Formal statement: $$\text{Utilitarianism}: \text{Right}(a) \Leftrightarrow \max_{a \in A} \sum_{i} U_i(a)$$ where $U_i(a)$ is the utility contribution of action $a$ to subject $i$. II. The Core Propositions of Utilitarianism Proposition 15.1 (The core propositions of utilitarianism) Utilitarianism includes the following core propositions:

  • Consequentialism: the moral value of an action depends entirely on its consequences
  • Welfarism: the only thing with intrinsic value is well-being
  • Aggregationism: the well-being of different subjects can be aggregated into overall well-being
  • Maximization: overall well-being ought to be maximized

Table 15.1 Main Variants of Utilitarianism | Variant | Core claim | Representative figures | |------|----------|----------| | Classical utilitarianism | Maximize pleasure, minimize pain | Bentham, Mill | | Preference utilitarianism | Maximize preference satisfaction | Hare, Singer | | Objective-list utilitarianism | Maximize the objective good list | Parfit | | Rule utilitarianism | Follow rules that maximize utility | Brandt | | Expected-utility utilitarianism | Maximize expected utility | Harsanyi | III. The Advantages of Utilitarianism Proposition 15.2 (The advantages of utilitarianism) Utilitarianism has the following theoretical advantages:

  • Simplicity: it provides a single criterion of evaluation
  • Universality: it applies to all subjects capable of experiencing well-being
  • Comparability: it provides a basis for comparing different actions
  • Reformatory character: it can criticize existing institutions and practices

IV. The Challenges of Utilitarianism Proposition 15.3 (The challenges facing utilitarianism) Utilitarianism faces the following major challenges:

  • The utility-measurement problem: how are the utilities of different subjects measured and compared?
  • The distributive-justice problem: does aggregation neglect the fairness of distribution?
  • The rights problem: may individual rights be sacrificed for overall well-being?
  • The deep-uncertainty problem: how is it applied when consequences are unpredictable?

§15.1.2 Commonalities between This Work and Utilitarianism I. Concern for Consequences Proposition 15.4 (Commonality of consequence concern between CRE and utilitarianism) Both CRE and utilitarianism are concerned with the consequences of actions. CRE's Three Principles (RFP, PNR, PR) all involve the assessment of the consequences of actions. Formal statement: $$\text{CRE} \cap \text{Utilitarianism}: \text{ConsequenceMatters}$$ Table 15.2 Comparison of Consequence Concern between CRE and Utilitarianism | Dimension | Utilitarianism | CRE | |------|----------|-----| | Concern for consequences | Yes | Yes | | Type of consequence | Well-being/utility | Space of possibilities, negentropy, reversibility | | Mode of assessment | Aggregative maximization | Multi-dimensional assessment | II. Universalism Proposition 15.5 (Commonality of universalism between CRE and utilitarianism) Both CRE and utilitarianism adopt a universalist stance and do not restrict moral concern to a particular group. Formal statement: $$\text{CRE} \cap \text{Utilitarianism}: \text{Universalism}$$ Argument 15.1 (Argument for the commonality of universalism) Premise P1: utilitarianism holds that all subjects capable of experiencing well-being ought to be taken into account Premise P2: CRE holds that all entities with the status of subject ought to be taken into account (based on NL-) Premise P3: neither restricts moral concern to humans or a particular group Conclusion: CRE and utilitarianism share a universalist stance III. Reformist Orientation Proposition 15.6 (Commonality of reformist orientation between CRE and utilitarianism) Both CRE and utilitarianism have a reformist orientation and can criticize existing institutions and practices. Examples:

  • Utilitarianism criticizes institutions that fail to maximize well-being
  • CRE criticizes institutions that compress the space of possibilities, damage sources of negentropy, and eliminate reversibility

IV. Cross-Species Concern Proposition 15.7 (Commonality of cross-species concern between CRE and utilitarianism) Both CRE and utilitarianism extend moral concern to non-human subjects. Table 15.3 Comparison of Cross-Species Concern | Dimension | Utilitarianism | CRE | |------|----------|-----| | Basis of extension | Sentience | Subject status (UCS) | | Scope of extension | Beings capable of experiencing pleasure and pain | All entities with the status of subject | | Including AI | Depends on whether the AI is sentient | Depends on the AI's UCS score |

§15.1.3 Differences between This Work and Utilitarianism I. Difference in Evaluative Criteria Proposition 15.8 (Difference in evaluative criteria) There is a fundamental difference between CRE and utilitarianism in evaluative criteria. Utilitarianism takes well-being/utility as its sole criterion, whereas CRE takes the space of possibilities, negentropy, and reversibility as multi-dimensional criteria. Formal statement: $$\text{Utilitarianism}: \text{Criterion} = \text{Welfare}$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Criterion} = \langle \text{PossibilitySpace}, \text{Negentropy}, \text{Reversibility} \rangle$$ Table 15.4 Differences in Evaluative Criteria | Dimension | Utilitarianism | CRE | |------|----------|-----| | Number of criteria | Single (well-being) | Multi-dimensional (the Three Principles) | | Source of criteria | Subjective experience | Physical-informational structure | | Measurability | Depends on subjective reports | Depends on structural analysis | | Cross-substrate applicability | Depends on sentience | Does not depend on a particular substrate | II. Difference in Mode of Aggregation Proposition 15.9 (Difference in mode of aggregation) Utilitarianism adopts simple aggregation (summation or averaging), whereas CRE adopts multi-dimensional integration and does not perform simple aggregation. Formal statement: $$\text{Utilitarianism}: \text{Value}(a) = \sum_i U_i(a) \text{ or } \frac{1}{n}\sum_i U_i(a)$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Value}(a) = f(\text{RFP}(a), \text{PNR}(a), \text{PR}(a))$$ Proposition 15.10 (Reasons why CRE rejects simple aggregation) CRE rejects simple aggregation because:

  • The space of possibilities, negentropy, and reversibility are different dimensions and cannot simply be added
  • Simple aggregation may conceal distributive injustice
  • Simple aggregation may permit sacrificing the individual for the aggregate

III. Difference in Absolute Constraints Proposition 15.11 (Difference in absolute constraints) Utilitarianism generally does not acknowledge absolute constraints, whereas CRE acknowledges taboo red lines as absolute constraints. Formal statement: $$\text{Utilitarianism}: \neg\exists a: \text{AbsolutelyForbidden}(a)$$ $$\text{CRE}: \exists FRL: \forall a \in FRL: \text{AbsolutelyForbidden}(a)$$ Argument 15.2 (Argument for the difference in absolute constraints) Premise P1: utilitarianism holds that any action can be justified by a sufficiently large gain in well-being Premise P2: CRE holds that actions within the taboo red lines are unacceptable regardless of their consequences Premise P3: these two claims are incompatible Conclusion: there is a fundamental difference between CRE and utilitarianism on the question of absolute constraints IV. Difference in Coping with Deep Uncertainty Proposition 15.12 (Difference in coping with deep uncertainty) Utilitarianism faces difficulties under deep uncertainty, whereas CRE has specifically designed mechanisms for coping with deep uncertainty. Table 15.5 Differences in Coping with Deep Uncertainty | Dimension | Utilitarianism | CRE | |------|----------|-----| | Standard method | Expected-utility maximization | Preservation of the space of possibilities | | Probability requirement | Requires probability assignments | Does not require probability assignments | | Under deep uncertainty | The method fails | The Reversibility Principle applies | | Worst case | Included in the expected-value calculation | Taboo red lines absolutely avoided | V. Difference in Temporal Perspective Proposition 15.13 (Difference in temporal perspective) Utilitarianism generally adopts temporal discounting, whereas CRE adopts a near-zero temporal discount rate. Formal statement: $$\text{Utilitarianism}: \text{Value}(a) = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \delta^t U_t(a), \quad \delta < 1$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Value}(a) = \sum_{t=0}^{T} \delta^t \text{CRE}_t(a), \quad \delta \approx 1$$

§15.1.4 Responses to Criticisms of Utilitarianism I. Possible Criticisms from Utilitarianism Proposition 15.14 (Possible criticisms of CRE from utilitarianism) From the utilitarian perspective, CRE may face the following criticisms:

  • Criticism 1: CRE's multi-dimensional criteria lack unity
  • Criticism 2: CRE's taboo red lines may lead to suboptimal consequences
  • Criticism 3: CRE's concept of the space of possibilities is too abstract
  • Criticism 4: CRE neglects the central place of well-being

II. Responses to the Criticisms Response 1: The Unity of the Multi-Dimensional Criteria Proposition 15.15 (Response on the unity of the multi-dimensional criteria) CRE's multi-dimensional criteria have a unified basis: maintaining the conditions for the survival of complex organization. The Three Principles are three aspects of this unified basis. Formal statement: $$\text{UnifiedBasis}(\text{CRE}) = \text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions}(\text{ComplexOrganizations}))$$ $$\text{RFP}, \text{PNR}, \text{PR} = \text{ThreeAspects}(\text{UnifiedBasis})$$ Response 2: Taboo Red Lines and Consequences Proposition 15.16 (Response on taboo red lines and consequences) Taboo red lines do not neglect consequences; rather, they are the absolute avoidance of the worst consequences. Under deep uncertainty, this is the more prudent consideration of consequences. Argument 15.3 (A consequentialist defense of taboo red lines) Premise P1: taboo red lines protect the most basic conditions of survival Premise P2: the consequences of violating taboo red lines are completely irreversible and catastrophic Premise P3: under deep uncertainty, the expected utility of violating taboo red lines cannot be reliably calculated Premise P4: prudent consideration of consequences requires avoiding the worst case Conclusion: taboo red lines are a prudent consideration of consequences, not a neglect of consequences Response 3: The Concreteness of the Space of Possibilities Proposition 15.17 (Response on the concreteness of the space of possibilities) The space of possibilities is not an abstract concept but a concrete one that can be operationalized through the RFD indicators. Examples:

  • Species extinction reduces the biological space of possibilities
  • Technological lock-in reduces the technological space of possibilities
  • Institutional rigidity reduces the social space of possibilities

Response 4: The Relation between Well-Being and the Conditions for Survival Proposition 15.18 (Response on the relation between well-being and the conditions for survival) CRE does not deny the importance of well-being; rather, it places well-being within a more fundamental framework of the conditions for survival. Survival is the precondition of well-being. Formal statement: $$\text{Welfare}(S) \rightarrow \text{Require}(\text{Survival}(S))$$ $$\text{Survival}(S) \rightarrow \text{Require}(\text{SurvivalConditions}(S))$$ Table 15.6 Summary of CRE's Responses to Utilitarian Criticisms | Criticism | Response | Core argument | |------|------|----------| | Multi-dimensional criteria lack unity | The unified basis is the conditions for survival | The Three Principles are three aspects of the unified basis | | Taboo red lines lead to suboptimal consequences | Taboo red lines are a prudent consideration of consequences | Avoid the worst case under deep uncertainty | | The space of possibilities is too abstract | It can be operationalized through the RFD | There are concrete measurement methods | | Neglect of the central place of well-being | Survival is the precondition of well-being | Does not deny well-being but places it in a more fundamental framework |

§15.2 Dialogue with Deontology

§15.2.1 The Core Claims of Deontology I. The Definition of Deontology Definition 15.2 (Deontology) Deontology is a theory of normative ethics that holds that the moral rightness of an action depends on whether the action itself conforms to moral rules or duties, and not merely on its consequences. Formal statement: $$\text{Deontology}: \text{Right}(a) \Leftrightarrow \text{ConformsTo}(a, \text{MoralRules})$$ II. The Core Propositions of Deontology Proposition 15.19 (The core propositions of deontology) Deontology includes the following core propositions:

  • Priority of rules: moral rules take priority over consideration of consequences
  • Absolute prohibitions: certain actions are wrong regardless of their consequences
  • Respect for persons: the personal dignity of rational beings ought to be respected
  • Universalizability requirement: moral rules ought to be universalizable

Table 15.7 Main Variants of Deontology | Variant | Core claim | Representative figures | |------|----------|----------| | Kantian deontology | The categorical imperative, personal dignity | Kant | | Rossian deontology | Prima facie duties, plural duties | Ross | | Contractual deontology | Principles that can be reasonably accepted | Scanlon | | Rights deontology | Rights as side-constraints | Nozick | III. The Advantages of Deontology Proposition 15.20 (The advantages of deontology) Deontology has the following theoretical advantages:

  • Respect for the individual: it does not permit sacrificing the individual for the aggregate
  • It provides determinacy: it offers clear guidance for action
  • Protection of rights: it treats rights as inviolable boundaries
  • Intuitive appeal: it accords with many moral intuitions

IV. The Challenges of Deontology Proposition 15.21 (The challenges facing deontology) Deontology faces the following major challenges:

  • The rule-conflict problem: how should conflicts between rules be handled?
  • The problem of neglecting consequences: does it excessively neglect consequences?
  • The difficulty of universalization: how is the universalization of a rule determined?
  • The cross-cultural applicability problem: do rules have cross-cultural validity?

§15.2.2 Commonalities between This Work and Deontology I. Absolute Constraints Proposition 15.22 (Commonality of absolute constraints between CRE and deontology) Both CRE and deontology acknowledge the existence of absolute constraints. CRE's taboo red lines are structurally similar to deontology's absolute prohibitions. Formal statement: $$\text{CRE} \cap \text{Deontology}: \exists a: \text{AbsolutelyForbidden}(a)$$ Table 15.8 Comparison of Absolute Constraints | Dimension | Deontology | CRE | |------|--------|-----| | Existence of absolute constraints | Yes | Yes | | Source of constraints | Moral rules/personal dignity | Conditions for survival/taboo red lines | | Content of constraints | E.g., the prohibition of killing the innocent | FRL-1 to FRL-5 | | Exceptions | Generally none | None | II. Respect for Subjects Proposition 15.23 (Commonality of respect for subjects between CRE and deontology) Both CRE and deontology emphasize respect for subjects and do not treat subjects merely as means. Argument 15.4 (Argument for the commonality of respect for subjects) Premise P1: deontology holds that the personal dignity of rational beings ought to be respected Premise P2: CRE holds that all entities with the status of subject ought to be respected Premise P3: both oppose treating subjects merely as means Conclusion: CRE and deontology share a stance of respect for subjects III. Rule Orientation Proposition 15.24 (Commonality of rule orientation between CRE and deontology) Both CRE and deontology provide rule-oriented guidance for action rather than relying solely on situational judgment. Examples:

  • Deontology provides the categorical imperative
  • CRE provides the Three Principles and the taboo red lines

IV. The Universalizability Requirement Proposition 15.25 (Commonality of the universalizability requirement between CRE and deontology) Both CRE and deontology require that principles be universalizable. Formal statement: $$\text{CRE} \cap \text{Deontology}: \text{Universalizable}(\text{Principles})$$

§15.2.3 Differences between This Work and Deontology I. Difference in the Source of Normativity Proposition 15.26 (Difference in the source of normativity) Deontology's normativity derives from pure reason (Kant) or moral intuition (Ross), whereas CRE's normativity derives from the Three New Views and the conditions for survival. Formal statement: $$\text{Deontology}: \text{Source}(\text{Normativity}) = \text{PureReason} \vee \text{MoralIntuition}$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Source}(\text{Normativity}) = \text{NewThreeViews} + \text{SurvivalConditions}$$ Table 15.9 Differences in the Source of Normativity | Dimension | Deontology | CRE | |------|--------|-----| | Source | Pure reason/moral intuition | The Three New Views + the conditions for survival | | Basis | A priori/intuition | Physical-informational structure | | Revisability | Generally low | Explicitly acknowledges revisability | | Empirical connection | Weaker | Stronger | II. Difference in the Scope of Subjects Proposition 15.27 (Difference in the scope of subjects) Deontology generally restricts moral concern to rational beings, whereas CRE extends moral concern to all entities with the status of subject. Formal statement: $$\text{Deontology}: \text{MoralPatients} = \text{RationalBeings}$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{MoralPatients} = \{S : \text{UCS}(S) > \theta\}$$ Argument 15.5 (Argument for the difference in the scope of subjects) Premise P1: deontology (especially Kantian deontology) takes rationality as the basis of moral status Premise P2: CRE takes subject status (UCS) as the basis of moral status Premise P3: UCS is a continuum and is not limited to rational beings Premise P4: CRE is based on NL- (the continuum of consciousness) Conclusion: CRE's scope of subjects is broader than that of traditional deontology III. Difference in the Consideration of Consequences Proposition 15.28 (Difference in the consideration of consequences) Deontology generally does not treat consequences as central to moral evaluation, whereas CRE, although not a purely consequentialist theory, explicitly takes consequences into account. Table 15.10 Differences in the Consideration of Consequences | Dimension | Deontology | CRE | |------|--------|-----| | Status of consequences | Not central | Important but not sole | | Type of consequence | Generally undifferentiated | Distinguishes the space of possibilities, negentropy, reversibility | | Consequences and rules | Rules take priority | Integrated consideration | IV. Difference in Revisability Proposition 15.29 (Difference in revisability) Deontology's rules are generally regarded as non-revisable, whereas CRE explicitly acknowledges the revisability of its principles. Formal statement: $$\text{Deontology}: \text{Revisable}(\text{MoralRules}) = \text{False} \text{ (generally)}$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Revisable}(\text{Principles}) = \text{True} \text{ (except the taboo red lines)}$$

§15.2.4 Responses to Criticisms of Deontology I. Possible Criticisms from Deontology Proposition 15.30 (Possible criticisms of CRE from deontology) From the deontological perspective, CRE may face the following criticisms:

  • Criticism 1: CRE focuses too much on consequences, weakening the status of rules
  • Criticism 2: CRE's source of normativity is not pure enough
  • Criticism 3: CRE's revisability may lead to moral relativism
  • Criticism 4: CRE's extension of the scope of subjects lacks sufficient justification

II. Responses to the Criticisms Response 1: The Integration of Rules and Consequences Proposition 15.31 (Response on the integration of rules and consequences) CRE does not weaken rules but integrates rules with consequences. The taboo red lines are absolute rules, and the Three Principles are consequence-oriented rules. Argument 15.6 (Argument for the integration of rules and consequences) Premise P1: CRE's taboo red lines are absolute rules that do not depend on the calculation of consequences Premise P2: CRE's Three Principles consider consequences but are not simple consequence-maximization Premise P3: this structure integrates the determinacy of rules with the relevance of consequences Conclusion: CRE integrates rules and consequences rather than weakening rules Response 2: The Sufficiency of the Source of Normativity Proposition 15.32 (Response on the sufficiency of the source of normativity) CRE's source of normativity is not less pure but more solid. The conditions for survival are the precondition of any normativity. Formal statement: $$\text{Normativity} \rightarrow \text{Require}(\text{Existence}(\text{NormativeAgents}))$$ $$\text{Existence}(\text{NormativeAgents}) \rightarrow \text{Require}(\text{SurvivalConditions})$$ Response 3: The Distinction between Revisability and Relativism Proposition 15.33 (Response on the distinction between revisability and relativism) Revisability is not equivalent to relativism. CRE's revisability is an expression of epistemic humility, not value relativism. Table 15.11 The Distinction between Revisability and Relativism | Dimension | Revisability | Relativism | |------|----------|----------| | View of truth | Acknowledges objective truth but holds that cognition may err | Denies objective truth | | Basis of revision | Better arguments and evidence | Culture or personal preference | | Taboo red lines | Extremely difficult to revise | No absolute constraints | | Epistemology | Fallibilism | Relativism | Response 4: The Reasons for Extending the Scope of Subjects Proposition 15.34 (Response on the reasons for extending the scope of subjects) CRE's extension of the scope of subjects is based on NL- (the continuum of consciousness) and the UCS indicators and has a sufficient theoretical and empirical basis. Argument 15.7 (Argument for the reasons for extending the scope of subjects) Premise P1 (NL-): consciousness is a continuum, not a binary present/absent Premise P2: UCS provides an operationalized method for assessing the status of subject Premise P3: restricting moral concern to rational beings is an arbitrary boundary Premise P4: extending the scope of subjects is consistent with scientific findings (animal consciousness, the possibility of AI) Conclusion: CRE's extension of the scope of subjects has sufficient justification Table 15.12 Summary of CRE's Responses to Deontological Criticisms | Criticism | Response | Core argument | |------|------|----------| | Focuses too much on consequences | Integrates rules and consequences | Taboo red lines are absolute rules | | The source of normativity is not pure enough | The conditions for survival are a more solid basis | Survival is the precondition of normativity | | Revisability leads to relativism | Revisability is not equivalent to relativism | Based on better arguments rather than preference | | Extension of the scope of subjects lacks justification | Based on NL- and UCS | Has a theoretical and empirical basis |

§15.3 Dialogue with Virtue Ethics

§15.3.1 The Core Claims of Virtue Ethics I. The Definition of Virtue Ethics Definition 15.3 (Virtue Ethics) Virtue ethics is a theory of normative ethics that holds that the core of moral evaluation is the character and virtue of the agent, rather than the consequences of actions or rules. Formal statement: $$\text{VirtueEthics}: \text{Right}(a) \Leftrightarrow \text{WouldBeDoneBy}(a, \text{VirtuousAgent})$$ II. The Core Propositions of Virtue Ethics Proposition 15.35 (The core propositions of virtue ethics) Virtue ethics includes the following core propositions:

  • Character-centered: the core of moral evaluation is character rather than action
  • Priority of virtue: virtue is the foundation of the moral life
  • Practical wisdom: moral judgment requires practical wisdom (phronesis)
  • The goal of flourishing: the goal of the moral life is human flourishing (eudaimonia)

Table 15.13 Main Variants of Virtue Ethics | Variant | Core claim | Representative figures | |------|----------|----------| | Aristotelian virtue ethics | Virtue, the mean, flourishing | Aristotle | | Neo-Aristotelianism | Revival of the Aristotelian tradition | MacIntyre, Foot | | Sentimentalist virtue ethics | The role of sentiment in virtue | Slote | | Confucian virtue ethics | Benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom | Confucius, Mencius | III. The Advantages of Virtue Ethics Proposition 15.36 (The advantages of virtue ethics) Virtue ethics has the following theoretical advantages:

  • Holism: it attends to the whole personality rather than isolated actions
  • Developmental character: it emphasizes moral development and growth
  • Situational sensitivity: it responds to complex situations through practical wisdom
  • Focus on motivation: it attends to the motives and character of action

IV. The Challenges of Virtue Ethics Proposition 15.37 (The challenges facing virtue ethics) Virtue ethics faces the following major challenges:

  • The action-guidance problem: how is concrete guidance for action derived from virtue?
  • The problem of the list of virtues: which are the genuine virtues?
  • The cultural-relativism problem: do virtues have cross-cultural validity?
  • The institutional-application problem: how is virtue ethics applied to institutional design?

§15.3.2 Commonalities between This Work and Virtue Ethics I. Practical Wisdom Proposition 15.38 (Commonality of practical wisdom between CRE and virtue ethics) Both CRE and virtue ethics emphasize the role of practical wisdom in moral judgment. CRE's context-dependent priority ordering and conflict resolution require practical wisdom. Formal statement: $$\text{CRE} \cap \text{VirtueEthics}: \text{Require}(\text{PracticalWisdom})$$ Examples:

  • CRE's priority ordering among the Three Principles is context-dependent and requires practical wisdom for judgment
  • CRE's conflict-resolution procedures require practical wisdom

II. Holistic Perspective Proposition 15.39 (Commonality of the holistic perspective between CRE and virtue ethics) Both CRE and virtue ethics adopt a holistic perspective and do not restrict moral evaluation to isolated actions. Table 15.14 Comparison of the Holistic Perspective | Dimension | Virtue ethics | CRE | |------|------------|-----| | Holistic object | Personality/character | Space of possibilities/system | | Temporal scope | A lifetime | Deep time | | Relational concern | Social relations | Cosmic relations | III. Developmental Orientation Proposition 15.40 (Commonality of developmental orientation between CRE and virtue ethics) Both CRE and virtue ethics have a developmental orientation and are concerned with growth and progress. Argument 15.8 (Argument for the commonality of developmental orientation) Premise P1: virtue ethics emphasizes the cultivation and development of virtue Premise P2: CRE emphasizes the maintenance and expansion of the space of possibilities Premise P3: both are concerned with development from the current state toward a better state Conclusion: CRE and virtue ethics share a developmental orientation IV. Epistemic Humility Proposition 15.41 (Commonality of epistemic humility between CRE and virtue ethics) Both CRE and virtue ethics emphasize epistemic humility. In virtue ethics it is expressed through practical wisdom; in CRE through revisability and the Reversibility Principle.

§15.3.3 Differences between This Work and Virtue Ethics I. Difference in Evaluative Focus Proposition 15.42 (Difference in evaluative focus) Virtue ethics' focus of evaluation is the character of the agent, whereas CRE's focus of evaluation is the impact of an action on the space of possibilities, negentropy, and reversibility. Formal statement: $$\text{VirtueEthics}: \text{Focus} = \text{Character}(\text{Agent})$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Focus} = \text{Impact}(a, \langle \text{PS}, \text{Neg}, \text{Rev} \rangle)$$ II. Difference in the Degree of Operationalization Proposition 15.43 (Difference in the degree of operationalization) Virtue ethics has a relatively low degree of operationalization, whereas CRE achieves a high degree of operationalization through its indicator system. Table 15.15 Differences in the Degree of Operationalization | Dimension | Virtue ethics | CRE | |------|------------|-----| | Degree of operationalization | Relatively low | Relatively high | | Method of assessment | Relies on judgment | Indicator systems (RFD, CDI, CRV) | | Institutional application | Difficult | Relatively easy | | Auditability | Relatively low | Relatively high | III. Difference in the Scope of Subjects Proposition 15.44 (Difference in the scope of subjects) Virtue ethics generally focuses on human agents, whereas CRE extends to all entities with the status of subject. IV. Difference in Temporal Scale Proposition 15.45 (Difference in temporal scale) Virtue ethics' temporal scale is generally the individual lifetime, whereas CRE's temporal scale is deep time. Formal statement: $$\text{VirtueEthics}: \text{TimeScale} = \text{Lifetime}$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{TimeScale} = \text{DeepTime}$$

§15.3.4 Responses to Criticisms of Virtue Ethics I. Possible Criticisms from Virtue Ethics Proposition 15.46 (Possible criticisms of CRE from virtue ethics) From the virtue-ethics perspective, CRE may face the following criticisms:

  • Criticism 1: CRE focuses too much on action and consequences and neglects character
  • Criticism 2: CRE's operationalization may lead to a mechanization of morality
  • Criticism 3: CRE lacks attention to moral motivation
  • Criticism 4: CRE's deep-time perspective may neglect present moral life

II. Responses to the Criticisms Response 1: The Relation between Character and Action Proposition 15.47 (Response on the relation between character and action) CRE does not deny the importance of character but regards character as one of the conditions for producing correct action. CRE is concerned with the structural impact of action, which is complementary to concern for character. Response 2: The Relation between Operationalization and Moral Judgment Proposition 15.48 (Response on the relation between operationalization and moral judgment) CRE's operationalization does not replace moral judgment but provides tools for it. Practical wisdom remains necessary. Argument 15.9 (Argument for the relation between operationalization and moral judgment) Premise P1: CRE's indicator system provides tools for assessment Premise P2: the application and interpretation of the indicators require practical wisdom Premise P3: conflict resolution and the determination of priorities require judgment Premise P4: operationalization assists rather than replaces moral judgment Conclusion: CRE's operationalization and moral judgment are complementary Response 3: The Status of Motivation Proposition 15.49 (Response on the status of motivation) CRE does not neglect motivation but places it within a broader framework. Epistemic humility, a sense of negentropy responsibility, and the like can be regarded as virtues under the CRE framework. Table 15.16 Virtues under the CRE Framework | Virtue | Content | Corresponding principle | |------|------|----------| | Epistemic humility | Acknowledging cognitive limits and remaining open | PR, revisability | | Sense of negentropy responsibility | Awareness of responsibility for sources of negentropy | PNR | | Sensitivity to the space of possibilities | Attending to the impact of action on the space of possibilities | RFP | | Deep-time concern | Concern for future generations | The deep-time perspective | Response 4: The Relation between Deep Time and the Present Proposition 15.50 (Response on the relation between deep time and the present) CRE's deep-time perspective does not neglect the present but places the present within a broader temporal framework. Present moral life is part of deep-time responsibility.

§15.4 Dialogue with Contractarianism

§15.4.1 The Core Claims of Contractarianism I. The Definition of Contractarianism Definition 15.4 (Contractarianism) Contractarianism/Contractualism is a theory of normative ethics that holds that the justification of moral principles derives from a (hypothetical) contract or agreement among rational agents. Formal statement: $$\text{Contractualism}: \text{Right}(P) \Leftrightarrow \text{WouldBeAgreedBy}(P, \text{RationalAgents})$$ II. The Core Propositions of Contractarianism Proposition 15.51 (The core propositions of contractarianism) Contractarianism includes the following core propositions:

  • Contractual basis: the justification of moral principles derives from agreement
  • Rational agents: the participants in the agreement are rational agents
  • Hypothetical contract: the contract is hypothetical rather than actual
  • Acceptability criterion: principles ought to be reasonably acceptable

Table 15.17 Main Variants of Contractarianism | Variant | Core claim | Representative figures | |------|----------|----------| | Hobbesian contractarianism | Self-interested rationality, the sovereign | Hobbes | | Rawlsian contractarianism | The veil of ignorance, the principle of fairness | Rawls | | Scanlonian contractarianism | Principles that can be reasonably rejected | Scanlon | | Gauthierian contractarianism | Rational bargaining, mutual advantage | Gauthier | III. The Advantages of Contractarianism Proposition 15.52 (The advantages of contractarianism) Contractarianism has the following theoretical advantages:

  • Democratic character: it emphasizes agreement and consent
  • Fairness: it guarantees fairness through procedure
  • Justifiability: principles can be justified to others
  • Institutional applicability: it suits institutional design

IV. The Challenges of Contractarianism Proposition 15.53 (The challenges facing contractarianism) Contractarianism faces the following major challenges:

  • The non-rational-subject problem: how should non-rational subjects be treated?
  • The future-generations problem: how do future generations participate in the contract?
  • The hypothetical-contract problem: whence comes the binding force of a hypothetical contract?
  • The cross-species problem: how do non-human subjects participate in the contract?

§15.4.2 Commonalities between This Work and Contractarianism I. Justifiability Proposition 15.54 (Commonality of justifiability between CRE and contractarianism) Both CRE and contractarianism emphasize the justifiability of principles. CRE's principles ought to be justifiable to all entities with the status of subject. Formal statement: $$\text{CRE} \cap \text{Contractualism}: \text{Justifiable}(\text{Principles}, \text{Others})$$ II. Procedural Justice Proposition 15.55 (Commonality of procedural justice between CRE and contractarianism) Both CRE and contractarianism value procedural justice. CRE's application procedures and institutional design embody a concern for procedural justice. Table 15.18 Comparison of Procedural Justice | Dimension | Contractarianism | CRE | |------|--------|-----| | Importance of procedure | High | High | | Content of procedure | Hypothetical contract | Application procedures, deliberative procedures | | Participants | Rational agents | All entities with the status of subject | III. Institutional Orientation Proposition 15.56 (Commonality of institutional orientation between CRE and contractarianism) Both CRE and contractarianism have an institutional orientation and are concerned with institutional design and institutional justice. IV. Intersubjectivity Proposition 15.57 (Commonality of intersubjectivity between CRE and contractarianism) Both CRE and contractarianism emphasize intersubjectivity. CRE's bridge principle BP- (the principle of intersubjectivity) is structurally similar to contractarianism's contractual basis.

§15.4.3 Differences between This Work and Contractarianism I. Difference in the Scope of Participants Proposition 15.58 (Difference in the scope of participants) Contractarianism's participants are generally limited to rational agents, whereas CRE extends to all entities with the status of subject. Formal statement: $$\text{Contractualism}: \text{Participants} = \text{RationalAgents}$$ $$\text{CRE}: \text{Participants} = \{S : \text{UCS}(S) > \theta\}$$ Argument 15.10 (Argument for the difference in the scope of participants) Premise P1: contractarianism takes rationality as the basis of eligibility for participation Premise P2: CRE takes subject status (UCS) as the basis of eligibility for participation Premise P3: UCS is not limited to rational beings Premise P4: CRE includes non-rational entities that nonetheless have the status of subject Conclusion: CRE's scope of participants is broader than that of contractarianism II. Difference in the Source of Justification Proposition 15.59 (Difference in the source of justification) Contractarianism's justification derives from agreement, whereas CRE's justification derives from the conditions for survival and the Three New Views. Table 15.19 Differences in the Source of Justification | Dimension | Contractarianism | CRE | |------|--------|-----| | Source of justification | Agreement/consent | Conditions for survival + the Three New Views | | Basis | Procedural | Substantive + procedural | | Independent of agreement | No | Partly | III. Difference in the Temporal Dimension Proposition 15.60 (Difference in the temporal dimension) Contractarianism finds it difficult to handle the problem of future generations, whereas CRE addresses this problem specifically through the deep-time perspective. Argument 15.11 (Argument for the difference in the temporal dimension) Premise P1: contractarianism requires that participants be able to take part in the agreement Premise P2: future generations cannot take part in the present agreement Premise P3: contractarianism finds it difficult to provide a basis for the interests of future generations Premise P4: CRE addresses this problem through the deep-time perspective and the principle of intergenerational responsibility Conclusion: CRE is more complete than contractarianism in the temporal dimension IV. Difference in Substantive Content Proposition 15.61 (Difference in substantive content) Contractarianism mainly provides a procedural framework, whereas CRE provides substantive principles (the Three Principles and the taboo red lines).

§15.4.4 Responses to Criticisms of Contractarianism I. Possible Criticisms from Contractarianism Proposition 15.62 (Possible criticisms of CRE from contractarianism) From the contractarian perspective, CRE may face the following criticisms:

  • Criticism 1: CRE's principles have not been agreed upon and lack justification
  • Criticism 2: CRE's extension of the scope of subjects lacks a contractual basis
  • Criticism 3: CRE's taboo red lines are arbitrary
  • Criticism 4: CRE neglects the importance of consent

II. Responses to the Criticisms Response 1: The Relation between Agreement and the Conditions for Survival Proposition 15.63 (Response on the relation between agreement and the conditions for survival) CRE's principles are not without agreement; rather, they are the conditions that any possible agreement must presuppose. The conditions for survival are the precondition of agreement. Argument 15.12 (Argument for the relation between agreement and the conditions for survival) Premise P1: agreement requires that participants exist Premise P2: the existence of participants requires the conditions for survival Premise P3: CRE's principles maintain the conditions for survival Premise P4: therefore CRE's principles are the precondition of any agreement Conclusion: CRE's principles do not bypass agreement but are its precondition Response 2: The Reasons for Extending the Scope of Subjects Proposition 15.64 (Response on the reasons for extending the scope of subjects) CRE's extension of the scope of subjects is not arbitrary but is based on NL- (the continuum of consciousness) and the UCS indicators. This extension can be regarded as an improvement on contractarianism. Response 3: The Justification of the Taboo Red Lines Proposition 15.65 (Response on the justification of the taboo red lines) The taboo red lines are not arbitrary but are based on plural foundations of justification (see Chapter 14, §14.2). The taboo red lines can be regarded as the bottom line that any rational subject would agree to. Response 4: The Status of Consent Proposition 15.66 (Response on the status of consent) CRE does not neglect consent but places it within a broader framework. FRL- (the prohibition of irreversible cognitive modification without consent) explicitly protects the importance of consent. Table 15.20 Summary of CRE's Responses to Contractarian Criticisms | Criticism | Response | Core argument| |------|------|----------| | Principles without agreement | The conditions for survival are the precondition of agreement | CRE's principles are the precondition of any agreement | | Extension of the scope of subjects lacks a contractual basis | Based on NL- and UCS | It is an improvement on contractarianism | | The taboo red lines are arbitrary | Plural foundations of justification | The bottom line that any rational subject would agree to | | Neglect of the importance of consent | FRL- protects consent | Consent is placed within a broader framework |

§15.5 The Distinctive Positioning of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics

§15.5.1 Transcending Traditional Classification I. The Limitations of Traditional Ethical Classification Proposition 15.67 (The limitations of traditional classification) Traditional ethics is usually divided into three major classes: consequentialism, deontology, and virtue ethics. Although useful, this classification has limitations:

  • It neglects the overlaps among the traditions
  • It finds it difficult to accommodate new ethical theories
  • It may lead to either/or thinking

Table 15.21 Traditional Classification of Ethics | Class | Core question | Focus of evaluation | |------|----------|----------| | Consequentialism | What consequences are good? | The consequences of action | | Deontology | What rules are right? | The action itself | | Virtue ethics | What character is good? | The character of the agent | II. How CRE Transcends Traditional Classification Proposition 15.68 (CRE transcends traditional classification) CRE cannot be simply assigned to any of the three traditional classes; rather, it transcends this classification. Argument 15.13 (Argument that CRE transcends traditional classification) Premise P1: CRE is concerned with consequences (the impact on the space of possibilities, negentropy, and reversibility) Premise P2: CRE includes absolute rules (the taboo red lines) Premise P3: CRE emphasizes practical wisdom and epistemic humility (virtue elements) Premise P4: CRE cannot be simply assigned to consequentialism, deontology, or virtue ethics Conclusion: CRE transcends the three traditional classes Table 15.22 The Relation between CRE and the Traditional Classification | Traditional class | Elements CRE contains | Aspects in which CRE transcends | |----------|---------------|---------------| | Consequentialism | Concern for consequences | Does not aim at utility maximization; has absolute constraints | | Deontology | Absolute rules (FRL) | Also considers consequences; different source of normativity | | Virtue ethics | Practical wisdom, epistemic humility | More concerned with action and institutions; highly operationalized | III. The Distinctive Features of CRE Proposition 15.69 (The distinctive features of CRE) CRE has the following distinctive features, which enable it to transcend traditional classification:

  • Multi-dimensional evaluation: it does not evaluate actions by a single criterion
  • Hierarchical structure: the hierarchy of taboo red lines, core principles, and derived principles
  • Cross-substrate applicability: it applies to subjects of different material substrates
  • Deep-time perspective: it extends ethical concern to deep time scales
  • Coping with deep uncertainty: specifically designed mechanisms for coping with deep uncertainty
  • Revisability: it explicitly acknowledges the revisability of its principles

§15.5.2 Integrating Multiple Traditions I. The Possibility of Integration Proposition 15.70 (The possibility of integrating multiple traditions) CRE can integrate multiple traditions because each tradition is concerned with a different aspect of the moral life rather than being a mutually exclusive alternative. Argument 15.14 (Argument for the possibility of integration) Premise P1: consequentialism is concerned with the consequences of action Premise P2: deontology is concerned with the conformity of action to rules Premise P3: virtue ethics is concerned with the character of the agent Premise P4: contractarianism is concerned with the acceptability of principles Premise P5: these concerns are complementary rather than mutually exclusive Conclusion: integrating multiple traditions is possible II. CRE's Integration Strategy Proposition 15.71 (CRE's integration strategy) CRE integrates multiple traditions through the following strategies:

  • Hierarchical integration: elements of different traditions are placed at different levels
  • Situational integration: elements of different traditions have different weights in different situations
  • Functional integration: elements of different traditions perform different functions

Table 15.23 CRE's Integration Strategies | Integration strategy | Content | Example | |----------|------|------| | Hierarchical integration | Different elements are placed at different levels | Taboo red lines (deontology) take priority over the Three Principles (concern for consequences) | | Situational integration | Different weights in different situations | Under deep uncertainty, the Reversibility Principle takes priority | | Functional integration | Different elements perform different functions | Practical wisdom is used for conflict resolution; indicators are used for assessment | III. The Specific Content of Integration Table 15.24 The Specific Content of CRE's Integration of Each Tradition | Tradition | Integrated elements | Position in CRE | |------|------------|---------------| | Consequentialism | Concern for consequences, universalism | The consequence assessment of the Three Principles | | Deontology | Absolute constraints, respect for subjects | Taboo red lines, subject status | | Virtue ethics | Practical wisdom, epistemic humility | Conflict resolution, revisability | | Contractarianism | Procedural justice, justifiability | Application procedures, deliberative procedures | IV. The Advantages of Integration Proposition 15.72 (The advantages of integration) CRE's integration strategy has the following advantages:

  • Comprehensiveness: it covers multiple aspects of the moral life
  • Flexibility: it can respond to different types of moral problems
  • Robustness: it does not depend on the assumptions of a single tradition
  • Inclusiveness: it can engage in dialogue with different traditions

§15.5.3 Facing Future Challenges I. New Challenges Facing Traditional Ethics Proposition 15.73 (New challenges facing traditional ethics) Traditional ethics faces new challenges in the era of interstellar civilization:

  • AI ethics: how should AI that may have the status of subject be treated?
  • Extraterrestrial-life ethics: how should possible extraterrestrial life be treated?
  • Deep-time ethics: how should subjects in the distant future be treated?
  • Deep-uncertainty ethics: how should moral decisions be made under deep uncertainty?

Table 15.25 New Challenges Facing Traditional Ethics | Challenge | Utilitarianism | Deontology | Virtue ethics | Contractarianism | |------|----------|--------|------------|--------| | AI ethics | Depends on whether the AI is sentient | Depends on whether the AI is rational | Difficult to apply | Depends on whether the AI can participate in a contract | | Extraterrestrial-life ethics | Depends on whether the extraterrestrial life is sentient | Depends on whether the extraterrestrial life is rational | Difficult to apply | Depends on whether the extraterrestrial life can participate in a contract | | Deep-time ethics | The discount-rate problem | The problem of duties to future subjects | Difficult to apply | Future subjects cannot participate in a contract | | Deep-uncertainty ethics | Expected utility fails | Difficulty in applying rules | Practical wisdom is limited | Difficulty of agreement | II. CRE's Responses to the New Challenges Proposition 15.74 (CRE's responses to the new challenges) CRE is specifically designed to respond to these new challenges:

  • AI ethics: assessing the subject status of AI through UCS
  • Extraterrestrial-life ethics: handling it through cross-substrate applicability
  • Deep-time ethics: handling it through the deep-time perspective and the principle of intergenerational responsibility
  • Deep-uncertainty ethics: handling it through the Reversibility Principle and the taboo red lines

Table 15.26 CRE's Responses to the New Challenges | Challenge | CRE's response | Specific mechanism | |------|----------|----------| | AI ethics | UCS assesses subject status | Multi-dimensional assessment that does not rely on a single criterion | | Extraterrestrial-life ethics | Cross-substrate applicability | Based on NL-1, not limited to a particular substrate | | Deep-time ethics | The deep-time perspective | A near-zero temporal discount rate; intergenerational responsibility | | Deep-uncertainty ethics | The Reversibility Principle + the taboo red lines | Maintaining the capacity for error correction; avoiding the worst case | III. The Forward-Looking Character of CRE Proposition 15.75 (The forward-looking character of CRE) CRE is forward-looking and can provide a framework for ethical problems that have not yet arisen. Argument 15.15 (Argument for CRE's forward-looking character) Premise P1: CRE is based on the Three New Views, which are a general understanding of the cosmos, life, and cognition Premise P2: CRE's principles (RFP, PNR, PR) are general principles and are not limited to particular situations Premise P3: CRE's indicator systems (UCS, RFD, etc.) are extensible Premise P4: CRE's revisability allows adjustment in light of new circumstances Conclusion: CRE is forward-looking and can meet future challenges

§15.5.4 Maintaining Open Dialogue I. The Necessity of Open Dialogue Proposition 15.76 (The necessity of open dialogue) CRE needs to maintain open dialogue with each ethical tradition because:

  • CRE is revisable and needs to absorb insights from each tradition
  • Each tradition may discover problems with CRE
  • Ethics is the product of collective intellect

II. The Principles of Dialogue Definition 15.5 (The principles of CRE's dialogue with each tradition) CRE's dialogue with each ethical tradition follows the following principles:

  • Charitable interpretation: adopt a charitable interpretation toward each tradition
  • Honest acknowledgment: honestly acknowledge CRE's limitations
  • Open learning: be willing to learn from each tradition
  • Mutual respect: respect the contributions of each tradition

III. The Domains of Dialogue Table 15.27 Domains of CRE's Dialogue with Each Tradition | Tradition | Domain of dialogue | What CRE can learn | |------|----------|-----------------| | Utilitarianism | Measurement of well-being, methods of aggregation | More refined methods of consequence assessment | | Deontology | The justification of rules, rights theory | A more solid basis for rules | | Virtue ethics | Cultivation of character, practical wisdom | A richer understanding of virtue | | Contractarianism | Procedure design, contract theory | A more complete procedural framework | IV. The Attitude of Dialogue Proposition 15.77 (CRE's attitude in dialogue) CRE maintains the following attitude toward each tradition:

  • Not a replacement: CRE does not seek to replace each tradition but to provide an integrative framework
  • Not an endpoint: CRE is not the endpoint of ethics but a revisable starting point
  • Not dogmatic: CRE is not a dogmatic doctrine but an open inquiry

Boundary Declaration 15.1 (The openness of CRE) CRE acknowledges its own limitations, is willing to learn from each ethical tradition, and revises itself in light of new arguments and evidence. CRE is an open framework, not a closed system.

Conclusion of Volume I: From Ontological Foundation to Normative Construction Conclusion of Volume I: From Ontological Foundation to Normative Construction

I. The Core Achievements of This Volume

1.1 Completion of the Theoretical Construction This volume has completed the most arduous theoretical task of the work: starting from the layer of physical constraints (L₀), passing through the layer of the ontological-epistemological framework (L₁), and arriving at the layer of normative principles (L₂). This chain of derivation can be formalized as: $$L_0 \xrightarrow{\text{explanation}} L_1 \xrightarrow{\text{bridge principles}} L_2$$ Specifically, this volume has completed the following core constructions: Table C.1 Core Construction Achievements of Volume I | Level | Construction Content | Core Output | Chapters | |------|----------|----------|----------| | L₀ | Elucidation of physical constraints | Constraints of thermodynamics, information theory, and complex systems | Chapters 1–3 | | L₁ | Framework of the New Three Views | NC-1 to NC-3, NL-1 to NL-3, NK-1 to NK-4 | Chapters 1–4 | | Bridge | Bridge principles | BP-1 to BP-3 | Chapter 5 | | L₂ | Normative principles | RFP, PNR, PR | Chapters 11–13 | | L₂ | Integration framework | CRE, FRL-1 to FRL-5 | Chapter 14 | | Dialogue | Theoretical positioning | Dialogue with the four great ethical traditions | Chapter 15 | 1.2 Establishment of the New Three Views The foremost achievement of this volume is the establishment of the New Three Views (the New Cosmological View, the New View of Life, and the New View of Cognition) as the ontological-epistemological foundation of interstellar civilization governance. Core propositions of the New Cosmological View (NC): $$\text{NC-1}: \text{Properties}(x) = f(\text{Relations}(x, \text{Context}))$$ $$\text{NC-2}: \text{Process} \succ \text{State}$$ $$\text{NC-3}: \text{Observation} \rightarrow \text{Participation}$$ Core propositions of the New View of Life (NL): $$\text{NL-1}: \text{Life} = \text{NegentropicOrganization}(\text{AnySubstrate})$$ $$\text{NL-2}: \text{Survival}(S) \rightarrow \text{Require}(\text{NegEntropyFlow}(S))$$ $$\text{NL-3}: \text{Consciousness} \in \text{Continuum}[0, 1]$$ Core propositions of the New View of Cognition (NK): $$\text{NK-1}: \text{Cognition} = \text{Participation}(\text{Agent}, \text{World})$$ $$\text{NK-2}: \text{Knowledge} = \text{SocialAchievement}(\text{Community})$$ $$\text{NK-3}: \text{Cognition} \rightarrow \text{Normative}$$ $$\text{NK-4}: \forall p: \text{Know}(S, p) \rightarrow \text{Revisable}(p)$$ These three views are not isolated but form a unified framework that mutually supports and cyclically co-constructs one another:

1.3 Establishment of the Bridge Principles The second achievement of this volume is the establishment of a bridge from the descriptive framework to normative principles. This bridge consists of three principles: Bridge Principle BP-1 (Principle of Survival Rationality): $$\text{RationalAgent}(S) \rightarrow O(\text{Maintain}(\text{SurvivalConditions}(S)))$$ Bridge Principle BP-2 (Principle of Epistemic Humility): $$\text{Fallible}(S) \rightarrow O(\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a)))$$ Bridge Principle BP-3 (Principle of Intersubjectivity): $$\text{Adopt}(P) \rightarrow \text{ReasonablyAcceptable}(P, \text{Others})$$ These three bridge principles respond to Hume's "is-ought" problem and provide a reasonable transition from facts to norms. 1.4 Derivation of the Normative Principles The third achievement of this volume is the derivation of three core normative principles from the New Three Views and the bridge principles: Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP): $$O(\text{Maintain}(\text{PossibilitySpace}) \vee \text{Expand}(\text{PossibilitySpace}))$$ Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (PNR): $$O(\text{Maintain}(\text{NegSource}) \wedge \neg\text{Externalize}(\text{EntropyCost}, \text{InnocentAgents}))$$ Principle of Reversibility (PR): $$\text{DeepUncertainty}(\text{Sit}) \rightarrow O(\text{Prefer}(\text{Reversible}(a)))$$ 1.5 Establishment of Cosmic Responsibility Ethics The fourth achievement of this volume is the integration of the three normative principles into Cosmic Responsibility Ethics (CRE) and the establishment of the forbidden red lines (FRL) as absolute constraints: List of Forbidden Red Lines: | No. | Name | Content | |------|------|------| | FRL-1 | Prohibition of intentional extinction | Prohibits intentionally eliminating any type that has subjecthood | | FRL-2 | Prohibition of irreversible large-scale environmental destruction | Prohibits causing irreversible environmental destruction at the planetary level or larger | | FRL-3 | Prohibition of non-consensual irreversible cognitive modification | Prohibits irreversible cognitive modification of an agent without consent | | FRL-4 | Prohibition of extreme intergenerational externalization of entropy costs | Prohibits externalizing extreme entropy costs onto future generations | | FRL-5 | Prohibition of disabling rollback mechanisms | Prohibits deploying systems that cannot be shut down or rolled back | 1.6 Clarification of Theoretical Positioning The fifth achievement of this volume is the clarification of CRE's theoretical positioning through a systematic dialogue with the four great ethical traditions (utilitarianism, deontology, virtue ethics, and contractualism): Table C.2 The Theoretical Positioning of CRE | Dimension | Positioning of CRE | |------|----------| | Relation to the traditional classification | Transcends the traditional trichotomy, lying at the intersection of the four great traditions | | Integration strategy | Hierarchical integration, contextual integration, functional integration | | Distinctive features | Cross-substrate applicability, deep time perspective, response to deep uncertainty, revisability | | Challenges addressed | AI ethics, extraterrestrial-life ethics, deep time ethics, ethics of deep uncertainty |

This is the task of Volume II: Table C.3 Core Tasks of Volume II | Task | Content | Corresponding Level | |------|------|----------| | Metric system development | UCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIA | L₄ | | Institutional prototype design | Multi-Intelligence Tribunal, cosmic-level IRB, intergenerational trust | L₃ | | Complete protocol stack architecture | Complete specification of the five-layer architecture | L₀-L₄ | | Versioned rollback mechanism | Design of the One Loop | Cross-level | 2.3 The Interface Between Theory and Operation The normative principles of this volume provide the normative foundation for the operational framework of Volume II: $$\text{RFP} \xrightarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{RFD}(\text{Recursive Freedom Degree})$$ $$\text{PNR} \xrightarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{CDI}(\text{Civilization Development Index})$$ $$\text{PR} \xrightarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{CRV}(\text{Commitment-Reversibility-Verification})$$ $$\text{NL-3} \xrightarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{UCS}(\text{Universal Consciousness Scale})$$ This interface ensures that the operational framework is not arbitrarily designed but has a solid normative foundation. 2.4 Methodological Contributions of This Volume This volume not only provides substantive theoretical content but also establishes a methodological paradigm: Features of engineered narrative: | Feature | Content | |------|------| | Definition first | Every core concept has a formalized definition | | Explicit constraints | Every proposition has a boundary statement | | Explicit argumentation | Key arguments are marked as "argument nodes" | | Testability | A three-tier testability architecture is provided | | Revisability | A versioned update mechanism | This methodology runs throughout the book, ensuring the traceability, testability, and revisability of the theoretical framework.

III. Preview of Volume II

3.1 Structure of Volume II Volume II, Operational Framework, will contain the following parts: Table C.4 Preview of the Structure of Volume II | Part | Title | Core Task | |------|------|----------| | Part Four | Metric system | Operationalize the New Three Views and the normative principles into computable metrics | | Part Five | Institutional design | Design institutional prototypes and the protocol stack architecture | 3.2 Preview of Part Four: The Metric System Part Four will develop six major metric systems: Table C.5 Preview of the Metric System | Metric | Full Name | Function | Theoretical Anchor | |------|------|------|----------| | UCS | Universal Consciousness Scale | Assesses the degree of subjecthood | NL-3 | | RFD | Recursive Freedom Degree | Measures changes in possibility space | RFP | | CRV | Commitment-Reversibility-Verification | Assesses the reversibility of commitments | PR | | CDI | Civilization Development Index | Assesses the fulfillment of a civilization's negentropy responsibility | PNR | | MBCL | Meme Biosafety Containment Level | Assesses information-hazard risk | NK-3 | | CSIA | Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment | Comprehensively assesses the impact of actions | CRE | Each metric will include:

  • Conceptual definition
  • Formalized formulation
  • Calculation method
  • Application procedure
  • Boundary statement

3.3 Preview of Part Five: Institutional Design Part Five will design the following institutional prototypes: Table C.6 Preview of Institutional Prototypes | Institution | Function | Theoretical Anchor | |------|------|----------| | Protocol stack architecture | A governance framework organized in layers | Full framework | | Multi-Intelligence Tribunal | Dispute resolution across subject types | NL-3, BP-3 | | Cosmic-level IRB | Ethical review at the cosmic scale | CRE | | Intergenerational trust | Institutionalization of intergenerational responsibility | PNR | | Versioned rollback mechanism | Guaranteeing the reversibility of institutions | PR | 3.4 The Logic from Volume I to Volume II The relationship between Volume I and Volume II can be expressed as: $$\text{Volume I}(\text{normative foundation}) \xrightarrow{\text{operationalization}} \text{Volume II}(\text{operational framework})$$ Specifically:

3.5 An Invitation to the Reader The completion of this volume marks that the normative foundation of Interstellar Civilization Studies has been laid. But this is only a beginning, not an end. This work invites readers to:

  1. Criticize: offer criticism of the arguments of this volume, pointing out logical gaps or empirical discrepancies
  2. Supplement: provide perspectives and arguments not covered by this volume
  3. Apply: attempt to apply the principles of this volume to concrete situations
  4. Develop: develop new theories and methods on the basis of this volume

As the New View of Cognition emphasizes, knowledge is a social achievement. This work is not a closed dogma but an open research program. Its value lies not in providing final answers but in opening up an inquiry that can continue to develop.

Summary of Boundary Statements for Volume I

Note: This summary collects all boundary statements in Volume I, arranged in chapter order. Boundary statements are a core component of the methodological commitments of this work, clarifying the scope and limitations of each proposition and argument.

Chapter 0 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 0.1 (Positioning of the Nature of This Work)

This work is a "provisional convention" rather than an "eternal truth," a "conceptual prototype" rather than a "mature product," and an "open system" rather than a "closed dogma."

Boundary Statement 0.2 (Restrictions on Use)

The content of this work should not be used to: (1) provide a theoretical basis for any form of discrimination or oppression; (2) provide the sole basis for decision-making regarding large-scale irreversible actions; (3) replace professional judgment in specialized domains.

Boundary Statement 0.3 (Maturity Statement)

Different parts of this work have different levels of maturity: the content at the L₀ layer is based on established scientific consensus (high maturity); the content at the L₁ layer is an interpretive framework (medium maturity); the content at the L₂ layer is a normative construction (medium-to-low maturity); and the content at the L₃–L₄ layers consists of institutional prototypes (low maturity).

Boundary Statement 0.4 (Revisability Statement)

All content of this work is revisable. The triggers for revision include: (1) discovery of a contradiction with facts at the L₀ layer; (2) discovery of internal logical inconsistency; (3) discovery of a better alternative; (4) discovery of serious problems in application.

Chapter 1 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 1.1 (Boundary of the Scientific Foundation)

The references in this chapter to quantum mechanics and relativity are "structural uses" rather than "concept hijacking." This work does not claim that quantum effects directly determine macroscopic phenomena, nor that relativity directly entails a particular ontological stance.

Boundary Statement 1.2 (Boundary of the New Cosmological View)

The New Cosmological View is an interpretive framework for the empirical facts at the L₀ layer, not a revision of those empirical facts. The New Cosmological View does not predict any new physical phenomena and does not challenge any established scientific conclusion.

Boundary Statement 1.3 (Boundary of Philosophical Sources)

This work has affinities with process philosophy, structural realism, and Eastern philosophy, but it does not fully adopt any one tradition. The position of this work is independent and requires independent assessment.

Chapter 2 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 2.1 (Boundary of the Scientific Foundation)

The references in this chapter to thermodynamics, information theory, and complex systems science are intended to provide a conceptual foundation, not to claim that these sciences directly entail the conclusions of the New View of Life.

Boundary Statement 2.2 (Boundary of Theories of Consciousness)

This work does not presuppose any particular theory of consciousness (IIT, GWT, HOT, etc.). The UCS is an operational scale and does not depend on resolving the question of the nature of consciousness.

Boundary Statement 2.3 (Boundary of Cross-Substrate Life)

Cross-substrate life is a conceptual possibility, not an empirical fact. This work does not claim that non-carbon-based life already exists; it only claims that this possibility cannot be ruled out a priori.

Chapter 3 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 3.1 (Boundary of the Scientific Foundation)

The references in this chapter to embodied cognition, social cognition, and predictive processing theory are intended to provide a conceptual foundation, not to claim that these sciences directly entail the conclusions of the New View of Cognition.

Boundary Statement 3.2 (Boundary of Epistemic Humility)

Epistemic humility is not skepticism. This work acknowledges the possibility of knowledge; it merely emphasizes the fallibility and revisability of knowledge.

Boundary Statement 3.3 (Boundary of Normative Cognition)

Normative cognition is not subjectivism. This work acknowledges the objectivity of cognition; it merely emphasizes that objectivity is an achievement of intersubjectivity rather than a subjectless given.

Chapter 4 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 4.1 (Boundary of the Unity of the Three Views)

The unity of the three views is a conclusion of argument, not a presupposition. If an irreconcilable contradiction is found among the three views, the claim of unity needs revision.

Boundary Statement 4.2 (Boundary of the Common Ground)

Relationality, processuality, and participation as common ground are claims of this work, not unquestionable axioms. These grounds themselves require justification.

Chapter 5 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 5.1 (Boundary of the Bridge Principles)

The bridge principles do not derive "ought" from a pure "is." The bridge principles themselves contain a normative component and require independent justification.

Boundary Statement 5.2 (Boundary of the Justification Argument)

The justification of the bridge principles is pluralistic, not singular. If one line of argument is refuted, other lines may still support the conclusion.

Boundary Statement 5.3 (Boundary of the Metaethical Stance)

The metaethical stance of this work is "weak realism" or "constructive realism," not fully adopting moral realism or anti-realism.

Chapter 11 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 11.1 (Boundary of the Principle of Recursive Freedom)

The Principle of Recursive Freedom is not absolute. In certain cases, it may be necessary to restrict the possibility space in order to protect more fundamental values.

Boundary Statement 11.2 (Boundary of the Possibility Space)

The possibility space is a conceptual tool, not a physical quantity that can be precisely measured. The RFD is an attempt at operationalization, but measurement difficulties exist.

Chapter 12 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 12.1 (Boundary of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility)

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility does not require zero entropy increase. All complex organization necessarily produces entropy; the responsibility lies in reasonable allocation and the avoidance of improper externalization.

Boundary Statement 12.2 (Boundary of the Allocation of Responsibility)

The principle of responsibility allocation is a general framework; specific allocation requires contextual judgment. This work does not provide specific allocation schemes for all situations.

Chapter 13 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 13.1 (Boundary of the Principle of Reversibility)

The Principle of Reversibility does not require that all actions be reversible. In certain cases, irreversible action may be necessary. The principle is to prefer reversible actions, not to prohibit irreversible actions.

Boundary Statement 13.2 (Boundary of the Assessment of Reversibility)

Reversibility is a matter of degree, not binary. Complete reversibility and complete irreversibility are two extremes; most actions lie in between.

Chapter 14 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 14.1 (Boundary of the Integration of the Three Principles)

The integration of the three principles is a construction of this work, not a logical necessity. If a better integration scheme is found, revision is required.

Boundary Statement 14.2 (Boundary of the Taboo Red Lines)

The specific content of the taboo red lines is revisable, but the threshold for revision is extremely high. The core region of the taboo red lines is absolute, while the boundary region requires deliberation to determine.

Boundary Statement 14.3 (Boundary of CRE)

CRE is a normative framework, not a predictive theory. CRE does not predict what will happen in the future; it only provides principles for evaluating and guiding action.

Chapter 15 Boundary Statements

Boundary Statement 15.1 (The Openness of CRE)

CRE acknowledges its own limitations, is willing to learn from the various ethical traditions, and revises itself in light of new arguments and evidence. CRE is an open framework, not a closed system.
